## Brāhmaṇas

**"Brahmanas" are specialized treatises that explain, at length, how the Samhita's mantras — which take the form of hymns of praise — are to be used in yajnas and similar rites: at what time which acts should be performed, and so on.** Taken as a whole, the Brahmanas serve as a kind of commentary (vyākhyāna) upon the Samhita. Each Veda has its own distinct Brahmanas.

**The Brahmanas connected with the Rigveda are the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and the Kauśītakī Brāhmaṇa.** Of these, the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is the principal and more ancient one. It comprises 40 Adhyāyas in total. It is said that one Mahīdāsa arranged this Brāhmaṇa. **The Kauśītakī Brāhmaṇa is also called the Sāṅkhyāyana Brāhmaṇa.** It comprises 30 Adhyāyas: the first six describe the procedure for the Darśapūrṇamāsa and similar rites, and Adhyāyas 7 through 30 describe the procedure for the Soma-yāga. The subject matter of this Brahmana broadly follows that of the Aitareya Brahmana.

**The Brahmana-portion, throughout, explains the procedure of the yajna in full.** Detailed discussion of the individual acts comprising the rite, the derivation of ritual terms, and similar matters are especially prominent here. Where the mantra-portion is bound to meter, the Brahmana-portion is generally in prose. **The Brahmanas may be regarded as representing the earliest stage of Sanskrit prose.**

**Of the two Brahmanas connected with the Rigveda, the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa belongs to the Śākala shakha, and the Kauśītakī Brāhmaṇa to the Bāṣkala shakha.** The reason for the name "Aitareya Brāhmaṇa" is this: Mahīdāsa, son of a woman named Itarā, once, at a yajna performed by his father, was not permitted to sit upon his father's lap alongside his other brothers. Grieved by this, he performed austerities directed to the Earth-goddess (Bhūdevī), and as the fruit of that penance obtained this Brāhmaṇa and its accompanying Āraṇyaka. **For this reason, these texts came to bear the names "Aitareya Brāhmaṇa" and "Aitareya Āraṇyaka" [after his mother Itarā].**

**This Brāhmaṇa is divided into 5 Pañcikās, each containing 8 Adhyāyas** *(cf. the 40-Adhyaya total already given above)*. The first several Adhyāyas concern the Agniṣṭoma-yāga; further Adhyāyas cover the Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, and Atirātra sacrifices, and so on. Other Adhyāyas describe the duties of the Hotṛ, the Yajamāna, the Grāvastut, the Subrahmaṇya, and six further officiants. **The final ten Adhyāyas describe the yajnas a Kṣatriya may perform, and explain the mutual relationship between Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.**

### Page 24

**Yajurveda Brahmanas** — for the Shukla Yajurveda, there is the **Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa**. Just as this Veda's Samhita has the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina shakhas, so too does this Brāhmaṇa. It comprises [several] Kāṇḍas and 100 Adhyāyas — and, having 100 Adhyāyas, bears the name "Śatapatha" ("Hundred-Path") Brāhmaṇa. **Its final portion is known as the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad.**

**For the Krishna Yajurveda, there is the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.** This Brāhmaṇa explains many matters not covered in the Samhita, and so may be regarded as a later portion of the Samhita itself. It comprises three Kāṇḍas and twenty-eight Adhyāyas.

**Besides these, this Veda has several further Brahmanas, now extinct and found nowhere. Only their names survive:** Caraka-brāhmaṇa, Kāṭhaka-brāhmaṇa, Śvetāśvatara-brāhmaṇa, Maitrāyaṇī-brāhmaṇa, Jābāla-brāhmaṇa, Khāṇḍikīya-brāhmaṇa, Aukheya-brāhmaṇa, Hāridravika-brāhmaṇa, Āpsaraka-brāhmaṇa, Kaṅkati-brāhmaṇa, Gālava-brāhmaṇa.

**Samaveda Brahmanas** — this Veda has three principal Brahmanas: **Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa, Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa**, and **Jaiminīya-brāhmaṇa** (also called Talavakāra-brāhmaṇa). Besides these, it has further Brahmanas: Mantra-brāhmaṇa, Daivata-brāhmaṇa, Sāmavidhāna-brāhmaṇa, Saṃhitopaniṣad-brāhmaṇa, Vaṃśa-brāhmaṇa, Jaiminīyārṣeya-brāhmaṇa, and Gopatha-brāhmaṇa. **A further, now-extinct set — Bhallavi, Śāṭyāyana, Kālabavi, Raurukī, Tumburu, Āruṇeya, Svaigi, Saulabha, Ailāli, Saṃśara, Māṣaśarāvi, Kāpeya, and Annākhyāna Brāhmaṇas — are known only by name, from mentions in the Sutra-literature, showing they were once current.** The Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa has 25 sections and so also bears the name "Pañcaviṃśa-brāhmaṇa"; the Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa is a later portion of this same text. **The Jaiminīya-brāhmaṇa is considered more ancient than the Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa.** Among these, there is yet another Samaveda Brahmana called "Śāḍyāyana" — the last two mentioned have not survived in complete form.

**Atharvaveda Brahmanas** — this Veda has only a single Brahmana, the **Gopatha-brāhmaṇa**.

## Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads

**The Āraṇyakas closely resemble the Brahmanas in most respects.**

> अरण्याध्ययनादेतदारण्यकमितीर्यते । अरण्ये तदधीयीतैवं वाक्यं प्रचक्षते ॥
> *araṇyādhyayanād etad āraṇyakam itīryate | araṇye tad adhīyīta evaṃ vākyaṃ pracakṣate ||*
> "It is called 'Āraṇyaka' from its being studied in the forest; texts declaring 'one should study this in the forest' pronounce it so."

**This verse is stated in connection with the subject matter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.** Because these portions exist [in a form requiring careful guidance], and because they must be studied specifically in the forest, and since they contain much deeply secret Vedāntic material...

*(This connects directly with the existing translation's "Page 25," which continues: "...because they exist [in a form requiring guidance], and because it was considered improper for these to be known to those not properly authorized, they were taught to disciples in the forest — for this reason, these texts came to be called 'Aranyakas' (forest texts).")*

### Page 25 *(resuming mid-paragraph)*

...because they exist [in a form requiring guidance], and because it was considered improper for these to be known to those not properly authorized, they were taught to disciples in the forest — for this reason, these texts came to be called "Aranyakas" (forest texts). Not all the subjects touched on within the Aranyakas have been explained in dedicated reference works, and even the scope of what they cover is a matter of some disagreement among scholars.

The Aranyakas discuss ritual action (karma) at a subtler, more philosophical level, leaning toward knowledge of Brahman, and are similar in character to the Upanishads. They suit the needs of a particular stage of life. Householders following the path of ritual action (karma-marga) — the Brahmanas — describe such rites in full external detail; the Aranyakas, by contrast, do not dwell on the external procedure but instead explain the deeper, hidden significance of these same acts. For this reason, the Aranyakas are associated with the path of renunciation (sannyasa), while those seeking the path of pure knowledge (jnana-marga) turn to the Upanishads. What belongs to the karma-marga is set out in the Brahmanas — though some hold, alternatively, that the three portions (Brahmana, Aranyaka, Upanishad) correspond respectively to the three paths of ritual action, meditative worship (upasana), and knowledge (jnana).

The most widely known and discussed portions of the Veda are the Upanishads, properly called "Vedanta" — the culminating portions of the Veda. Depending on the tradition, a given Upanishad may belong to a Brahmana, to an Aranyaka, or stand as an independent text. Tradition counts as many as 108 Upanishads, though scholars disagree on this, and only 10 or 11 are generally regarded as the principal ones deserving special attention.

The word "Upanishad" literally suggests "sitting near" (upa + ni + sad) — a disciple sitting close to the teacher — referring to knowledge conveyed in this intimate, one-to-one manner. As this concerns the guru-disciple relationship rather than our present subject, it need not be discussed further here.

> इदं वाव तच्छ्रेष्ठाय पुत्राय पिता ब्रह्म प्रब्रूयात्प्रणाय्याय वा चान्तेवासिने ।
>
> इदं वाव तच् छ्रेष्ठाय पुत्राय पिता ब्रह्म प्रब्रूयात् प्रणाय्याय वा चान्तेवासिने
> *idaṃ vāva tac chreṣṭhāya putrāya pitā brahma prabrūyāt praṇāyyāya vā cāntevāsine*
>
> "This indeed should a father teach to his most worthy son, or to a devoted resident-disciple."

The point: sacred knowledge should be imparted to a humble, deserving son or disciple. One who studies the Upanishads must be of refined character, well-disciplined, and genuinely eager to learn; the teacher, when a disciple comes to him, should examine him thoroughly before teaching. The dialogue between Nachiketas and Yama in the Katha Upanishad, and between Prajapati and Indra in the Chandogya Upanishad, both illustrate the qualities expected of a true disciple.

The Veda as a whole is one; among the Upanishads found within it, some belong to the Rigveda, some to the Kaushitaki tradition, some to the Samaveda, and others to the Chandogya, Kena, Taittiriya, Katha, and Shvetashvatara traditions, and to the Shukla Yajurveda's

### Page 26

Brihadaranyaka and Isha Upanishads; and to the Atharvaveda's Mundaka, Mandukya, and Prashna Upanishads. Thus the Brihadaranyaka, Aitareya, Chandogya, Taittiriya, Isha, Kena, Katha, Prashna, Mundaka, and Mandukya — these ten Upanishads — are the celebrated ones. They are not easy to understand: "What is this world? Who am I? What is the nature of the self? Where does ultimate truth reside?" — such questions are addressed across their various sections. Schools of thought such as Sankhya, Yoga, Vaisheshika, and Nyaya have all, in their own ways, drawn on and interpreted the Upanishads to support their own doctrines — worth noting, since each school's interpretation often stands opposed to another's, with authors frequently writing against rival schools. Still, one truth that emerges from the Upanishads beyond doubt [is affirmed, though the specific claim is not spelled out further here].

**The Aranyakas and Upanishads presently available, by Veda:**

**Rigveda:** the Aitareya Aranyaka and the Shankhayana Aranyaka; the Aitareya Upanishad; the Kaushitaki Aranyaka and the Kaushitaki Upanishad (also called the Kaushitaki-Brahmana-Upanishad).

**Shukla Yajurveda:** in the Shatapatha Brahmana (both the Kanva and Madhyandina recensions), the final portion of the last kanda serves as the Aranyaka; its concluding section is well known as the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. The last chapter of this Veda's Samhita is known as the Ishavasya Upanishad.

**Krishna Yajurveda:** the Taittiriya Aranyaka and the Maitrayaniya Aranyaka, containing the Taittiriya Upanishad, the Mahanarayana Upanishad, the Katha Upanishad, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad.

**Samaveda:** the closing portion of the Tandya-Mahabrahmana serves as this Veda's Aranyaka, containing the Chandogya Upanishad; also the Talavakara Aranyaka (or Jaiminiya Upanishad-Brahmana, also called the Jaiminiya-Aranyaka), containing the Kena Upanishad (also called the Talavakara Upanishad).

**Atharvaveda:** the Mundaka Upanishad, the Mandukya Upanishad, and the Prashna Upanishad.

These are the principal Aranyakas and Upanishads. Given their difficulty of language and philosophical depth, they are generally regarded as belonging to the very latest portion of the Vedas. Many ancient scholars and teachers have written numerous commentaries on them from many different viewpoints, and they have since been translated into languages around the world.

### Page 27

Beyond these [ten], many further Upanishads exist — tradition holds there are 108 in all, though manuscript copies of some 200 are actually available today. Many of these cannot be confidently assigned to a particular Vedic branch, and modern Western scholars differ on how to classify them; even so, since some display real literary depth, their importance cannot be dismissed outright. These can be broadly grouped into six categories:

1. Upanishads generally expounding Vedantic philosophy.
2. Upanishads explaining the practice of Yoga.
3. Upanishads expounding devotion to Vishnu.
4. Upanishads expounding devotion to Shiva.
5. Upanishads expounding Shakti (the Goddess).
6. Upanishads expounding renunciation (vairagya), the sannyasa order, and other deities such as Ganapati.

Listing every individual title is not essential here, so they are omitted.

## Chapter Three — The Vedangas

"Vedanga" does not simply mean correctly interpreting portions of the Veda — these are dedicated, specialized texts explaining subjects necessary for correctly understanding and reciting the Vedas. They are six: **Shiksha, Vyakarana (Grammar), Chandas (Metrics), Nirukta, Jyotisha (Astronomy), and Kalpa.** Let us examine each in turn.

### 1. Shiksha

Shiksha is the discipline teaching the correct pronunciation, accent, and clarity of Vedic mantras. Sayanacharya defines it:

> शिक्ष्यन्ते वेदमन्त्राणाम् उद्दिश्यन्ते स्वरवर्णादयो यत्रासौ शिक्षा ।
>
> शिक्ष्यन्ते वेद-मन्त्राणाम् उद्दिश्यन्ते स्वर-वर्णादयो यत्रासौ शिक्षा
> *śikṣyante veda-mantrāṇām uddiśyante svara-varṇādayo yatrāsau śikṣā*
>
> "That [text] in which the accents, sounds, and related features of Vedic mantras are taught — that is Shiksha."

At the start of the first chapter of the Taittiriya Upanishad (of the Krishna Yajurveda), there is a section beginning "śikṣāṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ" ("We shall now explain Shiksha"), concerning the [correct pronunciation of] Vedic mantras...

### Page 28

...and the associated rules that assist correct recitation are set out in Pratishakhya texts specific to each shakha (recension) — one Pratishakhya per shakha of a Veda. The Rigveda has two principal shakhas: Shakala and Bashkala, with no essential difference between them beyond arrangement and ritual custom. Among the authors of Shiksha-texts, the principal ones are Bharadvaja, Vyasa, Yajnavalkya, Narada, Panini, Vasishtha, Shaunaka, Shambhu, and Vararuchi; each shakha's Shiksha corresponds to its own Sutra-text, called a Pratishakhya.

For the Rigveda's Shakala recension, the Pratishakhya author is Shaunaka (who also authored the Atharvaveda's Chaturadhyayika Pratishakhya); for the Yajurveda, Katyayana. The Shakala Pratishakhya has 18 chapters (patalas), grouped into 6 larger sections. The first 3 patalas cover letters, accent, and consonants; patalas 4–5 cover the combined (Samhita) text, including vowel and consonant combination rules; patala 6 covers accent rules; patala 7, pronunciation method; patalas 8–9, consonant combinations; and patalas 10–18, further phonetic and accentual rules, along with matters of emphasis, meter, and related topics.

For Shukla Yajurveda, the Vajasaneyi Pratishakhya (8 chapters) was composed by the sage Katyayana, citing earlier Pratishakhya authors of the Shaunaka and Kashyapa lineages. For Krishna Yajurveda, the Taittiriya Pratishakhya names around 30 such authors. For the Samaveda, there are the Sama-Pratishakhya, the Pushpa-sutra, and the Sanchi-vidhi-sutra. For the Atharvaveda, the Atharva-Pratishakhya.

### 2. Vyakarana (Grammar)

The grammar tradition specifically tied to the Veda survives today only in scattered fragments. Among the earliest grammarians, Shakatayana, Gargya, Shakalya, and Yaska are the principal figures; Panini came after them. The prevailing view among grammarians is that all words ultimately derive from verbal roots (dhatus) denoting action. Panini composed his own grammar largely building on the views of these earlier authorities, addressing, among the Vedic material then in current use...


### Page 29

...tied to Vedic word-forms and their derivation. Since Paninian grammar became especially renowned, and no other principal grammar text exists apart from it, this is the one in current use today.

This work has eight chapters, hence its name "Ashtadhyayi." Exceptions to grammatical rule relevant specifically to the Veda are relatively scarce within it. Paninian grammar is celebrated for teaching correct classical Sanskrit usage, but for that very reason it cannot always be fully relied upon to reflect actual Vedic forms. In composing grammatical works generally, later authors have taken care not to disregard any part of received usage — this has become well-established practice.

Beyond Panini, the Unadi-sutras and Phit-sutras remain in use. The Unadi-sutras explain suffixes attached to particular roots — words formed this way are called "Unadi words," and are considered part of the broader Vedic grammatical tradition. The Phit-sutras, meanwhile, concern specifically the accentuation of Vedic mantra-words. Both, like the Pratishakhyas, are counted among the Vedangas.

### 3. Chandas-shastra (Metrics)

Chandas-shastra explains the metrical patterns of Vedic mantras. Pingala's treatise on this subject is the one in current use, though — unlike Paninian grammar — it is not the earliest such text. Discussions of meter already appear in the Brahmanas and Aranyakas, forming the real foundation on which Pingala's later, more systematic treatise builds. The key defining features of the meters found in the Rigveda are given in a separate chapter later in this book.

### 4. Nirukta

The Nirukta-shastra was composed by the sage Yaska, in two parts: the Nighantu and the Nirukta proper. The Nighantu gathers together Vedic words that share a common or synonymous meaning; the Nirukta then explains the form and derivation of these words, tracing their meaning in context and setting it out in connected, coherent form. This work is specifically and solely tied to the Veda.

The Nighantu (also called "Samamnaya") has three sections. The first section has three chapters; the remaining two sections together form one further chapter. The first section, the "Naighantuka-kanda," lists synonyms for various objects and concepts in its first chapter; earth, sky, and heaven in its second; and the qualities and epithets of living beings in its third.

### Page 30

The next section is the "Naigama-kanda": words that, though found only in the Veda, share their form with ordinary words but carry a different meaning there — these are gathered here. The final section is the "Daivata-kanda," listing the names of the various deities.

The Nirukta proper is the major work explaining the Nighantu's contents, and modern Sanskrit lexicography effectively begins from it — it is the earliest surviving text specifically devoted to explaining Vedic meaning. Yaska explains meaning independently, by his own method, though never in a way that would contradict the Veda's own intent; he states himself that his interpretations generally rest on the authority of the Brahmanas and the Aranyaka tradition.

The Nirukta has 14 chapters, plus two further supplementary chapters. The first three chapters explain the Naighantuka-kanda; chapters 4–6 explain the Naigama-kanda; from chapter 7 onward, the Daivata-kanda is explained. For Vedic study, the first and last chapters carry particular importance.

At the very outset, Yaska defines nouns, verbs, prepositions, and particles. The prevailing view — held even before Yaska — was that every noun derives from a verbal root; Yaska adopts this position too, deriving nominal forms from roots by showing a fitting semantic connection between them, wherever the explanation comes easily and naturally, and deciding between competing senses on the strength of the best-supported reading. Against this view, the grammarian Gargya is known to have dissented. Yaska also acknowledges that one and the same object may carry several names, or several objects may share one name (i.e., synonymy and homonymy both occur), and that not every word's origin can be traced to a clear founding principle — some function as mere conventional labels, a point grammar itself does not claim to fully resolve, and Yaska addresses this candidly in his own introduction.

Yaska then states the Nirukta's purpose: to help ascertain the Veda's meaning. This raises an objection some have posed — if words have no inherent, fixed connection to the things they denote, how can we even claim particular words correspond to particular meanings? The answer given is that the word–meaning relationship is established simply through convention (rudhi) and long usage. Ascertaining the Veda's true meaning is genuinely difficult, and only through sustained effort can one hope to grasp it...

### Page 31

...properly. Only by knowing the Veda's true meaning can its ultimate purpose be understood — with this, Yaska closes his first chapter. From the second chapter onward, wherever a word in the mantras admits multiple possible senses, he lays out the principles for settling on the correct one: chiefly, rules concerning pronunciation and rules concerning word-form. Meanings should accord with grammatical rule; irregular or unclear words should be traced to their root; interpreters should favor whichever reading is simplest and most natural; and where two senses seem equally plausible, the one with stronger textual support should be preferred. That the Nirukta's whole purpose is to aid correct understanding of the Veda is thus firmly established.

Yaska's own era, and how much of his work is original versus inherited, remains unclear — earlier, now-lost works on Nirukta likely existed and formed his foundation, though none survive today. Modern scholars, too, are uncertain of his precise date, though most agree he is the Nirukta's author, even if a few Vedic mantras' meanings may not have been entirely clear even to him. Two further complications are worth noting. First, Yaska is generally held to belong to a fairly ancient period: Panini's own grammar contains a sutra referencing the name "Yaska" (in the sense of his clan/gotra — Panini-sutra roughly 2.4.63), without further explanation, showing grammatical scholarship was already well established by then; yet Yaska, in the Nirukta, engages with and builds on earlier grammarians' views on nominal derivation, suggesting the Nirukta itself postdates the foundations of grammar. Second, some scholars question whether the compiler of the Nighantu and the author of the Nirukta are the same "Yaska," since the Nirukta occasionally appears to alter the Nighantu's exact word-order when explaining it — for instance, where the Nighantu reads "akāsārya dāvane," the Nirukta seems to restate it as "dāvane akāsārya." Even so, since a closing statement names Yaska as author, and this is accepted by those working on the Nighantu tradition as well, the two need not be regarded as different people.

### 5. Jyotisha-shastra (Astronomy)

Jyotisha does not dwell on planetary motion in great technical detail; rather, drawing on the actual observable state of the heavens, it provides the rules used to determine, precisely and impartially, favorable or unfavorable occasions for a person's practical affairs — above all, the correct timing and preparatory rites for yajnas. References to such matters appear scattered through the Brahmanas and Aranyakas, including the idea that time can be reckoned by the moon's motion through the lunar constellations. A compact treatise, the Jyotisha-Vedanga, exists for this purpose: 36 verses for the Rigveda tradition and 43 for the Yajurveda tradition, treating the sun, moon, constellations, and the twelvefold zodiacal division in careful detail — a discipline that helps determine the correct, auspicious timing for yajnas and similar rites.

### Page 32 — 6. Kalpa-sutras

These are texts composed to set out the practical rules and procedures governing mantras, yajnas, and related rites. Authorship of these texts varies by shakha — for instance, Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra is named for its author. They fall into four principal types: **Shrautasutra, Grihyasutra, Dharmasutra,** and **Shulbasutra**.

The **Shrautasutra** sets out, step by step, the procedure for yajnas and similar rites, together with the mantras required at each stage. The **Grihyasutra** explains the rules for life-cycle rites (samskaras) — birth-rites and the like — that Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas are to perform according to their station. The **Dharmasutra** sets out the general rules of right conduct expected of people. The **Shulbasutra** explains the construction of ritual structures — the fire-pit, the altar, and the sacrificial implements — including their precise measurements.

Each Veda (and each of its shakhas) traditionally had all four kinds of Sutra composed for it, though today only a fraction survive. These Sutra-texts are of great help in understanding Vedic meaning. Officiating priests, needing to know the correct procedure for the rites they performed, are why these Kalpa-sutras came to be composed in the first place. Sayanacharya puts it this way:

> बोधितानां कर्मणां सुखावबोधाय भगवान् बोधायनः कल्पसूत्रमकल्पयत् ।
>
> बोधितानां कर्मणां सुखावबोधाय भगवान् बोधायनः कल्पसूत्रम् अकल्पयत्
> *bodhitānāṃ karmaṇāṃ sukhāvabodhāya bhagavān bodhāyanaḥ kalpasūtram akalpayat*
>
> "For the easy comprehension of the rites already taught, the venerable Baudhayana composed the Kalpa-sutra."

The Brahmanas do describe yajnas and similar rites, but this material is interwoven with spiritual, historical, and etymological matter, making it hard to extract on its own — which is exactly why the Kalpa-sutras became indispensable for performing these rites correctly and in proper order.

Many Kalpa-sutras exist, one per shakha. For the Rigveda: the Ashvalayana and Shankhayana Sutras. The Ashvalayana Shrauta-sutra has two parts and twelve chapters in all, each chapter further divided into sections called Kandikas, describing the Darsha-Purnamasa (new-moon/full-moon) rites and others. For Krishna Yajurveda: the Baudhayana and Apastamba Sutras. For Shukla Yajurveda: the Katyayana Sutra. For the Samaveda: the Latyayana and Drahyayana Sutras.

It was through these Kalpa-sutras that a new era of Vedic study began — composed on the strength of long-established tradition, they came to hold real importance for the Veda...


### Page 33

...and this Kalpa-sutra tradition serves as the chief basis for it. Some works enlarge upon the Vedas, or on particular portions of them, and such derivative works are traditionally said to belong to that shakha's line of transmission. This same method of textual affiliation is used even in tracing gotra-pravara (clan lineage) matters, where scholars speak of the Ashvalayana, Baudhayana, and Apastamba schools, among others.

### Shrautasutras

These sutras primarily explain the procedure for performing yajnas. The person on whose behalf the yajna is performed is called the *yajamana*; priests called *purohitas* are engaged to help him carry out the mantras and ritual components correctly. As already noted, a yajna has four principal officiants — Hotr, Adhvaryu, Udgatr, and Brahma — with further assistant priests engaged depending on the yajna's scale. Three sacred fires are principal in a yajna: Dakshina-agni, Garhapatya, and Ahavaniya.

The first and most fundamental act in any yajna is establishing the sacred fire, either through the Agnyadheya rite or by transferring it from an already-consecrated fire. Fire is produced specifically by friction using two designated pieces of wood (Aranya) — only fire kindled this way may be used in a yajna; fire started by matches or other modern means is not proper. Maintaining this sacred fire involves numerous ancillary rites and mantras, and every element of a yajna proceeds strictly according to the Sutra-texts' prescribed rules.

Among yajnas, the Agnihotra, Darsha-Purnamasa, Soma, Chaturmasya, and Agnishtoma rites are the principal ones. "Darsha-Purnamasa" refers to the rites performed on the new-moon and full-moon days. The year's three seasonal divisions each begin with a rite called "Chaturmasya" (the four-monthly rite), itself with several sub-varieties. Soma-sacrifices likewise come in many distinct kinds, governed by particular rules concerning the relationship between the yajamana and the officiating priests from the initiation (Diksha) rite onward; a Soma-yaga may run continuously for a single day or, in its most elaborate form (the "Sattra"), for as long as a year.

Central to the Soma-yaga is the construction of the fire-altar (vedi) itself — the Agnishtoma rite requires it as an essential preliminary. The required number and type of bricks, their composition, and the exact sequence for laying them are described in painstaking detail, down to precisely when and with which mantras each brick is consecrated. An altar may use as many as several thousand bricks, requiring multiple officiating priests working to strict procedure — none of it left to improvisation. It is precisely this demand for exactness that makes these Sutra-texts so indispensable.

### Page 34

**For the Rigveda:** two Shrautasutras exist — the Ashvalayana and the Sankhyayana. The Sankhyayana Shrautasutra is especially current in Gujarat and northern regions, while the Ashvalayana is more widespread in parts of South India. There is no especially significant difference in subject matter between the two, though the Sankhyayana treats rites such as the Ashvamedha and Rajasuya in greater detail. The Sankhyayana Sutra generally follows the Kaushitaki Brahmana; its last two of several parts appear to be later additions, following material from the Kaushitaki Aranyaka specifically.

The Ashvalayana Shrautasutra includes a Grihya (domestic-rite) portion and generally follows the Aitareya Brahmana. Some say the sage Ashvalayana was a disciple of Shaunaka and also the author of the fourth chapter of the Aitareya Aranyaka.

**For Shukla Yajurveda:** the Katyayana Shrautasutra, in 26 chapters; the last three chapters relate to Samaveda matters and largely follow the Shatapatha Brahmana.

**For Krishna Yajurveda:** eight Shrautasutras exist, of which only a few have been printed. The Baudhayana and Bharadvaja Shrautasutras are quite ancient. The Apastamba Shrautasutra (30 chapters) has the Hiranyakeshiya as its supplementary text; both follow the Taittiriya tradition. The Manava Shrautasutra, connected to the Maitrayani Samhita, is very ancient. The Vaikhanasa Shrautasutra remains unprinted, surviving only in scattered manuscripts.

**For the Samaveda:** the Arsheya-kalpa (or Masaka-sutra), the Latyayana, Drahyayana, and Jaiminiya Shrautasutras, and the Samavidhana-Brahmana. Of these, the Masaka-, Latyayana, and Drahyayana Sutras are the principal ones in current circulation. The Masaka-sutra, the oldest of the three (also called "Arsheya-kalpa"), details the Soma-yaga rites described in the Panchavimsha Brahmana. The Latyayana Shrautasutra is the principal text for the Kauthuma shakha, following the Panchavimsha Brahmana; the Drahyayana is connected with the Ranayaniya shakha — the two do not differ significantly.

**For the Atharvaveda:** only the Vaitana Shrautasutra exists, closely following the Shukla Yajurveda's Katyayana Sutra and this Veda's own Gopatha Brahmana. This sutra does not appear to be especially ancient.

### Grihyasutras

These same authors composed further Sutra-texts as well — the Grihyasutras and the Samayacharika-sutras. Where the Shrautasutras belong to the Shruti tradition, these are *Smartasutras* (belonging to Smriti). The Grihyasutras set out the rules a householder should follow in family and domestic life, along with the customary practices expected of each person in society — hence also called Dharmasutras. Later works such as the Manusmriti and Yajnavalkya-smriti drew on these.

The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra has four chapters, each divided into further sections (Kandikas). Among its subjects: the Pakayajna, Balikarana, and the daily duties of a twice-born person — Chaula (tonsure), Upanayana (sacred-thread initiation), and other rites of passage, sixteen in number altogether. These rites are far simpler than the Shrauta rites, needing little preparation or material — reflecting the underlying principle that a person's own personal rites should be performed modestly, according to means, without excess or ostentation.

**For the Rigveda:** two Grihyasutras — Ashvalayana and Sankhyayana. The Sankhyayana Grihyasutra (6 parts) generally follows the Kaushitaki Brahmana; related to it is the Shambhavya Grihyasutra, covering some distinct matters, though unprinted and surviving only in manuscript. The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra is closely tied to the Aitareya Brahmana and is described as the latter portion of the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra, in four parts each divided into sections called "Pada."

**For Shukla Yajurveda:** the Parasvata (also called Kashyapa or Vajasaneya) Grihyasutra, largely following the Katyayana Shrautasutra's subject matter; its influence is visible in the Yajnavalkya Dharmasutra as well.

**For Krishna Yajurveda:** eight Grihyasutras, of which only 2–3 are printed. The Apastamba and Baudhayana Grihyasutras are especially popular in South India; the Hiranyakeshiya Kalpasutra closely follows Apastamba. The Bharadvaja Grihyasutra is not widely used. The Manava Grihyasutra mainly expounds subjects from its corresponding Shrautasutra and uniquely describes the Vinayaka-puja procedure, absent from other sutras. The later Karaka-Grihyasutra follows the Manava Grihyasutra, quoting many of its passages directly.

### Page 36

The Vaikhanasa Grihyasutra, though ancient, discusses many distinctive subjects of its own.

**For the Samaveda:** the principal Grihyasutra is the Gobhila Grihyasutra, unusually thorough and complete in its treatment. It follows mantras drawn from the Samaveda Samhita used specifically in domestic rites, in their traditional compiled order — a companion "Mantra-brahmana" gathers, in one place, exactly those domestic-rite mantras not found in the Rigveda, and is cited repeatedly within the Gobhila-sutra. Also notable is the Khadira Grihyasutra of the Drahyayana shakha, also used by the Ranayaniya and other shakhas, with no significant difference in content from the Gobhila-sutra.

**For the Atharvaveda:** the Kaushika Grihyasutra, which uniquely details the Atharvaveda's kamya-karmas (rites performed for specific desired outcomes) — a level of detail no other sutra provides, making this text especially valuable for understanding the social life of the Vedic era.

### The Sixteen Samskaras

From birth to death, a twice-born person undergoes numerous prescribed rites — around 40 in all — of which the principal ones are known as the "sixteen samskaras" (or, in a shorter reckoning, "ten"). The chief among them: Jatakarma, Namakarana, Chudakarma, Upanayana, Vivaha, Garbhadhana, Simantonnayana, and the Antyeshti (funeral rites).

**Jatakarma:** the rites performed immediately after birth, before the umbilical cord is cut.

**Namakarana:** the naming ceremony, in which parents give the child both a chosen name and one based on the birth star (nakshatra), usually performed on the tenth day after birth. Naming convention prescribes that a Brahmin's name end in "-sharma," a Kshatriya's in "-varma," and a Vaishya's in "-gupta."

**Chudakarma:** the first tonsure, ordinarily performed within the child's third year, timing varying by family tradition.

**Upanayana:** among the most important rites for a twice-born person — it is from this rite that one gains the authority (adhikara) to study the Vedas. The boy is dressed appropriately, invested with the sacred thread (yajnopavita), and taught the sacred Gayatri (Savitri) mantra by his guru. This rite is also called a "second birth" — hence Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, once they undergo it, are called "dvija" (twice-born).

### Page 37

This rite is prescribed for a Brahmin boy in his eighth year, a Kshatriya boy in his eleventh, and a Vaishya boy in his twelfth. Afterward, the boy either remains a lifelong celibate student (Naishthika-brahmachari) or lives in his guru's household, subsisting by begging alms and devoting himself continuously to Vedic study — performing the morning and evening twilight (sandhya) rites daily, living on alms alone, sleeping on the ground, speaking only when necessary, and acting according to the guru's instruction at all times. This entire way of life is called the Brahmacharya-ashrama; while some undertake it for life, most move on to the next life-stage once its prescribed period concludes — completing Vedic study, mastering other branches of learning, and, upon completing the Samavartana rite (marking the end of studentship) and proving themselves worthy, becoming eligible for marriage (vivaha).

The marriage rite includes several significant elements: Panigrahana (taking the bride's hand), circumambulation of the fire, Saptapadi (seven steps taken together), and the viewing of the pole star and the star Arundhati, among others — the Rigveda's Surya-sukta (Mandala 10, Sukta 85) supplies the mantras specifically used in marriage. Panigrahana signifies that the couple are no longer to be separated. Having the bride step on a stone (Ashmarohana) signifies she should remain as steadfast as that stone. The Saptapadi — seven steps taken together — signifies that from that point on, the couple will share equally in life's joys and sorrows. The Lajahoma is the bride's fire-offering of puffed rice. Provision for a widow's remarriage is indicated where circumstances allow. In the Dhruva-darshana, the couple view the fire and then the pole star; in the Arundhati-darshana, the bride views and venerates the star Arundhati — signifying that, following the example of the sage Vasishtha's devoted wife Arundhati, she should conduct herself as a virtuous wife who raises worthy children and manages the household well. Since these marriage customs have changed little since Vedic times, much the same practices continue even today. Through marriage, a man enters the householder stage (Grihastashrama) — regarded as foremost among the four life-stages, since it alone makes possible the fulfillment of all four aims of human life (purushartha).

Beyond these life-cycle rites, a householder has ongoing daily duties, among which the **Panchamahayajnas** (five great sacrifices) are most important. The Taittiriya Aranyaka (Krishna Yajurveda), Prapathaka 1, Anuvaka 2, states:

> पञ्च वा एते महायज्ञाः सततं प्रतायन्ते सततं संतिष्ठन्ते देवयज्ञः पितृयज्ञो भूतयज्ञो मनुष्ययज्ञो ब्रह्मयज्ञ इति ।
>
> पञ्च वा एते महायज्ञाः सततं प्रतायन्ते सततं संतिष्ठन्ते देव-यज्ञः पितृ-यज्ञो भूत-यज्ञो मनुष्य-यज्ञो ब्रह्म-यज्ञ इति
> *pañca vā ete mahāyajñāḥ satataṃ pratāyante satataṃ saṃtiṣṭhante deva-yajñaḥ pitṛ-yajño bhūta-yajño manuṣya-yajño brahma-yajña iti*
>
> "These five great sacrifices are continuously extended and continuously maintained: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to [all] beings, the sacrifice to humankind, and the sacrifice of sacred study."


### Page 38

That is: Devayajna, Pitriyajna, Bhutayajna, Manushyayajna, and Brahmayajna together make up the Panchamahayajna. These must be performed daily, begun and completed within the same day. The Taittiriya Aranyaka details each:

> यदग्नौ जुहोति तद्देवयज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यत्पितृभ्यः स्वधा करोति तत्पितृयज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यद्भूतेभ्यो बलिं हरति तद्भूतयज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यद्ब्राह्मणेभ्योऽन्नं ददाति तन्मनुष्ययज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यत्स्वाध्यायमधीयीतैकामप्यृचं यजुः साम वा तद्ब्रह्मयज्ञः संतिष्ठते ॥
>
> "Offering into the fire constitutes the sacrifice to the gods. Offering 'svadha' to the ancestors constitutes the sacrifice to the ancestors. Giving 'bali' (a food-offering) to [all] beings constitutes the sacrifice to beings. Giving food to fellow humans constitutes the sacrifice to humankind. Reciting even a single verse of the Rig, Yajus, or Sama constitutes the sacrifice of sacred study."

**Devayajna:** offering the Purodasha and other oblations into the fire with a simple homa, worshipping the intended deity — complete in a single such offering, requiring no elaborate effort.

**Pitriyajna:** since an ordinary householder cannot make elaborate offerings, he simply honors the ancestors with a water-offering accompanied by the "svadha" formula — this alone, via the Tarpana rite, completes the Pitriyajna.

**Bhutayajna:** as part of the Vaishvadeva rite and similar daily observances, offering food ("bali") to crows and other creatures.

**Manushyayajna:** giving food and other necessities, honestly earned, to Brahmins, guests, and people generally.

**Brahmayajna:** studying one's own Vedic shakha — or, having done so, studying one of the other Vedas as well. Its detailed procedure is described earlier in the text and will be revisited later in this book.

Those devoted to their duties perform these five great sacrifices daily even now.

Turning to practical customs: **Garbhadhana** is the rite performed to properly solemnize conception after a wife reaches fertility (also called "Nishekaprashasti"). Some hold it should be performed within a certain number of nights...

### Page 39

...following menses, alongside the other periodic (Panchamahayajna-related) rites — the new-moon, full-moon, and seasonal yajnas that a householder must perform. Optional (kamya) rites, such as the Soma sacrifice, may be undertaken as opportunity allows, with no strict obligation.

**Antyeshti:** after death, the rites performed on behalf of the departed — cremation (Dahana), gathering of the remains (Sanchayana), and further rites (Ekoddishta, Sapindikarana, Parvana-shraddha, Masika-shraddha, the annual Pitrimedha, and others) continuing for a fixed period and recurring yearly thereafter. These funeral (Shraddha) rites are distinct from the daily Pitriyajna discussed earlier, and are treated in great detail both in the Grihyasutras and in dedicated works such as the Hiranyakeshiya-Shraddhakalpa — not elaborated further here.

The subjects of the Grihyasutras have now been surveyed. While the overall pattern of these rites is broadly shared across all Vedas and shakhas, considerable variation exists in specific procedure and mantra.

### Dharmasutras

The reason for this name should already be clear; these texts are also called Samayacharika-sutras, since they teach proper conduct for the four social classes (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and the four life-stages (Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sannyasa) according to established custom — offering real insight into how thoroughly ancient society regulated conduct.

Tradition holds each Veda or shakha once had its own Dharmasutra, though only three survive today, all from the Taittiriya branch of Krishna Yajurveda. The **Apastamba Dharmasutra** is the most important, covering varna-ashrama customs, marriage, inheritance, and punishment for wrongdoing in detail; it predates even the Paninian era and remains current in South India. The **Hiranyakeshiya Dharmasutra**, though later, closely follows Apastamba with only minor wording differences, and is followed along the western (Konkan) coast. Third is the **Baudhayana Dharmasutra**, considered quite ancient — good evidence suggests Apastamba drew on Baudhayana rather than the reverse — and equally thorough

### Page 40

in its treatment of subject matter; it too remains current in South India. Sayanacharya himself, the celebrated Veda-commentator, belonged to the Baudhayana tradition. The sutra's later portion is thought to be a later addition rather than part of the original text.

Among these Dharmasutras is also the **Gautama-Dharmashastra**, traditionally linked to the Samaveda's Ranayaniya shakha — its ninth chapter closely follows the Samavidhana-Brahmana, supporting this connection, though its antiquity makes it hard to date with real confidence; it is provisionally placed around 800 BCE.

The **Vasishtha-Dharmashastra**, in 30 chapters, survives in error-ridden manuscripts with no reliable commentary; its later chapters seem to have a different origin than the earlier ones, and its middle portion includes verse material. It appears ancient, describes two distinct marriage procedures (per Apastamba's references to it), and is still studied by certain Rigveda-adherents today who claim it as their own — though it draws on other texts as authoritative in turn. Since northern Indian scholars relied on it for Vedic custom, it likely gained wider currency in the north; and since it quotes the Gautama-sutra while the Manava-Dharmashastra quotes it in turn, it is dated between the two — a few centuries BCE — though evidently followed by northern Rigvedins even earlier.

Beyond these, several other Dharmasutras are known only by citation in other texts. The **Manava-sutra** is notable among these, mixing prose and verse; some of its sentences are quoted elsewhere. A prose-verse Dharmashastra by certain scholars (surname reading approximately "Shambavi") survives similarly only in scattered citations, evidently once a substantial work, since it treated many subjects — later authors such as Parashara

### Page 41

cited many of its statements as authoritative. This text is thought connected to the Vajasaneya Samhita of Shukla Yajurveda, and is associated with Kumarila Bhatta (c. 700 CE), a conclusion supported by numerous corresponding passages.

**The Vaikhanasa Dharmasutra** is not very ancient. Its four-part Prashna section discusses matters connected to Narayana/Vishnu, alongside Varnashrama-dharma and the duties of the Vanaprastha stage, as in a Grihyasutra; it belongs to the Taittiriya tradition.

### Shulbasutras

These describe the construction of yajna-altars and are thus tied to the Shrautasutras. Only three survive: the **Apastamba, Baudhayana,** and **Katyayana Shulbasutras** — all connected to the Yajurveda; no equivalent texts are known for the other Vedas. The Apastamba Shulbasutra has three commentaries (Kapardi-bhashya, the oldest, in 6 patalas/82 khandas; Sundararaja's; and Karavindiya's) and has been printed in the Benares Sanskrit Series. The Baudhayana and Katyayana Shulbasutras have been translated into English with diagrams and printed in Calcutta, with commentaries by Dvarakanathayajvan (on Baudhayana) and by Someshvara's extensive *Somasudramanchandrika* (on Katyayana). These texts describe, in painstaking detail, the construction of the fire-pit and ritual implements, their use, and the precise dimensions required for the brick-built altar in the Agni-chayana rite — an established and carefully followed ancient custom. The Shulbasutras are considered the foundational source of the discipline of geometry/architecture (shilpa-shastra).

### Parishishtas (Supplements)

A few further Veda-related texts from this same era belong here: the Parishishta-sutras, the Anukramanikas, and the Charanavyuhas.

The Parishishta-sutras are generally composed, like the earlier Sutra-texts, in a compact style (in the Anushtubh meter), on Vedic subjects, though in a comparatively later style of composition. They fill in matters left incomplete in the Vedanga-related Kalpa-sutras — 

### Page 42

which, being composed concisely, left many such points untreated or barely touched on. Later generations, wanting fuller, more convenient guidance for performing yajna-related rites, compiled these more detailed supplementary works — hence "Parishishta": that which comprehensively completes what was left unaddressed.

Among the Parishishtas, the **Ashvalayana-Grihya-Parishishta** (4 chapters, all Rigveda-related) is important. The **Gobhila-Sangraha-Parishishta** is its Samaveda counterpart, covering domestic and especially kamya-karma rites. Related to it is the **Karma-pradipa** (also called Samagrihya, Chandogagrihya-Parishishta, or Gobhila-smriti), attributed either to Katyayana or to a Gobhila-follower, covering subjects that overlap with the main Grihyasutras plus additional material.

Katyayana, connected to Shukla Yajurveda, composed several further Parishishtas — three worth noting: one detailing sacred symbols; one (the "Svaradhyaya") giving the gotra-pravaras and genealogies of the rishis, useful for determining gotra in marriage matters; and the Charanavyuha, listing the names of the shakhas.

### Anukramanikas (Indices)

An "Anukramanika" is a systematic index of the mantras, words, and other elements occurring in a text, in their original sequence. The Rigveda's Anukramanikas list its suktas, rishis, meters, deities, and other details in the order they occur in the Samhita. About 8 such indices exist for the Rigveda, all attributed to Shaunaka; similar information also appears within the Rigveda's own Pratishakhya texts. The best known is Katyayana's **Sarvanukramanika**, covering every sukta's order along with rishi, deity, and meter, tied to the exposition of Vedartha; its closing section states it was composed ahead of six other, now-lost, Anukramani-type works, and it has since become the standard reference, superseding the others.

There is also, for the Rigveda, the **Arsha-Anukramani** (about 200 shlokas), listing which rishi composed which mantra. Similarly, the **Chandonukramani**...

### Page 43

...(about 200 shlokas) lists the meters used in each mantra by Mandala, with counts — though this reckoning covers only six of the available texts. The **Anuvakanukramani** (about 40 shlokas) gives the opening words of each Anuvaka and the number of suktas in each, stating the Rigveda's sukta count as 1,017 (or 1,025 by some manuscript traditions — the exact figure varies), along with syllable counts and related details.

The **Padanukramani** catalogs the Veda's individual words; the **Suktanukramani** would detail the suktas themselves, though this text does not appear to survive. The **Devatanukramani** lists the deity names, but only partially survives. Sage Shaunaka is also credited with the **Brihaddevata** and the **Rigvidhana**. The Brihaddevata (roughly 700 shlokas across 8 chapters) explains at length which deities belong to which sukta and the etymology of individual words; the Rigvidhana explains the practical ritual application of the Rigveda's mantras. Both are extremely ancient — suggesting that even while the Rigveda Samhita was still taking its final shape, its practical use and application were already evolving in various directions.

For Shukla Yajurveda's Madhyandina branch, Katyayana composed an Anukramanika broadly following the Rigveda's Sarvanukramani in covering rishi, deity, and meter (with some differences), and separately describing the Samhita's meters, based on the Rigveda's own model.

For Krishna Yajurveda, three Anukramanikas exist. The Atreya-shakha's has three parts (part one in prose, part two in verse), mostly just listing the Samhita's names without much further elaboration. The later **Charanavyuhanukramani** lists rishis and mantras in sequence but differs considerably from the Rigveda's own Sarvanukramani and contains many unfamiliar names; it is said to have been composed by an ascetic named (approximately) Lomagashti for his disciples.

For the Samaveda, the **Arsha** and **Daivata** Anukramanikas list rishis and deities respectively, following the Samaveda's

### Page 44

Saingiya-shakha tradition. Across these various indices, the names of Yaska, Shaunaka, Ashvalayana, and other sages, along with citations from their works, appear at many points.

Connected to the Atharvaveda's Parishishtas is one called the **Charanavyuha**. More than 70 Parishishtas exist for the Atharvaveda in total, this being one of them; it states that the Atharvaveda contains roughly 2,000 principal suktas.

**Prayoga and Paddhati texts:** beyond understanding ritual procedure in the abstract, separate practical manuals were composed to make actual performance convenient for ritual specialists — of great help to those handling Shrauta and Grihya rites. A **Prayoga** text lays out, step by step, exactly which act comes first and which follows, together with the specific mantra each officiant uses at each stage — invaluable to the ritvijas actually conducting the rite. A **Paddhati** gathers together, in one place, everything the Sutras say on a given ritual topic. Both genres are the work of later authors building on the older Sutras and their methods, typically composed in verse. Kumarila Bhatta (c. 700 CE) is the earliest known author in this genre.

## Chapter Four — The Shakhas (Branches) of the Veda

The previous chapter raised the question of how the Veda came to be divided into so many shakhas, and why. The Veda was originally a single, unified body of text. Consider first whether it would even be feasible for one person to study it in that undivided form: by ordinary human capacity, attempting to study it exactly as it originally existed would make serious Vedic study nearly impossible — and recognizing this is itself the reason behind its division:

> पूर्वं भगवता कृष्णद्वैपायनेन जगदुपकारार्थम् एकीभूतस्य तस्य वेदस्य व्यस्तम् ।
>
> पूर्वं भगवता कृष्ण-द्वैपायनेन जगद्-उपकारार्थम् एकी-भूतस्य तस्य वेदस्य व्यस्तम्
> *pūrvaṃ bhagavatā kṛṣṇa-dvaipāyanena jagad-upakārārtham ekī-bhūtasya tasya vedasya vyastam*
>
> "Formerly, by the venerable Krishna-Dvaipayana [Vyasa], for the benefit of the world, this Veda — which had been one unified whole — was divided."

> सकलवेदपरिपालनं तैश्चैव पुरुषेणेति शाखाभेदप्रवृत्तिः ।
>
> सकल-वेद-परिपालनं तैश् चैव पुरुषेणेति शाखा-भेद-प्रवृत्तिः
> *sakala-veda-paripālanaṃ taiś caiva puruṣeṇeti śākhā-bheda-pravṛttiḥ*
>
> "So that the entire Veda could be preserved by these very people [his disciples] — this is how the practice of dividing it into separate branches (shakhas) came about."

That is: Vyasa, having mastered the whole Veda himself, divided it and taught its parts separately to different disciples, who carried their respective portions forward within their own family traditions — whatever one makes of this account, dividing the Veda clearly became a practical necessity. This explains why the Veda was first split into its four parts. But this alone doesn't fully capture what "shakha" means: a shakha is not a distinct portion of content so much as a distinct line of oral transmission — since different gurus took on the task of teaching disciples, each taught according to his own particular tradition, and although it was one and the same Veda, small variations crept in simply because the teaching lineages differed. That is: even within a single shakha, mantras handed down in different manuscript lines occasionally differ slightly from one another...


### Page 45

...and even the sequence of pronunciation could vary from teacher to teacher — though no substantial difference of principle exists between shakhas. This is why some are said to follow the "Shakala reading" and others the "Bashkala reading" when studying the Rigveda — both traditions remain current today.

All four Vedas originally had numerous shakhas; only a handful survive in practice now, and some are known only by name. The Rigveda currently has two well-known shakhas: Ashvalayana and Sankhyayana. The Yajurveda first splits into Shukla and Krishna; Shukla Yajurveda has two well-known shakhas (Kanva and Madhyandina), and Krishna Yajurveda several, of which Apastamba is well known. The Samaveda reputedly once had a thousand shakhas; only a few survive today, of which Kauthuma is well known. The Atharvaveda has nine shakhas, of which Shaunaka is well known. These are all Samhita-portions.

Brahmana-portions are believed to have once existed for many of these shakhas too, though only a few survive: for the Rigveda, the Aitareya and Kaushitaki; for the Yajurveda, the Shatapatha, Taittiriya, Maitrayaniya, and Kathaka; for the Samaveda, the Tandya, Shadvimsha, and Jaiminiya; and for the Atharvaveda, the Gopatha Brahmana.

Shakhas do not differ significantly in antiquity, but do show some variation in matters of pronunciation and recitation sequence — for instance, the Shakala-shakha recites certain suktas (such as ones connected to Gotama and a Kshatriya rishi) in a particular order that the Bashkala-shakha omits or handles differently, and the Ashvalayana followers are thought not to include certain Khila-suktas that the Bashkala tradition does. Such differences are essentially a matter of textual lineage rather than substance.
