## Chapter [Twenty-One] — Subjects Expounded in the Veda: Differing Opinions on This Point

*(Chapter number as legible; sequence continues.)*

### The Traditional (Vedic/Astika) View

**Astikas**, who accept the Veda's authority, hold that the Vedas are beginningless (anādi) and eternal (nitya) — never originating at any point in time, having existed since beginningless time. Whatever needs to be known in this vast universe is held to be contained, in compressed form, within the Veda — the ultimate authority. The Shatapatha Brahmana states: "Prajapati, wishing to create, needed to know the complete range of eternal ritual-forms and materials needed for creation. He then considered these three: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda — known to contain everything." All meters, revealed texts (shrutis), life-force, and deities are said to be contained within it. This is eternal, beginningless, and alone called "Sat" (Being) from time without beginning — the Veda encompassing everything, with no question of it deriving from anything prior. This same subject is discussed in the Purusha-sukta...


### Page 318

> तस्माद्यज्ञात्सर्वहुत ऋचः सामानि जज्ञिरे । छन्दांसि जज्ञिरे तस्माद्यजुस्तस्मादजायत ॥ (Purusha Sukta, RV 10.90.9)
>
> "From that all-offering yajna, the Riks and Samans were born; the meters were born from it, and the Yajus arose from it."

That is: from that yajna (the Supreme Being), the Riks, Samans, and Yajus all came into being — the same view of the Veda's non-human origin (apaurusheya) found across the texts cited above.

But the Samhita portion is chiefly concerned with ritual action (karma) — pleasing the deities through worship and yajna to accumulate merit — and many texts hold this to be a lesser pursuit than the knowledge (jnana) taught in the Upanishads as the true cause of liberation. The Bhambhoyoga Upanishad states:

> सोऽहं भगवो मन्त्रविदेवास्मि नात्मवित् । श्रुतं ह्येव मे भगवद्दृशेभ्यस्तरति शोकमात्मविदिति सोऽहं भगवः शोचामि तं मा भगवाच्छोकस्य पारं तारयत्विति । तं होवाच यद्वै किंचैतदध्यगीष्ठा नामैवैतत् । नाम वा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः...
>
> "'I am, reverend one, a knower of mantras, but not a knower of the Self; yet I have heard from the likes of your reverence that one who knows the Self crosses beyond sorrow. I am full of sorrow, O reverend one — may you carry me to sorrow's far shore.' He replied: 'Whatever you have studied is merely name. Name alone is the Rigveda, the Yajurveda...'"

Many hold that the Veda-Samhitas and related shastras, however celebrated, cannot resolve the sorrow of worldly existence (samsara-duhkha) — that liberating the Self lies beyond their scope. The Gita expresses this same view:

> यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके । तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः ॥ (Bhagavad Gita 2.46)
>
> "As much use as there is in a well when floodwater surrounds it on every side, so much use do all the Vedas hold for a Brahmin who has attained true knowledge."

Put simply: the Veda describes rituals granting heaven and worldly/other-worldly pleasure — of no further use to one who has attained knowledge of Brahman.

**Madhavacharya**, in his *Vedartha-prakasha*, defines the Veda thus:

> इष्टप्राप्त्यनिष्टपरिहारयोरलौकिकमुपायं यो ग्रन्थो वेदयति स वेदः । अलौकिकदेशे प्रत्यक्षानुमाने व्यावर्त्येति ।
>
> "That text which teaches a transcendent (alaukika) means for obtaining what is desired and avoiding what is undesired — that is the Veda. 'Transcendent' excludes ordinary perception and inference as the means in question."

That is: the Veda teaches a path — distinct from perception and inference — for both attaining desired ends and avoiding undesired ones.


### Page 319

Many texts discuss the Veda's non-human origin (apaurusheyatva) at length, especially in Sayana-related literature — the core doctrine holding that the Veda is apaurusheya, eternal, and of ultimate/transcendent significance.

On this point, the *Vedanta-paribhasha*'s introduction states:

> न हि तावत्पुरुषेणोच्चार्यमाणत्वं पौरुषेयत्वम् । गुरुमुखेऽपि अध्यापकसंप्रदाया पौरुषेयत्वाशक्त्ये । नासि पुरुषाभीनोत्पत्तिकत्वं पौरुषेयत्वम्...किंतु सजातीयोच्चारणानेक्षोच्चारणविषयत्वम् । तथा च सर्गाद्यकाले परमेश्वरः पूर्वसर्गसिद्धवेदानुस्पूर्विसमानानुस्पूर्विकं वेदं विरचितवान् न तु तद्विजातीयं वेदमिति न सजातीयोच्चारणानेक्षोच्चारणविषयत्वं पौरुषेयत्वं वेदानाम् । भारतादीनां तु सजातीयोच्चारणमनपेक्ष्योच्चारणमिति तेषां पौरुषेयत्वम् ॥
>
> *(A technical Vedanta-paribhasha argument distinguishing mere recitation by a person from actual authorship: since the Creator, at each creation-cycle, reproduces the Veda in the exact same sequence as the prior cycle's Veda — rather than composing something new and different — the Veda does not qualify as "authored" (paurusheya) the way texts like the Mahabharata, freely composed without such fixed precedent, do. Precise phrase-level parsing is difficult at this resolution, but the overall argument is clear.)*

That is: the Supreme Being, at each creation, reproduces the Vedas exactly as in the prior creation-cycle — "*dhātā yathā pūrvam akalpayat*" ("the Creator fashioned it just as before") — and because the Vedas continue unchanged across every successive cycle, they are called apaurusheya and eternal.

This represents the view found across various texts. But what does the Veda itself suggest, upon direct examination? Consider:

> इदं ब्रह्म क्रियमाणं नवीयः (2.35.40[?]) ब्रह्म कृण्वन्तो हरिवो वसिष्ठाः (1.12.4[?]) ब्रह्मेन्द्राय वज्रिणे अकारि (6.42.6[?]) इत्यादि ।
>
> *(Citations referencing prayers/hymns being "newly composed" or "fashioned" by named rishis — e.g., "this prayer being newly made," "the Vasishthas fashioning a prayer," "a prayer was made for thunderbolt-wielding Indra" — precise mantra locations given as best legible.)*

Two things become clear from such statements:

**(1)** The mantras were composed by rishis or knowledgeable persons.
**(2)** There are both older and newer rishis, and correspondingly older and newer suktas.

Supporting this same view are mantras using verb-roots meaning "to take form/be born" (jāta) or "birth" (janya) in connection with the mantras themselves.


### Page 320

> मन्त्रं ये वारं नर्या अतक्षन् (2.34.1) । अवस्यवो न वयुनानि तक्षुः (1.19.7) । विश्वान्यर्यो भुवना जजान (3.31.1) । इन्द्र ब्रह्माणि जनयन्त विप्राः (2.13.8) । तस्मा उक्थं जनये यज्जुजोष (2.19.1) । इन्द्राय ब्रह्म जनयन्त विप्राः (2.10.10) ।
>
> *(Citations of mantras describing themselves as "carved," "fashioned," or "generated" by rishis/inspired poets — precise locations given as best legible.)*

But these contexts may simply indicate the time and rishi associated with a mantra's ritual use, rather than proving the mantra was newly created then — the "old rishi/new rishi" distinction discussed earlier isn't so easily dismissed either.

Elsewhere, statements convey the directly opposite view — that mantras became perceptible to rishis purely through divine grace, with Speech herself personified and praised as their true source:

> यज्ज्ञेन वाचः पदवीयमायन् तामन्वविन्दन्नृषिषु प्रविष्टाम् । तामाभृत्या व्यदधाप्यर्भुधे तां सप्तरेभा अभि सं नवन्ते ॥ (10.71.3)
>
> "When, through the yajna, they traced Speech's path, they found her having entered into the rishis; having received her, they distributed her further; the seven singers together celebrate her."

Rishis' own utterances are elsewhere attributed extraordinary power:

> विश्वामित्रस्य रक्षति ब्रह्मेदं भारतं जनम् (3.33.11) । विनेन्न कं दाशराज्ञे सुदासं प्रावदिन्द्रो ब्रह्मणा वसिष्ठाः (7.33.3) । वसिष्ठस्य स्तुवत इन्द्रोऽश्चोदुरुं कृत्स्न्यभ्यो अकृणोदुलोकम् (7.33.5) ।
>
> *(Citing Vishvamitra's prayer protecting the Bharata people, and Indra aiding Sudas in the Battle of Ten Kings through the power of the Vasishthas' prayer — precise locations as best legible.)*

Yet elsewhere still, rishis express genuine doubt about their own poetic power and admit their own insufficiency (RV 1.164.37, 6.37).

Such genuinely divergent views coexist within the Veda itself, making any single, tidy determination difficult — even as texts grounded in Vedic authority insist, without qualification, that the Vedas are apaurusheya and faultless, a claim not easily reconciled with the Veda's own varied self-descriptions.

One plausible resolution: the rishis originally lacked full confidence in their own poetic power, and so came to believe their own utterances were not truly their own composition, but something that dawned on them through divine grace — lacking the courage to consider this belief mistaken. **This very belief may be the seed from which the later, firmer doctrine of Vedic apaurusheyatva grew**, becoming progressively more entrenched over time.


### Page 321

Those investigating the Upanishads' philosophical principles hold that view superior to the ritualistic one; even critically-minded scholars share this preference, while Sayanacharya emphasizes the Veda's practical ritual value instead. This represents the ancient scholarly view; now consider the modern view:

> "The Primitive Aryans were children easily susceptible to the influence of their surroundings, highly imaginative, simple and innocent."

That is: early Aryans were simpler than their descendants, not fully grasping natural phenomena, and thus prone to personify and imagine — believing in deities corresponding to natural causes, performing rituals out of unreasoned fear, and composing prayers and hymns from whatever satisfaction or feeling moved them, before having faced great hardship. This isn't a conclusion drawn from the mantras' content directly, but from their careful composition and thoughtfulness, it becomes clear their composers were, from early on, actually quite intellectually mature.

**Another view** holds that the Vedas are neither especially modern nor ancient — their true era becomes clear from careful examination of the mantras themselves: their meters, distinguishing stylistic features, and structural conventions all point to a mature compositional era.

**Yet another view** holds that the Rigveda is not a systematic philosophical text at all, but simply a collection of the earliest hymns — pointing to war-themed suktas and the stories of Sarama, Bhrigu, and Angiras as evidence. Drawing comparisons to Phoenician civilization and its interactions with Assyria, Babylonia, Egypt, and Greece, this view holds that linguistic evidence connects ancient Aryan civilization to a broader trade network — the Ganges region once connected to the Mediterranean by water routes now lost to history, explaining why European and Hindu regions later grew disconnected. This remains one hypothesis among several.


### Page 322

The Rigveda's content can be divided several ways: mantras of ordinary/everyday concern, spiritual (adhyatmic) mantras, and practical/ritual mantras. Deity-focused mantras generally aim to please the deities, concerned with sons, progeny, cattle, and similar worldly goods. Spiritual mantras are comparatively few, including cosmological/metaphysical inquiry alongside more worldly questions — genuinely difficult territory, since even certain deity-worship can be understood in either a worldly or spiritual register, and the line between "practical" and "spiritual" mantras isn't always sharp.

Among clearly ritual/practical suktas: the marriage sukta, funeral suktas, and the gambling sukta stand out. Mandala 10's Yama-sukta (the Yama-Yami dialogue) addresses matters connected to marriage and kinship.

One striking marriage-sukta verse has the bride declare her own domestic authority:

> "...having pleased my husband's mind, may I experience happiness; I have made no vow against a shared household. Aryama, Bhaga, Savitri, and Purandhi and the other deities have placed the role of household-deity upon me alone." (~10.85.46)

This closing verse of the marriage sukta reveals how sacred marriage was held to be in a woman's worldly life, and elsewhere she declares her wish for authority above all other women of the household — the mother-in-law, the daughters-in-law, and other kin — a natural desire for one's own rightful domain (~10.85.46).

The marriage sukta connects to nearly every important rule governing the institution — a rare and carefully composed sukta deserving special mention.

Genuinely historically-informative suktas, however, are few. Where they exist, they generally serve to illuminate some royal lineage's history, praising a king's generosity or Indra's favor, revealing how far kings honored the deities and giving the historical basis for the Purohita's role — the rishis maintaining their relationship with the deities through devotion and the expectation of generous gifts in return. (~7.18; 6.16 series; 1.2; 4.5, etc.)


### Page 323

**Danastuti** (praise-of-gift) hymns praise the donor's qualities, name the gift itself, and record the donor's lineage, the poet's own name, family, and gotra (see 5.61.5-6; 4.2.10, etc.).

A famous humorous sukta (10.108[?] — Gambler's Lament) portrays a compulsive gambler's addiction with real wit — some read it as pure humor, others more seriously, but either way it connects to the gambler's own household troubles and his wife, serving as a genuine warning against gambling's material and moral dangers.

On women, a few notable verses appear:

> "A woman does not walk an easy path." (8.33.17)
> "There is no such thing as friendship with a woman; her heart is like a hyena's heart." (10.95.15)
> "Many women, on many occasions, surpass men." (5.60.6, 2)

It's also noted (10.39.14) that young women are courted for the sake of wealth.

Following the Nyaya tradition, the Atharvaveda-adjacent material includes necessary medicinal plants and remedies for physical weakness and disease:

> "This is a medicine for every disease." (10.97.6)

Indra restores a skin-disease-afflicted woman to health (8.90; 10.14.1, 3); one at death's door is saved (10.18.2, 8); a woman seeking to marry a man drives off her rival and binds him to her (10.145); and a woman awaiting her lover casts all the household to sleep (4.54.5-8).

Finally, **Brahmodyas** are a form of riddle-hymn — describing someone's qualities rather than naming them directly. In one set of mantras (~8.4[?]), the unnamed deities are, in sequence, Indra, Rudra, Vishnu, and the Ashvins — inferable from description alone, and relatively easy riddles. Far harder Brahmodyas apply this technique to earth and sky, sun and moon, wind, cloud, and rain — Sukta 1.164 being the prime example.


## Chapter Twenty-Two — The Rigveda: Its Doctrine

### Page 324

As discussed earlier, the great majority of Rigveda suktas connect to some doctrine or belief tied to the deities — determining a sukta's context, its divine connection, and its dedicated deity requires real care. Two aspects of the Rigveda's content deserve special note. First: these mantras of praise (stuti) each belonged to a specific rishi — not every rishi's mantra held equal renown, and what survives as "the Rigveda's view" is really a merger of many individual views across a long period, so any general statement about its "intent" necessarily glosses over real historical variation, capturing only shared, common qualities.

One view holds that the Vedic-era Aryans, being entirely uncivilized, were simply awestruck by natural phenomena, personifying nature and composing hymns to praise the cattle-wealth they possessed. I cannot fully accept this — the claim of extreme primitiveness, however often repeated, doesn't hold up.

Even granting limited planning, the rishis clearly composed with real worldly awareness — their careful attention to meter and structure, each mantra crafted with a specific purpose, each deity praised to secure favor for a particular yajna, mantras revised and refined over time, and appropriate mantras composed as community needs demanded within inherited compositional conventions (1.104.1; 1.63.1[?]; 3.16.7, etc.) — none of this is the work of uncivilized, primitive people. This is my counter-argument.

The Vedic doctrine's most important trait, and its practical value, lies in its embodiment of ritual action (karma) — of great use to practitioners and result-seekers alike. The Rigveda's genuine poetic spirit suggests an era where sacrificial practice was already well-established and mature...


### Page 325

...the ritual acts of yajnas — composed with a poet's rhythmic care, or sung with a warrior's rallying spirit — sought longevity, wealth, fame, sons, and cattle for the community through fire-offerings and Soma-libations (see e.g. 1.1.8; 1.1.9).

The Rigveda, being primarily connected to the **Purohita** class, naturally reflects their own worldview — where priestly matters took priority, devotion to the deities was steadfast, and prayer went well beyond basic subsistence. In war, kings prayed for victory through their Purohita, pleasing their chosen deity and considering it improper to abandon that deity for a rival one once devotion had been pledged. Mandala 7's suktas show Vasishtha's own royal patron relying jointly on Indra and Varuna for aid in the same battle — even while helping one side, no hesitation existed about opposing the other:

> "Hear my prayer, all-knowing Indra; look upon these battle-difficulties. Many pray to you; I too pray, trusting in you." (7.18.1)

This confirms that faith in the deities, mediated through the Purohita, was believed capable of securing victory — righteousness and divine reliance together constituting the true path to success.

Purohitas performing yajnas would receive a tenth share (dakshina) of what was gained from the king, offering divine assistance in return — a mutual relationship where both sides had to remain satisfied for the arrangement to succeed. Generous praise-gifts to Purohitas are recorded as Danastutis.

In the Vedic era, deities were **not enshrined in temples** for worship, nor worshipped individually within households — only invoked in sequence during yajnas and pleased through Soma-offerings and similar rites. Among the deities, Agni and Indra held the highest importance; a full treatment of all the deities appears elsewhere in this book.

---

*(This concludes Chapter Twenty-Two.)*


## Chapter Twenty-Three — Social Life in the Vedic Era

### Page 326

Modern researchers, using **comparative philology**, have established with reasonable confidence that Indians, Persians, Greeks, Germans, and Italians all once formed a single unified group, living together in one place. The **Avesta**'s language shows close similarity to the Rigveda's language, indicating that, in ancient times, one group split off, another remained, and both continued residing side by side for a long period. Later, the Hindus entered India specifically. It can be determined, with reasonable precision, from the names of rivers appearing in the Rigveda, which places the Aryans first settled. Following the Ganga river's route, further eastward-region rivers' names occur less frequently. The Sindhu and its own tributary rivers — the **Vitasta** (present-day Jhelum), **Asikni** (Chenab), **Parushni** (Ravi), **Vipas** (Beas), and **Shutudri** (Sutlej) — all appear by these names in the Rigveda. The Ganga river's name appears just once, in a single place (10.75.5). This suggests that, when much of the Rigveda was composed, the Aryans had not yet penetrated as far as the Ganga's banks. The **Kubha** (Kabul) and **Suvastu** (the Swat) river-names also occur, confirming that at the time much of the Rigveda was composed, the Aryans were settled across the region spanning Kabul to the Punjab.

Villages, forts, and cities built of brick are also mentioned, alongside forts of stone (1.104.1; 1.44.10; 7.6.5; 7.15.14; 7.18.1[?]) — though whether these were the deities' own fortresses or genuinely fortified structures used decoratively remains a debated point.

Among people's chief occupations were **agriculture** and **animal husbandry**. Every deity is prayed to, at some point, for crops, wealth, horses, and cattle — praying for cattle in particular is especially common. People valued these as their wealth. No other name for wealth appears elsewhere in the Veda quite so often — only in the Atharvaveda does "Akshaya" (imperishable wealth) occur as a term.

> प्रीहिमत्रं यवमत्रमथो माषमथो तिलम् । (Atharva — 8.70[?].2)


### Page 327

Roasted grains and crushed handfuls mixed with ghee were offered to deities (2.1[?].5; 2.13.2[?]). Various domesticated animal species are named, especially oxen and horses (5.19.3; 5.83.7; 10.121[?]); ox-meat cooking is occasionally mentioned too (5.5[?].2; 8.3[?].3; 8.66.10) — though whether such practices reflect universal custom or occasional exception is hard to determine, much as with Soma consumption itself, since some later ritual texts explicitly restrict it.

Rishis of this era excelled in chariot construction, and skilled craftsmen (kushalaru) practiced this trade — chariot-building imagery recurs frequently in poetic metaphor. Weaving was likewise common, its imagery ("thread") also used metaphorically in mantra composition. Woodworking/carpentry, leatherwork, and metalwork are all mentioned as Aryan crafts.

Trade is scarcely mentioned, and seafaring activity even less so — what boat-usage appears seems oriented toward river-crossing rather than genuine sea voyages.

Marriage was arranged by the father; widow remarriage appears to have been considered acceptable. Details of husband-wife relations are scarce, but the **wife held a significant position within the household** — "household deity, mistress of the household" — with authority over domestic affairs; there's little evidence of exclusive husbandly authority in this domain. A house without a mistress, it's noted, could not properly function; a newly arrived young bride becomes the household's own yajamana (ritual mistress). This blessing was offered to a bride newly arriving in her husband's home:

> सम्राज्ञी श्वशुरे भव सम्राज्ञी श्वश्र्वां भव । ननान्दरि सम्राज्ञी भव सम्राज्ञी अधि देवृषु ॥ (10.85.46)
>
> "Be sovereign over your father-in-law; be sovereign over your mother-in-law. Be sovereign over your sister-in-law; be sovereign over your brothers-in-law too."

That is: may you hold authority over your in-laws — meaning, may you look after their welfare (yogakshema). Elsewhere, further—


### Page 328

> "From the very beginning, before the father-in-law's time itself, this position remains fixed" — meaning her authority over mother-in-law and household affairs was established from the outset. That is: women held an honored place in domestic life, connected to maintaining household happiness (10.85).

On the wider question of women's authority, the term "kshatriya" (used elsewhere for the warrior class) and terms for "wife" appear used in overlapping ways (1.109.2[?]; 1.126.1[?]; 1.109.8; 10.86.9[?]; 6.75.19; 8.75.9[?]; 10.95.1[?]). A woman is described achieving independence by bringing an errant husband back under control (10.34.11-12[?]).

Marriage aimed at mutual companionship and establishing a lineage — prayers commonly requested sons for one's family, with the eldest son apparently holding special priority (including a special inheritance share), though whether daughters held inheritance rights is unclear. No evidence suggests anything but genuine mutual affection within Vedic-era families.

Whether monogamy or polygamy was the established norm isn't entirely clear — some Rigveda passages place no restriction on plural wives (4.5.5[?]), and specific status for co-wives appears unfixed in places (10.72.8[?]; 10.71.4[?]).

Remarriage after divorce doesn't appear to have been common practice — marriage was held to be a supremely sacred act, and mantras generally express the wish that a woman's marriage remain permanently fixed to one husband, without dissolution:

> कुणस्सिद्ध्योष्णा कुण वस्त्रोऽरश्चिना कुहाभिसिक्तं करकः कुहोषतुः । को वां शयुत्रा विधवेव देवरं मर्यं न योषा कृणुते सधस्थ आ ॥ (10.40.2)
>
> *(A difficult passage concerning marital fidelity and the comparison of an abandoned woman to a widow turning to a brother-in-law; precise construction uncertain at this resolution.)*

**Manu** (9.46.20) similarly permits a widow to marry her husband's brother (devara) under certain circumstances — but the same chapter (9.46.10) restricts such a marriage to lasting only until she bears a son.

Abandonment of marital duty and infidelity are both known to have occurred (10.34.4; 10.40.6; 3.53.1), and one mantra describes women as headstrong and fickle-minded (8.33.17).


### Page 329

Infidelity was believed to bring destruction, with the deities prayed to for the ruin of an unfaithful person's lineage (1.167.4[?]; 4.5.5; 4.5.6[?]).

**People lived organized in tribal groups.** Each tribe was distinct and independent, joining forces only temporarily during war; each had its own king with his own lineage, and each royal household maintained its own Purohita (2.42.1[?]; 2.11.8[?]) — kings gave a portion of earned wealth to Indra as tribute, while the Purohita's task was to pray for wealth and the destruction of enemies, receiving a share of royal gifts in return, as many Danastuti hymns attest (10.148[?]).

On deity-worship, already discussed — but whether Vedic-era practice included **idol worship** remains genuinely unclear. Max Müller and others hold that it did not:

> "The Religion of the Veda knows of no idols. The worship of idols in India is a secondary formation, a later degradation of the more primitive worship of ideal gods."

That is: no image-worship ritual is mentioned in the Vedic era; idol-worship developed later, a corruption of an earlier, more imaginative form of worship. Dr. Bollensen opposes this view, citing passages (3.53.8; 8.83.8[?]) suggesting deities were understood to have physical bodies and hold weapons — a genuinely unresolved scholarly question.

### On Caste (Varna)

The caste system is one of Hindu society's most defining, enduring features, still distinctly maintained today by inherited custom — and some scholars hold that caste distinction is not a very ancient feature at all, but a later development in our country's history.

Indeed, through Mandala 9, the Rigveda shows no established basis for caste distinctions. Only in Mandala 10's **Purusha Sukta** (10.90) does the fourfold varna system first appear:

> ब्राह्मणोऽस्य मुखमासीद्बाहू राजन्यः कृतः । ऊरू तदस्य यद्वैश्यः पद्भ्यां शूद्रो अजायत ॥ (RV 10.90.12)
>
> ब्राह्मणोऽस्य मुखम् आसीद् बाहू राजन्यः कृतः । ऊरू तद् अस्य यद् वैश्यः पद्भ्यां शूद्रो अजायत ॥
> *brāhmaṇo'sya mukham āsīd bāhū rājanyaḥ kṛtaḥ | ūrū tad asya yad vaiśyaḥ padbhyāṃ śūdro ajāyata ||*
>
> "The Brahmin was his mouth; the Rajanya (Kshatriya) was made his arms; that which became the Vaishya was his thighs; from his feet the Shudra was born."


### Page 330

...from the Virat-Purusha's face the Brahmin was born, from his arms the king (Kshatriya), from his thigh-region the Vaishya, and from his feet the Shudra.

Some scholars hold that this sukta stands apart from the Rigveda's general flow and style, suggesting a later addition — though others dispute this. One theory holds that the body-part imagery reflects a functional division: Brahmins, born of the mouth/head, took up knowledge and learning, becoming particularly devoted to deity-worship and governance-adjacent affairs; those relying on physical strength for society's protection became Kshatriyas; trade and agriculture fell to Vaishyas; and whatever labor supported the body's basic needs and other humbler tasks fell to Shudras. This suggests occupational necessity, rather than everyone being assigned a single fixed task from birth, gave rise to these four divisions naturally. Puranic and related texts, however, state plainly that the four-varna division is fixed by birth (janmataḥ siddha).

The Gita states:

> "चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः"
>
> "The fourfold varna was created by me, according to the division of qualities (guna) and actions (karma)."

That is: the four varnas were organized according to their respective qualities and work — not fixed by birth as such. But since, over time, the qualities of Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra families came to be inherited by birth in practice, some argue — based on the word "sṛṣṭam" ("created") in this very verse — that the division was intended as a birth-based lineage system from the very beginning.

---

*(This concludes the chapter's discussion of the Rigveda's social world.)*


## Chapter Twenty-Four — Special Grammatical Features in the Rigveda

### Page 331

Comparing Vedic Sanskrit with classical Sanskrit reveals considerable differences on both sides — verb-forms and noun-declensions differ significantly, though case-formation still follows one underlying method, with a more restricted range of alternate forms than classical usage typically shows (two or three variant forms for a single word being common). Verb (tiṅanta) forms differ slightly too; the Veda makes wide use of potential/subjunctive-like mood-marking, present in classical Sanskrit only in more limited, indicative-restricted form. The Veda's sandhi (euphonic combination) rules show many differences from classical practice — a few key points are examined below.

**Sandhi frequently doesn't occur where classical grammar would expect it**, though it is generally applied throughout the Veda. Classical rule holds that visarga does not occur before consonant-initial words at a word-boundary — but the Veda shows many exceptions, generally where meter demands preserving a required syllable-count; sandhi is even applied mid-word in some cases where meter requires it:

> त्वं सुतस्य पीतये सद्यो वृद्धो अजायथाः (1.8.4)
>
> "You, for the drinking of the pressed Soma, instantly became grown/strong."

> अथा ते अन्तमानां विद्याम सुमतीनाम् (1.4.3)
>
> "And may we know the innermost of your favors."

And also 1.1.2, 1.1.7, 1.1.4, 1.1.11, 1.1.19, and others.

Classical grammar holds that no sandhi occurs where a word ending in *ī, ū,* or single-mora *ṛ* precedes a following vowel — but the Veda shows many exceptions, especially where the word "iva" follows:

> ब्रह्माणि नृपतीव जिन्वतम् । (2.104[?].6)
> अन्तर्मने रोदसीव मे — (2.81.1)
> अविनासं रोदसी धिष्ण्येमे — (2.11.1)

*(These citations illustrate sandhi occurring across "iva" in Vedic recitation contrary to the classical rule; precise phrase-level translation is difficult at this resolution given the technical grammatical register.)*


### Page 332

In certain consonant contexts, classical rule requires a following "na" sound — but the Veda shows variant forms with na-sound or sha-sound, particularly around the particles "ena" and "ina."

Vowel-lengthening for prosodic (metrical) purposes affects words like *atha, adha, pibha, śrutata, vidya, yuṣma, veda, kṛdhi, śṛṇuhi* especially often.

Two related matters deserve note. In noun-declension, third-person dual forms and words like "ena" vary according to the meter's required syllable-count:

> अश्विना पुरुदंससा नरा शवीरया धिया (1.3.3)
> कवीनो मित्रावरुणा तुविजाता उरुक्षया (1.2.9)
> यमश्विना ददथुः श्वेतमश्वम् (1.116.9)
> ता विद्वांसा हवामहे (1.130.9)

In some places, both dual-form variants occur within the very same mantra:

> ता वामद्य तावसरं हुवेम (1.44.1)

In the **plural of Nominative and Vocative cases**, "āsa" often replaces plain "ā":

> विश्वे देवास आगत । (1.3.2)
> ब्राह्मणासः पितरः सोम्यासः (6.75.10)
> सोमासो दध्याशिरः (1.37.5)

"Devāsaḥ," "brāhmaṇāsaḥ," "somāsaḥ" and similar forms are ancient usages; alongside them, the more recent forms — "devāḥ," "brāhmaṇāḥ," "somāḥ" — also occur abundantly.

In the **neuter plural of a-stem nouns**, both "-ā" and "-āni" occur — the Rigveda favoring "-ā," the Atharvaveda favoring "-āni" more heavily, with both forms occasionally appearing together in the same passage. Examples—


### Page 333

> इनो अग्ने वीततमानि हव्या (2.1.17[?]) । कृषु यदन्ना समवृक्त जंभैः (2.8.4[?]) । पिता नो अग्ने सौभगा दिदीहि (2.8.10[?]) । यो दैव्यानि मानुषा जनूंषि (2.5.1[?]) — इत्यादि ।

In the **Instrumental plural**, both "bhiḥ" and "aiḥ" forms occur — but the "aiḥ" form appears increasingly rarely, surviving mainly among pronominal words:

> पावका नः सरस्वती वाजेभिर्वाजिनीवती (1.3[?].10) । देवो देवेभिरागमत् (1.1[?].5) — इत्यादि ।

For **a-stem feminine nouns**, the Instrumental singular shows both "-ā" and "-ayā" forms. Examples:

> माशेषसोऽवीरता सरि त्वा (2.1[?].10) । सहस्रसाध्या अक्षरा सनेति (2.1[?].4) । गव्या कृत्स्नभो अजगन् युधा स्वः (2.75[?].2) । आ यो विश्वानि शवसा तताना (2-91[?]-1) । श्रद्धा इत्ये मघवन् पार्ये दिवि (2-92[?]-14) — इत्यादि ।

For **i-stem words**, the Instrumental singular's "-i" lengthens to "-ī." Examples:

> हस्त्यश्च्युती जनयंत प्रशस्युम् (2-1[?]-1) । सुदीत्यी सूनो सहसो दिदीहि (2-1[?]-20[?]) । प्रावीण्न वीरो जरितारनूती (2-90[?]-2) । तन प्रणीती हर्यश्व सूरिभिः (2-92[?]-19[?]) । न दुष्ट्रुती मत्र्यो विंदते वसु (2-92[?]-20[?]) — इत्यादि ।

For the **Locative singular**, some words retain the "i"-stem, while a few show a shift to "a"-stem or "ā"-stem-style endings:

> त्वं धृष्णो धृषता वीतहव्यम् (2-19[?]-3) । युत्वायर्आ युनजते धियस्काः (2-91[?]-1) — इत्यादि ।

*(Given the extreme grammatical density of this page — worked case-ending examples across several noun classes — citations are transcribed as faithfully as legible; the mantra reference numbers marked "[?]" carry some uncertainty given the compressed numerals in the original typeface, though the Sanskrit text itself and grammatical point being illustrated are clear.)*


### Page 334

In the **Genitive singular**, the stem-vowel takes guna, with only the case-suffix attaching (e.g., *ari + as = aryaḥ*). For i-stem feminine nouns, the Nominative plural also lengthens — e.g., *bhūmyaḥ*.

A table of variant forms found among masculine and neuter nouns:

| Form (with citation) | Description | Standard equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| वस्नः (2.[?].5) | u-stem masc., Genitive sing. | (vasoḥ) |
| कृत्ये (2.[?].5) | " , Dative sing. | (kṛtave) |
| सानवि | neuter, Locative sing. | (sānau) |
| कृत्वा (2.[?].6) | masc., Instrumental sing. | (kṛtunā) |
| देवीः (2.[?].7) | ī-stem fem., Nom. plural | (devyaḥ) |
| शमा | " , Instr. singular | (śamyā) |
| कुचे | i-stem neuter, Nom. plural | (kucīni) |
| अप्रती (2.[?].2) | " " " | (apratīni) |
| मातरा (2.[?].2) | r-stem fem., Nom. dual | (mātarau) |
| युष्मे | yuṣmad-stem, Nom. plural | (yūyam) |
| अस्मे | asmad-stem, Nom. plural | (vayam) |
| व्योमन् | n-stem neuter, Nom. sing. | (vyoma / vyomāni) |
| सरिज्ञन् | " " " | (sarijñi) |

*(Given the highly technical, tabular nature of this page's grammatical comparisons across multiple noun-classes, forms are transcribed as legible; some individual mantra-reference numerals carry residual uncertainty.)*

Some words show no case-suffix at all in either declension.

**Non-standard (aśrutya) suffixes:** verb-roots occasionally take non-classical suffixes, producing variant forms noted throughout. For the second-person plural imperative suffix "mas," the Veda regularly uses "masi" in its place instead — sometimes rendered simply "mas." In the Rigveda, "masi" occurs 112 times, "mas" 30 times, and in other Brahmana texts "masi" occurs twice and "mas" four times — confirming that in classical usage, the "mas" form for imperative verbs is not the established convention. Example:

> मिनीमसि (1.[?].[?]) । बोधामसि (2.[?].1)

For first-person singular Atmanepada verbs, "e" traditionally replaces "i" — but "śṛṇute" appears where "śṛṣṇe" would traditionally be expected instead (2.8[?].5; 2.9[?].4).

The Injunctive mood, middle-voice second-person singular, shows many variant forms — often ending in "dhi" (also seen as "hi," e.g., "śaśādhi," "kṛdhi," "śrudhi" — per Panini, either "dhi" ending is correct). Forms like "śṛṇudhi" and "gṛbhi" also occur.


### Page 335

In the middle-voice second-person plural, "dhve" and "dhvam" replace classical "dhvam" and "dhvam" variants. Imperative first-person singular forms take an extra "si" suffix — examples: kṣeṣi (2.[?].3), bhakṣi (2.[?].3), riṣṭi and veśi (2.[?].8[?]).

Present participles occur in many varied forms; the suffix "tam" is generally used, though the Veda uses "avitane" (2.[?].1) and "aśnevatane" (2.[?].8) in the same sense. Among these:

- ending in "tve": haṃtve, khātve
- ending in "se": cikṣṇase, jīvase
- ending in "taye": pīśhitaye, ūtaye
- ending in "dhyai": iṣadhyai, sṛṇudhyai, śucidhyai
- ending in "mane": vitomāḥ, kartomāḥ, and similar forms — all used in the sense of an infinitive.

In place of forms ending in the "tvā" suffix, "tvāya" or "tvī" are also used — hantvāya, kṛtvī, pītvī, bhūtvī, etc.

**Potential-mood forms** are relatively few; the negating particle "mā" often used alone, combined with root-forms and mood-neutral forms of the base, without the potential-suffix strictly attached — this "mā"-based construction is common in the Veda in the potential sense. The Veda gives such forms the technical name "Let" (imperative/prohibitive). Examples: bhavāti (2.[?].5), patāti (2.[?].1), tāriṣat, joṣiṣet, mādayaithe — all illustrating this prohibitive/optative-adjacent construction.

In classical Sanskrit, prefixes (upasargas) are used joined directly to the verb root as a matter of convention — but this rule doesn't apply strictly in the Veda:

> इन्द्र त्वोकास आ वयं वज्रं घना दधीमहि । जयेम सं युधि स्पृधः ॥ (1.8[?].3)

Here, "ādadhīmahi" and "saṃjayema" are the intended verbs — but in the first, several words come between the prefix and the root, and in the second, the prefix follows the verb root instead of preceding it:

> उप यामेति युवतिः सुदक्षं दोषावस्तोर्दिविष्टिषु प्रचेती । उप स्वैनमरमतिर्वसूयुः ॥ (2.1[?].6)
> अव द्युग्नानि पित्र्या सृजा नोऽव यां वयं चक्रुमा तनूभिः । अव राजन्पशुतृपं न तायुं........ (2.[?].3)

and so on.


### Page 336

A verb-prefix is sometimes used once joined to its verb, then repeated again alone, detached, later in the same sentence:

> प्र सम्राजो असुरस्य प्रशस्तिं पुंसः कृष्टीनामनुमाद्यस्य । इन्द्रस्यैव प्र तवसस्कृतानि वन्दे दारुं वन्दमानो नि वक्मि ॥ (2.[?].1) इत्यादि ।
>
> *(Praising the mighty sovereign lord's deeds, extolling Indra's powerful acts; precise phrase-level construction is difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

Only a small selection of special grammatical forms has been illustrated in this chapter for representative purposes — such variations are far too numerous to detail exhaustively here. They will be discussed at length, with full grammatical reasoning, when explaining each individual mantra's meaning, and again in the dedicated "Vyakarana-prakriya" (Grammatical Process) section.

*(This concludes Chapter Twenty-Four.)*

---

## Chapter Twenty-Five — The Age of the Vedas

### Page 336 (continued)

No one has definitively settled the question of the Vedas' age. Among scholars who have attempted to date them, no consensus exists, and it cannot be said that any single determination has become firmly established. Whether this question is even worth pursuing further might itself be questioned — but it matters because comparative philology, social/political history, and linguistics all converge on this point: our nation's own culture, and the foundations of ancient Hindu-Aryan civilization, cannot be properly understood without knowing the Veda's era. A complete historical understanding of our own past requires it.

Among surviving texts of our country, the Vedas are held to be the most ancient — a settled matter. But whether the Aryans were already present in our land at that time, or arrived from elsewhere, remains unresolved, and the era of Vedic composition demands careful examination. Among the Vedas, the **Rigveda** is held to be the most ancient, and many scholars have attempted to determine its era.


### Page 337

Scholars attempting to date the Rigveda have offered various bases for their conclusions, but none has proven definitively correct — the Rigveda's true era remains undetermined by anyone. It's worth clarifying at the outset what is and isn't actually known.

Comparative-mythology scholars broadly agree the Vedas are extremely ancient. **Friedrich Schlegel** held that the Vedas offer "enlightenment upon the history of the primitive world, so dark till now." **A. Weber**, in his 1852 *History of Indian Literature*, wrote:

> "We are justified in regarding the literature of India as the most ancient literature of which written records on an extensive scale have been handed down to us."

Compared with all surviving world literatures, Indian literature is reasonably held to be the most ancient of its kind, preserved on this scale.

In the Rigvedic era, the Aryans lived organized in tribes, with the Rigveda predating the other Vedas and belonging to a period before full settlement of the Gangetic plains. The Puranas record Brahmanical religion's later spread southward across the peninsula — a process that, even today, continues incorporating remote regions, not something confined to the Rigvedic period alone. The Rigveda's own mantric worship-tradition has persisted continuously since, integrated deeply into ongoing philosophical and devotional practice, alongside many differing later forms of worship and belief — a broad picture Weber himself never disputed, and there is little point disputing further.

**Max Müller** was the first to attempt a fixed dating, in his 1859 *History of Ancient Sanskrit Literature*, working backward from the known beginning of Buddhism as an anchor point.

Brahmanism (Vedic doctrine) was already well established before Buddhism arose. Buddhism developed specifically as a reaction against Vedic custom and worldview, its own texts spreading extensively in opposition to Vedic ideology...


### Page 338

...must be factored in — the Sutra texts, being the latest-composed Vedic layer, are estimated to span roughly 600–200 BCE. The Brahmana texts, distinguished by their emphasis on birth-based Brahmin ritual status (unlike earlier layers), are placed in a separate, earlier era. By this reckoning, the Vedas' earliest layer is estimated at roughly 2000 BCE — though since the mantras themselves were composed over a long span, no single fixed date applies to "the" composition era; later contributors kept adding to an existing body of material. On this reasoning, the Vedic era's beginning is often placed around **1200 BCE**.

Max Müller's own original dating is not considered decisive — essentially an educated guess without firm grounding, since assigning a fixed number of years to each successive textual layer (Samhita, Brahmana, Sutra) has no genuinely scientific basis; civilizational development doesn't proceed in neat, countable increments. Max Müller himself, in his later 1889 Gifford Lectures on *Physical Religion*, revisited the subject and famously admitted:

> "No power on earth will ever determine [the exact date of the Vedic period]."

A merely impressionistic acceptance, without genuine critical examination, isn't appropriate here — though Max Müller's rough 1200 BCE estimate is not accepted point-by-point by everyone, other scholars have arrived at broadly similar figures independently. **L. Von Schroeder** boldly proposed 1500 BCE. **H. Jacobi** and others argued for a considerably more ancient date still, basing their conclusions on **astronomical evidence** — drawing on Jyotisha-shastra (astronomical science) to support their dating. **Ludwig**, similarly, attempted a clear determination based on solar eclipse references.

In ancient Hindu society, before undertaking any ritual action, households would consult auspicious timing and decide on marriage-dates and similar matters before beginning — and the Brahmanas and Sutras contain material related to Jyotisha-shastra (astronomy)...


### Page 339

...astronomical references are numerous, especially concerning the 28 **nakshatras** (lunar mansions), through which the moon's movement was tracked to establish the calendar — roughly one nakshatra per day, cycling through all 28 to form a month, with 12 such months forming a year. The Vedas record precisely which nakshatra the moon occupied in a given month.

Certain ancient texts also track the sun's position at year's start against this same backdrop — the precession of this solar reference point across successive years provides another dating tool, one Ludwig and Jacobi both drew upon.

Using this astronomical evidence, **Jacobi** and the Indian scholar **B. G. Tilak** independently arrived at strikingly similar conclusions, both dating the Vedic era to roughly **4500 BCE**.

The Brahmana-era ritual calendar begins its sequence with the Krittika (Pleiades) constellation, while the earlier Samhita portions instead begin the nakshatra sequence with Mrigashira — on this basis, the Samhita era is estimated at roughly 4000 BCE, and the Brahmana era somewhat later, around 3000 BCE, drawing on this same body of astronomical evidence.

Using this same evidence, however, other scholars — including Jayaswal — reach a considerably more modest figure, placing the era around 1180 BCE, a conclusion disputed by others still.

The Brahmana-era ritual texts also reference the equinox point (Mesha-sankranti) at the sequence's start; but even earlier Samhita material places the equinox instead at the Krittika constellation — a precessional shift used to estimate the Samhita era at roughly 4000 BCE and the somewhat later Brahmana era at roughly 3000 BCE, per this method. Ludwig's independent estimate reportedly arrives at a broadly similar picture...


### Page 340

...one nakshatra shifting to the next westward, cycling back to the pole-star (Dhruva) region over roughly 25,000 years — currently, the pole-star's associated nakshatra-group is Abhijit (Vega). This dating method's scientific certainty is considered limited; a 1893 publication specifically addressing the Dhruva-nakshatra question concluded this method isn't fully applicable to the Rigveda, and thus can't firmly establish its era.

Other historians hold differing views on this debate. The Shatapatha Brahmana's own Krittika-constellation reference does point toward a specific era with reasonable agreement (~3000 BCE) — and on this basis, an agricultural-era date of roughly 2800 BCE is considered a fair estimate, corroborated by additional evidence and generally accepted.

But applying this same precise method to the Rigveda itself has no comparably solid basis — the Rigveda's own era cannot be firmly fixed this way, and none of these precision dating-attempts for the Veda proper rest on solid ground; they shouldn't be relied upon as decisive.

Jacobi's and Tilak's conclusions are not universally accepted, and further research remains necessary. Where earlier historians confined Indian culture's founding to within the last 100–800 years, it's now clearly established that portions of the Rigveda belong to a much earlier society. Evidence from Ashoka's inscriptions, recording missionaries sent to South India, confirms Buddhism (and by extension, prior Aryan presence) had already reached the far south by around **500 BCE** — well before Ashoka's own time.

Around 500–800 BCE, the Aryans were the dominant influence...


### Page 341

...gradual assimilation and cultural spread over generations seems entirely plausible, requiring its own additional span of time to account for — this is **G. Buhler's** view.

**Oldenberg** differs, holding that meaningful linguistic change doesn't require even 200 years — comparing rates of change observed in American-continent languages within similar timeframes to argue for faster change than Buhler assumes.

But American linguistic-social change and Indian conditions differ considerably — Vedic-era Aryans maintained a remarkably conservative language and ritual system across generations, treasuring even single words and half-verses of received mantras with great care.

**Bloomfield** notes that many Rigveda mantras recur repeatedly across different contexts within the text itself — showing that much of the Rigveda's material already existed in fixed, traditional form before being incorporated, later generations adapting it to their own needs.

The Rigveda's mantras and those found in other Vedic texts show comparable language, style, and worship-practices with little variation — and the close relationship between Brahmana-texts and their associated shakhas suggests continuous transmission over a considerable span, not a brief one; the Samhita portions cannot simply be assigned to a later era's authorship.

The Veda was never composed as a single unified "textbook" — no fixed date can be assigned to it as a whole. But systematic comparison across sources leads most historians to conclude that the Vedic corpus, and its various portions, must span several centuries — the Brahmana literature alone likely took many centuries to fully develop. Some suktas explicitly reference earlier suktas, sometimes naming their composers or patrons directly, confirming relative chronology within the text — the same method used to establish relative dating among Upanishadic teachers' lineages.

Beyond this, tracing the Aryans' own migration — from the Gangetic frontier gradually southward into the Deccan and beyond, and the corresponding spread of Brahmanical communities — Oldenberg argues this process, too, cannot have been brief, a conclusion some further evidence supports.


### Page 342

Max Müller, taking the spread of Buddhism (~600 BCE) as an anchor point, held that Vedic religion was already fully developed by then; Oldenberg and others hold that the Upanishads and early Buddhism are closely connected within a few centuries of each other, even though Buddhism explicitly rejected Vedic textual authority. The Buddha's own traditional date (~560 BCE) provides a further fixed reference. **G. Buhler** argues this is the correct starting point, and that the Veda's true age must extend considerably further back still.

A genuinely remarkable piece of evidence comes from **Boghazkoi** (Hattusa): ancient artifacts discovered there by **Hugo Winckler** in 1907 CE included treaty documents from the ancient **Hittite Kingdom**. Among them, a treaty between the Hittites and the **Mitanni** kingdom, dated to roughly **1400 BCE**, survives in its concluding portion — where the two parties invoke their own deities as witnesses to the treaty. Among the named deities are **Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and Nasatya** — all recognizably Hindu deity-names. This discovery has been a matter of major scholarly significance, and its authenticity is universally accepted.

The historian **Meyer** holds that these deities belong to a shared ancient Aryan-Iranian heritage, predating the Aryans' eventual arrival in India — the Aryans having crossed through the Mesopotamian region and spread further west before some branch eventually reached India, with mantra-composition beginning sometime after. **Oldenberg** shares this view, explicitly rejecting the claim that the Vedas themselves date to this earlier (Mitanni-treaty) period.

It's not strictly necessary to claim these deities belonged *exclusively* to Vedic worship even at that early date — their worship may have spread into other regions before Vedic tradition, as we know it, later arrived in India along a related cultural stream. Considering this, some scholars in the field hold that an ancient, broadly Vedic-adjacent tradition already existed and extended over a considerable period, well established in various places by the 1400 BCE century, with continuous worship-practice for a long time already behind it.

**J. Hertel** argues the Veda's birthplace was not India at all, but Persia, dating its composition to the era of Zoroaster (~950 BCE). **G. Husing**...


### Page 343

**Husing** argues that the Rigveda references figures connected to a Caspian/Iran-adjacent kingdom predating its arrival in India, placing full Vedic composition after this point — though his own supporting basis is not firmly grounded.

It can be stated with confidence that the Vedas are not merely 3,500 years old and no more — but whether their true origin lies in Persia or in India remains disputed, and the linguistic resemblances found between the two traditions can be explained either way with comparable plausibility; both regions may simply share a common ancestral settlement group. Since languages change at variable, non-uniform rates — some quickly, some slowly — conclusions drawn from language comparison alone provide no fully reliable dating basis.

Even so, languages do generally change gradually across generations, and this much can be accepted with confidence. Whether the Vedas are 3,500 or 4,000 years old cannot be determined with full confidence purely through astronomical or geo-historical methods — yet, weighing the various strands of evidence together, scholars from differing backgrounds have independently converged on roughly similar eras, which itself carries some weight, even amid genuine, unresolved disagreement on details. The connections between Vedic and ancient Iranian legal/political traditions remain relevant to this discussion regardless of which specific dating (3,500–4,000 years) is accepted.

**In summary, three points bear on this question:**

**1.** Attempts to date the Veda through Jyotisha-shastra (astronomical evidence) have not proven conclusive — Vedic astronomical references admit too many differing interpretations to settle the matter.

**2.** Historical evidence — inscriptions from Syria and elsewhere naming Vedic deities, and the broader question of Hindu-Aryan civic/cultural continuity — carries real evidentiary weight, though not fully decisive on its own; taken together, however, several such elements point toward a Vedic date of roughly **1300 BCE** for the Hindus specifically.

**3.** Linguistic evidence — the Vedic language's natural resemblance to related ancient and modern languages — likewise cannot yield a fully confident, definitive determination on its own.


### Page 344 — Chapter Conclusion

**4.** Since the rate of linguistic change is itself variable, any conclusion drawn from language-resemblance alone can only ever yield an approximate value for the Vedic era — a genuine limitation worth stating plainly rather than glossing over.

**5.** In the absence of firm textual proof settling the matter, examining our own country's broader literary and cultural record offers the best remaining path to an estimate. It can be reliably established that, before the teachings of **Parshvanatha, Mahavira,** and the **Buddha** spread, the Vedas and Vedangas had already reached their complete, established form. On this basis, the Vedas' composition can reasonably be estimated to have **begun around 2500–3000 BCE**, reaching **completion around 1500–2000 BCE**. Fixing a more precise date beyond this general range — while avoiding both excessive antiquity and unwarranted recency — remains the most reasonable and methodologically sound path available with current evidence.

---

**— This concludes the chapter on the Age of the Vedas. —**

# PART II: Sāyaṇācārya's Ṛgveda-Bhāṣya-Bhūmikā
*("ಸಾಯಣಾಚಾರ್ಯಕೃತ ಋಗ್ವೇದಭಾಷ್ಯಭೂಮಿಕೆ" — Sayana's Preface to His Rigveda Commentary. Printed pages 345–593 of the source. Restructured into 18 chapters below, following the source's own descriptive table-of-contents outline (pp. xvii–xix of the front matter), with each chapter's original Kannada title given alongside its English translation.)*

## Chapter 1. Invocatory Verses
*Original title: "Maṅgalācaraṇa"*
**Printed pages 345–349 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter as of the last review.)*

### Title Page

**श्रीगणाधिपतये नमः।**
*śrī gaṇādhipataye namaḥ*
"Salutations to Sri Ganapati (Lord of the Ganas)."

**सायणाचार्यकृता ऋग्वेदभाष्यभूमिका**
*(Composed by Sayanacharya: The Introduction (Bhumika) to the Rigveda-Bhashya)*

**Kannada Translation of Sayanacharya's Rigveda-Bhashya-Bhumika**

### Opening

Shri Sayanacharya was a great scholar of the Vijayanagara royal court — highly accomplished in the Vedas, Vedangas, statecraft (rajaniti), the doctrines of Purva-Mimamsa, logic (tarka-shastra), grammar, and other disciplines, and the elder-brother-scholar in tradition with Madhavacharya, renowned as a foremost authority across all the shastras, and the author of many independent works.

Recognizing his scholarly mastery, the king asked him to compose a Rigveda commentary for the benefit of the world (lokopakara). Sayana responded: "O great king, you yourself are equal to this task." But the king, though himself accomplished across the shastras, understood the sheer difficulty of Vedic exegesis and judged that undertaking it personally would take far too long — so he turned to Sayanacharya and requested that he take up the work instead.

Since the Yajurveda held particular usefulness for yajna-related matters, Sayana composed its commentary first, turning to the Rigveda only afterward. Following the ancient tradition of disciples, he opened his very first verse with an auspicious invocation (mangalacharana) honoring **Ganapati**:

> "āśīr-namaskriyā vā vastu-nirdeśo vā" — auspicious invocations take one of three forms: a blessing (āśīrvāda), a salutation (namaskāra), or a statement of the subject-matter (vastu-nirdeśa). Since the deity who removes obstacles (Vighneshvara/Ganapati) is especially favored at the start of any undertaking, Sayana composed his opening verse as a hymn of praise to this very deity, so that his own great endeavor might proceed free of obstacles.


### Page 346

**Verse 1:**

> वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस्तं नमामि गजाननम् ॥ १ ॥
>
> वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानाम् उपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस् तं नमामि गजाननम् ॥ १ ॥
> *vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānām upakrame | yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syus taṃ namāmi gajānanam || 1 ||*
>
> "I bow to that elephant-faced one, bowing to whom, at the start of all undertakings, even the wise ones beginning with Vagisha (the Lord of Speech) become accomplished in their purpose."

That is: Chaturmukha-Brahma and other deities, before beginning yajnas, going to war, or any other undertaking, first bow to elephant-faced Ganapati and thereby become successful in their tasks. Sayana bows to this same obstacle-removing Ganapati so that the Rigveda-commentary he is about to begin may reach completion without hindrance.

Ganapati is famously known in the Puranas as "Vighnaraja" (Lord of Obstacles) — granting his worshippers success without hindrance. The Shiva Purana recounts that at the burning of Tripura, when Shiva set out to destroy the three cities without first worshipping Ganapati, the cities could not even be seen; only after worshipping Ganapati did they become visible, and the destruction proceeded effortlessly. Vishnu, Brahma, Indra, and other deities likewise began their own undertakings only after worshipping Ganapati first — and if even the gods do so, mortals certainly must. It is customary to worship Ganapati first at the start of education, marriage and other auspicious rites, vows, and deity-worship generally. Sayanacharya follows this same learned tradition here.

**Verse 2:**

> यस्य निःश्वसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तमहं वन्दे विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरम् ॥ २ ॥
>
> यस्य निःश्वसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तम् अहं वन्दे विद्यातीर्थ-महेश्वरम् ॥ २ ॥
> *yasya niḥśvasitaṃ vedā yo vedebhyo'khilaṃ jagat | nirmame tam ahaṃ vande vidyātīrtha-maheśvaram || 2 ||*
>
> "I worship him — Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara — whose very breath the Vedas are, and who, from the Vedas, fashioned this entire universe."

Having bowed to Ganapati, Sayana next bows to the Blessed Lord Ishvara — identifying his own guru, Vidyatirtha, with Maheshvara himself.

## English Translation of Sayana's Preface to the Rigveda

*(The source document itself presents an existing English scholarly translation of this preface alongside the Sanskrit and Kannada — reproduced here in full as it appears, per the user's explicit request to retain both the Sanskrit and this English rendering together.)*

**1.** I bow down to the elephant-faced Ganapati, to whom (even all other) deities with the Lord of speech (Brihaspati or Brahma) at their head, bow down at the beginning of all their undertakings, and (thereby) become successful in their attempts.

**2.** I worship Him—Vidyatirtha, (my Guru) Who is (identical with) Maheswara, Whose breath the Vedas are, (and) Who from the Vedas created the whole world.


### Page 347

Whichever supreme deity is both the material and efficient cause of the Veda's own form, and whichever supreme soul created, from within the Veda itself, all sentient and insentient beings together with the entire universe — Sayanacharya bows to his own guru Vidyatirtha, regarding him as identical with that very deity, in bodily presence as much as in essence.

For a seeker of knowledge, Indian tradition holds the guru to be worthy of worship equal to the divine itself — "*guru reva maheśvaraḥ*" ("the guru alone is Maheshvara"), as scripture states — and a disciple should regard his guru as identical with Parameshvara (the Supreme Lord) on this basis. This is precisely why Sayanacharya, regarding his own guru Vidyatirtha as one with Ishvara, bows to him here.

The Vedas hold the Supreme to be non-dual — "*tat sat, tad vā dvaita*" (that which is Being, whether described as non-dual or dual) — as the Upanishads generally establish. Since the Vedas belong to Parameshvara alone, and since Parameshvara alone created the world and became all beings, and since this same Bhagavan is the ultimate source of all knowledge and every discipline — it follows that, in composing a Veda-commentary, the relationship between every seeker of knowledge and their guru (celebrated as the foremost authority) carries this same weight. With this understanding, Sayana performs his mangalacharana at the very opening of the text.

That he composed the Yajurveda commentary first, before undertaking the Rigveda's, has already been stated — but why explain the Yajurveda first, when the Rigveda is the first among the Vedas? This verse gives the answer.

In yajnas, the **Adhvaryu** priest's role is primary — "*adhvaryur vā ṛtijñaṃ prabhavo yajñe*" ("the Adhvaryu is indeed the foremost knower of the sacrificial order"), as the Yajurveda itself states. An Adhvaryu cannot perform his duties without thorough knowledge of the Yajurveda. Correspondingly, the **Hotr** priest must be deeply versed in the Rigveda. Yajnas involve four principal priests — Hotr, Adhvaryu, Udgatr, and Brahma — and though many assistant priests may participate in various rites, these four remain the principal officiants. The Hotr must have mastered Rigveda study along with its Shrauta (ritual-application) portion. Yajna-mantras fall into two categories: purohita-vakya and yajya; inviting the deities and directing the fire-offering is the Hotr's chief duty. The Adhvaryu, correspondingly, must thoroughly study the Yajurveda and diligently practice its Shrauta portion...

Since even this remains incomplete without the Rigveda, the **Brahma** priest must know all four Vedas and be broadly versed in every ritual matter — overseeing the correct, sequential offering of oblations throughout the yajna, a role that stands above all the other three priests.

II. 2, 34); considerations of propriety, therefore, demand that the Rigveda should have been commented upon first of all. The primacy of the Rigveda is quite apparent from the Purushasukta:—
>
> "From that 'yajna' invoked by all, the Riks (hymns) and Samans (chants) were born; the metres were born from it; the Yajus (sacrificial formula in prose) was born from it." (R. V. X. 90. 9).


### Page 352

...pervasive and omnipotent — this same **यज्ञ-पुरुष** (*yajña-puruṣa*, "the Yajna as Person," i.e. the great **पुरुष** *puruṣa* with a thousand heads described at Rigveda 10.90.1), called **परमेश्वर** (*parameśvara*, "the Supreme Lord"), is worshipped throughout every yajna, by everyone. Here "यज्ञ" (*yajña*) carries the sense of "**यजनीय**" (*yajanīya*) — "that to which sacrifice is offered," i.e., an object of worship — and "**सर्वहुतः**" (*sarvahutaḥ*) means "invoked/offered to by all" — that is, worthy of worship, invoked universally. This describes Parameshvara alone.

Here, an objection may be raised: is it a fixed rule that in Vedic mantras, any reference must refer to Parameshvara alone? Why, then, do some mantras invoke Agni, Indra, or other deities specifically, if the same underlying being is meant? The answer: though these deities are invoked separately in different mantras, since Parameshvara alone is omniscient, omnipotent, and all-pervading, he alone underlies and takes on all these various divine forms — so when a devotee invokes Agni, it is Parameshvara who is truly being invoked. The word "sarvahutaḥ," applied to Parameshvara, is thus without contradiction.

Further mantras confirm this same point — when people invoke Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, or Garutman under these differing names, wise scholars recognize that one and the same deity is being addressed throughout, whatever name is used. Or, alternatively: whichever name a deity is invoked under, the worshipper simply regards that name as referring to that same deity.

The followers of the Vajasaneyi (Shukla Yajurveda) tradition state something similar: though various deities appear worshipped under different names here and there, no genuinely separate deity is being worshipped — it is that same great deity existing in the forms of Indra and the others. Whichever deity is invoked or worshipped, Parameshvara alone is ultimately being addressed.

### Page 354

...this same pattern holds in the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda alike. Each Veda has its own Brahmana portion explaining the manner of performing yajna-rites — and in supporting their own statements, these Brahmanas cite "thus it is said in the Rigveda," using the Rigveda itself as authority. This confirms that the other Vedas and their Brahmanas rely on the Rigveda. Even in the Yajurveda's own mantra-section, the mantras the Adhvaryu priest must actually recite are often not found in his own Veda at all — the Rigveda's own Riks must be recited instead. The same holds for many Samaveda mantras that are themselves drawn from the Rigveda, and a large portion of the Atharvaveda likewise consists of Rigveda verses. Since every Veda relies upon the Rigveda in this way, and all revere it accordingly, the Rigveda's foremost, most venerable position is confirmed.

**The followers of the Chandogya tradition** recite Narada's own words to this effect:

> ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदमाथर्वणं चतुर्थमिति । (Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.2)
>
> ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदम् आथर्वणं चतुर्थम् इति ।
> *ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo'dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam ātharvaṇaṃ caturtham iti |*
>
> "O revered one, I have studied the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the fourth — the Atharvana."

**The followers of the Mundaka Upanishad** likewise state:

> ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेद इति । (Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.5)
>
> ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेद इति ।
> *ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo'tharvaveda iti |*
>
> "Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda."

Other Upanishadic traditions similarly prescribe the order of study for the whole body of mantras:

> ऋक्सामाथर्वणाश्चैव स्कन्धो वेदाः सांगाः सशाखाश्च स्वारक साधा भवन्तीति । (Taittiriya Aranyaka 1.2[?])
>
> *(Naming the Rik, Sama, and Atharvan branches together with the Vedangas and shakhas as together constituting the full body of Vedic learning; precise construction difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

## Chapter 3. Uttara-pakṣa's Defense — It Was Proper, for the Convenience of Yajna-Performance, to Compose the Yajurveda Commentary First
*Original title: "Yajñānuṣṭhānasaukaryakkāgi Yajurvēdakke modalu bhāṣyavannu racisidudu yuktavendu uttarapakṣasamarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 355–361 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter as of the last review.)*

### Page 355

The Chandogas first cite Narada's own words to Sanatkumara: "O revered one, I have studied the Rigveda, and also the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the Atharvaveda" — even here, listing all four Vedas studied, the Rigveda is named first. The Mundaka Upanishad likewise states: "The Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda — these are the four Vedas." The Tapaniya Upanishad, describing the "feet" of the sovereign mantra and prescribing the order of study, states: "The Riks, the Yajus, the Sama, and the Atharvana — the Vedas are these four; together with their limbs (the Vedangas) and their branches (shakhas), they form the four feet." Many more such examples could be cited. Wherever one looks, the Rigveda holds primacy — so it would only have been proper for this preeminent text to be commented upon first.

> एवं सर्वत्रोदाहरणीयम् । तस्मादृग्वेदस्य भूरिष्ठत्वादादौ व्याख्यानमुचितमिति । तान् प्रत्येतदुच्यते—
>
> *evaṃ sarvatrodāharaṇīyam | tasmād ṛgvedasya bhūriṣṭhatvād ādau vyākhyānam ucitam iti | tān pratyetad ucyate—*
>
> "Such examples can be cited everywhere. Therefore, given the Rigveda's preeminence, its commentary ought to have been undertaken first. To this, the following reply is given—"

### The Resolution (Siddhanta) Begins

> अस्त्येवं सर्ववेदाध्ययनकत्वात् आचारण ब्रह्मयज्ञ जपसाधा-ऋग्वेदस्यैव प्राथम्यम् । अर्थज्ञानस्य तु यज्ञानुष्ठानार्थत्वात् तु यजुर्वेदस्यैव प्रधानत्वात् व्याख्यानप्रयोगेऽदौ युक्तम् । तस्मात्प्राधान्यं काचिद् गेवाच—
>
> *asty evaṃ sarva-vedādhyayanakatvāt ācāraṇa brahmayajña japasādhā-ṛgvedasyaiva prāthamyam | arthajñānasya tu yajñānuṣṭhānārthatvāt tu yajurvedasyaiva pradhānatvāt vyākhyāna-prayoge'dau yuktam | tasmāt prādhānyaṃ kācid gevāca—*
>
> "It is indeed true that, so far as the practice of studying all the Vedas, the daily Brahma-yajna, muttering of mantras, and similar customary observances are concerned, the Rigveda holds primacy. But since understanding meaning (artha-jñāna) exists specifically for the purpose of performing yajnas — and since, for that purpose, the Yajurveda holds the primary place — it was proper for its commentary to be undertaken first. Therefore, whatever primacy [the Rigveda holds elsewhere]..."

...regarding the Yajurveda's meaning being essential for yajna-performance, the Yajurveda's commentary needed to be composed first. This same point, Sayana notes, is suitably supported by a verse of the Rigveda itself:

> ऋचां त्वः पोषमास्ते पुपुष्वान् गायत्रं त्वो गायति शक्वरीषु । ब्रह्मा त्वो वदति जातविद्यां यज्ञस्य मात्रां विमिमीत उ त्वः ॥ (RV 10.71.11)
>
> ऋचां त्वः पोषम् आस्ते पुपुष्वान् गायत्रं त्वो गायति शक्वरीषु । ब्रह्मा त्वो वदति जातविद्यां यज्ञस्य मात्रां विमिमीत उ त्वः ॥
> *ṛcāṃ tvaḥ poṣam āste pupuṣvān gāyatraṃ tvo gāyati śakvarīṣu | brahmā tvo vadati jātavidyāṃ yajñasya mātrāṃ vimimīta u tvaḥ ||*
>
> "One, having nourished it, tends the growth of the Riks; another sings the Gayatra chant among the Shakvari meters; the Brahmin speaks forth innate knowledge; and another measures out the proper form of the yajna."

Yaska, author of the Nirukta, briefly explains this verse's purport (Nirukta 1.8): it "determines the sphere of application of priestly duties" — that is, it explains which specific tasks each of the priests must perform, distinguishing their respective roles.

**Nirukta** is one of the six Vedangas (alongside Shiksha, Vyakarana, Chandas, Nirukta, Jyotisha, and Kalpa), in which Yaska clarifies the meaning of certain difficult Riks — the very first text composed in the form of a Rigveda commentary. Though the Aitareya Brahmana and similar texts also explain portions of the Veda, since the Brahmanas are themselves considered part of the Veda, no one calls them commentaries or bhashyas upon it. Yaska therefore stands as the first to attempt explaining the Veda's meaning as such. But since the Nirukta explains only select Riks here and there, and even there conveys only the hidden sense rather than the full meaning, understanding the Veda's meaning through the Nirukta's help alone remains impossible.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source (continuing the footnote from the previous page):**

> ...concerned. But [it should be carefully noted that] the knowledge of the meaning [of the Vedas] is insisted upon] for the performance of the sacrifices, and in that respect Yajurveda undisputedly enjoys the position of supreme importance; and so it stands to reason that Yajurveda should be commented upon first. And this supremacy [of the Yajurveda] is plainly stated in a verse of the Rigveda itself (Rig. 10-71-11).
>
> Yaska, the author of the Nirukta, gives in brief the purport of this Rik verse as follows (Ni. I. 8):—"(It) determines (the sphere of) the application of the duties of priests". Again, the same author explains the first quarter—One (priest) i.e. Hotr nourishes the Riks; Rik is equivalent to *arcani* (panegyric). The meaning of this is as follows:—The word 'tva' is the synonym of 'eka' (one) and qualifies 'Hotr'. One priest called Hotr, at the time of the sacrifice, makes a culture of the Rik verses found in his own Veda. In other words, he makes a collection of the verses read in various places, determines that this much constitutes this Sastra;—this is what is called here culture or nourishment (pusti). The word *archani* is given as the meaning of the word Rik; The etymology of the word Rik implies that by it a particular deity, or a particular rite or a particular instrument of a rite—is eulogised.

> "This indeed is the yajna, having mind and speech as its twofold path; the Brahma corrects one of these [the mind-path] with his mind, while the Hotr, Adhvaryu, and Udgatr correct the other [the speech-path] with speech."

Even if an error occurs during the yajna, the whole rite need not be considered incomplete — it can be properly rectified through the mind, while the mantras of the three Vedas are recited through speech. The Hotr and his two counterparts (Adhvaryu, Udgatr) together correct the yajna's speech-path; but the Brahma alone corrects its mind-path, in its entirety, by himself. This is his special capability.

**Continuing the explanation of the third quarter:** while the yajna proceeds, the priest called Brahma instructs the other priests on precisely how each rite should be performed, being himself the most knowledgeable of all. Many subsidiary rites occur as part of a yajna's proper conduct, and the important ones require the Brahma priest's explicit sanction. For example, at the water-fetching rite, the Adhvaryu requests permission: "O Brahman, shall I fetch the water into this vessel?" — to which the Brahma replies, "Om, fetch it" — granting permission. Even pouring water from one vessel into another requires the Brahma's approval, since "apaḥ praṇayana" (the water-fetching rite) is itself an important ritual act — filling the "praṇīta" or "pūrṇa" vessel with water as a purificatory step. In all such ritual components, work may proceed only with the Brahma's sanction, since he alone is thoroughly versed in the ritual procedures laid out across all the Vedas, knowing precisely what should be done, and when — and he accordingly watches for errors throughout the yajna. Should an error occur through inattention, he identifies the necessary remedy and sets it right. The followers of the Samaveda (Chandogas) describe the Brahma's capability in just this way — describing the yajna as having both a mind-form and...

>
> "Thus it being established that the yajna's own body is formed specifically within the Yajurveda, connected to the Adhvaryu — the remaining elements, in the form of hymn (stotra) and recitation (shastra), are supplied by the other Vedas..."

This is the pivotal conclusion of the entire discussion: since the yajna's essential body/structure resides in the Yajurveda, and the Rigveda and Samaveda merely furnish its accompanying hymn and recitation elements, the Yajurveda holds the dominant, foundational role — justifying why it was explained first. And since the Samaveda's own verses are entirely drawn from the Rigveda, between these latter two, the Rigveda rightly comes next — which is precisely the task Sayana now undertakes.

## Chapter 4. Purva-pakṣa — Since the Veda Has No Defining Marks or Proofs, No Such Text as "the Veda" Exists
*Original title: "Vēdakke lakṣaṇapramāṇādigaḷu illaddarinda vēdavemba granthavē illavendu pūrvapakṣavu"*
**Printed pages 362–367 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter — pp.364 and 366 repaired during the Phase B review: Devanagari added for the Nyaya definitional-flaw terms (ativyāpti/avyāpti/asambhava) on p.364, and the Chandogya Upanishad citation restored in full on p.366.)*

### Page 362

> द्वैयेन पूर्ग्येके इत्येव जीव्यस्य यजुर्वेदस्य प्रभुगुण व्याख्यानं युक्तम् । तत ऊध्वं साम्नामृगात्मकत्वादुभयोर्मध्ये प्रभुमके ऋग्व्याख्यानं युक्तमिति सिद्धे इदानीं व्याख्यायते ॥
>
> *(Concluding: since the yajna's essential body resides in the Yajurveda, its commentary rightly came first; and since the Samaveda is itself constituted of Riks, between the Rigveda and Samaveda, the Rigveda rightly comes next — this now being settled, the Rigveda-commentary is undertaken.)*

Keeping this reasoning in mind, Yaska Maharshi clarifies the etymology showing that the Yajurveda — the Adhvaryu's own Veda — holds the power to establish the yajna's essential form: "manana" (reflection) yields "mantra"; "chādana" (covering/binding together) yields "chandas"; "praising" yields "stoma." The yajna's principal form must therefore arise from the Yajurveda, with the Rik and Sama Vedas serving a supporting, auxiliary role. This establishes that the Yajurveda holds primacy for yajna-performance — justifying its commentary being composed first. And since every Samaveda mantra is itself found within the Rigveda, between these remaining two, the Rigveda rightly comes next. **Accordingly, the Rigveda-commentary now begins.**

## The Rigveda-Bhashya Proper Begins: A Logical Challenge to the Veda's Very Existence

> लक्षणप्रमाणाभ्यां वेदस्यावधारण इति पूर्वे पक्षे—
>
> *lakṣaṇa-pramāṇābhyāṃ vedasyāvadhāraṇa iti pūrve pakṣe—*
>
> "In the objection concerning the determination of the Veda through definition and proof—"

> ननु वेद एव तावन्नास्ति । कुतस्तदवान्तरभेद ऋग्वेदः ? तथा हि । कोऽयं वेदो नाम ? न हि तत्र लक्षणं प्रमाणं वास्ति । न च तदुभयमृते किंचित्सिध्यति । लक्षणप्रमाणाभ्यां हि वस्तुसिद्धिरिति न्यायविदां मतम् ॥
>
> ननु वेद एव तावन् नास्ति । कुतस् तद्-अवान्तर-भेद ऋग्वेदः । तथा हि । कोऽयं वेदो नाम । न हि तत्र लक्षणं प्रमाणं वास्ति । न च तद्-उभयम् ऋते किंचित् सिध्यति । लक्षण-प्रमाणाभ्यां हि वस्तु-सिद्धिर् इति न्याय-विदां मतम् ॥
> *nanu veda eva tāvan nāsti | kutas tad-avāntara-bheda ṛgvedaḥ | tathā hi | ko'yaṃ vedo nāma | na hi tatra lakṣaṇaṃ pramāṇaṃ vāsti | na ca tad-ubhayam ṛte kiṃcit sidhyati | lakṣaṇa-pramāṇābhyāṃ hi vastu-siddhir iti nyāya-vidāṃ matam ||*
>
> "Objection: The Veda itself does not exist at all — how then can there be a subdivision of it called the Rigveda? Consider: what is this thing called 'Veda'? Neither a definition (lakṣaṇa) nor a proof (pramāṇa) of it exists. And without both of these, nothing whatsoever can be established — for it is the settled view of logicians (Naiyayikas) that the establishment of any entity requires both definition and proof."

...a distinguishing mark by which something can be pointed out. "Pramana" (proof) means stating separately, "this object bears such-and-such a mark" — the means by which an object's true nature is determined through its own characteristic marks. Logicians hold that a thing's real nature becomes known only through such proofs. Since the Veda has neither a definition nor a proof, how can the entity called "Veda" be established to exist at all?
