### Page 364

Regarding the three proofs of knowledge — perception (**प्रत्यक्ष** *pratyakṣa*), inference (**अनुमान** *anumāna*), and revealed word (**आगम** *āgama*) — even if the last of these, "āgama," is proposed as the Veda's defining mark, this fails: since Manu's and other Smritis also possess this same "āgama" quality, the flaw of over-extension (**अतिव्याप्ति** *ativyāpti*) results, since they too would have to count as "Veda." A sound definition (**लक्षण** *lakṣaṇa*) must avoid three classical flaws:

- **अतिव्याप्ति** (*ativyāpti*, over-extension): the stated mark applies to other things too (e.g., defining milk as "that which is white" also catches lime).
- **अव्याप्ति** (*avyāpti*, under-extension): the stated mark fails to cover part of the intended thing (e.g., defining horses by "red color" excludes horses of other colors).
- **असंभव** (*asambhava*, impossibility): stating a quality the thing doesn't actually possess at all.

Whatever definition of "Veda" one proposes free of these three flaws will, since Manu's and similar Smritis share the same "āgama" quality, still fall into ativyāpti. The characteristic of being "āgama" therefore cannot serve as the Veda's true defining mark.

**Fourth attempted definition, and its refutation** (regarding embodiment):

If you say the "body" in question is specifically one produced by the karmic results of a past life — and that the Veda's own author has no such body, which is what you really mean by "non-human origin" — this too fails. For the Vedas are described as produced through such beings as Agni, Vayu, and Aditya: "The Rigveda was born from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya" — confirming that Parameshvara composed the Vedas at the instigation of Agni and the others.

**Fifth attempted definition, and its refutation** (mantra + brahmana):

You might next suggest that "Veda" simply names the collected body of mantras and brahmanas. This too fails — since no one has yet clearly established what precisely constitutes a "mantra" or a "brahmana." It is therefore clear that no adequate definition of the term "Veda" exists.

If, finally, you propose that "apauruṣeyatva" (non-human origin) itself simply *is* the Veda's defining mark — since the Veda is not made by any finite person — this too fails, for the Veda is itself [made by] Parameshvara...

---

### Page 365

...since it is made by someone, the quality of "personal origin" (pauruṣeyatva) necessarily follows — and countless texts are made by persons, so why should the Veda deserve any special regard on that basis? If the Veda is instead called apauruṣeya because no embodied living being made it — that too fails, since the Veda itself states "sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ" (the thousand-headed Purusha), affirming Ishvara's own possession of a body. And if apauruṣeya means merely "not made by one embodied through karmic result," this too fails: the Veda states it was born from special beings — Agni, Vayu, Aditya — the Rigveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya — meaning Parameshvara, who impels Agni and the others, is himself the true author of the Shruti. And if "Veda" simply names the collected group of mantras and brahmanas, that too fails, since no one has ever clearly determined what precisely qualifies as a "mantra" or a "brahmana." **The Veda, in short, has no valid defining characteristic whatsoever.**

If we cite the Yajnavalkya-Smriti's statement, "the Veda alone is the highest means of ultimate good for the twice-born," as proof that the Vedas exist — that too fails. All Smritis are rooted in Shruti — that is, they follow Shruti itself — so the very same fallacy of self-dependence arises here too. The Vedas' existence cannot be established through Smriti statements either.

In everyday affairs, no one can deny things visible to the eye — so shouldn't everyone accept perceptual proof? Should we accept the Veda's existence simply because the subject is widely renowned, and everyone visibly engages with Vedic matters? No — because many things considered "perceptually evident" in ordinary life turn out to rest on mere illusion, just as it is commonly (but falsely) held that the sky is blue-colored. Is this anything but illusion? Therefore, there is no valid basis for accepting that an entity called "Veda," lacking both definition and proof, exists. **This concludes the objection (purva-paksha).**

### A Methodological Note: Purva-Paksha and Siddhanta

When examining any subject, pointing out its flaws and objections through careful, reasoned argument to show "this is not correct" is called the **purva-paksha** (prior view, or objection). Correspondingly, resolving those very flaws and objections one by one, with sound reasoning, and firmly establishing the subject's true nature, is called the **siddhanta** (established conclusion). To properly grasp the subjects expounded in the shastras, tradition holds that the purva-paksha should be presented first, with the siddhanta established afterward. This purva-...

> It is then clear that since the Veda is not capable of definition or proof, it cannot be admitted that there is such a thing. This is the prima facie case.

...-paksha, siddhanta, and related components together form what is called an "adhikarana." Its definition:

> विषयोऽविषयश्चेति पूर्वसंपक्षिस्फोत्तरं । निर्णयश्चेति संबद्धं शास्त्रेऽधिकरणं मतम् ॥
>
> "Subject-matter and doubt, together with the objection and its answer, and the determination — this combination is considered an 'adhikarana' in the shastras."

That is: an adhikarana comprises five distinct parts — the subject-matter (vishaya), the doubt (samshaya), the objection (purva-paksha), its answer, and the final determination (siddhanta). Each is examined in turn before the siddhanta is finally established as correct.

We now state the resolution (samādhāna) to the objection. Calling the body of words comprising mantras and brahmanas "the Veda" is, in fact, a faultless definition. As for the objection that "mantra" and "brahmana" themselves remain undefined — the answer is that whatever the shastra-tradition designates as "mantra" is indeed mantra, and the remainder is brahmana. This is exactly why the great sage **Apastamba**, in his *Yajna-paribhasha-sutra*, states: "mantra-brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam" — the name "Veda" applies to both mantras and brahmanas together.

## Chapter 5. Siddhanta — the Veda Does Have Defining Marks and Proofs; and Why a Commentary Is Needed at All
*Original title: "Vēdakke lakṣaṇapramāṇādigaḷu iveyendu siddhāntasamarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 368–373 of the source.**

> **⚠ Known issues in this subchapter (pending verification against source images):**
> - p.368 — mostly repaired during Phase B (the "granted the Veda exists, but is it authoritative?" citation restored); one compound near the end of that citation has an uncertain reading, flagged inline.

### Page 368

This is accepted. This point will be settled further ahead. Similarly, on the question of "apauruṣeyatva," we shall clarify our stated definition later. The three types of proof — shruti (revealed word), smriti (tradition), and loka-vyavahara (common human practice) — must all be accepted together as establishing the Veda's existence.

Consider: jars and similar objects have no self-illuminating power — they depend on other light sources and cannot shine on their own. But does this mean *everything* luminous must depend on another's help to shine? The sun, moon, and stars shine of their own accord, without needing any external light. A pot's lack of self-illumination doesn't contradict the sun's genuine self-luminosity. Likewise: just because an ordinary human, however skilled, cannot climb onto his own shoulder, does that mean the Veda — possessing unlimited power — cannot illuminate itself the same way? No. **The Veda's power is unobstructed**, and it can therefore reveal and prove itself, just as it reveals everything else. The fallacy of self-dependence, then, simply does not arise for a text of such undiminished power. As those versed in ancient tradition say of the Veda's own unblunted power:

> "The Veda can make clear what has been, what is, and what is to be — what is near, and what is far off."

This being so, proof drawn from Smriti (itself rooted in the Veda), as well as proof drawn from common notoriety (rooted in both Shruti and Smriti), must also be accepted. **It therefore stands firmly established that the Veda, duly proven by both definition and proof, cannot be overturned by any skeptic.**

### A New Objection: Even If the Veda Exists, Is It Authoritative?

> *nanv astu nāma vedākhyaḥ kaścit padārthaḥ | tathāpi nāsau vyākhyānam arhati | apramāṇatvenānupayuktatvāt | na hi vedaḥ pramāṇam | pramāṇa-lakṣaṇasya tatra duḥsampādatvāt | tathā hi | samyak...* *(the final compound's exact reading is uncertain at this resolution; the sense is confirmed by the embedded English translation below)*

"Very well — we grant that the thing called 'Veda' exists. Still, it isn't worth commenting on, since it carries no authority (pramāṇya), and being without authority, it is of no real use. The Veda is of no authority. Why? Because you cannot show that the defining mark of valid proof (pramāṇa) resides in it." Some define "pramāṇa" as the instrument of right knowledge; others say it is the means of acquiring [knowledge]...

> *anubhava-sādhanaṃ pramāṇam iti kecil lakṣaṇam āhuḥ | apare tṛ-ṣaṣṭy-adhigatārtha-gantṛ pramāṇam ity ācakṣate | na caitad ubhayaṃ vede saṃbhavati | mantra-brāhmaṇātmako hi vedaḥ | tatra mantrāḥ kecid abodhakāḥ | ... na hy etair mantraiḥ kiṃcij jñeyārtho'vagacchate | viśeṣataḥ saṃbhava eva yadā nāsti tadā tasya jñāna-kāraṇa-sādhanatvaṃ ca dūrāsthitam ||*
>
> "Some define 'pramana' (valid proof) as 'the means of [right] experience.' Others say it is 'that which leads to knowledge of an object not previously known.' Neither definition applies to the Veda. For the Veda consists of mantras and Brahmanas — and among the mantras, some convey no discernible meaning at all: 'amyak sa ta indra ṛṣṭir' is one such mantra; 'yad rismin dhāyi tam apaśyayā vidad ṛkṣaḥ' is another; 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītu' another; and 'apāntamanyus tripala-prabharmiḥ' and similar besides may be cited. These mantras yield no discernible meaning whatsoever. And when there is no possibility of meaning at all, being a means or cause of knowledge is all the more remote."

We grant, then, that an entity called "Veda" exists — but what need is there to compose commentary on it? Since the Veda carries no valid authority (pramana) and yields no genuine use, commenting on it serves no purpose. The Veda cannot count as "pramana," since it lacks the defining marks proposed for valid proof: some define pramana as "the means productive of correct experience"; others define it as "that which reveals an object not previously known." Neither definition applies to the Veda. As already stated, the Veda consists of two parts — mantra and Brahmana. Taking the mantra portion first: does either definition of pramana apply there? It does not — and several mantras are cited here as examples: "amyak sa ta indra ṛṣṭi," "yad rismin dhāyi tam apaśyayā vidat," "sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītu," and "apāntamanyus tripala-prabharmā." These mantras convey no meaning at all. And if they convey no meaning whatsoever, then their serving as a means to correct knowledge becomes, quite obviously, altogether impossible.

---

And others such, for example, as "apantamanyus tripalaprabharma," could be cited. These mantras yield no sense at all. > *adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīd iti (RV 10.129.5) mantrasya bodhakatve'pi sthāṇur vā puruṣo vety ādi-vākyavat saṃdigdhārtha-bodhakatvān na prāmāṇyam ||*
>
> "The mantra 'adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt' (was it below, or was it above?) (RV 10.129.5), though it conveys some meaning, conveys only a doubtful, ambiguous sense — like the statement 'is it a post, or is it a man?' — and therefore lacks authority."

Take the mantra "adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt." Even though its words convey a meaning of sorts, it leaves genuine room for doubt — much like asking whether something is a stump or a man. Since it fails to convey a settled, coherent meaning, how could such a mantra carry any authority?

> ओषधे त्रायस्वैनमिति (Taittiriya Samhita 1.2.1.1) मन्त्रे दर्भविषयः । (Ashvalayana Grihyasutra 1.12.4) स्वधिते मैनं हिंसीरिति क्षुरविषयः । (Taittiriya Samhita 1.3.1.3) श्रुणोत ग्रावाण इति पाषाणविषयः । एतेष्वचेतनानां दर्भक्षुरपाषाणानां चेतनवत्संबोधनं श्रूयते । द्वौ चन्द्रौ चन्द्रमसाविति वाक्यवद्विसंवादिबोधकत्वात्प्रामाण्यम् ॥
>
> ओषधे त्रायस्वैनम् इति मन्त्रे दर्भ-विषयः । स्वधिते मैनं हिंसीर् इति क्षुर-विषयः । शृणोत ग्रावाण इति पाषाण-विषयः । एतेष्व् अचेतनानां दर्भ-क्षुर-पाषाणानां चेतनवत् सम्बोधनं श्रूयते । द्वौ चन्द्रौ चन्द्रमसाव् इति वाक्यवद् विसंवादि-बोधकत्वात् प्रामाण्यम् ॥
> *oṣadhe trāyasvainam iti mantre darbha-viṣayaḥ | svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīr iti kṣura-viṣayaḥ | śṛṇota grāvāṇa iti pāṣāṇa-viṣayaḥ | eteṣv acetanānāṃ darbha-kṣura-pāṣāṇānāṃ cetanavat sambodhanaṃ śrūyate | dvau candrau candramasāv iti vākyavad visaṃvādi-bodhakatvāt prāmāṇyam ||*
>
> "In the mantra 'oṣadhe trāyasvainam' ('O herb, protect him'), the subject is sacred grass (darbha). 'Svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīḥ' ('O razor, do not harm him') concerns a razor. 'Śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ' ('Hear, O stones') concerns stones. In these, inanimate things — grass, razor, and stones — are addressed as though sentient beings. Such statements, conveying something self-contradictory (like saying 'there are two moons'), cannot carry authority."

That is: the mantras "O herb, protect him" address grass (darbha), "O razor, do not harm him" address a razor, and "Hear, O stones" address stones — in each case treating lifeless objects as if they were conscious beings capable of understanding and acting on a command. This, the objection argues, is as absurd as claiming there are two moons — and such statements therefore cannot possibly be authoritative.

One mantra states that Parameshvara, as Rudra, exists alone with no equal second; another states there are thousands upon thousands of Rudras in the world. These two statements plainly contradict each other — like a man declaring, "as long as I live, I remain silent" — the very act of speaking the claim contradicts it. How can the claim of silence hold, once spoken aloud? A mantra conveying mutually contradictory meanings in this way cannot carry authority.

That is: these mantras merely describe customs already familiar from ordinary life — pouring water while shaving, placing a garland at a wedding — conveying nothing genuinely new. Since valid proof must reveal something not already known, even this portion of the Veda fails to qualify as pramana.

**This is Sayana's own resolution** to the preceding objection: while the *outward act* described (pouring water, placing a garland) may be common knowledge, the specific *divine favor* connected to performing it in the prescribed ritual manner is not — and it is precisely this previously-unknown element that the mantra reveals, satisfying the very definition of valid proof.

### Page 375

A "sutra" is a sentence composed with the fewest possible words to convey many subjects concisely, without any loss of meaning. In ancient times, many rishis composed their treatises in this style — the Yoga, Vyakarana, and other philosophical schools (darshanas) are similarly composed, and, being terse, require commentary to unpack. We now turn to explaining several sutras from Jaimini's own Purva-Mimamsa-sutras concerning the meaning of mantras, beginning with the objection (purva-paksha) as Jaimini himself states it.

> चेदर्थशास्त्रत (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.31) स विनाभिधेयो यस्य शास्त्रे ब्राह्मणवाक्ये तदर्थशास्त्रम् । तस्माच्चाविशक्तार्थो मन्त्र इत्यर्थः । इत्येवं हि । उक्तं हि (Taittiriya Samhita 1.1.1; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.1.1.4) मन्त्रेण प्रथमप्रभनमुभयीयते । पुरोडाशं प्रथयिष्येति (Taittiriya Samhita 1.1.1; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.2.1.1) ब्राह्मणेऽपि तदेवाभिप्रेत्य प्रस्तुतचोदनाय प्रवृत्तं ब्राह्मणवाक्यम् प्रवृत्तम् । तथा सति मन्त्रेणाप्ययमेवार्थो बोधाय प्रवृत्तः ।
>

> "The mantras convey no [independent] meaning, since there exists an 'artha-shastra' — a separate text explaining their meaning — namely, the Brahmana [portion]. For instance: it is said that the first application is conveyed through the mantra, and the statement 'I shall set forth the puroḍāśa cake' occurring in a Brahmana passage was made with this same intent, using the Brahmana's own sentence to direct the ongoing rite — showing that the mantra was employed to convey this very same meaning [already given by the Brahmana]."

That is: from the sutra "ced artha-shastrata" through to the sutra on "vidhi-shabda" (injunction-words), a single adhikarana (topic-section) runs, with each sutra explained in turn. The opening sutra's meaning: mantras have no independent meaning, because a separate "artha-shastra" (meaning-explaining text) — namely, the Brahmana — already exists to explain them. If a mantra genuinely had its own meaning, people would grasp it directly, with no need for an accompanying Brahmana passage. Since a Brahmana explanation *is* needed, this shows the mantra itself conveys no independent meaning — illustrated by the Brahmana statement "I shall set forth the puroḍāśa cake," used precisely to supply the meaning the mantra alone fails to convey.

### Page 376

For instance, the mantra "uru prathasva" refers to spreading out the purodāśa cake — and this same act is described in the Brahmana passage "purodāśaṃ prathayati" ("the Adhvaryu spreads the purodāśa"). Since the Brahmana merely restates what the mantra already conveys, what genuine use does such a Brahmana serve? If the mantra's meaning is already clear on its own, the Brahmana statement becomes pointless. But if instead the mantra's own meaning is what remains unclear, and the Brahmana serves to clarify its **viniyoga** — the procedure and context in which the mantra should be applied — then the Brahmana genuinely earns its purpose. On this view, if mere recitation of the mantra during the yajna is held to be its primary function, we must then accept that recitation serves some **adṛṣṭa** (unseen, imperceptible) purpose.

On this, the upholder of the doctrine to be controverted states another argument:

> ननूच्चारणार्थत्वे सत्यनिष्टं प्रयोजनं परिकल्प्येत । अर्थाभिधायकत्वे तु दृष्टं लभ्यते । तस्माद् व्याख्यानस्यानुवादकत्वम् अभ्युपेत्य मन्त्रा अभिधानार्थत्वेनैवेत्य् आशङ्क्य उत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *nanūccāraṇārthatve saty aniṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ parikalpyeta | arthābhidhāyakatve tu dṛṣṭaṃ labhyate | tasmād vyākhyānasyānuvādakatvam abhyupetya mantrā abhidhānārthatvenaivety āśaṅkya uttaraṃ sūtrayati ||* *(the exact word-division here is uncertain at this resolution; the sense — that if mantras existed merely to be recited, an unwelcome unseen purpose would have to be posited, whereas taking them as meaning-conveying yields a directly observable purpose instead — is confirmed by the Kannada explanation and the embedded English below)*

But suppose instead we say the very purpose of reciting mantras at the yajna is to convey their meaning — this would establish a **dṛṣṭa** (directly perceivable) purpose for the mantras. Between the two kinds of purpose, perceived and unperceived, an unperceived purpose should only be invoked when no perceived purpose can be found. If the Brahmana merely repeats the mantra's own meaning, then the meaning of mantras recited during the yajna...

### "Vakya-niyamat" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.32)

> अग्निर्मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (RV 8.44.16) इत्येवमेव वाक्यं पठितव्यमिति मन्त्रे नियम उपलभ्यते । अर्थप्रत्यायनं तु मूर्ध्वाग्निरित्येवं वृत्त्यपि स्वेष्टेव भवत्येव । तस्मान्नियतपाठक्रमफलायोच्चारणमेव मन्त्रप्रयोजनम् । ननु पाठक्रमनियममात्रात्स्याद्यष्ट्वार्थज्ञेऽपि मन्त्रपाठक्रमबोधार्थं चेवेत्याशंक्य तत्र दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> अग्निर् मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (र्व् ८.४४.१६) इत्य् एवम् एव वाक्यं पठितव्यम् इति मन्त्रे नियम उपलभ्यते । अर्थप्रत्यायनं तु मूर्ध्वाग्निर् इत्य् एवं वृत्त्यपि स्वेष्टैव भवत्य् एव । तस्मान् नियत-पाठ-क्रम-फलायोच्चारणम् एव मन्त्र-प्रयोजनम् । ...
> *agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut (RV 8.44.16) ity evam eva vākyaṃ paṭhitavyam iti mantre niyama upalabhyate | arthapratyāyanaṃ tu mūrdhvāgnir ity evaṃ vṛttyapi sveṣṭaiva bhavaty eva | tasmān niyata-pāṭha-krama-phalāyoccāraṇam eva mantra-prayojanam | ...*
>
> "It is a settled rule that the mantra 'agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut' must be recited in exactly this word-order, and no other. Yet conveying its meaning would work equally well in a rearranged form such as 'mūrdhāgnir...' Therefore, the mantra's purpose lies solely in its recitation according to a fixed word-order — for the sake of that order's own fruit, not for conveying meaning. One might object that even granting this fixed order, its purpose could still be to teach the proper recitation-sequence to someone who already knows the mantra's meaning. Anticipating this, Jaimini now formulates a further objection identifying an additional flaw in that view."

>

> *agnīd agnīn vihara (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.1.1) iti eṣa mantraḥ prayoga-kāle paṭhyate | tac cāgni-viharaṇādikam āgnīdhreṇādhyayana-kāla eva svakartavyatvena buddham | tasya ca buddhārthasya punar mantreṇa śāsanam anarthakam | na hi sopānatkaḥ pāde pratimuñcati | ...*
>
> "'Agnīd, distribute the fires' (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1.1) — this mantra is recited during the ritual performance. But distributing the fire and similar duties have already been learned by the Agnidh priest, as his own responsibility, during his period of study. Instructing him again, through a mantra, about something he already knows serves no purpose. Indeed, no one puts a second shoe on a foot that already wears one."

That is: the objection here is that mantras convey no meaning, since their sole function is recitation — not instruction, because reciting an already-known meaning serves no purpose. It was already established that mantras must follow a fixed recitation-order (per the previous sutra); now a further flaw is illustrated. "Agnīd agnīn vihara" is an injunctive mantra (vidhi-mantra), also called a "prescriptive" (preṣaṇa) mantra, recited during the yajna to direct the priest performing a task while he performs it. In every yajna, fire is kept burning in the Agnidh's own fire-pit before the ritual begins, and before the rites commence, this fire is carried from the Agnidh's altar to the other altars — this mantra commands precisely that act. But this mantra's meaning is already generally known to every priest participating in the yajna. What purpose is served by restating something everyone already knows?

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Since the command is already known.
>
> "Agnid agnin vihara" is a directory text, which is recited at the time of sacrifice. Now the duty of distributing the fire or the like has already been learnt as part of his work by the priest when engaged in study. It is a useless proceeding to instruct him by a mantra with regard to a thing which he has already learnt. If your foot has a shoe on you do not clap another on the top of it.


### Page 379

Generally, yajnas employ sixteen priests, organized into four groups (**गण** *gaṇa*):

- **होतृगण** (*hotṛgaṇa*, Hotr-group) — मैत्रावरुण/प्रशास्त्र (*maitrāvaruṇa*/*praśāstra*), अच्छावाक (*acchāvāka*), ग्रावस्तुत् (*grāvastut*) — priests connected to the Rigveda.
- **अध्वर्युगण** (*adhvaryugaṇa*, Adhvaryu-group) — प्रतिप्रस्थाता (*pratiprasthātā*), नेष्टा (*neṣṭā*), उन्नेता (*unnetā*) — priests connected to the Yajurveda.
- **उद्गातृगण** (*udgātṛgaṇa*, Udgatr-group) — प्रस्तोता (*prastotā*), प्रतिहर्ता (*pratihartā*), सुब्रह्मण्य (*subrahmaṇya*) — Samaveda priests.
- **ब्रह्मगण** (*brahmagaṇa*, Brahma-group) — ब्राह्मणाच्छंसी (*brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*), आग्नीध्र (*āgnīdhra*), पोता (*potā*) — priests who must be learned across all the Vedas.

The Shatapatha Brahmana (10.4.1.7) states that a yajna should not proceed with only sixteen priests — followers of the Kaushitaki shakha therefore appoint a seventeenth priest, the **सदस्य** (*sadasya*), who oversees the entire proceeding to ensure everything runs correctly (this appointment is not customary among Ashvalayana-shakha followers).

The mantra "Agnīd agnīn vihara," discussed above, is used specifically when carrying fire from the Agnidh's altar to the other altars. But the Agnidh and other priests such as the Adhvaryu already know their duties, and the meaning and purpose of the mantras, from their period of Vedic study. Restating what is already known is therefore pointless — as pointless, the objection says, as putting a second shoe over a foot already shod.

This might be answered as follows: what the mantras state may indeed already be known — but it could be forgotten through carelessness, and the mantras then serve a genuinely useful reminding function. Very well — let us grant that mantras can serve to remind priests of forgotten matters. But some mantras assert things that are outright impossible. This is addressed in the next sutra.

---

> It may, however, be said that the mantra may be a useful reminder for the avoidance of a careless forgetfulness. To guard against this he brings forward another objection in the next sutra.

> अदितिर्द्यौरदितिरन्तरिक्षम् (RV 1.89.10[?]) इति मन्त्र आम्नायते । यद् एव द्यौः तद् एवान्तरिक्षम् इति अपि-प्रतिṣiddham । एवं विषयं एव रुद्रः (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.6.1) सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्राः (Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.1.1) इत्याद्यपि अत्र किल कथम् ।
>
> अदितिर् द्यौर् अदितिर् अन्तरिक्षम् इति मन्त्र आम्नायते । यद् एव द्यौः तद् एवान्तरिक्षम् इत्य् अपि-प्रतिषिद्धम् । एवं विषयं एव रुद्रः ... सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्राः ... इत्य् आद्यपि अत्र किल कथम् ।
> *aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam iti mantra āmnāyate | yad eva dyauḥ tad evāntarikṣam ity api-pratiṣiddham | evaṃ viṣayaṃ eva rudraḥ ... sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrāḥ ... ity ādyapi atra kila katham |*
>
> "The mantra states: 'Aditi is Dyaus (Heaven), Aditi is Antariksha (the mid-region).' But to say that what is Dyaus is the very same as Antariksha is a self-contradiction. Similarly, one might cite here 'Rudra is one only' alongside 'the Rudras in their thousands.'"

The objection: since a single mantra identifies Aditi simultaneously with two distinct cosmic regions (Heaven and the mid-air), and separate mantras contradictorily describe Rudra as both singular and countless-in-thousands, such mutually inconsistent statements cannot be meaningful or authoritative.

>
> "A certain woman named Purnika is pounding grain with a pestle. Nearby, a young brahmin student, engaged in his daily lesson, happens to be reciting the pestle-mantra (avaghāta-mantra). Just as this mantra, though recited during study, conveys no meaning relevant to Purnika, so too it will convey no meaning even when recited during the actual ritual."

That is: just as a mantra's meaning goes unattended during rote study, so too its ritual application conveys no genuine meaning — since the objection holds that mantra-recitation and the accompanying ritual action (here, pounding grain) proceed with no real connection between them, mantras recited without understood meaning yield no fruit for the rite performed alongside them.

**Resolution to the Purnika objection:** there is no intention of conveying meaning when the student recites the mantra during rote study, and Purnika herself has no capacity to grasp it. But in yajna-rites proper, the Adhvaryu priest reciting mantras does know their meaning, does intend to convey it, and those present are capable of understanding it. The claim that mantras are meaningless does not hold.

> *keṣāñcin mantrāṇām artho vijñātuṃ na śakyate | tad yathā | amyaksa ta indra ṛṣṭir asme ity eko mantraḥ | sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū ity aparo mantraḥ | nanv etasmān mantrārtha-bodhāyaiva nigama-nirukta-vyākaraṇāni santīty āśaṅkya doṣāntaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "The meaning of some mantras cannot be ascertained at all. For example: 'amyaksa ta indra ṛṣṭir asme' is one such mantra; 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū' is another. One might object that Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana exist precisely to illuminate such mantras' meaning — anticipating this, a further objection is formulated."

That is: since the meaning of numerous mantras cannot be properly determined at all — these two being prime examples — it follows that mantras exist merely for recitation, not meaning.

**A resolution is then offered:** it is precisely to explain such difficult mantras' meaning that disciplines like Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana arose; with their help, understanding mantra-meaning is readily achievable — the claim of impossibility does not hold.

This being so, it follows that the mantra must postdate King Pramaganda's era. Thus, for these reasons — along with the shastra-based arguments already given — mantras serve no purpose in conveying meaning; their purpose lies instead in the unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa) obtained through mere recitation. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

That is: since mantras mention transient, historically-bound proper names — a country, a city, a king — accepting that mantras convey meaning would force one to admit the Vedas are non-eternal, contradicting the doctrine that they are beginningless (anādi) and non-human (apauruṣeya). Therefore, only the unseen fruit of recitation itself can be the mantras' purpose — no other fruit exists.

**This concludes the full nine-part objection (purva-paksha)**, spanning from "Buddha-shastrat" through this final sutra — nine separate arguments marshaled to establish that mantras serve recitation alone. **Jaimini's own resolution follows in the next sutra.**

### Page 386 — A Methodological Note, then Jaimini's Own Resolution Begins

In his Purva-Mimamsa sutras, before establishing that mantras do carry meaning, Jaimini himself first gathered every possible objection on the subject and presented them as the purva-paksha. Sayanacharya, rather than composing his own independent arguments, works directly through Jaimini's own sutras — though in places he interprets them along a path somewhat different from the classical commentators (Shabara, Kumarila, and others), who did not, sutra by sutra, anticipate the siddhantin's coming resolution before commenting on each subsequent sutra.

One notable divergence: Mimamsakas do not generally accept resolutions like "lifeless objects have presiding deities" or "yogis possess extraordinary powers" as doing genuine argumentative work — Shabara's own commentary instead holds that reciting mantras with meaning as the primary intention involves no fault at all. Sayanacharya, however, resolves this very objection using the sutra "abhimāninyaḥ pa-devatāḥ" ("the deities are the presiding spirits [of these objects]"). By anticipating objections this way throughout, Sayana's argument reads as complete and self-contained. We follow Sayanacharya's own interpretation of Jaimini's sutras from here onward.

**There, Jaimini formulates the siddhanta (resolution):**

### "Api śiṣṭasya vākyārthaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.42)

That is: mantra-meaning is established through the relation of action and its instruments, exactly as in ordinary speech — this holds equally for sacred and secular language alike. The word "tu" ("but") in this sutra rejects the earlier objection's claim that mantras serve merely recitation and not meaning; a new meaning, once revealed by a mantra, is what makes ritual action possible, and this alone is the mantra's directly observable (dṛṣṭa) purpose — not some purely "spiritual"/unseen one. Just as an ordinary sentence is uttered specifically to convey its meaning, so too must a Vedic mantra be understood as functioning the same way.

A further objection is then raised: consider the sequence of mantras running from "abhrir asi nārir asi" through "traiṣṭubhena cchandasā dade" — on your view, this passage fully describes the taking-up of the "ābhri" (a ritual implement). If so, the Brahmana's separate injunction "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" ("one takes up the ābhri with four [strokes/portions]") becomes entirely redundant. Jaimini anticipates and answers this objection in the next sutra.

That being so, just as in common talk a sentence is uttered in order that it may convey its meaning, the same law must be recognized in the case of a Vedic sacrifice. For only the rite which is illustrated by a mantra can be performed, not that which is not so illustrated. Therefore the recitation of the mantras has one immediate use and one such use only, and that is not a mystical one. They are recited in order that they may convey their meaning.

In that view the direction to that effect contained in the brahmana "chaturbhir abhrim adatte" became perfectly useless. He anticipates and answers this objection in the next sutra.


### Page 388

The general point: acting according to a purpose already understood is the aim [of ritual action] — one must be able to say *why* a given act is performed, since even if the act itself succeeds mechanically, uttering words devoid of meaning cannot explain "why" it was done. The reason each individual mantra is recited must be known; without this, others simply perform the action mechanically. Since this defeats the purpose behind ritual acts, a mantra's meaning must be understood as serving a genuinely observable (dṛṣṭa) purpose — precisely what its "prāptaviṣṭyaṃ prayojanam" (immediately applicable purpose) consists in, per the Shabara-bhashya. Meaning is therefore not a matter of unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose alone — it is directly observable purpose. To claim otherwise contradicts how language works in ordinary human affairs, where sentences are understood specifically to convey meaning; the same applies to Vedic sentences. The unseen fruit that arises specifically from the *act of recitation itself* is a separate matter — but understanding the meaning is what makes the resulting Dharmic fruit (dharma) possible, and this is what both types of purpose ultimately serve together.

If a mantra's meaning is granted, but the Brahmana's own separate injunction (e.g., regarding the fourfold use of the "abhri") becomes redundant given this — that objection was raised on the previous page. It is resolved as follows: this mantra alone does not specify by itself *how many strokes* constitute proper use of the "abhri" — that detail must be learned from elsewhere. Even granting the mantra's own meaning, the Brahmana statement "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" still serves an independent, non-redundant purpose, specifying the count — resolving the apparent contradiction between the objection and the resolution.

### "Guṇārthena punaḥ-śrutiḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.43)

> मन्त्रेण प्रतीतस्यार्थस्य ब्राह्मणे यत् पुनःश्रुतिस्तद्देशे चतुःसंख्यालक्षणगुणविधानार्थत्वेनोपयुज्यते । एकस्य विधानस्याभावे चतुर्भ्रां मन्त्राणां मध्ये येन केनाभ्रिं आदद्यीत । तन्निमित्तं वाग्भ्रतश्च (Taittiriya Samhita 4.1.2.1[?]) इत्येतच्छस्त्राभिधानाद्ये । (Taittiriya Samhita 3.1.2.1) इत्येतत्र मन्त्रसामर्थ्येन प्राप्तस्य रचनादानस्य पुनर्ब्राह्मणवाक्यं विनियोजकमाम्नायते । तदेतत्तु न्यर्थमित्याशंक्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *(Jaimini's own resolution formula: where a mantra's meaning is restated in a Brahmana passage, that repetition serves the specific purpose of specifying a quantifying detail — here, the "fourfold" count — not otherwise established by the mantra alone. Precise word-level construction is difficult to render with full confidence at this resolution, though the overall doctrine is confirmed by the embedded English translation below.)*

That is: where a mantra's own already-understood meaning is repeated in a Brahmana passage, that repetition is not redundant — it serves to specify a quantifying detail (here, that exactly four applications are required), a detail the mantra by itself leaves open, since without such specification, a priest might assume he had the option to use any single one of the four mantras referenced.

## Chapter 7. The Definition of Pariṣaṅkhyā
*Original title: "Pariṣaṅkhyālakṣaṇa"*
**Printed pages 389–393 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter as of the last review.)*

### Page 389

The sutra's meaning: restating what is already said serves to indicate a distinctive point contained within it. Why repeat, in the Brahmana, what the mantra already states? Because the mantra contains a directive about the "abhri" (spade), followed by three further similar mantras — but if one simply followed the mantra alone, the act of taking up the tool could be completed using just one of the four, leaving the remaining three mantras' purpose unclear. The Brahmana resolves this by stating "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" — one must recite all four mantras before taking up the tool. Since "caturbhiḥ" ("with four") appears nowhere in the mantra itself, without the Brahmana's help, an Adhvaryu might recite only one mantra of his choosing and consider the act complete — improperly performed by shastric standards. The Brahmana's repetition thus serves specifically to supply this missing detail.

But consider the Taittiriya Samhita's mantra "imām agṛbhṇan" ("I have grasped this"), which clearly instructs taking up a rope. The Taittiriya Brahmana restates the same matter: "aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" ("one takes up the rope called ashva"). Here too, one might object that the mantra's application becomes redundant. Anticipating this, the sutra "parisaṅkhyā" follows.

### "Pariṣaṅkhyā" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.44)

> गर्दभाभिधानीं नादत्त इति निषेधः परिसंख्या । तदर्थमिदं ब्राह्मणवाक्यम् ॥
>
> गर्दभाभिधानीं नादत्त इति निषेधः परिषङ्ख्या । तदर्थम् इदं ब्राह्मण-वाक्यम् ॥
> *gardabhābhidhānīṃ nādatta iti niṣedhaḥ pariṣaṅkhyā | tadartham idaṃ brāhmaṇa-vākyam ||*
>
> "'One does not take up the rope called gardabha [donkey-rope]' — this implied prohibition is called pariṣaṅkhyā (exclusive specification). The Brahmana statement exists precisely for this purpose."

That is: the Brahmana's repetition here isn't redundant either — it implicitly *excludes* an alternative (a "donkey-rope," as opposed to the "horse-rope" specified), a specification the mantra alone cannot convey.

> *(A dense technical Mimamsa argument on the "pariṣaṅkhyā" (exclusive specification) doctrine and its relationship to what the mantra literally establishes vs. what the Brahmana's word "takes" adds or restricts; precise phrase-level construction is very difficult to render with confidence at this resolution — the embedded English translation below is the more reliable guide to this passage's content.)*

The sutra's meaning: "This Brahmana statement is a prohibitive injunction (niṣedha-vidhi)." Before following Sayanacharya's own argument, it helps to understand the classical Mimamsa taxonomy of injunctive statements (**vidhi**) — sentences prescribing that a given act be performed in a given way. Mimamsa authorities recognize three kinds:

**(1) Apūrva-vidhi** ("wholly new" injunction) — a sentence prescribing an act knowable by no other means. "One who desires heaven should perform yajna"; "one should sprinkle the grain [with mantra]" — these are apurva-vidhis, since no alternative path exists to fulfill the stated aim.

**(2) Niyama-vidhi** (restrictive injunction) — where two possible methods exist for performing some act, and a sentence specifies that only one of them should be adopted...

---

**(3) Pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi** — its defining characteristic:

> विधिर्द्व्यन्तमप्राप्ते नियमः स्यादुके गतिः । तत्र चान्यत्र च प्राप्ते परिसंख्येति कीर्त्यते ॥
>
> विधिर् द्व्य्-अन्तम् अप्राप्ते नियमः स्याद् उके गतिः । तत्र चान्यत्र च प्राप्ते परिषङ्ख्येति कीर्त्यते ॥
> *vidhir dvy-antam aprāpte niyamaḥ syād uke gatiḥ | tatra cānyatra ca prāpte pariṣaṅkhyeti kīrtyate ||*
>
> "Where nothing else is otherwise attained, that instruction is 'vidhi'; where one of two paths is already established and the instruction directs toward one, that is 'niyama'; where both this and another alternative are equally attained, and one is exclusively specified, that is called 'pariṣaṅkhyā.'"

That is: where no path besides the stated one can accomplish a given task, it is vidhi; where either of two paths would work and only one is prescribed, it is niyama; where more than one path is simultaneously viable and one is exclusively singled out, it is pariṣaṅkhyā. Such a statement — prescribing that only one of several available options be taken, the rest set aside — may seem unnecessary, since the situation alone would suggest which path to take anyway; but it earns its purpose precisely by *prohibiting* the other paths.

Example: "**pañca pañca-nakhā bhakṣyāḥ**" ("the five five-clawed [animals] are edible") — meaning only these five specified clawed animals may be eaten; other animals may not, though there's no requirement that all five must be eaten. This is precisely why pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi differs from apūrva- and niyama-vidhi: failing to perform what is stated in the latter two counts as a defect (karma-lopa) in the rite, but this defect does not apply to pariṣaṅkhyā.

Pariṣaṅkhyā itself comes in two kinds: **Shrauti** (explicit, marked by words like "eva," "only") and **Lakshaniki** (implied, established through the sentence's own structure without such marker-words). The sentence under discussion belongs to this second, implied category — which is precisely why further discussion is needed.

The mantra "imāmu gṛbhṇan" is used in the fire-altar construction rite (agnichayana): bricks are needed for the fire-pit, horses and donkeys carry the required earth, and ropes are needed to lead them — this mantra is recited while taking hold of such a rope. Without the Brahmana statement "ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" ("thus he takes the horse-named rope"), the mantra might be recited while taking up either the horse's or the donkey's rope; this Brahmana statement clarifies that it should specifically accompany taking up the horse's rope, not the donkey's — precisely the pariṣaṅkhyā function.

An objection arises: without this Brahmana statement, three flaws would follow if the mantra alone were held to demand taking up any rope indiscriminately — abandoning the natural meaning of "ādāna/grahaṇa" (taking/holding), assuming a foreign meaning ("not taking"), and failing to exclude the donkey's rope, which the general word "rope" would otherwise include. Taking up the donkey's rope only becomes "attained" after several intervening steps — merely reciting the mantra doesn't make it directly applicable; only after grasping various intervening matters does the donkey-rope possibility even arise. But once the Brahmana statement "ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" is understood, none of this difficulty arises: it becomes clear that the mantra must accompany taking up specifically the horse's rope. Since the donkey's rope was never genuinely "attained" as a live option, there's no room for the "barring what is established" flaw — and without that flaw, "abandoning one's own meaning" doesn't arise either. With neither flaw applicable, the sutra calls this a pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi precisely in the sense that it excludes the (never truly viable) taking of the donkey's rope.

On further reflection, however, this statement arguably isn't pariṣaṅkhyā in the strict classical sense at all — pariṣaṅkhyā's defining mark is excluding *other genuinely available* means to accomplish a task, but here no other means was ever truly possible. Once the Brahmana statement clearly prescribes the intended means without ambiguity, the question of grasping the unwanted donkey-rope never arises. This same point appears in the Tantravartika:

> ननु एवमप्राप्तिविधिरेवायं संजात इति न वक्तव्यम् । परिसंख्येति फलेनैवं अभिधानाद्दोषः । (तन्त्रवार्तिक)

> *nanv evam aprāpti-vidhir evāyaṃ saṃjāta iti na vaktavyam | pariṣaṅkhyeti phalenaivam abhidhānād doṣaḥ | (Tantravārtika)*
>
> "One might object: this then simply becomes an ordinary injunction (for something not otherwise attained), and the term 'pariṣaṅkhyā' should not apply. But calling it pariṣaṅkhyā on the strength of its resulting function, rather than its strict formal structure, involves no real flaw."

In sum, whether or not this statement technically counts as pariṣaṅkhyā, one point stands firmly established: there is no room whatsoever for the flaw the objector (pūrvapakṣin) alleges. The Brahmana statement conveys a genuinely new point not otherwise present in the mantra.

> *adhvaryuḥ puroḍāśam uddiśya mantre prathasvety evam abhidhatte | tasmād abhidhānād adhvaryu-kartṛkaṃ prathanaṃ prāptam | yathā loke yaḥ kurv iti brūte sa kārayaty eva tathātrāpi yaḥ prathasveti brūte sa prathayaty eva |*

Sutra's meaning: since a mantra's own hidden/deeper meaning can be directly examined, mantras are not without purpose. The word "vā" (or) here signals this. Connected with "uru prathasveti prathayati" ("spread wide," he spreads) is an arthavāda: "yajñapatim eva tat prathayati" ("it spreads out the yajamāna himself"). The Adhvaryu recites this mantra while spreading the puroḍāśa cake — and just as the cake expands, so too the yajamāna gains growth in wealth and grain, per this arthavāda's own intended meaning. The Brahmana statement exists precisely to connect this arthavāda to the mantra.

### On Arthavāda

According to the Mimamsakas, the Veda's overriding purpose is performing yajnas to obtain unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit — the Brahmanas prescribe the ritual acts, while the Samhita supplies the mantras recited while performing them. But Brahmana texts don't consist solely of injunctions (vidhi-vākya) — some portions fit neither prescription nor prohibition. Rather than dismiss these as meaningless (which would compromise the Veda's own defining coherence), Mimamsakas hold that such passages support the Veda's central purpose indirectly — setting aside their surface/literal sense to grasp a different, connective meaning tied to the injunctions nearby. Such statements are called **arthavāda**, generally either praising an enjoined act or condemning a prohibited one. Arthavāda divides into four kinds:

**(1) Praśaṃsā** — praise (of what is enjoined).
**(2) Nindā** — censure (of what is prohibited).

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> From its mention in the mantra.
>
> The adhvaryu, referring to the purodasa quotes the mantra and says, Spread it out. And because he says this we understand the act of spreading it out to be the work of the...


### Page 396

**(3) Parakṛti** — relating that some great person in the past performed the enjoined act.
**(4) Purākalpa** — narrating an ancient historical account.

These statements convey that fruit accrues from performing an enjoined act, helping a person decide whether to undertake it, by clarifying its good or bad aspects — supporting the injunctions in this way.

Corresponding to the three pramanas (perception, inference, revealed word), arthavādas are likewise classified into three kinds:

**(1) गुणवाद (Guṇavāda)** — where the stated meaning contradicts direct perception, it is called guṇavāda (a metaphorical statement). Example:

> आदित्यो यूपः ।
> *āditya yūpaḥ |*
> "The sun is the sacrificial post"

— taken literally this is meaningless; the intended sense is that the post, like the sun, shines with brilliance — brilliance being their shared quality (guṇa).

**(2) अनुवाद (Anuvāda)** — restating an already-known fact. Example:

> अग्निर्हिमस्य भेषजम् ।
> *agnir himasya bheṣajam |*
> "Fire is the remedy for cold"

— common knowledge to everyone.

**(3) भूतार्थवाद (Bhūtārthavāda)** — matters impossible to establish through perception or inference. Example:

> इन्द्रो वृत्राय वज्रम् उदयच्छत् ।
> *indro vṛtrāya vajram udayacchat |*
> "Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vritra"

On this third category, a genuine disagreement exists between Agama-authority proponents (like Badarayana and Sayana) and the Mimamsakas. Sayanacharya holds that rejecting the literal truth of bhūtārthavāda statements would render *all* texts — Veda, Purana, Itihasa alike — unauthoritative. The Mimamsakas instead hold that bhūtārthavādas must be read purely as praise or censure, not literal fact. But the Mimamsaka position doesn't fully hold up: consider that the "Ratrisukta" yajna's own mantras nowhere state the rite's fruit — that fruit appears only in the associated arthavāda. Even the Mimamsakas must therefore accept that arthavāda genuinely conveys authoritative new information in such cases.

### Page 397

The Mimamsakas' "fruit-authority" doctrine (that every Vedic statement is authoritative only insofar as it supports yajna-performance) meets genuine resistance in the Upanishads and Gita.

**In the Chandogya Upanishad:**

> तद्यथेह कर्मचितो लोकः क्षीयते एवमेवामुत्र पुण्यचितो लोकः क्षीयते (Chandogya Upanishad 8.1.6)
>
> तद् यथा इह कर्म-चितो लोकः क्षीयते एवम् एवामुत्र पुण्य-चितो लोकः क्षीयते
> *tad yathā iha karma-cito lokaḥ kṣīyate evam evāmutra puṇya-cito lokaḥ kṣīyate*
>
> "Just as here, a world built through action decays, so too, in the next world, a world built through merit likewise decays."

**And in the Bhagavad Gita:**

> यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः । वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः ॥ (Bhagavad Gita 2.42)
>
> याम् इमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्य् अविपश्चितः । वेद-वाद-रताः पार्थ नान्यद् अस्तीति वादिनः ॥
> *yām imāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadanty avipaścitaḥ | veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha nānyad astīti vādinaḥ ||*
>
> "That flowery speech which the unwise proclaim, O Partha, devoted to the letter of the Veda, declaring 'there is nothing else [beyond ritual fruit]'..."

That is: just as worldly fruit is transient, so too are the heavenly pleasures gained through yajna — both texts hold that those who claim yajna-fruit as the only, ultimate reward are "avipaścitaḥ," the unwise (i.e., the Mimamsakas).

**Returning to resolve the earlier fixed-word-order objection:** in statements like "uru prathasva," the word "prathayati" was construed as connected to an arthavāda — but then where does the actual injunction to spread the puroḍāśa come from? The sutra "mantrābhidhānāt" answers this: the Adhvaryu addresses the puroḍāśa directly — "O puroḍāśa, spread yourself out" — and by this address alone, it becomes clear that the Adhvaryu himself must perform the spreading. This mirrors ordinary experience: if one person tells another to do something, carrying it out becomes that person's own responsibility — no separate injunction is needed.

*(Note: "mantrābhidhānāt" is not itself one of Jaimini's own sutras — it is a Shabara-bhashya sentence Sayana has interspersed while working through Jaimini's sutras, itself carrying sutra-like concision, a technique commentators occasionally employ.)*

> *paraṃ dvitīya-sūtroktaṃ syāt ... na hi ayaṃ sākala-krama-niyamādṛṣṭyaṃ nivārayāmaḥ || kiṃ tarhi || mantreṇa jāyamānam artha-pratyāyanaṃ dṛṣṭa-prayojanatvān nopekṣitavyam iti brūmaḥ | nanu prokṣaṇīr āsādaya iti mantro buddham evārthaṃ śāsti | tad ayuktam |*
>
> "What was said in the second sutra is not contradicted by us — we do not deny the unseen benefit of the fixed recitation-order. What then is our point? We say that the meaning-conveying function arising through the mantra, being a directly observable benefit, must not be overlooked. But doesn't the mantra 'prokṣaṇīr āsādaya' merely prescribe an already-known matter? That objection does not hold."

Sutra's meaning: what the second sutra states is not opposed to our view. The intent of "vākya-niyamāt" (the second sutra) was that altering the mantra's word-order yields an improper result — this we don't deny; reciting mantras does yield a fruit. But our own position is: reciting a mantra also produces knowledge of its meaning, which helps carry out yajnas properly — and this directly observable benefit (dṛṣṭa-prayojana) must not be neglected or denied. Mantras, in other words, possess both the unseen fruit the objector claims *and* a directly observable one.

**This answers the third original objection ("buddha-shāstrāt")** — recall the "agnīd agnīn vihara" example, objected to as useless repetition of already-known matter. Here, the Vajasaneyi Samhita's "prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" is cited: reciting this mantra, one places the mantra-sanctified water...

### "Sampreṣakarmaṇo garhānupalambhe saṃskāratvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.48)

> संप्रेषकर्मणो गर्हा त्वदुक्त दोषो नोपलभ्यते । बुद्धस्यापि अर्थस्य मन्त्रेणानुसंस्करणान्नियमाद्दृष्टलक्षणस्य संस्कारस्य सद्भावात् । यच्चोक्तं चत्वारि शृंगेति मन्त्रेऽसंभवमेवार्थमभिधत्त इति तस्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> संप्रेष-कर्मणो गर्हा त्वद्-उक्त दोषो नोपलभ्यते । बुद्धस्याप्य् अर्थस्य मन्त्रेणानुसंस्करणान् नियमाद् दृष्ट-लक्षणस्य संस्कारस्य सद्भावात् । यच् चोक्तं चत्वारि शृङ्गेति मन्त्रेऽसंभवम् एवार्थम् अभिधत्त इति तस्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *saṃpreṣa-karmaṇo garhā tvad-ukta doṣo nopalabhyate | buddhasyāpy arthasya mantreṇānusaṃskaraṇān niyamād dṛṣṭa-lakṣaṇasya saṃskārasya sadbhāvāt | yac coktaṃ catvāri śṛṅgeti mantre'saṃbhavam evārtham abhidhatta iti tasyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "The fault you alleged for acts commanded by 'presha' (directive) mantras is not actually found. Even for already-known matter, reciting the mantra confers a directly-observable refinement (saṃskāra) upon the act, following the established rule. As for the earlier objection that the 'four-horned' mantra states something self-evidently impossible, an answer to that follows too."

Sutra's meaning: since an injunctive statement conveys ritual refinement (saṃskāra), it escapes the objection. Mantras like "prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" and "agnīd agnīn vihara" are **presha-mantras** — directive mantras commanding that certain acts be performed. Their stated meaning may already be known, but reciting the mantra to re-announce the act carries a special unseen fruit precisely through following this rule.

Though one learns during study what acts must be performed at their proper time, this knowledge doesn't remain constantly active in memory — it stays latent. Some means is needed to bring it to conscious attention; one could try to recall it through deliberate focus alone, but the rule requiring the act be performed specifically accompanied by this mantra rules out other means of recollection. The claim that presha-mantras are meaningless therefore does not hold.

The Garhapatya and other sacred fires, together with the seven meters, are its 'hands.' It is bound threefold through the Rigveda and the other Vedas. 'It fulfills desires' — hence it is called a 'bull' (vṛṣabha); it 'roars' — that is, the hymn of praise — and, from the word 'etc.,' does so repeatedly. This same great deity (Mahādeva), this life-breath in the form of the sacrifice, has entered mortals — hence humans having two principal [organs/heads] need not be taken too literally. Metaphorical usage is seen in ordinary life too — as when we call a woman 'swan-toothed' or 'Kashi's own curly-locked one,' describing her as embodying these qualities directly. Likewise, addresses to inanimate things — 'O herb, protect him,' 'hear, O stones' — should be understood as oriented toward praise. This is the celebrated allegorical reading of the "four-horned bull" mantra: rather than describing a literal impossible creature, it poetically describes the yajna itself — its four priests as horns, its three daily pressings as feet, its sacred fires and meters as hands, and its threefold Vedic foundation as its binding — resolving the fourth objection entirely.

### Page 401

Sutra's meaning: in a context stating a non-existent thing, that sentence carries a special, secondary meaning. Where any sentence describes non-existent things, a different, secondary meaning must be construed — setting aside the apparent literal meaning. Non-Vedic literature uses such devices too: describing a river as "**चक्रवाकस्तनी**" (*cakravāka-stanī*, having chakravaka birds as her breasts), "**हंसदन्तावली**" (*haṃsa-dantāvalī*, rows of swans as her teeth), **काश** (*kāśa*) grass as her garment, **शैवल** (*śaivala*) moss as her hair — one naturally understands a meaning beyond the literal claim. The same principle applies to the objector's cited mantra "**चत्वारि शृङ्गा**" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*) — it need not describe a literal four-horned, three-footed creature at all:

**चत्वारि शृङ्गाणि** (*catvāri śṛṅgāṇi*, Four Horns) — the four principal priests carrying out the yajna's work: **होतृ** (*hotṛ*), **अध्वर्यु** (*adhvaryu*), **उद्गातृ** (*udgātṛ*), and **ब्रह्मा** (*brahmā*).

**त्रयः पादाः** (*trayaḥ pādāḥ*, Three Feet) — the morning pressing (**प्रातःसवन** *prātaḥ-savana*), midday pressing (**माध्यंदिनसवन** *mādhyandina-savana*), and evening pressing (**सायंसवन** *sāyaṃ-savana*).

**द्वे शीर्षे** (*dve śīrṣe*, Two Heads) — the **यजमान** (*yajamāna*, patron of the sacrifice) and his wife.

**सप्त हस्ताः** (*sapta hastāḥ*, Seven Hands) — the **गायत्री** (*gāyatrī*) and the other Vedic meters (seven in number).

**त्रिधा बद्धः** (*tridhā baddhaḥ*, Threefold Bound) — bound together through the Rigveda and the other Vedas.

**वृषभः** (*vṛṣabhaḥ*, Bull) — one who "rains down" (**वर्षति** *varṣati*) desired boons, like rainfall.

**रोरवीति** (*roravīti*, "Roars") — he who repeatedly recites the mantras in the form of **स्तोत्र** (*stotra*) and **शस्त्र** (*śastra*) (hymn and recitation).

**Great God (Maho Deva)** — this deity in the form of the yajna itself.
**Entered Mortals** — has taken abode within humans, meaning: the authority to perform this yajna belongs to human beings alone.

That is: this mantra's real purport is that the above elements are the principal constituents of every yajna-rite — not a description of some strange creature. Recognizing the secondary meaning elsewhere too shows the claim that mantras are meaningless to be groundless.

Similarly, sentences addressing inanimate objects serve to praise the associated act. "Oṣadhe trāyasvainam" belongs to the yajamāna's shaving-ritual: addressing the darbha grass, "protect the yajamāna," the point is — if the grass itself protects the yajamāna seated for shaving, how much more should the one performing the shaving protect him. Likewise "śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ" ("listen, O stones"), recited before the dawn hymns (prātar-anuvāka): if even inanimate stones listen to these hymns, how much more attentively should the assembled learned Brahmins listen — this is the intended point.

### "Vidyā-vacanam-asaṃyogāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.51)

> *veda-vidyā-grahaṇa-kāle'rthasya yad avacanaṃ tad ayajña-saṃyogād upapadyate | na hi pūrṇikāyā avaghātako yajña-saṃyuktaḥ | nāpi māṇavako yajñam anutiṣṭhati | ato yajñānuṣṭhārān na tatrārtha-vivakṣā | ...*

> "That meaning goes unconveyed during Vedic study is explained by the absence of any connection to an actual yajna. Purnika's pounding is not connected to a yajna, nor is the student performing one — hence, absent yajna-performance, there is no intention to convey meaning in that context. As for the claim that meaning cannot be determined in texts like 'amyaksā ta indra' or 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū,' an answer to that follows next."

That is: the student's silence on meaning during rote study isn't evidence mantras lack meaning generally — it simply reflects that neither Purnika's work nor the student's recitation is actually part of a yajna. Where no yajna is being performed, there's no occasion to intend conveying meaning at all — this doesn't undermine the mantra's meaning when genuinely used in ritual context.

Sutra's meaning: during rote practice/study, since the mantra bears no connection to any yajna-related ritual act, no meaning is conveyed. The objection holds that meaning-grasping fails to occur during Vedic study — but when mantras are genuinely applied in yajnas, real efforts at conveying and understanding meaning take place; during mere memorization, no such occasion arises. In the pestle-mantra case, since Purnika's husking isn't part of a yajna, no rule ties the mantra's recitation to the pounding — and the student's own recitation likewise isn't yajna-related. Where no yajna-connection exists, the absence of meaning-knowledge is simply not a flaw at all.

That is: the meaning is genuinely present in such mantras, but goes unnoticed through carelessness or inattention — not because it's inherently absent. Careful etymological analysis via Nirukta and grammar, cross-checked against parallel passages, reveals that even the famously obscure "jarbhari turpharitu" refers to the twin Ashvin deities, confirmed by the dual grammatical forms and the hymn's overall Ashvin-context.

One can indeed determine the meaning of such texts. For difficult words like these, gathering other Vedic passages using similar constructions, with Nirukta and grammar's help, one determines the underlying verbal root and infers meaning accordingly. Working through the cited example: "jarbharī" and "turpharītū" are clearly dual-number words, occurring in verse 6 of Rigveda Mandala 10, Sukta 106 — a sukta dedicated to the Ashvins, confirmed by that same sukta's own line "aśvinoḥ kāmam aprāḥ" ("you fulfilled the Ashvins' desire"). Therefore "jarbharī" and "turpharītū" refer to the Ashvin deities. The Nirukta itself, holding this same view, glosses "jarbharī" as "those who nourish/give shelter" and "turpharītū" as "those who destroy [obstacles]." The same method of inference applies to "amyak sā ta" and similar texts.

**The ninth and final objection-sutra: "Anitya-saṃyogān mantrānarthakyaṃ."** The Veda mentions non-eternal things — Pramaganda, Babara, Prātaḥsavana, and similar proper names of persons who lived and then perished. Either the claim that the Veda is beginningless (anādi) is false, the objector argues, or the Vedas have no meaning at all — mere recitation must be their sole purpose.

> *paraṃ tu śruti-sāmānya-mātram |*
>
> "But this rests merely on a similarity of sounds."

This is Jaimini's answer: such words resemble ordinary words only in sound and letter-sequence, not in meaning. The siddhanta holds: "Kathaka," "Kalapaka," and similar terms denote different Vedic branches/schools; "Babara" and similar words merely resemble ordinary proper names in their letter-sequence — there was no actual person named "Babara." Rather, "babara" is the very sound wind makes while blowing — so "babaraḥ" here means "the wind that makes that sound," and "prāvāhaṇīḥ" means "one whose nature is to blow swiftly/forcefully." The same reasoning applies to words like "Pramaganda."

In this way, no flaw whatsoever remains regarding mantra-meaning — mantras genuinely exist to convey meaning, and each mantra should be applied precisely where its stated meaning holds genuine use.

**A further doubt arises:** the siddhanta-sutras have logically established that mantras reveal meaning and possess directly observable purpose — but one might object that no actual scriptural (śruti) statement supports this conclusion. Jaimini anticipates this and answers next.

Sutra's meaning: ritual terms are used precisely to indicate meaning. "Āgneyyāgnidhram upatiṣṭheta" is a Brahmana statement indicating the mantra to recite while approaching the Agnidh's platform with one's wife for worship. "Āgneyyā" means "by the mantra whose presiding deity is Agni" — referring to the mantra beginning "agne naya." Rather than naming that mantra directly, the Brahmana uses the grammatically-derived (taddhita) term "āgneyī" ("Agni-related [verse]") — itself proof that the mantra is understood to carry genuine meaning, since only a meaning-bearing verse could be classified by its subject-deity this way. Since mantras thus demonstrably convey meaning, they must be recited at their proper application. Further proofs follow.

The original mantra must sometimes be recited with slight modification across different contexts — changing certain words, or substituting others in their place — this practice is called **ūha** (adaptation), found here and there in ritual application. A Brahmana statement confirms this required adaptation, stating simply:

> न माता वर्धते न पिता ।
> *na mātā vardhate na pitā |*
> "The mother is not increased, nor the father."

Here, "vṛddhi" (increase) could mean either of two things: age-related growth (childhood through youth to old age), or grammatical number-change (the singular "mātā"/"pitā" becoming dual "mātarau"/"pitarau" or plural "mātaraḥ"/"pitaraḥ"). Age-related growth obviously cannot be denied — it's plainly observable. So the Brahmana's real point must be grammatical: the words "mātṛ" and "pitṛ" specifically should NOT change in number. Since this restriction applies only to those two words, it follows that the remaining word "enam" *must* instead take the appropriate dual or plural form depending on context. If mantras carried no meaning at all, why would this kind of careful word-adaptation even be necessary? This confirms that mantras do indeed convey genuine meaning.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> ...is the original form of a mantra referring to the sacrifice of an animal. When there are two animals to be sacrificed the form of this mantra is altered, and they say, "enau ('these two') mata manyatam." When there are more than two there is a different uha and they say "enan ('these') mata manyatam."
>
> Of this mantra there is an interpretative brahmana, "Na mata vardhate na pita," "The mother does not increase, nor the father." Here the thought must arise, is the increase, which is in this brahmana forbidden, increase of the body, or is it increase of the word? By increase of the word of course is meant the change of the singular "matri" to the dual "matarau," or to the plural "matarah." Now it is not possible to prohibit increase of the body. For we see it increase before our eyes, according to the change from child to girl, from girl to woman. We are left with the increase of the word. And the special prohibition against any increase of the words matri and pitri in this text is intended to indicate that the other word enam is to be increased, according to the sense, to enau or enan. But if the meaning of the mantra is not intended to be conveyed by its recitation, then where is the necessity of introducing the dual when two beasts are to be sacrificed, or the plural when more than two beasts are to be sacrificed?
>
> In the same matter he brings forward still another indication from scripture in the next sutra.

> *mantra-vyākhyāna-rūpo brāhmaṇikaḥ śabdo vidhi-śabda ity ucyate | sa caivam āmnāyate | śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam ity evaitad āha iti | tatra śataṃ himā ity etad vyākhyeya-mantrasya pratīkam | avaśiṣṭaṃ tu tasya tātparya-vyākhyānam | mantrasyāvivakṣitārthatve tu kiṃ nāma tātparyaṃ mantre vyākhyāyeta | tasmād vivakṣitārthā mantrāḥ prayoga-kāle svārtha-prakāśanāyaivoccāryanta ity āha ||*
>
> "A Brahmana statement that takes the form of explaining a mantra is called a 'vidhi-śabda.' One such is recorded: 'śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam' ('may I live a hundred winters, a hundred years') — this is what is meant. Here, 'śataṃ himāḥ' is the pratīka (opening phrase) of the mantra being explained; the rest explains its purport. If the mantra carried no intended meaning at all, what purport could possibly be explained? This shows that mantras, carrying real intended meaning, are recited at their application specifically to reveal that meaning."

Sutra's meaning: vidhi-śabda words embedded in Brahmanas likewise support that mantras carry meaning. Brahmanas contain many mantra-explanatory statements (the earliest form of Vedic commentary) — such statements are called vidhi-śabda. In "śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam ity evaitad āha" (Shatapatha Brahmana 2.3.4.10), "śataṃ himāḥ" is the mantra-portion, and the rest explains its purport — that it means "may we live a hundred years." Had mantras no meaning, there would be no need to explain their purport at all. This too proves mantras carry genuine meaning.

## Chapter 9. Examination of the Authority of the Brahmana-Portion (the Vidhi/Injunctive Mantras)
*Original title: "Brāhmaṇātmaka-mantrabhāgada prāmāṇyavicāravimarśeyu — vidhivākyapramāṇa samarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 412–419 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter — pp.416 and 417 repaired during Phase B: the yajna taxonomy and stotra/shastra terminology now carry Devanagari, and the "atiratre shodasinam" contradiction example is restored in full.)*

### Page 412

Here, the objector's (pūrvapakṣa) view is presented as a question, and the siddhanta as its answer.

**Question:** Do mantras like "uru prathasva" yield only an unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit, or do they clarify actual ritual procedures — such as spreading the puroḍāśa — in the yajnas where they occur?

**The objector's prima facie answer:** since Brahmana statements already explain the acts to be performed in yajnas, mantras must be said to yield only unseen merit (puṇya).

**Siddhanta:** mantras do not yield merit alone as their fruit — the meanings they express are clearly useful for performing yajna-related acts. A directly observable (dṛṣṭa) fruit is always the superior explanation; mantras therefore do convey meaning, contrary to the claim that mere recitation is their only purpose.

**A new question opens:** granting the mantra-portion's authority, does the Brahmana-portion itself carry the same authority?

> नन्वस्तु मन्त्रभागस्य प्रामाण्यम् । ब्राह्मणभागस्य तु न तदस्त्येक्ष्यते । तथा हि । द्विविधं ब्राह्मणम् । विधिरर्थवादश्चेति । तथा चासद्बन्धः । कर्मचोदना ब्राह्मणानि ब्राह्मणशेषोऽर्थवादः (Jaimini... 2.1.33[?]) इति । विधिरपि द्विविधः । अप्रवृत्तप्रवर्तनमज्ञातज्ञापनं चेति । यथा पुरोडाशं निर्वपन्ति दीक्षणीयायाम् (Shatapatha Brahmana 1.1[?]) इत्याद्या कर्मकाण्डगतविधयोऽप्रवृत्तिप्रवर्तकाः । आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् (Shatapatha Aranyaka 1.4.1[?]) इत्याद्यो ब्रह्मकाण्डगता अज्ञातज्ञापकाः । तत्र कर्मकाण्डगतानां जर्तिलैर्यवानाग्नौ जुहुयाद् वीरुधः कल्पयाग्ना वा (तैत्तिरीय संहिता 3.1.3.1[?]) इत्यादिविधीनां नास्ति प्रामाण्यम् । प्रवृत्त्युद्यप्रवृत्युद्रव्यविधानेन सम्यगनुभवसाधनत्वाभावात् । अयोग्यत्वं च वाक्यशेषे समाम्नातम् । अनाहुतिर्वै जर्तिलाश्च गवीधु...

Let us accept the Samhita (mantra) portion as authoritative, as already established. But applying that same status to the **Brahmana portion** is not straightforward. Brahmanas fall into two kinds — **vidhi** (injunction) and **arthavāda** (explanatory statement). Apastamba's sutra defines them: "karma-codanā brāhmaṇāni" — statements that impel ritual acts are Brahmanas (vidhis); the remainder is arthavāda. Vidhi itself divides further into two kinds: those that initiate a not-otherwise-performed act, and those that reveal a previously unknown matter. Karma-kanda statements like "āgnāvaiṣṇavam..." and similar...

The brahmana portion is of two kinds, called respectively vidhi and arthavada. So, for example, Apastamba says, "Some brahmanas relate to works, that is, are vidhis, precepts: and all the remaining brahmanas are of the nature of arthavada." Vidhis, too, are of two kinds, according as they enjoin the performance of something that has not been performed, or make known something that is not known. Such vidhis as, for example,

> सोमयागे प्रवृत्तस्य यजमानस्य संस्कारो दीक्षणम् । तस्मै च संस्कारस्य हेतुः कर्मविशेषो दीक्षणीयाच्च्यवाच्यः ॥ (Sampranabhashya 6, Brahmana 1.1.1)
>
> सोमयागे प्रवृत्तस्य यजमानस्य संस्कारो दीक्षणम् । तस्मै च संस्कारस्य हेतुः कर्म-विशेषो दीक्षणीयाच् च्यवाच्यः ॥
> *somayāge pravṛttasya yajamānasya saṃskāro dīkṣaṇam | tasmai ca saṃskārasya hetuḥ karma-viśeṣo dīkṣaṇīyāc cyavācyaḥ ||*
>
> "For the yajamāna undertaking a Soma-yaga, initiation (dīkṣaṇa) is the necessary consecration; the specific ritual act causing that consecration is termed 'dīkṣaṇīyā.'"

The yajamāna undertaking a Soma-yaga must undergo certain consecrations, including bodily purification — this purifying rite is called "dīkṣaṇīyā(-iṣṭi)," described in the Taittiriya Samhita's sixth kanda, first chapter, first anuvaka. In this iṣṭi, a puroḍāśa cake is offered to Agni and Vishnu together ("āgnāvaiṣṇava"). Since no one would undertake such an act without being told to, this statement counts as **apravṛtta-pravartaka** vidhi (initiating what wouldn't otherwise occur).

The second category of vidhi reveals previously unknown matters. "Ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt" ("in the beginning, this was the Self alone") and similar statements on the relationship between the individual soul and Brahman belong to the **brahma-kāṇḍa** — the Aranyakas and Upanishads. Since such truths cannot otherwise be known, this category is called **ajñāta-jñāpaka** vidhi (revealing the unknown). Vidhi thus divides into these two kinds.

But within the karma-kāṇḍa, statements like "jartilayavāgvā..." (concerning forest-grown sesame and wheat as valid oblation materials) lack genuine authority — since the same scriptural tradition elsewhere states that forest-grown sesame and wheat are *not* suitable oblation materials. A statement permitting the use of unsuitable substances cannot itself be considered authoritative.

Similarly, in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, and other Brahmanas, many matters are prohibited using phrases like "this should not be regarded" or "this should not be done that way." Consider two examples: the Aitareya Brahmana repeatedly condemns performing homa before sunrise as useless:

> "tasmād udite hotavyam" — "therefore, homa should be performed only after sunrise" — stated again and again.

The Taittiriya Brahmana states similarly through "yad anudite... juhoti" and related passages — if homa is performed before sunrise, the offering goes entirely to Agni rather than reaching Surya; therefore the morning-homa (prātar-homa) must occur only after sunrise. Yet the same tradition also criticizes performing it *after* sunrise:

> यदुदिते सूर्ये प्रातर्जुहुयात् । यथातिथये प्रयुतायै शून्यायावसथायागच्छेत् । आद्यैव स्यात् । (Taittiriya Brahmana 2.1.2.1)
>
> यद् उदिते सूर्ये प्रातर् जुहुयात् । यथातिथये प्रदुतायै शून्यायावसथायागच्छेत् । आद्यैव स्यात् ।
> *yad udite sūrye prātar juhuyāt | yathātithaye pradutāyai śūnyāyāvasathāyāgacchet | ādyaiva syāt |*
>
> "If one performs the morning homa after the sun has already risen — it is like a guest arriving at an empty house after the food meant for him has already been sent away; it would have been better offered promptly."

Thus, contradictory statements exist on this exact same point.

**The Taittiriya Brahmana offers a mythological account explaining this:** long ago, Prajapati (Brahma), preparing to offer havis to Agni, was approached by Surya, who insisted the offering be made to him instead. Agni and Surya then debated and reached an agreement: daytime homa belongs to Surya, nighttime homa belongs to Agni — a reasonable arrangement, since Surya's influence predominates by day and Agni's by night. Therefore, homa performed before sunrise (still counted as "night") belongs to Agni, while homa from sunrise to sunset belongs to Surya. Daytime homa thus belongs to Surya, nighttime homa to Agni.

### Page 416

A homa performed contrary to this arrangement, the argument holds, fails to reach its intended deity and becomes useless. Similarly, the Atiratra yajna's rule requiring the Shodashi-stotra and Shastra is directly contradicted by another passage prohibiting their use in that same rite. And while the Jyotishtoma yajna is said to secure heaven (with similar specific fruits attributed to other yajnas), none of these outcomes can be verified through direct experience — unlike "eating brings satisfaction," which is confirmed by observation. Since karma-kāṇḍa vidhi statements' promised fruits cannot be similarly verified, the objection concludes they carry no authority whatsoever.

**Before proceeding, a clear understanding of yajnas' actual structure is needed** — their main ritual components, subdivisions of injunction, method of performance, and technical vocabulary — to properly follow the Mimamsa-sutras' argument. We therefore briefly explain the classification of yajnas here.

**Yajnas are of two kinds: सोमयज्ञ (Soma-yajña) and हविर्यज्ञ (Havir-yajña)** — Soma-juice as the offering-substance defines the former; ordinary havis (oblation material) the latter. Soma-yagas divide into three kinds:

**एकाह (Ekāha)** — completed within a single day.
**अहीन (Ahīna)** — completed within two to twelve days.
**सत्र (Sattra)** — continuing beyond twelve days.

Among Ekāhas, the most important is the **ज्योतिष्टोम (Jyotiṣṭoma)**, itself of seven kinds (the "seven संस्था *saṃsthā*"):

1. अग्निष्टोम (Agniṣṭoma) 2. अत्यग्निष्टोम (Atyagniṣṭoma) 3. उक्थ्य (Ukthya) 4. षोडशी (Ṣoḍaśī) 5. वाजपेय (Vājapeya) 6. अतिरात्र (Atirātra) 7. आप्तोर्याम (Āptoryāma)

Of these, **Agnishtoma is the primary form**, the remaining six being its variants — hence Agnishtoma is called the "prakṛti" (base form) and the other six the "vikṛti" (modified forms). In the Agnishtoma, the designated Stotras (hymns, or Sama-chants/mantras) are sung, and after each Stotra-recitation, the accompanying priests — Maitravaruna, Brahmanacchamsi, Achchavaka, and others...

> *ajñāta-jñāpakeṣu brahma-vidhiṣv api paraspara-virodhān nāsti prāmāṇyam | ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt ity aitareyeṇa āmnanti | asad vā idam agra āsīt iti taittirīyakāḥ | so'yaṃ virodhaḥ | tasmād eva vidhi-bhāgaḥ sarvo'py apramāṇam iti prāpte brūmaḥ ||*
>
> "Even among the brahma-kāṇḍa's 'revealing the unknown' vidhis, no authority exists, due to mutual contradiction. The Aitareyins state: 'ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt' (in the beginning, this was the Self alone). The Taittiriyas state: 'asad vā idam agra āsīt' (in the beginning, this was non-being alone). This is a direct contradiction. Given this, the entire vidhi-portion is claimed to be without authority — to which we now respond—"

Just as karma-kāṇḍa contains contradictions, the brahma-kāṇḍa does too — hence its statements are likewise claimed as unauthoritative. The Aitareya Aranyaka (Aitareya Upanishad 1.1) states that at the world's beginning, the Self (ātman) alone existed; the Taittiriya Aranyaka states instead that at the beginning, only "asat" (non-being/void) existed — a direct contradiction between these two Upanishadic statements.

**Given that the entire vidhi-portion — both karma-kāṇḍa and brahma-kāṇḍa — stands accused of lacking authority, a resolution now follows, establishing the vidhi-portion's genuine authority.**

Sutta's argument now resolves the objection fully: the statements "jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt gavīdhukayavāgvā vā" and "anāhutir vai jartilāś ca gavīdhukāś ca" (cited as contradictory) genuinely do lack authority — but without any actual flaw, since these vidhi-statements were never meant to be followed in the first place. The truly prescribed oblation-substance — goat's milk — appears shortly after, in "ajakṣīreṇa juhoti." Goat's milk is the excellent oblation-substance; jartila and gavidhuka were mentioned first, and then declared unsuitable, precisely to praise goat's milk by contrast — that is, jartila and similar substances...
