> If you say here that in accordance with this reasoning vidhis such as that about forest grain, though rejected in the passage before us, must be authoritative in some other Sakha, just as goats and the like are beasts, though in that way of speaking they are declared not to be beasts, we will accept that. But they will be authoritative only to a follower of that Sakha. The case is on all fours with eating the food of a stranger which, forbidden in one stage of life, is lawful in another. Reasoning in this way we can resolve all contradictions between precepts or vidhis and prohibitions by referring them to differences in the man.


### Page 421

The vidhi-statements should be understood as arthavāda. Many such statements exist. The Taittiriya Brahmana states:

> अपशवो वा अन्ये गोऽश्वेभ्यः ।
> *apaśavo vā anye go'śvebhyaḥ |*
> "Apart from cows and horses, there are no [true] beasts."

This doesn't literally deny goats' status as animals — its real point is that cows and horses are superior in this context. There's a maxim:

> न हि निन्दा निन्द्यं निन्दितुं प्रवर्तते, अपि तु विधेयं स्तोतुम् ।
> *na hi nindā nindyaṃ ninditum pravartate, api tu vidheyaṃ stotum |*
> "Censure is not truly meant to condemn what's censured, but rather to praise what's prescribed."

Statements of censure aim to elevate what's prescribed, not genuinely denigrate what's censured. The same logic applies to jartila: its real point is praising goat's milk as the superior oblation-substance. If goats count as valid "beasts" in some other Vedic school, jartila might likewise be a valid oblation-substance there too — but this would apply only to followers of that particular school.

**A household-duty example illustrates this same principle:**

> परस्साकरुणिः स्यात् ।
> *paras-sākaruṇiḥ syāt |* (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1.112)

— prohibits eating others' food for a householder;

> भिक्षार्थी ग्राममाश्रयेत् ।
> *bhikṣārthī grāmam āśrayet |*

— requires a sannyasi to beg for alms in the village (food from others being his only means);

> ब्रह्मचारी स्थितो नैकमन्नमद्यादनापदि ।
> *brahmacārī sthito naikam annam adyād anāpadi |*

— requires a Brahmachari student to eat from *many* households rather than just one, except in genuine hardship. What's prohibited in one life-stage (āśrama) is thus prescribed in another.

Following this same reasoning, mutually contradictory injunctions and prohibitions should be applied according to the specific person following them. Even mantras show this pattern across different schools (śākhā) — a rule stated in one context becomes prohibited in another. The Taittiriya Samhita contains the mantra:

> न आयवस्थोपायवस्था देवो वः ।
> *nāyavastho-pāyavasthā devo vaḥ |*

The same mantra appears in the Vajasaneyi Samhita too — but there, only "**न आयवस्था देवो वः**" (*nāyavasthā devo vaḥ*) appears, omitting "upāyavasthā" entirely. The Vajasaneyi Samhita's own Brahmana...

In the same way the Taittiriyas, in their "suktavaka" mantra, quote the reading of another Sakha, and reject it in favour of the reading of their own. The passage in which the reading of their another Sakha is rejected is "yad bruyat supavasana cha svadhyavasana cheti pramayuko yajamana syat." And the passage in which the other reading is enjoined is "supacharana cha svadhicharana chetyeva bruyat." A contradiction like this can only be resolved by a difference in the sacrificers. And the same rule must be applied to conflicting vidhis.

Whichever reading is stated belongs to followers of that specific school (śākhā) — another school prescribes a different reading. In all such cases, the correct reading is determined by who recites or performs it. The same principle applies to vidhi-statements generally: whether a statement functions as injunction or prohibition must be judged relative to the specific person performing the act.

**Turning to resolve the Ātman/Asat contradiction:** "ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt" means the Self alone existed before creation; "asad vā idam agra āsīt" means only the unmanifest form called "asat" existed — these two Shruti statements appear directly contradictory. The answer is given in the Brahma-sutra, first adhyaya, fourth pada, fourteenth sutra:

> "कारणत्वेन चाकाशादिषु यथा व्यपदिष्टोक्तेः"
> "kāraṇatvena cākāśādiṣu yathā vyapadiṣṭokteḥ" (Vedanta Sutra 1.4.14)
>
> *(As with the sky and other elements, designated according to their causal role — the "asat" reference likewise describes Brahman's own unmanifest, pre-creative state as cause, not literal non-existence.)*

Badarayana, and Jaimini following him, hold that all the Upanishads together establish one and the same underlying doctrine: that Brahman alone is eternal — a conclusion drawn from the Upanishads as a whole...

### Page 423

...the subject already established; the apparent contradictions we find are only superficial, not genuinely opposed in real intent — on this foundation, Badarayana and Jaimini composed their respective works.

Regarding creation, contexts do differ over which entity was created first, and one place calls the cause of creation "sat" (being), another "asat" (non-being) — apparently opposed views. The Vedanta-sutra answers this:

Though schools differ over the *sequence* and specific entities of creation, no genuine difference exists regarding **Brahman itself** as the ultimate cause — the same Brahman is called the cause of the sky in one place and other elements elsewhere (Vedanta Sutra 1.4.14). Sequence-related statements are not decisive on their own; not every created thing is even named in them. The Taittiriya Upanishad explains this matter fully, establishing that the creator is one alone.

**On the specific meaning of "asat":** the Brahma-sutra's third adhyaya, first pada, addresses the Taittiriya Upanishad's own "asad vā idam agra āsīt":

> "असद्-व्यपदेशान् नेति चेन् न धर्मान्तरेण वाक्य-शेषात्"
> "asad-vyapadeśān neti cen na dharmāntareṇa vākya-śeṣāt" (Vedanta Sutra 2.1.17)
>
> "If it be objected that, because it is called 'non-existent' [Brahman cannot be its cause] — we say no, since the remainder of the passage indicates a different attribute [i.e., an unmanifest state, not literal non-existence]."

Using the word "asat" does not mean nothing at all existed at the beginning. Here, "asat" doesn't mean "void" — it means "not-sat," that is, not yet in a clearly manifest form, existing instead in an unmanifest state. This meaning is confirmed by the statements that follow in the same passage. Therefore, "sat" and "asat" carry no real, fundamental difference: one indicates the manifest state, the other the unmanifest state preceding manifestation — "asat" simply marks this distinct, pre-manifest condition, not literal nothingness.

And in the first adhikarana of the first pada of the second adhyaya the sutra "asadvyapadesan neti chen na dharmantarena vakyaseshat" shows that the word "asat" in the Taittiriya text does not mean "non-existent" but "unevolved."

### Page 424

That is: since the flaws alleged in the objection do not actually hold, vidhi-statements stand established as authoritative. Jaimini and Badarayana both affirm this in their own foundational sutras.

> "चोदना-लक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः"
> "codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.2)
>
> "Dharma is that which is characterized by [Vedic] injunction."

In this sutra, Jaimini establishes that dharma is whatever is conducive to a person's ultimate good — and since vidhi-statements themselves state which acts are conducive to that good, vidhi-statements are thereby authoritative. This authority is further affirmed by the sutra known as the "autpattika-sutra":

> "औत्पत्तिकस् तु शब्दस्यार्थेन सम्बन्धस् तस्य ज्ञानम् उपदेशोऽव्यतिरेकश् चार्थेऽनुपलब्धे तत् प्रमाणं बादरायणस्यानपेक्ष्यात्"
> "autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena sambandhas tasya jñānam upadeśo'vyatirekaś cārthe'nupalabdhe tat pramāṇaṃ bādarāyaṇasyānapekṣyāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.5)
>
> "The relationship between word and meaning is innate; knowledge of this relationship constitutes instruction; and where no perceivable contradiction exists [in the matter concerned], this instruction is itself valid proof — because, per Badarayana, it [dharma] depends on nothing else for its validity."

Word and word-meaning are both naturally arising and eternal — every phoneme is eternal, not created. The entire Veda is likewise "shruta" (heard/revealed) — eternal and faultless. For dharma and its karmic fruits, the Veda alone is authoritative, since these cannot be known through perception or inference. Jaimini himself anticipates every conceivable objection here and answers each in his own systematic way — only a full study of the Mimamsa-shastra can properly evaluate whether his conclusions hold.

**Vyasa parallels this in the Brahma-sutra:**

> "śāstra-yonitvāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.3)

Sayanacharya glosses this sutra two ways: (1) "śāstrasya yoniḥ (brahma)" — the Supreme Self alone is the cause of all shastras, including the Vedas; or (2) "śāstre yoniḥ yasya" — he for whom the shastras alone serve as the basis of being known. This is affirmed further in "tat tu samanvayāt" ("and this, from harmonious coherence [across scripture]").

### Page 425

This second meaning is the better-known one; the first is merely the general sense — it isn't especially significant to say the creator of the whole universe also created the shastras. What matters is that shastra be the sole reliable means for knowing such a being — this is Badarayana's real point. But if it's objected that, since many differing statements exist within the Veda itself, treating all shastras as pointing to the Supreme Self risks the Veda's own authority — this is answered by:

> "तत् तु समन्वयात्"
> "tat tu samanvayāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.4)
>
> "But that [Brahman as the unified meaning of all Vedantic texts] is established through their coherence/harmony."

The apparent mutual contradiction is not genuine — it only appears so on the surface; all seemingly conflicting statements must be harmonized as ultimately pointing to the Supreme Self. Indeed, most of the Brahma-sutras exist precisely to resolve such apparent contradictions. As the Nirukta states, for one unfamiliar with Mimamsa-shastra:

> "नैष स्थाणोर् अपराधो यद् एनम् अन्धो न शक्नोति"
> "naiṣa sthāṇor aparādho yad enam andho na śaknoti" (Nirukta, Naighantuka-kanda, Purvapada 1.1)
>
> "It is not the post's fault that a blind man cannot see it."

That is: if a blind man fails to see the tree-stump before him, the fault isn't the stump's — and likewise, it's only reasonable that someone unfamiliar with Purva-Mimamsa cannot grasp the Vedas' true meaning.

**The vidhi-portion's authority is now fully established. Turning to the second kind of Brahmana content — arthavāda —** the sage Jaimini takes great pains to establish its authority as well. The objection's opening sutra:

> "आम्नायस्य क्रियार्थत्वाद् आनर्थक्यम् अतदर्थानां तस्माद् अनित्यम् उच्यते"
> "āmnāyasya kriyārthatvād ānarthakyam atadarthānāṃ tasmād anityam ucyate" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.1)
>
> "Since revelation exists for the sake of ritual action, whatever doesn't relate to that action is meaningless — and is therefore called 'anitya' (non-eternal/non-authoritative)."

No genuine meaning could be intended for such statements — hence they're called "anitya." In this sense, they're "anitya" much like ordinary poetic statements.

### "Śāstra-dṛṣṭa-nirodhāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.2)

Sutra's meaning: since arthavādas contradict both shastra and direct experience, the arthavāda-portion is not authoritative.

Sutta's meaning: since arthavādas contradict both shastra and direct experience, the arthavāda-portion cannot be authoritative — this establishes a threefold taxonomy of contradiction found across various arthavāda passages, to be worked through with specific examples.

### Page 428

Statements like "so'rodīt" might lack authority regarding dharma-matters specifically, but their literal meaning must still be accepted as authoritative in itself — so one cannot claim they entirely lack authority. However, some arthavāda statements' meanings directly contradict perceptual and other proofs — such statements genuinely must be called unauthoritative, and on this basis, the next sutra argues for extending non-authority to all arthavādas.

**Three kinds of contradiction found in arthavādas, each illustrated:**

**Śāstra-virodha** (contradiction with shastra) — a view opposed to the Veda's own stated intent:

> स्तेनं मनः ।
> *stenaṃ manaḥ |*
> "The mind is a thief" — [continuing] "speech a teller of lies." One might wrongly conclude theft and lying are thereby permitted — directly contradicting the prohibitive shastra against theft and falsehood.

**Dṛṣṭi-virodha** (contradiction with direct experience):

> तस्माद्धूम एवाग्नेर्दिवा दृश्यते । नार्चिः । तस्मादर्चिरेवाग्नेर्नक्तं दृश्यते । न धूमः ॥
> *tasmād dhūma evāgner divā dṛśyate | nārciḥ | tasmād arcir evāgner naktaṃ dṛśyate | na dhūmaḥ ||* (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.6.1.4)
> "By day only smoke is seen, not flame; by night only flame is seen, not smoke" — contradicting our ordinary observation.

> न चैतद्विद्मो वयं ब्राह्मणा वा स्मोऽब्राह्मणा वा ॥
> *na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā ||* (Maitrayani Samhita 1.4.11)
> "We don't even know whether we are brahmins or not" — likewise contrary to experience.

**Śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodha** (undermining the Veda's own authority) — where one Vedic statement damages another's credibility:

> स्वर्गकामो यजेत ।
> *svargakāmo yajeta |*
> "One desiring heaven should perform yajna" — clearly asserting heaven's existence. Yet:

> को हि तद्वेद यद्यमुष्मिन् लोकेऽस्ति वा न वा ॥
> *ko hi tad veda yad yamuṣmin loke'sti vā na vā ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1.1)
> "Who indeed knows whether that [heavenly world] exists or not" — directly undermines the authority of the very statement promising heaven as yajna's reward.

**On the Purnahuti itself:** among the fire-offerings performed within Shrauta, Smarta, and Grihya rites, many "pradhana-homas" (principal offerings) are made to the yajna's chief deities. Afterward, "prayashchitta-homas" (expiatory offerings) remedy any lapses, followed by the "srishtikrit" offering, and finally the "Purnahuti" — the very last oblation of the sequence.

**A digression on yajna classification, for context:** Sayanacharya's introduction and commentary cites many portions from Mimamsa texts throughout — properly following these arguments requires familiarity with yajnas, so a brief technical outline follows here.

Vedic yajnas are of two kinds: **(1) Shrauta-yajna** and **(2) Grihya-yajna**. Taking Grihya-yajnas first — also called **Pakayajnas** — their procedures are described across various Grihya-sutras, using the fire called "Grihyagni." Pakayajnas exist in seven varieties (samsthas) across all traditions — no more, no less:

**Per the Gobhila Brahmana (1.4.3):**
1. सायंप्रातर्होम (*Sāyaṃprātar-homa*) 2. स्थालीपाक (*Sthālīpāka*) 3. नवयज्ञ (*Navayajña*) 4. बलि/वैश्वदेवबलि (*Bali*/*Vaiśvadeva-bali*) 5. पितृयज्ञ (*Pitṛyajña*) 6. अष्टक (*Aṣṭaka*) 7. पशु (*Paśu*)

**Per the Gautama Dharmasutra (1.8.10):**
1. अष्टक (*Aṣṭaka*) 2. पार्वण (*Pārvaṇa*) 3. श्राद्ध/मासिकश्राद्ध (*Śrāddha*/*Māsika-śrāddha*) 4. श्रावणी (*Śrāvaṇī*) 5. आग्रहायणी (*Āgrahāyaṇī*) 6. चैत्री (*Caitrī*) 7. आश्वयुजी (*Āśvayujī*)

**Per Dhurtasvami's commentary on the Apastamba Yajna-paribhasha-sutra:**
1. औपासनहोम (*Aupāsana-homa*) 2. वैश्वदेव (*Vaiśvadeva*) 3. पार्वण (*Pārvaṇa*) 4. अष्टक (*Aṣṭaka*) 5. मासिश्राद्ध (*Māsi-śrāddha*) 6. सर्पबलि (*Sarpa-bali*) 7. ईशानबलि/शूलगव (*Īśāna-bali*/*Śūlagava*)

Pakayajnas differ according to each branch's own tradition. Among Shrauta-yajnas too, there are two kinds: Soma-yajnas (using Soma-juice for homas) and Havir-yajnas (using ordinary havis). Soma-yajnas were briefly introduced earlier (page 416).

**हविर्यज्ञ (Havir-yajña)** number seven across all traditions — no disagreement on the count, though which specific rites are included varies by school:

**(1) Per Sayanacharya's own Aitareya-Brahmana-bhashya (2.1):**
अग्न्याधेय (*Agnyādheya*), अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), दर्शपूर्णमास (*Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*), आग्रयण (*Āgrayaṇa*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), दाक्षायणयज्ञ (*Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña*), कौण्डपायिनायन/सौत्रामणि (*Kauṇḍapāyina-māyana* or *Sautrāmaṇi*)

**(2) Per Dhurtasvami's Yajna-paribhasha-sutra commentary:**
अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), दर्शपूर्णमास (*Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*), आग्रयण (*Āgrayaṇa*), पिण्डपितृयज्ञ (*Piṇḍa-pitṛyajña*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), निरूढपशुबन्ध (*Nirūḍha-paśubandha*), सौत्रामणि (*Sautrāmaṇi*)

**(3) Per the Gautama Dharmasutra (8.20):**
अग्न्याधेय (*Agnyādheya*), अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), दर्शपूर्णमास (*Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*), आग्रयण (*Āgrayaṇa*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), निरूढपशुबन्ध (*Nirūḍha-paśubandha*), सौत्रामणि (*Sautrāmaṇi*)

**(4) Per the Gobhila Brahmana (1.4.2):**
अग्न्याधेय (*Agnyādheya*), अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), पौर्णमासी (*Pūrṇamāsī*), अमावास्या (*Amāvāsyā*), नवेष्टि (*Naveṣṭi*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), पशुबन्ध (*Paśubandha*)

**On the दर्शपूर्णमासेष्टि (Darsha-Purnamasa-iṣṭis)** — performed at new moon and full moon, called "**इष्टि**" (*iṣṭi*) — these form the structural foundation for all other iṣṭis, identical in both ritual technique (tantra) and essential form. The main offering-substance for the **पुरोडाश** (*puroḍāśa*) is wheat, made into flour and baked to become "puroḍāśa," prepared separately in earthen-dish fragments called "**कपाल**" (*kapāla*). The first homa addresses Agni: the puroḍāśa baked in eight kapalas ("**आग्नेयमष्टाकपालम्**" *āgneyam aṣṭākapālam*) is offered. The second homa addresses Agni and Soma jointly: the puroḍāśa in eleven kapalas ("**आग्नीषोमीयमेकादशकपालम्**" *āgnīṣomīyam ekādaśakapālam*) is offered. Different deities correspondingly require different numbers of kapalas.

### Page 434

These ishtis require four priests: **(1) अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu)** — performs all the technical/procedural work; **(2) होतृ (Hotṛ)** — recites mantras and invites the deities; **(3) ब्रह्मा (Brahmā)** — oversees the correct performance of the above two; **(4) आग्नीध्र (Āgnīdhra)** — Brahma's assistant.

The rites described so far occur on the new-moon or full-moon day itself, but preliminary rites are performed the day before: in the morning, the **अग्न्याधान (Agnyādhāna)** rite (placing kindling in the Garhapatya, Ahavaniya, and Dakshinagni fires with mantras); then the yajamana is ritually shaved, eats purified food, and, standing near the three fire-pits, takes certain vows (**व्रतग्रहण** *Vratagrahaṇa*) — after which he is considered "dīkṣā-bound." That night, both he and his wife (also diksha-bound) must remain within the sacrificial hall; the yaga proper begins the following morning.

After the Agnihotra: **(1)** priest-selection (**ऋत्विग्वरण** *Ṛtvigvaraṇa*); then, for minor deities' favor, the **प्रयाज (Prayāja)** rites (subsidiary to the main act); **(2)** one Ajya-homa (ghee-offering) each to Agni and Soma; **(3)** the puroḍāśa offered first to Agni (eight kapalas), then jointly to Agni-Soma (eleven kapalas) — the yajna's central act. Between these two, a softly-recited Ajya-homa to Agni-Soma jointly is called **उपांशुयाग (Upāṃśu-yāga)**; **(4)** the **सुहुतकृत्/शिष्टकृत् (Śiṣṭikṛt)** rite, offering the remainder of the puroḍāśa already used; **(5)** finally, the **अनुयाज (Anuyāja)s** — homas addressing three [further] deities.

### पूर्णाहुति (Pūrṇāhuti)

The final, principal offering made at the close of the Agnyadhana is called **Pūrṇāhuti**. Agnyadhana is also called **अग्न्याधेय (Agnyādheya)** — meaning the establishing or consecration of fire within the sacrificial hall. This Shrauta-fire consecration [is undertaken by] a householder [following his] marriage...

### Page 435

The main ritual act one gains the right to perform only after undertaking householder-life (**गार्हस्थ्य** *gārhasthya*) requires establishing three fires: **गार्हपत्य (Gārhapatya)**, **आहवनीय (Āhavanīya)**, and **दक्षिणाग्नि (Dakṣiṇāgni)**.

A square platform is built in the middle of the yajna-hall — to its west, a long rectangular pit for the Garhapatya-fire; to its east, a circular pit for the Ahavaniya-fire; to its south, a semicircular pit for the Dakshinagni-fire. The Garhapatya represents the yajamāna himself (as "**गृहपति**" *gṛhapati*, household-master); the Ahavaniya belongs to the deities, so all deity-offerings must be made there; other homas use the Dakshinagni.

**Preliminary rites the day before:** the Adhvaryu brings fire from a fixed source into the Garhapatya-pit. The yajamāna, with his wife, enters the yajna-hall that evening and keeps vigil through the night — solely to keep the Garhapatya-fire burning, continually feeding it kindling.

**The next morning**, fire is newly produced through "**अग्निमन्थन**" (*Agni-manthana*, fire-churning), with a horse readied for the occasion. The Adhvaryu ignites a stick from this new fire and places it in the Garhapatya-pit while the Brahma priest performs the Sama-chant. A procession then forms: the Adhvaryu carrying fire leads, the horse follows, then the yajamāna. The horse, facing west, places one leg into the Ahavaniya-pit; the Adhvaryu touches the fire to the horse's foot before placing it in the pit. He then carries fire once more from the Garhapatya into the Dakshinagni-pit. Everyone circumambulates the fires, and the horse is released.

**This is the moment of Pūrṇāhuti.** Ghee is melted over the Garhapatya-fire; the Adhvaryu, using a wooden ladle called "**जुहू**" (*juhū*), offers it into the Ahavaniya-fire while reciting Yajus mantras — further mantras follow with further offerings. Since the Adhvaryu performs this homa on the yajamāna's behalf, the yajamāna touches the Adhvaryu throughout. This final offering is what's called **Pūrṇāhuti** — the last act of the Agnyadhana rite. Even after this yajna concludes, the yajamāna must remain bound by certain observances for some further days. In this yajna...

### Page 436

The Garhapatya-fire must never go out, day or night — this rule doesn't apply to the other two fires. Every householder must perform this Agnyadhana; one who completes it properly is called **"Āhitāgni"** (one who has established the fire) — a status required before any other Shrauta yajna can be undertaken. Purnahuti is the final act of Agnyadhana as described, though two differing views exist on whether Agnyadhana properly concludes with a homa or with an ishti.

### Agnihotra

Every householder who is an Ahitagni must perform this rite daily. In the morning, addressing the Sun-deity, one recites—

> ॐ भूर्भुवस्स्वः । ॐ सूर्यो ज्योतिर्ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा ।
> *oṃ bhūr bhuvas svaḥ | oṃ sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā |*

—and offers a homa in the Ahavaniya-fire, using milk as the offering-substance — heated in an earthen vessel over the Garhapatya-fire, then offered using wooden spoons: a small "**स्रुव**" (*sruva*), and a larger "**अग्निहोत्रहवनी**" (*agnihotra-havanī*). Four or five sruva-dips of milk are transferred into the larger spoon for offering.

The Garhapatya-fire must always stay lit. The yajamāna, with his wife, enters the fire-hall and lights the Ahavaniya and Dakshinagni from it, offers a kindling-stick homa in the Ahavaniya, and then, once consumed, offers two milk-portions with the agnihotra-havani spoon — the first addressing the Sun (with mantra), the second addressing Prajapati (without mantra). He then similarly offers two milk-portions in the Garhapatya (for Agni-Grihapati, then Prajapati) and two more in the Dakshinagni (for Agni-Annapati, then Prajapati). The heated milk isn't offered undivided; the leftover portion is consumed by the yajamāna himself.

The evening rite follows the same structure, but addresses Agni instead of Surya, with the mantra—

> अग्निर्ज्योतिर्ज्योतिरग्निः स्वाहा ।
> *agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā |*

—the evening Agnihotra must be performed at sunset...

### पशुबन्ध (Paśubandha, or निरूढपशुबन्ध Nirūḍha-Paśubandha)

Among the many animal-sacrifice varieties, one is obligatory: the **निरूढपशुबन्ध (Nirūḍha-Paśubandha)**, performed on the rainy season's full-moon or new-moon day (some hold it should instead fall at the winter/summer Sankranti transitions). Six priests officiate: अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu), होतृ (Hotṛ), ब्रह्मा (Brahmā), आग्नीध्र (Āgnīdhra, Brahma's assistant), प्रतिप्रस्थाता (Pratiprasthātā, Adhvaryu's assistant), and मैत्रावरुण (Maitrāvaruṇa, Hotr's assistant).

As in the ishtis, a platform is built; east of the Ahavaniya-pit, at a slight distance, a further platform called "**पशुक** (*Pāśuka*)" is constructed, atop which a smaller platform, "**उत्तरवेदि** (*Uttaravedi*)," is built. A pole (**यूप** *Yūpa*) is planted one cubit into the ground there, to which the sacrificial animal is tied. Numerous small mantric acts follow. Before the main homa, several "**प्रयाज** (*Prayāja*)" offerings are performed, each accompanied by its own "**आप्री** (*Āprī*)" hymn of praise.

The main homa follows immediately, dedicated to **इन्द्र (Indra)** and **अग्नि (Agni)**. The animal's fat and other portions are consecrated with mantras; the Adhvaryu offers the puroḍāśa and fat as homa, while the Maitravaruna and Hotr recite the appropriate Anuvaka-verses and "**याज्या** (*Yājyā*)" mantras respectively. An offering to please Agni ("**रुद्र** *Rudra*" in this ritual context) follows — the **शिष्टिकृत्-होम (Śiṣṭikṛt-homa)** — then "**इडाभक्षण** (*Iḍā-bhakṣaṇa*)," the partaking of the leftover offering ("iḍā") by the yajamāna, priests, and all present.

This completes the yajna's central portion, though further minor acts remain before the rite concludes properly: the "**अनुयाज** (*Anuyāja*)" offerings (using curd-mixed grain as the substance, honoring eleven deities), followed by the "**उपयाज** (*Upayāja*)" — the Adhvaryu's assistant, the Pratiprasthata, offering the animal's meat without mantra-recitation — performed only in animal-sacrifice yajnas specifically.

### "Abhāgi-pratiṣedhāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.5)

> न पृथिव्याम् अग्निश् चेतव्यो नान्तरिक्षे न दिवीत्य् एतस्य च दिवि प्रतिषेध-भागित्वं नास्ति । तत्र चयनस्य कृनगस्याभावात् । मा भूत्य् अर्षि निषेधानां प्रामाण्यं । बबरः प्रावाहणेर् अमयतेऽस्मायशऋचादीनां पूर्व-पुरुषन्यत्तन्ताभिधायिनाम् निरोधानुपलम्भाद् अस्तु प्रामाण्यम् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> na pṛthivyām agniś cetavyo nāntarikṣe na divīty etasya ca divi pratiṣedha-bhāgitvaṃ nāsti | tatra cayanasya kṛnagasyābhāvāt | mā bhūty arṣi niṣedhānāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇer amayate'smāyaśaṛcādīnāṃ pūrva-puruṣanyattantābhidhāyinām nirodhānupalambhād astu prāmāṇyam ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> *(Introducing the objection that certain arthavada prohibitions apply to circumstances that could never actually occur — e.g., a rule against building a fire-altar "in the sky" makes no sense, since no one would ever attempt to build a sacrificial fire-altar in the sky in the first place. Such prohibitions, having nothing genuine to prohibit, are argued to be purposeless, extending the charge of non-authority even to the prohibitive class of arthavada statements.)*

Sutra's meaning: since the prohibitive statements found within arthavāda address situations that could never arise, arthavāda is not authoritative on these grounds either.

Granting, as the previous sutras argued, that fruit-promising statements lack authority — this same flaw shouldn't extend to prohibitive statements, since no view anywhere opposes them; one might therefore argue prohibitive arthavadas at least remain authoritative. Anticipating this, the objector raises a further point: since prohibitions address impossible situations, they too serve no purpose. The Taittiriya Samhita contains a statement regarding fire-altar construction (agni-chayana) — declaring that fire should not be established "on earth," "in the atmosphere," or "in the sky"...

> In the arthavada "na prithivyam agnis chetavyo nantarikshe na divi" there is no room for the prohibition as regards the mid-heaven or the sky. For the act forbidden to be done there, the raising an altar for the sacrificial fire, could not in any case be done in either of these two places.

...a falcon-shaped altar is customarily constructed (in the Agni-chayana rite) — this Soma-related form being a portion of Prajapati, whom the rite addresses. The fire is established upon a golden plate (symbolizing the Sun), atop which a human-shaped golden image (representing Prajapati) is set, surrounded by layered bricks ("svayamātṛṇṇāḥ") thought to occupy the positions of earth, atmosphere, and sky — the whole rite depicting the creation of the universe, with the yajamāna coming to feel unity with Prajapati and the mantra-invoked deities.

Very well, let prohibitive statements lack authority — but surely narrative statements like "Pravāhaṇa's son sought out Babara" carry no such doubt, containing only a sage's own historical account with no contradictory content at all? Anticipating this defense, the next sutra follows.

### The Siddhāntin's Resolution Begins

> "विधिना त्व् एक-वाक्यत्वात् स्तुत्यर्थेन विधीनां स्युः"
> "vidhinā tv eka-vākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.7)
>
> "But since arthavādas form a single syntactical unit together with their corresponding vidhi, they must be understood as existing to praise those very vidhis."

> तुशब्दोऽर्थवादानाम् अप्रामाण्यं वारयति । वायुर् वै क्षेपिष्ठा देवता वायव्यं श्वेतम् आलभेत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित २.१.१[?]) इत्य् आदिना विधिना सैकवाक्यत्वाद् धर्मे प्रामाण्यम् । न च विधि-वाक्य-स्यार्थ-वादात् नैः सर्वे क्षेत्रण सदास्ति-यसंपूर्के स्तार्थ-वादानां नास्त्येक-योग इति शङ्कनीयम् । तेष्व् अर्थ-वादानां पुरुष-प्रवृत्ति-मात्र-कांक्षतां विधीनां स्तुत्यर्थ-स्येनोपयुक्ताः स्युः । स्तुत्या च पुरुष-प्रवृत्ति-श्रवण । तेनार्थ-वादानां प्रमाद-शमिते-क्षेपाणीय-क्त्वा तस्मिन् एवैकवाक्यता-प्रत्य् आसत्वाच्-छन्क्य्-अकः ॥
> tuśabdo'rthavādānām aprāmāṇyaṃ vārayati | vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta (Taittiriya Samhita 2.1.1[?]) ity ādinā vidhinā saikavākyatvād dharme prāmāṇyam | na ca vidhi-vākya-syārtha-vādāt naiḥ sarve kṣetraṇa sadāsti-yasaṃpūrke stārtha-vādānāṃ nāstyeka-yoga iti śaṅkanīyam | teṣv artha-vādānāṃ puruṣa-pravṛtti-mātra-kāṃkṣatāṃ vidhīnāṃ stutyartha-syenopayuktāḥ syuḥ | stutyā ca puruṣa-pravṛtti-śravaṇa | tenārtha-vādānāṃ pramāda-śamite-kṣepāṇīya-ktvā tasmin evaikavākyatā-praty āsatvāc-chanky-akaḥ ||
>
> *(This dense commentary establishes: since arthavādas are grammatically and syntactically bound to the vidhi-statement they accompany — forming one continuous unit of meaning — the entire combined statement takes on the vidhi's own authority. The arthavāda's role is specifically to encourage a person's motivation to act on the injunction, through praise, and this "praise function" is what grants it derivative authority — not any standalone claim to convey new facts.)*

Sutta's meaning: arthavādas exist to praise the very meaning conveyed by vidhi-statements — this is the point of censuring them independently. Since one accepts the objector's own earlier concession that vidhi-statements are proven authoritative through the sutras, that same authority extends here: the very first sutra, "vidhinā tv eka-vākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ," establishes that both vidhi and arthavāda together form a single grammatical unit — and, being one unit, the arthavādas relevant portions in the current discussion are themselves praise-statements strengthening the vidhi's own force.

The word "**tu**" ("but") in this sutra rejects the objection's claim of arthavāda's non-authority. It is not correct that "stenaṃ manaḥ" and similar statements become inauthoritative through shastra-contradiction — since they say nothing about actual yajna performance at all. Shastra-contradiction would arise only if theft were being literally prescribed for performance; nowhere does this happen — only the literal word-meaning of "theft" occurs, without any action-oriented sense. Since the mere presence of this word produces no genuine shastra-contradiction, this arthavāda retains its authority.

**A further, genuinely subtle objection now arises:** granting that arthavādas exist to praise vidhis — forming, together, one complete sentence — surely the vidhi-portion alone should be accepted as authoritative, while the arthavāda-portion, addressing an entirely *different* subject, cannot be? Consider:

> "वेतस-शाखया चावकाभिश् चाग्निं विकर्ष्यापो वै शान्ताः"
> "vetasa-śākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣyāpo vai śāntāḥ"

Here, "vetasa-śākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣati" ("one draws away the fire using branches of the vetasa and avaka plants") is the vidhi-portion. "Āpo vai śāntāḥ" ("waters indeed possess a calm nature") is a separate statement. What connection does water's calm nature have with extinguishing fire using plant-branches? Given such apparently unrelated subject-matter combined within a single vidhi-arthavāda passage, how can we accept its authority as a unified whole? — This is the objection. The resolution is given in the next sutra.

### Page 445

Sutra's meaning: in such statements, one portion states a quality belonging to what the other portion describes — so the two portions of the statement do share a genuine mutual connection. The word "tu" (but) resolves the flaw of "vaiyadhikaraṇya" (mismatched subject-matter) — where a vidhi addresses one thing and its arthavāda seems to address another entirely. As in ordinary life: "when Kashmir is praised, Devadatta, native to Kashmir, considers himself praised too" — likewise, praising "waters are calm" implicitly praises the vetasa and avaka plants growing in that water, since they share water's calm nature and thereby pacify misfortune for the yajamāna. Stating this shared quality is the arthavāda's whole purpose.

> so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam | yad apkṣīyata kad rajataṃ hiraṇyam abhavat svāpkarjataṃ hiraṇyam adakṣiṇam utpṛjad ghi yo barhiṣi dadāti purastāt saṃvatsarād dhy e rudanti tasmād barhiṣi na deyam || (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.1)
>
> सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् । यद् अपक्षीयत तद् रजतं हिरण्यम् अभवत् स्वापकर्जतं हिरण्यम् अदक्षिणम् । उत्पृज्य हि यो बर्हिषि ददाति पुरस्तात् संवत्सराद् अस्य रुदन्ति तस्माद् बर्हिषि न देयम् ॥
> *so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam | yad apakṣīyata tad rajataṃ hiraṇyam abhavat svāpakarjataṃ hiraṇyam adakṣiṇam | utpṛjya hi yo barhiṣi dadāti purastāt saṃvatsarād asya rudanti tasmād barhiṣi na deyam ||*
>
> "He wept; because he wept, that is Rudra's own 'Rudra-ness.' What flowed out [from his weeping] became silver-gold; silver-gold is therefore not fit as a sacrificial fee. For whoever, discarding [this warning], gives it upon the sacrificial grass — within that year, there is weeping in his household. Therefore it should not be given upon the sacrificial grass."

**This is the resolution.** The corresponding **vidhi** (injunction) here simply states: silver should not be given as the priest's fee at a sacrifice. The "Rudra wept" narrative is an **arthavāda** built entirely to reinforce that one rule — deriving the god Rudra's name from the root for "weeping," and then figuratively tying that weeping to silver ("what flowed from his tears became silver"). The intended, purely figurative point is simple: if silver is given as payment, there will be "weeping" — misfortune — in that household within the year. Sayana states plainly that there is **no literal truth** in the story that Rudra's tears turned into silver; the narrative exists solely to emphasize and recommend the vidhi against paying priests in silver, through a vivid, memorable etymological pun.

That is: "He (Rudra) wept — that is, cried. Because he wept, he came to be named 'Rudra.' The tears that fell from him became silver. Having now shown resolutions to the shastra-contradiction cases, we turn to those raised as contradicting direct sense-perception: "stenaṃ manaḥ, anṛtavādinī vāk" — and a further doubt about how arthavāda statements' apparent absurdity should be resolved is addressed via the next sutra.

### "Rūpasattvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.11)

> हिरण्यं हस्ते भवत्य् अथ गृह्णाति त्यकं विधिः स्तोकमयम् अर्थवाद उच्यते । यथा लोके किम् पुरुषा देवदत्त एव । पूज्यते इव? देव-दत्ते पूज्यमाने पूज्यं स्वयम् इत्य् उच्यते ।

>
> *(Introducing a new sutra concerned with arthavāda passages whose surface form appears to contradict what we plainly observe — here, gold "being in the hand" before the priest actually grasps it — resolved by recognizing this as ordinary hyperbolic emphasis, the same way one might say "isn't Devadatta the only person who matters" without literally denying every other person exists.)*

Sutra's meaning: statements whose surface appearance seems inconsistent [with reality], being simply common usage, must be understood as intending an emphatic (exaggerated) sense — not as literal factual claims.

As with the earlier examples ("stenaṃ manaḥ, anṛtavādinī vāk"), this next arthavāda-statement is used only to encourage a person toward what's genuinely worth pursuing — not to convey a literal factual claim. Gold [in the phrase] "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavati"...

### Page 449

We now explain the arthavāda praising the vidhi "haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" (Taittiriya Samhita 4.7.3.1). "Kiṃ puruṣā devadatta eva pūjyāḥ" ("What! Is Devadatta the only person worthy of honor?") — such an expression doesn't imply others aren't worthy; it exists solely to *emphasize* Devadatta's own worthiness. Likewise, "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" ("gold comes to be in the hand, then he grasps it") — this arthavāda praises the vidhi that gold should be taken as sacrificial fee, by declaring gold's own preciousness.

In the same way, "stenaṃ manaḥ" ("the mind is a thief") should be read figuratively: thieves remain hidden and unseen; the mind too stays hidden within the body, unseen. Since concealment is a shared quality between thieves and the mind, the mind is compared to a thief — stating this figurative sense is exactly this statement's purpose.

Likewise, "anṛtavādinī vāk" ("speech is a false-speaker"): since speech is commonly observed, in ordinary human life, to speak falsely, one must grasp the figurative sense here too, setting aside a literal reading. As for "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" — that gold visibly sits in the hand is plain to everyone, not hidden or false at all; this arthavāda's purpose is simply to praise the vidhi by declaring gold worth wearing on the hand.

**On these falsehood-statements, the Taittiriya Brahmana adds:**

> अनृतं वै वाचा वदति । अनृतं मनसा ध्यायति । चक्षुर् वै सत्यम् । अद्या हि घृताह अदर्शम् इति । सत्यैव ॥
> anṛtaṃ vai vācā vadati | anṛtaṃ manasā dhyāyati | cakṣur vai satyam | adyā hi ghṛtāha adarśam iti | satyaiva || (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.1.4)
>
> "Speech indeed speaks falsehood; the mind indeed dwells on falsehood — but the eye is indeed truthful, for when one says 'I saw [it] today,' that itself is truth."

### Page 450

A sentence carries two kinds of meaning: one, the direct meaning conveyed by the words themselves — "the fire burns"; another, a further meaning conveyed indirectly through that literal sense as a stepping-stone — the "secondary meaning" (gauṇārtha), as in "Devadatta burns like fire," where "burning" must be reinterpreted (through anger, desire, etc.) to fit Devadatta sensibly. The first is the primary meaning; the second, the secondary meaning — meaning derived by pointing at a shared quality.

Having thus resolved the shastra-contradiction objection, we turn to the dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction with direct perception) examples — statements like "bhūmā vāgnir dinā dṛśye" (only smoke, not flame, is visible by day) — addressed in the next sutra.

### "Dūra-bhūyastvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.12)

> अग्निर् ज्योतिर् ज्योतिर् अग्निः स्वाहा सायं जुहोति । सूर्यो ज्योतिर् ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा प्रातर् इत्य् एतौ विधी स्तोतुं सोऽर्थवादः । यस्माद् अर्चिर् दिना न दृश्ये तस्मात् केषां प्रयोक्ष्ये यस्माद् रात्रौ प्रयोक्ष्ये इत्य् एतं तयोर् मन्त्रयोः स्मृतिः क तस्माद् अग्नि-मन्त्रेण रात्रौ प्रयोक्ष्य इति । भूमार्चिस् सोमदर्शनोऽस्य प्राप्तिः । भूम्या दूर-भूयस्य गुणस्य विशिष्टे । भूम्य् असि हि दूरे पर्येऽग्न्येर् वैश्वादयोऽपि न विशिष्ट्या दृश्यन्ते । किं तु कृष्णा-दृश्येन तेषां दर्शनाभाव एव ।
> agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā sāyaṃ juhoti | sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā prātar ity etau vidhī stotuṃ so'rthavādaḥ | yasmād arcir dinā na dṛśye tasmāt keṣāṃ prayokṣye yasmād rātrau prayokṣye ity etaṃ tayor mantrayoḥ smṛtiḥ ka tasmād agni-mantreṇa rātrau prayokṣya iti | bhūmārcis somadarśano'sya prāptiḥ | bhūmyā dūra-bhūyasya guṇasya viśiṣṭe | bhūmy asi hi dūre parye'gnyer vaiśvādayo'pi na viśiṣṭyā dṛśyante | kiṃ tu kṛṣṇā-dṛśyena teṣāṃ darśanābhāva eva |
>
> अग्निर् ज्योतिर् ज्योतिर् अग्निः स्वाहा सायं जुहोति । सूर्यो ज्योतिर् ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा प्रातर् इत्य् एतौ विधी स्तोतुं सोऽर्थवादः । यस्माद् अर्चिर् दिना न दृश्ये तस्मात् केषां प्रयोक्ष्ये । यस्माद् रात्रौ प्रयोक्ष्ये इत्य् एतम् उभयोः मन्त्रयोः स्मरणं । तस्माद् अग्नि-मन्त्रेण रात्रौ प्रयोक्तव्य इति । भूयांश् चर्चिषो दर्शनम् अस्य प्राप्तिः । भूम्या दूर-भूयस्त्व-गुणस्य विशेषः । भूम्यां हि दूरे पर्य् अग्नेर् वैश्वादयोऽपि न विशेषेण दृश्यन्ते । किं तु कृष्णा-दृश्यत्वेन तेषां दर्शनाभाव एव ।
> *agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā sāyaṃ juhoti | sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā prātar ity etau vidhī stotuṃ so'rthavādaḥ | yasmād arcir dinā na dṛśye tasmāt keṣāṃ prayokṣye | yasmād rātrau prayokṣye ity etam ubhayoḥ mantrayoḥ smaraṇaṃ | tasmād agni-mantreṇa rātrau prayoktavya iti | bhūyāṃś carciṣo darśanam asya prāptiḥ | bhūmyā dūra-bhūyastva-guṇasya viśeṣaḥ | bhūmyāṃ hi dūre pary agner vaiśvādayo'pi na viśeṣeṇa dṛśyante | kiṃ tu kṛṣṇā-dṛśyatvena teṣāṃ darśanābhāva eva |*
>
> "'Agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā' [is offered] in the evening; 'sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā' [is offered] in the morning — this arthavāda exists to praise these two vidhis. Since flame is not visible by day, [one might ask] for what purpose should I use [the fire-mantra then]? — and since [it should be] used at night, this itself is the recollection [rationale] behind the two mantras: therefore the Agni-mantra must be used at night. The greater visibility of the flame [at night] is what's actually being conveyed — a distinction owing to the sheer distance [between earth and the visible daytime sky-glow]. For at a distance, in daylight, even conspicuous things like [smoke and] fire's other features are not seen distinctly — not because they don't exist, but simply because their dark-visible quality goes unseen [against the bright sky]."

Sutra's meaning: the "smoke by day, flame by night" arthavāda isn't a false claim about physical reality — it explains, and thereby reinforces, exactly which mantra (Sun or Agni) belongs to which time of day, with the visibility difference serving as a memorable, praise-oriented justification rather than a literal scientific claim.

### Page 451

These are the two vidhis this arthavāda exists to praise. Since flame isn't visible by day, the sun-mantra suits the morning; since flame alone is visible at night, the fire-mantra suits the night — "day, the sun-mantra" is the praise these vidhis (mantras) receive.

The objection held this contradicts direct perception — flame *is* visible before our eyes, so how can the text say otherwise? The resolution: if a fire burns at a distance during daylight, the sun's superior brightness prevents the flame from being visible — only the dark smoke registers. This is confirmed by ordinary experience: with sufficient distance, even trees atop a hill lose their distinct shape and look like mere blades of grass. The same principle applies here.

> *striyā aparādho bhavati tatra kartur utpādayitur jārasyāpi putro dṛśyate | ataḥ patyupapatyor ubhayoḥ putra-darśanāt kīdṛśyam jyāyasa idṛśam iti durjñānam | anenābhiprāyeṇa prayuktāv na asti tatra dṛṣṭi-virodhaḥ | na hi tatra dṛśyamānaṃ sva-brāhmaṇyam apahriyata iva "na caitad vidmaḥ" ity asatya-sattvam |*
>
> "Where a woman commits an offense [of infidelity], the son may be seen to belong to her actual paramour, the true begetter. Therefore, given the possibility of the son belonging to either the husband or the paramour, which of the two is genuinely the case remains difficult to know with certainty. Understood with this intent, no contradiction with direct perception arises here — for one's own visible brahmin-status isn't thereby actually denied; the statement 'we do not know this' does not assert something false."

Sutra's meaning: because of a woman's infidelity, a son born [to her] might in fact be her lover's son (rather than her husband's) — therefore that son's true lineage cannot be determined with full certainty.

The statement "na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā" ("we don't know whether we are brahmins or not") is spoken by the officiating priests — who are, by definition, always brahmins. So why would doubt about one's own brahmin-status even arise? Isn't everyone supposed to simply know their own caste? The resolution: in ordinary human affairs, when a son is born, whom does he properly belong to — mother or father? A son always belongs to the father (not the mother), and it is well-established, both by common recognition and by shastra, that a son belongs to whichever caste his father belongs to. But in some cases, through a mother's infidelity, the son born to her may in fact have been fathered by her lover — in which case, though publicly treated as his legal father's son, he is, in strict truth, the lover's son, and takes the lover's own caste. Such situations are not at all uncommon in ordinary life. Therefore, as stated above, genuine doubt can arise even regarding whether "we" (the officiants) are truly brahmins — and this example is accordingly classified as a case of dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction with direct perception).

### Page 453

"Pravare pravriyamāṇe brūyād devāḥ pitaraḥ" (Vajasaneyi Samhita 1.4.11) is the vidhi: when reciting one's pravara (ancestral lineage), one should recite the mantra "devāḥ pitaraḥ." If the yajamāna does so, then even a non-brahmin becomes a brahmin through that mantra's power — this is the praise conveyed. The admission "na caitad vidma" ("we do not know") isn't a firm claim of ignorance, but a statement that certainty is genuinely unattainable: where a woman has erred, her son may in fact be her lover's child; since he is then socially treated as son to both the husband and the lover, whose son he truly is remains genuinely unclear — hence no contradiction with direct perception. "Na caitad vidma" is not meant to deny one's own plainly-evident brahmin status.

**Having resolved dṛṣṭi-virodha, we turn to the shastra-contradiction example still outstanding:** "ko hi tad veda yad yamuṣmin loke'sti vā na vā" ("who indeed knows whether that heavenly world exists or not"). The next sutra resolves this doubt.

### "Ākālikeṣṭā" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.14)

> दिक्षाश् चीकास्थानश् चास्थंश द्वार-विधिः । तस्य शेषोऽयं को हि तद् वेदेति । धूमाद्य्-अप्रद्रवस-परिकरेण प्रत्यक्षेण फलेन द्वार-विधिः स्तूयते । स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिरूपं तु फलम् आकालिकम् । अकाले भवम् आकालिकम् । विप्रुष्टकालीनं न त्रिदानीम्-तनम् इत्य् अर्थः । तस्येष्टा प्राप्तिम् इच्छा । सा च को हि तद् वेदेत्य् अज्ञयोऽस्थानस्य कारणम् । यथा भाविकालिकः पौत्र प्रसौत्रादि त्वं को निश्चेतुं शक्नुते । तद्वत् स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिर् भाविकालीनेत्य् गुण-योगाद् इष्टयोपस्थिते इष्टाभिप्रायः ।
> dikṣāś cīkāsthānaś cāsthaṃśa dvāra-vidhiḥ | tasya śeṣo'yaṃ ko hi tad vedeti | dhūmādy-apradravasa-parikareṇa pratyakṣeṇa phalena dvāra-vidhiḥ stūyate | svarga-prāptirūpaṃ tu phalam ākālikam | akāle bhavam ākālikam | vipruṣṭakālīnaṃ na tridānīm-tanam ity arthaḥ | tasyeṣṭā prāptim icchā | sā ca ko hi tad vedety ajñayo'sthānasya kāraṇam | yathā bhāvikālikaḥ pautra prasautrādi tvaṃ ko niścetuṃ śaknute | tadvat svarga-prāptir bhāvikālīnety guṇa-yogād iṣṭayopasthite iṣṭābhiprāyaḥ |
>
> दिक्ष्वातिकासन-करोति द्वार-विधिः । तस्य शेषोऽयं "को हि तद् वेद" इति । धूमाद्य्-अप्रदृश्य-सापरिकरेण प्रत्यक्षेण फलेन द्वार-विधिः स्तूयते । स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिरूपं तु फलम् आकालिकम् । अकाले भवम् आकालिकम् । विप्ररुष्ट-कालीनं न तद्-इदानीम्-तनम् इत्य् अर्थः । तस्येष्टा प्राप्तिम् इच्छा । सा च "को हि तद् वेद" इत्य् अज्ञान-वचन-कारणम् । यथा भावि-कालिकः पौत्र-प्रपौत्रादि-भावः को निश्चेतुं शक्नोति । तद्वत् स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिर् भावि-कालीनेत्य् अत्र गुण-योगाद् इष्टवती उपस्थितेत्य् अभिप्रायः ।
> *dikṣvātikāsana-karoti dvāra-vidhiḥ | tasya śeṣo'yaṃ "ko hi tad veda" iti | dhūmādy-apradṛśya-sāparikareṇa pratyakṣeṇa phalena dvāra-vidhiḥ stūyate | svarga-prāptirūpaṃ tu phalam ākālikam | akāle bhavam ākālikam | vipraruṣṭa-kālīnaṃ na tad-idānīm-tanam ity arthaḥ | tasyeṣṭā prāptim icchā | sā ca "ko hi tad veda" ity ajñāna-vacana-kāraṇam | yathā bhāvi-kālikaḥ pautra-prapautrādi-bhāvaḥ ko niścetuṃ śaknoti | tadvat svarga-prāptir bhāvi-kālīnety atra guṇa-yogād iṣṭavatī upasthitety abhiprāyaḥ |*
>
> "'Dikṣvātikāsana-karoti' is the 'dvāra' (doorway) vidhi [performed] on the east side [of the altar]. 'Ko hi tad veda' ('who indeed knows this') is the arthavāda completing that vidhi. The dvāra-vidhi is praised through an immediately observable result, involving smoke and similar visible signs. But the fruit in the form of attaining heaven belongs to a *future* time. 'Ākālika' means 'occurring at [some] non-present time' — that is, it pertains to a time yet to come, not the present moment. 'Iṣṭā' means the desire for its attainment. And 'ko hi tad veda' is precisely the reason this admission of not-knowing is stated — just as no one can say with certainty whether a grandson or great-grandson will be born [to them] in the future, likewise, heaven's attainment, belonging to future time, is here connected with this same quality — this is the statement's intended meaning."

That is: no one doubts whether a *future* good — a grandchild not yet born — will actually occur; such uncertainty about future events is simply the nature of anything not-yet-present. In exactly the same way, "who indeed knows whether heaven exists" isn't a skeptical denial of heaven's reality — it merely acknowledges that heaven's attainment, being a *future* fruit, shares this same natural uncertainty that all future outcomes carry. The statement doesn't undermine the vidhi's authority at all; it simply reflects how one properly speaks about anything belonging to time yet to come.

### Page 454

When statements like "**स्वर्गकामो यजेत**" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) declare that heaven and similar worlds exist, statements like "**को हि तद्वेद**" (*ko hi tad veda*), which appear to cast doubt on this, are classified as śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction damaging the shastra's own authority).

**The resolution:** "ko hi tad veda," cited by the objector, is actually the closing portion of a longer statement about ritual "openings" (atikāśa) —

> दिक्ष्वातिकाशान् करोति ।
> *dikṣv-ātikāśān karoti |* (Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1)

— occurring in the ancient-lineage section of the Soma-yaga discussion. Without grasping the whole statement, its final fragment cannot be properly understood in isolation. "**अतिकाश**" (*atikāśa*) refers to doorway-openings made on the eastern and other sides of the yajna-platform, allowing smoke to escape freely — this is the passage's directly observable, immediate benefit (dṛṣṭa-phala).

Heaven's attainment, by contrast, is a *future* fruit — it doesn't materialize immediately. It's therefore entirely natural to express uncertainty about exactly *when* it will occur; "ko hi tad veda" exists precisely to convey this. The sutra's word "**आकालिक**" (*ākālika*, आकाले भवम् आकालिकम् *ākāle bhavam ākālikam*) means "occurring at another [future] time" — not the present, but the time to come. No one can say with certainty what will become of children not yet born; likewise, no one can specify with certainty exactly when a future fruit like heaven's attainment will occur. This uncertainty about *timing* is what "ko hi tad veda" conveys — not doubt about heaven's *existence*.

Notably, slightly earlier in this very same passage, it's stated plainly:

> अम्बर्हिः को हि देवलोके मनुष्यलोकात् ।
> *ambarhiḥ ko hi devaloke manuṣyalokāt |*

— that the divine world and the human world are interwoven with each other. This confirms unambiguously that no genuine doubt about the existence of heaven and similar worlds is intended anywhere here.

**Turning to the last remaining shastra-dṛṣṭi-virodha example** —

> शोभतेऽस्य मुखं य एवं वेद ।
> *śobhate'sya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ veda |* (Tandya Mahabrahmana 20.14.3)

— the next sutra explains this.

>
> सोऽयं गर्गत्रिरात्र-विधेः शेषः । तद्-विषयं वेदनम् अस्य मुख-शोभा-हेतुः किम् उतानुष्ठानम् इति स्तूयते । यथा कर्णाभरणादिना मुखं शोभितं भवत्य् एवं वेदितुस् त्व् एव विकसितं वदनं शोभितम् इव शिष्यैर् उदीक्ष्यते । अतः शोभा-सादृश्य-गुण-योगात् शोभत इत्य् उच्यते ।
> *so'yaṃ gargatrirātra-vidheḥ śeṣaḥ | tad-viṣayaṃ vedanam asya mukha-śobhā-hetuḥ kim utānuṣṭhānam iti stūyate | yathā karṇābharaṇādinā mukhaṃ śobhitaṃ bhavaty evaṃ veditus tv eva vikasitaṃ vadanaṃ śobhitam iva śiṣyair udīkṣyate | ataḥ śobhā-sādṛśya-guṇa-yogāt śobhata ity ucyate |*
>
> "This [statement] is the complement of the Gargatriratra vidhi. Merely knowing about that rite is itself said to be a cause of facial radiance — how much more so its actual performance! Just as ear-ornaments and similar adornments make a face radiant, so too a knower's beaming face is regarded by his students as radiant. This is stated on the basis of a shared quality resembling literal radiance."

Sutra's meaning: this is a statement made in praise of knowledge itself. "Śobhate'sya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ veda" ("his face shines, whoever knows this") is the Gargatriratra vidhi's companion arthavāda. The point: mere knowledge of this rite brings radiance to the face — how much more so its actual performance? Just as ear-ornaments enhance a face's radiance, knowing the Gargaratri and similar Vedic portions produces a genuine effect on the mind, which then emanates outward and becomes visible on the face as an unprecedented glow. The difference between the countenance of one endowed with knowledge and humility, and that of an ignorant fool, is perceptible even to ordinary people — so a Veda-scholar's facial radiance becomes swiftly apparent to his students and others...

**Resolving the "swift descendant" example** ("asya prajāyāṃ vājī jāyate ya evaṃ veda") — this arthavāda companions the vidhi about reciting the Veda to one's son. Following the same a-fortiori logic already established: the son of a Veda-learned father becomes learned himself through his father's instruction, then serves as officiating priest in yajnas, thereby earning substantial wealth — hence food and livelihood come to him. This is the meaning of "a swift one is born to his offspring." Stating this quality is what connects the arthavāda to its vidhi — the arthavāda praises the vidhi's own underlying value.

>
> "Youth, wealth, power, and lack of discernment — even a single one of these can lead to ruin; how much more so when all four occur together! [Any] one alone is a source and dwelling-place for every kind of impropriety — how much more so when they converge!"

That is: imagine a person possessing these four qualities — youth, wealth, authority, and lack of judgment. Youth alone risks entanglement with others' spouses and similar misdeeds; wealth alone breeds attachment to sense-pleasures, neglect of duty, and cruelty toward the poor; authority alone leads to harming others; lack of discernment alone leaves no wrongdoing unattempted. Each single vice is sufficient to ruin a person's worth on its own. Four...

### "Sarva-śabdādhikārikam" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.16)

> पूर्णाहुतिं जुहुयाद् इत्य् अस्य विधेः शेषोऽयं । सर्व-कामावाप्ति-हेतुत्वेन स्तूयमानं पूर्णाहुतिर् इति सूच्यते । यथा सर्वे ब्राह्मणा भोजयितव्या इत्य् अत्र सर्वत्वं स्व-गृह-गत-ब्राह्मण-विषयं । एवं पूर्णाहुत्याः कर्म-सङ्गत्ये यत् फलं तस्याधिकारे प्रस्तावे सम्भावितं तद्-विषयं सर्वत्वं द्रष्टव्यम् । पूर्णाहुतेर् अभावे कर्माङ्ग-विकलं भवति । तच् चेन् नैश्चल्यं पूर्णाहुत्या समाधीयत इत्य् एष कामः । तस्मिन् सम्ये सत्याहवनीयाद्य्-अग्नि-होत्रादि-कर्मसु योग्यो भवतीत्य् अयम् अप्य् एष कामः । कैश् च कर्मभिस् तैस् तैस् फलं प्राप्यत इति कामान्तरम् ।
> pūrṇāhutiṃ juhuyād ity asya vidheḥ śeṣo'yaṃ | sarva-kāmāvāpti-hetutvena stūyamānaṃ pūrṇāhutir iti sūcyate | yathā sarve brāhmaṇā bhojayitavyā ity atra sarvatvaṃ sva-gṛha-gata-brāhmaṇa-viṣayaṃ | evaṃ pūrṇāhutyāḥ karma-saṅgatye yat phalaṃ tasyādhikāre prastāve sambhāvitaṃ tad-viṣayaṃ sarvatvaṃ draṣṭavyam | pūrṇāhuter abhāve karmāṅga-vikalaṃ bhavati | tac cen naiścalyaṃ pūrṇāhutyā samādhīyata ity eṣa kāmaḥ | tasmin samye satyāhavanīyādy-agni-hotrādi-karmasu yogyo bhavatīty ayam apy eṣa kāmaḥ | kaiś ca karmabhis tais tais phalaṃ prāpyata iti kāmāntaram |
>
> पूर्णाहुतिं जुहुयाद् इत्य् अस्य विधेः शेषोऽयं । सर्व-कामावाप्ति-हेतुत्वेन स्तूयमानं पूर्णाहुतिर् इति सूच्यते । यथा सर्वे ब्राह्मणा भोजयितव्या इत्य् अत्र सर्वत्वं स्व-गृह-गत-ब्राह्मण-विषयं । एवं पूर्णाहुत्याः कर्म-सङ्गत्ये यत् फलं तस्याधिकारे प्रस्तावे सम्भावितं तद्-विषयं सर्वत्वं द्रष्टव्यम् ।
> *pūrṇāhutiṃ juhuyād ity asya vidheḥ śeṣo'yaṃ | sarva-kāmāvāpti-hetutvena stūyamānaṃ pūrṇāhutir iti sūcyate | yathā sarve brāhmaṇā bhojayitavyā ity atra sarvatvaṃ sva-gṛha-gata-brāhmaṇa-viṣayaṃ | evaṃ pūrṇāhutyāḥ karma-saṅgatye yat phalaṃ tasyādhikāre prastāve sambhāvitaṃ tad-viṣayaṃ sarvatvaṃ draṣṭavyam |*
>
> "This is the complement of the vidhi 'one should offer the Purnahuti.' The Purnahuti is praised as the cause of obtaining all desired ends. Just as, in 'all brahmins should be fed,' the word 'all' refers only to the brahmins present in one's own household [not literally every brahmin everywhere] — so too here, the 'all' [in the Purnahuti's praise] should be understood as restricted to the specific fruit relevant to the ritual context (adhikāra) in which the Purnahuti occurs, given its connection to that particular rite. Its absence would leave that particular ritual act incomplete; ensuring its stability/completeness is the specific 'desire' addressed here — and, at that proper ritual moment, becoming fit for the Ahavaniya-fire, Agnihotra, and similar acts is likewise this same 'desire.' Different rites yield their own respective fruits through their own respective means."

Sutra's meaning: the word "sarva" (all), occurring in such statements, must be understood as scoped specifically to the ritual context at hand — not as an unrestricted, universal claim covering literally every possible desire across all rites.

### Page 458

...depends on the qualified performer entitled to it — or, alternatively, pertains only to the specific ritual act named there.

> पूर्णाहुत्या सर्वान् कामानवाप्नोति ।
> *pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān avāpnoti |*

is the concluding portion of the vidhi—

> पूर्णाहुतिं जुहुयात् ।
> *pūrṇāhutiṃ juhuyāt |*

That is, this statement is the final component of just the Purnahuti-rite's own context — not a claim about literally every desire attainable through any offering whatsoever. One cannot, for instance, obtain sky-flight powers through the Purnahuti — nothing of that kind is claimed here. Just as saying "today, all the rice should be cooked" means only the rice in one's own house (not all the rice in the world), and "all brahmins should be fed" means the brahmin-guests present at one's own house — "sarva" (all) is used in this restricted sense throughout. Likewise here: "all fruits" means the desires specifically attainable through the ritual acts (like Adhana) relevant to this particular context — obtainable through the Purnahuti-homa alone.

The Adhana rite currently underway would otherwise remain deficient; the Purnahuti remedies this deficiency — **that** is one benefit. By completing the Adhana rite through the Purnahuti, one gains qualification to perform subsequent rites (Agnihotra, and homas in the Ahavaniya and other fires) — a **second** benefit. And the fruit promised by shastra for properly performing these subsequent rites is **yet another** benefit. If it's asked whether these same benefits might apply equally to other oblations besides the Purnahuti — very well, let it be so; what is lost to us by that? Praising the Purnahuti in this way loses nothing at all.

Another desire secured for us by the purnahuti is that, the maimed condition of the rite being averted, the ahavaniya and other fires become fit for use at the agnihotra and other sacrifices. Yet another desire is that by these rites thus rendered possible, such and such fruits are obtained. Perhaps you will say that if this is all that is meant by asserting that the purnahuti procures for the worshipper all desires the same is true of other oblations than the purnahuti. Good. How are we touched? That does not detract from the eulogy of the purnahuti here.
>
> This, however, may be said. The purnahuti is part of a larger rite, and mention made of a reward for it may be in this way explained as a case of an arthavada merely


### Page 459

Very well — Purnahuti is merely a component of one ritual act, and its fruit-declaring Shruti-statement, being arthavāda, is oriented purely toward praise, since it concerns substance, consecration, and ritual acts performed for another's (i.e., a further) sake. But "paśubandha-yājī sarvāl lokān abhijayati" ("one who performs pashubandha conquers all worlds") both prescribes an act *and* declares its own principal fruit — if we accept the Purnahuti resolution as given, doesn't one of these two statements become purposeless? The next sutra resolves this.

### "Phalasya karma-niṣṭheṣu lokavat parimāṇakaḥ sāratho vā phala-viśeṣaḥ syāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.2.17)

> पृथिव्य्-अन्तरिक्ष-स्वर्-गेषु तमलोक-अभिजय-रूपं फलं पशुबन्ध-कर्मणा निष्पाद्यत इति शेषः । इतरेषां च प्रेणादीनां फलानां कर्मान्तरेण परिमाणाधिक्यं सारत्वं वा सम्पद्येत । ततः फल-विशेषः स्याद् इति नास्त्य् अनर्थक्यम् । लोक-वद् अपि प्रत्यक्ष-प्रमाणः दृष्टान्तः । यथा लोके निष्टिकिनः खारी-परिमितापि रीणे री श्रियं निष्पाद्य अन्तरेन पुनः क्रिये सति परिमाणाधिक्यं भवति । यथा वा निष्ठेन वस्त्र-मात्रं अल्पे निष्पद्यकेन तु सार-भूतं संकुलम् । तथा भोगाधिक्यं भोग-सारत्वं वा कर्मान्तरेण दृश्यम् । ब्रह्म-हत्याया अपि मानस्याः स्वल्पाया वेदन-मात्रेण तरणं कायिक्या महत्या अश्वमेधेन इति नास्त्य् अनर्थक्यम् ।
> pṛthivy-antarikṣa-svar-geṣu tamaloka-abhijaya-rūpaṃ phalaṃ paśubandha-karmaṇā niṣpādyata iti śeṣaḥ | itareṣāṃ ca preṇādīnāṃ phalānāṃ karmāntareṇa parimāṇādhikyaṃ sāratvaṃ vā sampadyeta | tataḥ phala-viśeṣaḥ syād iti nāsty anarthakyam | loka-vad api pratyakṣa-pramāṇaḥ dṛṣṭāntaḥ | yathā loke niṣṭikinaḥ khārī-parimitāpi rīṇe rī śriyaṃ niṣpādya antarena punaḥ kriye sati parimāṇādhikyaṃ bhavati | yathā vā niṣṭhena vastra-mātraṃ alpe niṣpadyakena tu sāra-bhūtaṃ saṃkulam | tathā bhogādhikyaṃ bhoga-sāratvaṃ vā karmāntareṇa dṛśyam | brahma-hatyāyā api mānasyāḥ svalpāyā vedana-mātreṇa taraṇaṃ kāyikyā mahatyā aśvamedhena iti nāsty anarthakyam |
>
> *(Establishing that the fruit of "conquering all worlds" — across the terrestrial, mid-heaven, and celestial realms — is obtained through the pashubandha rite specifically, while other rites performed further can yield an increase in the same fruit's degree or quality, not a wholly separate fruit. The parallel given: just as a fixed amount of raw grain, when processed, might yield the same quantity of a superior grade, or a greater quantity of an ordinary grade, depending on how it's worked — so too, rites performed in addition to the pashubandha can enhance the degree or quality of the "world-conquest" already secured, rather than rendering the pashubandha's own promised fruit redundant. Similarly, the "crossing beyond mental brahmin-slaying sin through mere knowledge" (a smaller sin) versus "crossing beyond even grave bodily brahmin-slaying sin through the Ashvamedha" reflects the same scaling principle — no genuine redundancy exists.)*

That is: no true redundancy exists between such fruit-statements. Just as in ordinary life, the same quantity of raw material, processed differently, might yield either a greater quantity of an ordinary product or the same quantity of a superior one — rewards across different rites can likewise differ in *degree* or *quality* rather than being entirely separate, competing claims. The Pashubandha secures "conquest of all worlds" as its base fruit; further rites performed afterward enhance that same fruit's magnitude or refinement, rather than duplicating or invalidating it.

### Page 460

Sutra's meaning: variations in how ritual acts are performed produce corresponding variations in their fruits — differing in either quantity or quality, just as in ordinary human affairs.

Since the Pashubandha secures the yajamāna all worlds — earth, atmosphere, heaven, and beyond — and other rites promise similar fruits, what special value does the Pashubandha specifically offer? Answer: other rites do secure heaven and similar worlds, and so does Pashubandha — but through Pashubandha, one obtains a *more excellent* fruit than what other rites yield. Consider an ordinary example: one nishka (gold coin) buys one khāri of rice; two nishkas buy two khāris — an increase in *quantity*. Or, one nishka buys ordinary cotton cloth; two nishkas buy silk — an increase in *quality*. The first shows quantitative increase; the second, qualitative increase (silk being superior to cotton).

A further illustration: imagine two farmers cultivating separate fields. One farms carelessly — minimal ploughing, no fertilizer, weeds left unpulled. The other farms attentively — proper ploughing, timely fertilizer, weeding, and protection from pests and birds. At harvest time, both obtain grain — but not equally. One gets little, the other gets his due measure...

Here you have increase in bulk and increase in quality respectively. In the same way it must be recognised that additional sacrifices will procure for the worshipper increased or higher enjoyments. A mentally-committed, comparatively minor sin like brahmin-slaying can be removed merely through others declaring it (i.e., through knowledge/confession); a grave, physically-committed sin of the same kind requires the Ashvamedha to remove it. Therefore, no genuine flaw of purposelessness (ānarthakya) applies to any of these statements.

Therefore, as already explained, its connection here serves a praise-oriented purpose, resolved in precisely the same manner as before. **This closes the entire arthavāda objection cycle.** Both remaining examples are answered by simply invoking resolutions already established: the "impossible prohibition" is, once again, understood as praise-oriented arthavāda attached to a genuine vidhi (just as with the earlier Kashmir/vetasa examples), and "Babara" is, exactly as resolved many pages earlier in the vidhi-authority discussion, understood as onomatopoeia for wind's sound — not a historical person's name at all, closing off any claim that the passage depends on a "non-eternal" human referent.

Thus, since no genuine cause for lack of authority exists among the three portions present in the Veda — mantra, vidhi, and arthavāda — and since authority has now been established for each of these contested categories, **the Veda's authority, in every respect, stands proven.**

This proper understanding was already established in the final adhikarana of the first pada of Jaimini's sutras.

In the Kavya-pashu-kanda section, two connected statements occur: **(1)** "vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta bhūtikāmaḥ" — "one desiring prosperity should offer a white [animal] to Vayu" — the vidhi; **(2)** "vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyum eva svena bhāgadheyenopadhāvati sa enaṃ bhūtiṃ gamayati" — "since Vayu is the swiftest-natured deity, the wind-god swiftly grants prosperity to his own worshipper" — the arthavāda.

If it's asked whether the arthavāda words here, being independently capable of conveying complete sense on their own, are truly authoritative in matters of dharma — some argue that vidhi and arthavāda, being separate, unconnected statements, means arthavāda carries no such authority. But the correct view: the arthavāda praises the vidhi. Without it, a person, told merely "offer a white animal to Vayu," might hesitate — why perform this act at all, what fruit results? The arthavāda resolves this doubt directly, stating that prosperity comes swiftly through this offering — thereby motivating action. Since vidhi and its praising arthavāda are thus mutually connected, arthavāda carries the same authority in matters of dharma that vidhi does.

## Chapter 11. Refuting, with Proper Proofs, the Claim That the Veda Is of Human Origin — the Defense of Apauruṣeyatva
*Original title: "Vēdavu puruṣaracitavemba vādavannu pramāṇapurassaravāgi nirākarisi vēdāpauruṣeyatvasamarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 465–475 of the source.**

### Page 465

...quickly gives fruit — this arthavāda instills the confidence needed to motivate action, making the vidhi's dependence on arthavāda's help genuinely necessary; an incomplete vidhi lacking this support would not be authoritative — this concludes the objection.

**The siddhānta's resolution:** if acts are performed with a desire for fruit — just as serving and pleasing a king yields reward — then pleasing a deity likewise yields fruit, and the scripturally-authoritative vidhi needs no further external proof. Stating that a fruit-giving deity should be worshipped conveys the *praiseworthiness* of the act itself; since vidhi and arthavāda together convey "the praiseworthy act should be performed," their mutual connection is thereby established, and the siddhānta concludes: vidhi statements are indeed authoritative.

**A summary reflection:** the Veda's karma-kāṇḍa (ritual-action portion) discusses attainable actions; its jñāna-kāṇḍa (knowledge portion) discusses the established truth of the Self. Only the karma-kāṇḍa concerns the Mimamsakas, who divide it into mantra, vidhi, and arthavāda — this framework doesn't apply to jñāna-kāṇḍa. Since no genuine cause for doubt remains regarding these three portions, and each is accepted as inherently self-authoritative, the entire Veda stands established as authoritative.

### A New Major Topic: The Statement of the Veda's Human Origin, Followed by Establishment of Its Non-Human Origin

> नन्व् एवम् अपि वेदस्य पौरुषेयत्वेन विप्रलम्भक-वाक्यवद् अप्रामाण्यं स्यात् । पौरुषेयत्वं च प्रथम-साध्ये पूर्वपक्षे जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास (पुर्व मिमम्स १.१.२७–३२) । वेदांश्ये सन्निकर्षं पुरुषाख्या ॥
> nanv evam api vedasya pauruṣeyatvena vipralambhaka-vākyavad aprāmāṇyaṃ syāt | pauruṣeyatvaṃ ca prathama-sādhye pūrvapakṣe jaiminiḥ sūtrayāmāsa (Purva Mimamsa 1.1.27–32) | vedāṃśye sannikarṣaṃ puruṣākhyā || (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.27)
>
> नन्व् एवम् अपि वेदस्य पौरुषेयत्वेन विप्रलम्भक-वाक्यवद् अप्रामाण्यं स्यात् । पौरुषेयत्वं च प्रथम-साध्ये पूर्वपक्षे जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास । वेदेऽंश्ये सन्निकर्षं पुरुषाख्या ॥
> *nanv evam api vedasya pauruṣeyatvena vipralambhaka-vākyavad aprāmāṇyaṃ syāt | pauruṣeyatvaṃ ca prathama-sādhye pūrvapakṣe jaiminiḥ sūtrayāmāsa | vede'ṃśye sannikarṣaṃ puruṣākhyā ||*
>
> "But even granting all this, might the Veda still be unauthoritative on account of its human origin — like the speech of one who utters a deliberate falsehood? Jaimini formulates, as the very first matter to be established, the objection (pūrvapakṣa) asserting the Veda's human origin: 'Within Vedic portions, there occurs mention connecting to specific persons' (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.27)."

This opens a genuinely major new discussion — one of the most significant debates in all of Mimamsa philosophy: whether the Veda is of human authorship (pauruṣeya) or entirely without human origin (apauruṣeya). Jaimini himself first states the objection favoring human authorship, before Sayana works through its resolution.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> We have thus shown that the reasons alleged against the authoritativeness of the Veda in its three parts of mantra, vidhi and arthavada have no existence, and we have accepted the reasons for such authoritativeness. The authority of the whole Veda therefore stands sure.
>
> But even granting this, may it not be that the Veda, on account of its human authorship, may be unauthoritative like the speech of one who utters a fallacy? The human authorship of the Veda is set out in sutras by Jaimini, speaking as the holder of the view that is to be controverted, as follows.

> तेऽत्र दृष्टान्ततया समुच्चीयन्ते । यथा रघुवंशादय इदानीम्-तनास् तथा वेदा अपि । न तु वेदा अनादयः । अत एव वेद-कर्तृत्वेन पुरुषा आम्नायन्ते । व्यासासिकं भारतम्, वाल्मीकीयं रामायणम् इत्य् अत्र यथा भारतादि-कर्तृत्वेन व्यासादिं व्यपदिश्य आम्नायन्ते तथा काथकं कौथुमं तैत्तिरीयम् इत्य् एवं तथा वेद-शाखा-कर्तृत्वेन कथादीनाम् आख्यातत्वाद् वेदाः पौरुषेयाः । नन्व् इतीनाम् एव सतां वेदानाम् अध्याय-वंश-सम्प्रदाय-प्रवर्तकत्वेन काठकादि-समाख्या स्याद् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> te'tra dṛṣṭāntatayā samuccīyante | yathā raghuvaṃśādaya idānīm-tanās tathā vedā api | na tu vedā anādayaḥ | ata eva veda-kartṛtvena puruṣā āmnāyante | vyāsāsikaṃ bhāratam, vālmīkīyaṃ rāmāyaṇam ity atra yathā bhāratādi-kartṛtvena vyāsādiṃ vyapadiśya āmnāyante tathā kāthakaṃ kauthumaṃ taittirīyam ity evaṃ tathā veda-śākhā-kartṛtvena kathādīnām ākhyātatvād vedāḥ pauruṣeyāḥ | nanv itīnām eva satāṃ vedānām adhyāya-vaṃśa-sampradāya-pravartakatvena kāṭhakādi-samākhyā syād ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "These [book-examples] are cited here as parallel illustrations: just as the Raghuvamsha and similar works belong to recent times, the Vedas too [are argued to be recent] — the Vedas are not beginningless. This is precisely why persons are cited as the Veda's authors. Just as, in 'Vyāsāsikaṃ Bhāratam' (Vyasa's Bharata) and 'Vālmīkīyaṃ Rāmāyaṇam' (Valmiki's Ramayana), Vyasa and others are explicitly named as authors, so too, in 'Kāthakam,' 'Kauthumam,' 'Taittirīyam,' and similar [Vedic school-names], Katha and other [sages] are named as authors of their respective Vedic branches — the Vedas are therefore of human origin. [An objector might counter:] perhaps such names as 'Kathaka' arose simply because these individuals were the ones who established the tradition of study and transmission [of an already-existing text] — anticipating this, the answer follows in the next sutra."

Sutra's meaning: some hold that the Vedas were composed by human authors, because the Veda's various portions bear many names — and these names are the names of the persons who composed them. Jaimini himself first constructs this objection in his Purva-Mimamsa-sutra, before establishing the Veda's non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) in response.

Some argue that the Vedas, like recent literary works, were composed by specific persons not long ago. Their reasoning: everyone knows the Raghuvamsha and similar works, composed by poets like Kalidasa, are recent compositions. By the same logic, the Vedas too are recent works composed by certain persons. The word "ca" ("too") in the sutra signals this comparison — just as Raghuvamsha and similar works are human-composed, so too are the Vedas...

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Of the Vedas, too, some predicate nearness to us in time. There is mention of the men who composed them.
>
> Some disputants predicate nearness of the Vedas. The word "too" in the sutra links the Vedas to books like the Raghuvansa, the works of Kalidasa and the like. For they are in this sentence brought together with the Vedas by way of comparison. As books like the Raghuvansa belong to our own time, so, too, the Vedas. They are not without beginning. And that is why we find men mentioned as the authors of them. In the familiar designations of these books—the Vaiyasika Bharata, the Valmikiya Ramayana, and the like—Vyasa and other writers are clearly indicated as the authors of these books. Just so it is with the titles—the Kathaka, the Kauthama, the Taittiriya. These titles indicate Katha and other writers as the authors of various Sakhas of the Vedas, and the Vedas are therefore of human origin.

### Page 467

It cannot be said the Vedas are beginningless — it is customary to attach the names of composers alongside them, exactly as with "Vyāyasikaṃ bhāratam" (Vyasa's Bharata) and "Vālmīkīyaṃ rāmāyaṇam" (Valmiki's Ramayana), which clearly name their authors. Similarly, "Kāthaka," "Kauthuma," "Taittiri," and "Pippalāda" name the actual composers of their respective Vedic branches. Therefore, the Vedas are human-composed works. (This concludes the first argument of the objection.)

**A possible counter-response, and a further objection anticipating it:** some might reply that Katha and similar figures were merely teachers who established a tradition of study — their students' recitation-lineage simply came to bear the teacher's name, without implying literal authorship. Anticipating and questioning this defense, a further sutra advances another argument.

### "Anitya-darśanāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.28)

> अनित्या जनन-मरणवन्तो बबरादयो वेदे श्रूयन्ते । बबरः प्रावाहणिर् अकामयत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित ४.१.१.३) कुसुरुबिन्द औद्दालकिर् अकामयत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित ३.१.३.१) इति । तथा सति बबरादिभ्यः पूर्वम् अभावाद् अनित्या वेदाः । विमतं वेद-वाक्यं पौरुषेयं सांक्यत्वात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवद् इत्य् अनुमान-समुच्चयार्थश् च कारः ॥
> anityā janana-maraṇavanto babarādayo vede śrūyante | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata (Taittiriya Samhita 4.1.1.3) kusurubinda auddālakir akāmayata (Taittiriya Samhita 3.1.3.1) iti | tathā sati babarādibhyaḥ pūrvam abhāvād anityā vedāḥ | vimataṃ veda-vākyaṃ pauruṣeyaṃ sāṃkyatvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavad ity anumāna-samuccayārthaś ca kāraḥ ||
>
> अनित्या जनन-मरणवन्तो बबरादयो वेदे श्रूयन्ते । बबरः प्रावाहणिर् अकामयत । कुसुरुबिन्द औद्दालकिर् अकामयत इति । तथा सति बबरादिभ्यः पूर्वम् अभावाद् अनित्या वेदाः । विमतं वेद-वाक्यं पौरुषेयं वाक्यत्वात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवद् इत्य् अनुमान-समुच्चयार्थश् च "च"-कारः ॥
> *anityā janana-maraṇavanto babarādayo vede śrūyante | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata | kusurubinda auddālakir akāmayata iti | tathā sati babarādibhyaḥ pūrvam abhāvād anityā vedāḥ | vimataṃ veda-vākyaṃ pauruṣeyaṃ vākyatvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavad ity anumāna-samuccayārthaś ca "ca"-kāraḥ ||*
>
> "Non-eternal beings, subject to birth and death — Babara and similar figures — are spoken of in the Veda: 'Babara, son of Pravahana, desired [this]' (Taittiriya Samhita 4.1.1.3); 'Kusurubinda, son of Uddalaka, desired [this]' (Taittiriya Samhita 3.1.3.1). This being so, the Vedas cannot have existed before Babara and these other figures — therefore the Vedas are not beginningless. The disputed Veda-statement is of human origin, since it is a statement [like any other] — just like statements by Kalidasa and similar poets. The word 'ca' (also) here links this inferential argument to what was said before."

Sutra's meaning: since the Vedas contain descriptions of non-eternal things — names of persons and similar — the Vedas, discussing such non-eternal matters, are themselves non-eternal, that is, composed by persons. (This is a further objection.)
