**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> In the next sutra, bethinking that it may be said that the Vedas are eternal, and that these titles merely mean that Katha and others like teachers were busy in handing down the traditional knowledge of the Vedas, he puts forward another argument in favour of their human origin.
>
> Also because we see mention made of things that are not eternal.
>
> People like Babara, who were not eternal, but were born and have died, are spoken of in the Veda. "Babarah pravahanir akamayata kusurubinda auddalikir akamayata." This being so the Vedas, which cannot be placed prior to Babara and others mentioned in them, are not without beginning. The word "also" in the sutra links this argument to such other...


### Page 468

In the Veda, statements occur: "babaraḥ prāvāhaṇeḥ kāmayata" ("he sought after Babara, son of Pravahana") and "kusurubinda auddālakir akāmayata" ("he sought after Kusurubinda, son of Uddalaka"). Since Babara and Kusurubinda are human, they're subject to birth, death, and similar changes — non-eternal beings. Statements discussing such figures necessarily postdate their birth; these Vedic passages cannot have existed before those persons lived. Therefore, the Vedas are non-eternal — and, like the works of poets such as Kalidasa, human-composed. The word "ca" ("also") in the sutra marks this as an additional argument, beyond the earlier human-authorship claim, specifically establishing the Veda's non-eternality.

**Having thus completed the objection — that the Veda is human-composed and, discussing non-eternal things, is itself non-eternal — the siddhānta (resolution), that the Veda is in fact apauruṣeya (non-human in origin) and eternal, is now established in the sutras that follow.**

### The Siddhāntin's Resolution Begins

### "Uktaṃ tu śabda-pūrvakam" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.29)

> तु-शब्दो वैमानाम् अनित्यत्वं वारयति । शब्दस्य वेद-रूपस्य कथादि-पुरुषेभ्यः पूर्वत्वम् अनादित्वं प्राचीनैर् एव सूत्रे उक्तम् । "औत्पत्तिकस् तु शब्दस्यार्थेन सम्बन्धः" (पुर्व मिमम्स १.१.५) इत्य् अस्मिन् सूत्रे औत्पत्तिक-शब्देन सर्वेषां शब्दानां वेदानां तद्-अर्थानां तद्-उभय-सम्बन्धानां च नित्यत्वं प्रतिज्ञायोक्तराभ्यां शब्दाधिकरण-वाक्याधिकरणाभ्याम् उपसादितत्वात् तर्हि कथाद्य्-आख्याया गतिः का शङ्क्य सम्प्रदाय-प्रवर्तनापेक्षयैव उपसद्यत इत्य् उत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> tu-śabdo vaimānām anityatvaṃ vārayati | śabdasya veda-rūpasya kathādi-puruṣebhyaḥ pūrvatvam anāditvaṃ prācīnair eva sūtre uktam | "autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena sambandhaḥ" (Purva Mimamsa 1.1.5) ity asmin sūtre autpattika-śabdena sarveṣāṃ śabdānāṃ vedānāṃ tad-arthānāṃ tad-ubhaya-sambandhānāṃ ca nityatvaṃ pratijñāyoktarābhyāṃ śabdādhikaraṇa-vākyādhikaraṇābhyām upasāditatvāt tarhi kathādy-ākhyāyā gatiḥ kā śaṅkya sampradāya-pravartanāpekṣayaiva upasadyata ity uttaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "The word 'tu' (but) rules out the [claim of] non-eternality [regarding sound]. That the sound constituting the Veda existed prior to — and independently of — Katha and similar persons was already stated by the ancient [sages] in the sutra: 'the connection between word and meaning is innate/original' (Purva Mimamsa 1.1.5). In this sutra, by the term 'autpattika' (innate), the eternality of all words, of the Vedas, of their meanings, and of the very relationship between the two, was already established through both the assertion and its subsequent proof, across the sections on word (śabdādhikaraṇa) and sentence (vākyādhikaraṇa). One might then ask: what, then, is the actual purpose of names like 'Kathaka'? Anticipating this doubt, the answer is that such names arise solely from the need to designate who established a given tradition [of transmission] — this is now formulated as the resolution."

**This is the pivot of the entire debate.** The Veda's own sound (śabda) is eternal and precedes even sages like Katha — already established earlier in the very foundational discussion of word-meaning relationships. The names "Kathaka" and similar do not indicate authorship at all — they simply mark which teacher established a particular tradition of transmission.

### Page 469

Sutra's meaning: it was already established that words — including those constituting the Vedas — are eternal. The word "tu" rules out the claim of non-eternality: the Veda's own sound-form existed even before figures like Katha, its beginninglessness having already been established through a sequence of prior sutras — from "karmaike tatra darśanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.1) through "liṅgadarśanāc ca" (1.1.21), spanning the sixth adhikarana of the first pada of the first adhyaya of Jaimini's own Purva-Mimamsa-sutra. (These intervening sutras are not detailed here, to keep this Bhashya-Bhumika from growing too long — interested readers may consult them directly.)

**One might then ask: why, then, do names like "Kathaka" appear at all?** The next sutra answers: these names arose because these persons propagated Vedic knowledge through teaching and recitation.

### "Abhyāsa-pravacanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.30)

> अस्त्य् एव आख्याया गतिः । तेषां परं बबराद्य्-अनित्य-दर्शनं । यद् उक्तं तस्य किम् उत्तरम् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> asty eva ākhyāyā gatiḥ | teṣāṃ paraṃ babarādy-anitya-darśanaṃ | yad uktaṃ tasya kim uttaram ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "There does indeed exist [a valid] explanation for these names. As for the remaining objection — the appearance of non-eternal figures like Babara — what answer can be given to that? Anticipating this doubt, the resolution is formulated next."

Sutra's meaning: this is the correct interpretation of names like "Katha" and similar. This resolves the entire naming-based objection. But regarding mantras that discuss non-eternal beings like Babara — what should be said about this? The next sutra answers this remaining doubt.

### Page 470

Sutra's meaning: it is customary to name each Vedic branch (śākhā) after the celebrated rishi who traditionally taught it, according to a fixed method, to students proficient in that portion.

Take the Kāthaka-śākhā as an example: this doesn't mean the branch was *composed* by a man named Katha — rather, teachers who mastered that branch taught it to their students in a fixed, traditional sequence, and among them was one particularly gifted teacher named Katha, after whom the branch came to be named. The same holds for other branches.

**Very well — but what of "Babara" and similar words referring to non-eternal persons?**

### "Paraṃ tu śruti-sāmānya-mātram" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.31)

> यत् परं बबरादिकं तच् छब्द-सामान्यम् एव न तु मनुष्यो बबर-नामकोऽत्र प्रतिपाद्यते । बबर-ध्वनि-युक्त प्रवहन-स्वभावस्य वायोर् वचः शक्यत्वात् । ननु वेदे क्वचिद् एवं श्रूयते । वनस्पतिः सत्रम् आसत सर्पाः सत्रम् आसतेति । तत्र वनस्पतीनाम् अचेतनत्वात् सर्पाणां चेतनत्वेऽपि विद्या-रहितत्वात् तद्-अनुष्ठानं न सम्भवति । अत उन्मत्त-बाल-प्रलपित-मद्रकाणि इत्य् आदिर् वेदो मनुष्य-कृत इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> yat paraṃ babarādikaṃ tac chabda-sāmānyam eva na tu manuṣyo babara-nāmako'tra pratipādyate | babara-dhvani-yukta pravahana-svabhāvasya vāyor vacaḥ śakyatvāt | nanu vede kvacid evaṃ śrūyate | vanaspatiḥ satram āsata sarpāḥ satram āsateti | tatra vanaspatīnām acetanatvāt sarpāṇāṃ cetanatve'pi vidyā-rahitatvāt tad-anuṣṭhānaṃ na sambhavati | ata unmatta-bāla-pralapita-madrakāṇi ity ādir vedo manuṣya-kṛta ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "The remaining case — 'Babara' and similar — is simply a matter of shared sound; no man actually named Babara is being spoken of here. The wind, characterized by the sound 'babara' and whose very nature is to blow forth (pravahana), is capable of being described this way. But one might object: don't we find such statements as 'the trees performed a sattra [ritual session]; the serpents performed a sattra'? Trees are insentient; serpents, though sentient, lack knowledge — for either to actually perform such a rite is impossible. Given this, and given examples like the babble of a madman or child ('jaradgavo gāyati madrakāṇi'), it would seem the Veda must be human-composed after all. Anticipating this doubt, the resolution follows in the next sutra."

Sutra's meaning: among Vedic words, some words resembling ordinary [human/animal] names are simply that — ordinary shared words. They do not actually indicate any specific human person.

In the case under examination, though the word "Babara" appears to name a man, it is not actually a proper name — merely an ordinary word. Combined with the sound "ba-ba-ra," it means "wind blowing forcefully." "Babara" is therefore not any man's name.

Yet the Veda does contain exactly this kind of assertion, unverifiable by any human means...

### Page 473

Sutra's meaning: though many seemingly incoherent statements ("**वनस्पतयः सत्रमासत**" *vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata* — "the trees performed the sacrifice," and similar) occur in the Vedas, they exist only to clarify certain ritual acts and their proper relationships.

**Working through the reasoning with a concrete example:** suppose someone claims a man composed

> ज्योतिष्टोमेन स्वर्गकामो यजेत ।
> *jyotiṣṭomena svargakāmo yajeta |*
> "One desiring heaven should perform the jyotiṣṭoma" Any man could say "perform the jyotiṣṭoma" — but no man can foresee that this specific act yields that specific future fruit. Humans have the capacity to perform acts, not to know which acts yield which unobservable future results. Such statements resemble a sovereign's authoritative command, requiring three essential components: **bhāvya** (the fruit sought), **karaṇa** (the means/instrument), and **itikartavyatā** (the proper method). Just as "feed the brahmins" implies satisfaction (goal), food (instrument), and accompaniments like vegetables and soup (method) — "perform the jyotiṣṭoma" implies heaven (goal), soma (instrument), and the full consecration-and-subsidiary-rite sequence (method). How could such a carefully structured statement resemble a madman's ravings?

**But this same explanation doesn't cleanly cover "**वनस्पतयः सत्रमासत**" (*vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata*)** — true, and a different kind of explanation is needed there. When interpreting a sentence, one must take the complete statement as a whole; taking only one fragment and declaring it senseless is not a fair reading...

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Neither are passages like that about the sacrifices performed by trees open to that charge. Logicians say that the meaning to be assigned to an expression must vary with the purport or context. Now the passage about the jyotishtoma is preceptive, and its purport is the performance of the rite. The passage about the sacrifice performed by the serpents is of the character of an arthavada, and its purport is eulogy of the rite. Such a eulogy can be made by means even of a thing that has no existence. If senseless trees and unlearned serpents perform a sacrifice, how much more should sentient and learned brahmins do so? In this way the sacrifice is eulogised.


### Page 474

How could it be otherwise? Examining a sentence's preceding and following context resolves what first seemed inconsistent. The "**वनस्पतयः सत्रमासत**" (*vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata*) statement, connected as it is with jyotiṣṭoma-type sattra statements, is not comparable to a madman's ravings. Logicians hold that a word's meaning shifts with context: statements like the jyotiṣṭoma exist to declare a duty — that is their function; statements like this are arthavāda, existing purely to convey praise, regardless of whether their literal content is possible or impossible. The point isn't literal plausibility — it's the praise itself: "if even insentient, unknowing creatures managed to perform such a rite, how much more should sentient, learned brahmins do so!" — this a-fortiori eulogy of the sattra-yajna is the statement's whole purpose.

**Siddhānta — the true conclusion:** names like "Kathaka" and "Kauthuma" do not indicate the persons who composed those Vedic branches — they were composed by no human being at all. Because these figures traditionally taught those branches to their students, the branches came to bear their names...

...became customary. Unlike the Raghuvamsha and similar works of Kalidasa and other poets — which always close each canto with an author's colophon, "iti kālidāsa-kṛtau" ("thus, in the work composed by Kalidasa") — no such author's name-marker appears anywhere in the Vedas. Therefore, the Vedas are not human-composed; they are apauruṣeya.

**A closing summary verse, in question-and-answer form:**

> "Is the Veda of human origin? Yes, since it is known by titles such as Kathaka, and since it is made up of sentences that have the same nature as other sentences." — "No: these titles refer to men who taught the Veda, not composed it. And that other argument has already been refuted by the fact that no author's name is mentioned."

**A doubt then arises:** hasn't the holy Badarayana himself stated that the Veda is the work of Brahman? — "śāstra-yonitvāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1.1.3), meaning Brahman is omniscient, having created the Rigveda and all other shastras. Granted — but this doesn't establish the Veda's *human* origin; it was not made by a [mere embodied] person. This same Badarayana, in the Devatā-adhikaraṇa section, establishes that for all beings who have not attained final liberation, the Veda is eternal, like the sky itself — "ata eva ca nityatvam" ("and for this very reason, its eternality follows").

**Both Shruti and Smriti confirm this:**

> स्ह्रुति: "वाचा विरूपा नित्यया"
> Shruti: "vācā virūpā nityayā" ("with speech, of varied form, eternal")
> स्म्रिति: "अनादि-निधना नित्या वाग् उत्सृष्टा स्वयम्भुवा"
> Smriti: "anādi-nidhanā nityā vāg utsṛṣṭā svayambhuvā" ("beginningless and endless, eternal is the speech emitted by the Self-existent One")

**Therefore, no possibility of an authorial flaw arises for the Veda — it has no author at all. The authority of the Veda, comprising both mantra and Brahmana, thus stands firmly and unobstructedly established.**

—carry a valid definition [of "mantra"], or not? Since no definition can be given that avoids all these flaws, this passage fails to qualify as a defining case of "mantra."

**Siddhānta:** whatever priests customarily call "mantra" during a yajna's performance — that itself is mantra. This definition is free from flaw, since they simply use it as such during ritual practice — that alone suffices; there's no further need to test whether this designation avoids over- or under-extension.

At the Adhana rite (already explained on page 431), the mantra—

> अहे बुध्निय मन्त्रं मे गोपाय ।
> *ahe budhniya mantraṃ me gopāya |* (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.2.1.14)

—is recited. Here the question is raised: what is mantra's proper definition? Any such definition must avoid avyāpti and ativyāpti — but no such flawless definition can actually be stated. If mantra is defined as "a statement conveying an injunctive shastric meaning," the mantra—

> वसन्ताय कपिञ्जलानालभेत ।
> *vasantāya kapiñjalān ālabheta |* (Vajasaneyi Samhita 24.20)

—itself declaring a new injunction — would fail to qualify. If mantra is derived etymologically from "**मनन**" (*manana*, reflective mental deliberation), Brahmana statements would wrongly qualify too (ativyāpti). Definitions based on grammatical person (second-person vs. first-person endings) each exclude valid mantras of the other type. Given these compounding difficulties, mantra appears to have no coherent definition at all — and therefore [the objector concludes] such "mantras" cannot properly constitute part of the Veda. (This concludes the objection.)

**The resolution:** not so. Whatever the priests declare to be "mantra" — that itself is mantra; this usage-based designation is itself the flawless defining mark, since it can be recognized alongside the already-understood procedures of ritual application. For example: "**उरु प्रथस्व**" (*uru prathasva*) and similar mantras convey the proper sequence of ritual performance...

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> mantra is such. This denomination alone it is which indicates that texts used in directing the mantras and others are mantras. "Uru prathasva" and similar texts direct the sacrifice. "Agnim ile purohitam" and other similar texts are in praise of the gods. "Ishe tva" and the texts which follow end in the word "tva." "Agna a yahi vitaye" and texts like it are invocations. Such texts as "agnid agnin vihara" are directory. Such texts as "adhah svid asid upari svid asit" are philosophical hymns. Such texts as "ambe ambike ambalike na ma nayati kaschana" are lamentations. Such texts as "prichchhami tva param antam prithivyah" are questions. And so on with others. Since the mantras are so various in kind, except denomination there is no common quality which will serve for a definition. But the need of some definition has been shown by old teachers.


### Page 479

**A functional taxonomy of mantras, by type:**

- **"अग्निमीळे पुरोहितम्"** (*Agnimīḷe purohitam*, Rigveda Samhita 1.1.1) and similar — **praise-form** mantras.
- **"इषे त्वा"** (*Iṣe tvā*, Vajasaneyi Samhita 1.1) and similar — **"tvā"-ending** mantras (concluding with the word "tvā").
- **"अग्न आयाहि वीतये"** (*Agna āyāhi vītaye*, Samaveda Samhita 1.1) and similar — **invocations**, calling the deities to come.
- **"अग्नीदग्नीन्विहर"** (*Agnīd agnīn vihara*, Taittiriya Samhita 6.1.1.3) and similar — **preṣa (command)-form** mantras.
- **"अधः स्विदासीदुपरि स्विदासीदु"** (*Adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīd u*, Rigveda Samhita 10.129.1) and similar — **philosophical** mantras, conveying ultimate truth (tattva).
- **"अम्बे अम्बालिके न मा नयति कश्चन"** (*Ambe ambālike na mā nayati kaścana*, Taittiriya Samhita 3.4.1.1) and similar — **grief-expressing** mantras.
- **"पृच्छामि त्वा परमं पृथिव्याः"** (*Pṛcchāmi tvā paramaṃ pṛthivyāḥ*, Taittiriya Samhita 4.7.8.3) and similar — **question-form** mantras.
- **"वेदिमाच्छः परमं पृथिव्याः"** (*Vedim ācchaḥ paramaṃ pṛthivyāḥ*, Taittiriya Samhita 4.7.8.3) and similar — **answer-form** mantras.

Many more examples could be given. Given such genuinely diverse statements, no single characteristic — beyond simple designation (whatever priests customarily call "mantra") — can be stated as a definition without falling into ativyāpti or avyāpti. What, then, is a definition even for? A defining mark, as a tool for recognizing things, ideally applies uniformly — and the great importance of this requirement was shown long ago by the ancient teachers:

> ऋषयोऽपि न शक्नुवन्नेकैकश्यात्पदार्थान् परीक्षितुम् । सामान्यतोदृष्टया चैषां लक्ष्यन्ते समवायिनः ॥
> *ṛṣayo'pi na śaknuvann ekaikaśyāt padārthān parīkṣitum | sāmānyato-dṛṣṭyā caiṣāṃ lakṣyante samavāyinaḥ ||*
>
> "Even the rishis, who knew all the shastras, were not capable of examining every single object in the world individually and stating its defining marks. But dividing objects into natural groups, and stating the characteristics naturally shared within each group, is the easier method — one the wise follow. Doing so, a defining mark may indeed be stated for all things in the world in this uniform way."

**Therefore, when the learned — the wise, the discerning, ritual practitioners — simply say "this is mantra," that suffices. That itself is mantra; their own statement is the proof. This very designation — their own customary usage — is itself the definition.**

---

> "Even the rishis could not come to the end of things taken one by one: it is only when things are comprehended under a definition that learned men can master them."
>
> "So the denomination of the mantras, as they are used, in the words, This is a mantra, is the definition."

### Page 480

### The Eighth Adhikarana Is Now Formulated

> नास्त्य् एतद् व्याछक्षीत वा ब्राह्मणेत्य् अत्र लक्षणं विद्यतेऽथवा । नास्ति यंको वेद-भागा इह च एवं स्युर् भावकः ॥ मन्त्रस्य ब्राह्मणं शेषेत्य् एतौ द्वौ भागौ तेन मन्त्रकः । अन्यद् वा ब्राह्मणम् इत्य् एव द्वा ब्राह्मण-लक्षणम् ॥
> nāsty etad vyāchakṣīta vā brāhmaṇety atra lakṣaṇaṃ vidyate'thavā | nāsti yaṃko veda-bhāgā iha ca evaṃ syur bhāvakaḥ || mantrasya brāhmaṇaṃ śeṣety etau dvau bhāgau tena mantrakaḥ | anyad vā brāhmaṇam ity eva dvā brāhmaṇa-lakṣaṇam || (Jaimini-nyaya-mala 2.1.8)
>
> "Is there, or is there not, a definition of 'brahmana' with reference to the text 'etad brahmana'? There is none — because no one has shown how much of the Veda is mantra, and how much is brahmana. [Reply:] there is. Since the Veda divides into these two parts, mantra and its remainder [brahmana], whatever in the Veda is not mantra is itself brahmana — this is brahmana's definition."

**The objection develops through the Chaturmasya-ishti example:** "etad brāhmaṇān eva pañca-havīṃṣi" (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.2.7.1) — here, [it's argued,] no definition of "brahmana" exists, because the Vedic portions themselves haven't been clearly delimited, leaving both the mantra-portion (already discussed) and the remaining portions without a coherent shared characteristic. These "other portions" can be shown to include vastly different content-types — nindā (censure), as in "anamīdhya vai māṣāḥ"; praśaṃsā (praise), as in "vāyus tvai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā"; saṃśaya (doubt), as in "śatruṣ cikitsat kim bahavānīrma poṣā"; vidhi (injunction), as in "yajamānena sannimitādambarī bhavati"; parakṛti (deeds of others), as in "mā prāpā neva mahyaṃ pātanti"; purākalpa (ancient narrative), as in "purā brāhmaṇā abhyāṣāriśi"; and viśeṣāvadhāraṇa (specific determination), as in "yāvato'śvair niṣṭhīvet yāvato vāruṇāc cāturāśāt sarvaṃ vet." Given content-types this varied, no single shared characteristic — beyond simple exclusion from the mantra-category — can serve as a proper definition of brahmana.

...(as established earlier) the Veda's own portions, any definition seeking to distinguish "brahmana" precisely from other content would either over- or under-include. The mantra-portion, already discussed, is one part; the remaining portions have been summarized by the ancient teachers thus:

> हेतुर् निर्वचनं निन्दा प्रशंसा संशयो विधिः । परक्रिया पुराकल्पो व्यवधारण-कल्पना ॥

> "Reason (hetu), etymology (nirvacana), censure (nindā), praise (praśaṃsā), doubt (saṃśaya), injunction (vidhi), another's act (parakriyā), ancient narrative (purākalpa), and specific determination (vyavadhāraṇa-kalpanā) — [these nine constitute the remaining Brahmana-content types]."

**Each illustrated with a precise example:**

- **"Tena hy annaṃ kriyate"** — a **hetu** (reason).
- **"Tad dadhno dadhitvam"** — a **nirvacana** (etymology).
- **"Amedhya vai māṣāḥ"** — a **nindā** (censure).
- **"Vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā"** — a **praśaṃsā** (praise).
- **"Tad vyacikitsaj juhavāni mā hauṣam"** — a **saṃśaya** (doubt).
- **"Yajamānena sammitāṇḍumbhāri bhavati"** — a **vidhi** (injunction).
- **"Māṣān eva mahyaṃ pacanti"** — a **parakriyā** (another's deed).
- **"Purā brāhmaṇā abhaiṣuḥ"** — a **purākalpa** (ancient narrative).
- **"Yāvato'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt tāvato vāruṇāṃś cātuṣkapālān nirvapet"** — a **viśeṣāvadhāraṇa-kalpanā** (specific determination).

Other examples could be given as well. None of these nine content-types, taken individually, can serve as a coherent positive definition of "brahmana" — since mantras too, at times, exhibit similar features (as in "amba ambike" and similar). Therefore, the only workable definition remains the exclusionary one already established: whatever in the Veda is not mantra is brahmana.

### Page 482

Having examined the seventh adhikarana (Mantra-nirvacana), we now turn to the eighth (Brahmana-nirvacana). The summary verses mean as follows:

**Objection:** does a definition exist for statements like

> एतद्ब्राह्मणानेव सप्त हवींषि ।
> *etad brāhmaṇān eva sapta havīṃṣi |*

or not? My view: none exists, since even though it's not doubted how much overall is mantra versus brahmana, no explicit rule states precisely "this much is mantra, this much is brahmana" — so any attempted definition falls into avyāpti or ativyāpti. Therefore, brahmana has no valid definition.

**Siddhānta:** it is well-established that the Veda comprises two portions — mantra and brahmana. The mantra-portion's own defining characteristic has already been given [in the seventh adhikarana]; whatever remaining Vedic content is not mantra may properly be called brahmana — this itself serves as brahmana's definition.

In the Chaturmasya-yashti yajna, the mantra "etad brāhmaṇān eva sapta havīṃṣi" (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.2.7.1) is used — yet no explicit definition of brahmana is stated there. Without knowing precisely which portion is mantra and which is brahmana, any attempted definition risks avyāpti/ativyāpti even for the brahmana-portion. (This concludes the objection.)

**The true resolution:** within the Veda's mantra-and-brahmana-composed text, whatever is not mantra is brahmana. "Mantra" was earlier defined as whatever the ancient teachers, during ritual performance, customarily call "mantra." But merely being *any* Vedic statement isn't sufficient — a statement genuinely recognized and transmitted by disciples as mantra, without even the slightest word-variation, alone qualifies. Jaimini himself states this precisely in his own Purva-Mimamsa-sutra:

> आम्नायोक्तमन्त्रश्च ऐतिह्यात्सा हि विभागः ।
> *āmnāyokta-mantraś ca aitihyāt sā hi vibhāgaḥ |* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.33)

— [affirming] that this very distinction [between mantra and its remainder] rests on such established recognition. Accordingly, a Vedic statement bearing these characteristics is mantra; the Veda's remaining content is brahmana — as the sutra states,

> शेषे ब्राह्मणशब्दः ।
> *śeṣe brāhmaṇa-śabdaḥ |* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.33)
> "'Brahmana' is the term applied to the remainder."

---

### Page 483

Up to this point, matters have been discussed clarifying, in careful detail, which portions of Vedic statements are mantra and which are brahmana. In identifying the brahmana-portion specifically, the ancient teachers state it can be marked by: **हेतु** (*hetu*, reason), **निर्वचन** (*nirvacana*, subject-clarification), **निन्दा** (*nindā*, attributing a flaw), **प्रशंसा** (*praśaṃsā*, praise), **संशय** (*saṃśaya*, doubt), **विधि** (*vidhi*, command), **परक्रिया** (*parakriyā*, describing another's matter), **पुराकल्प** (*purākalpa*, ancient history), and **व्यवधारणकल्पना** (*vyavadhāraṇa-kalpanā*, stating "if this is done, that results"). One example for each mark is given:

**Hetu:** तेन ह्यन्नं क्रियते (*tena hy annaṃ kriyate*, Shabara Bhashya 1.2.7.1)
**Nirvacana:** तद्व्याघ्नं दधित्वम् (*tad-vyaghna dadhitvam*, Taittiriya Samhita 2.8.6.4)
**Nindā:** अमेध्या वै माषाः (*amedhyā vai māṣāḥ*, Taittiriya Samhita 5.1.9.1)
**Praśaṃsā:** वायुर्वै क्षेपिष्ठा देवता (*vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā*, Taittiriya Samhita 2.1.1.1)
**Saṃśaya:** तद्व्यचिकित्सेज्जुहवानि मा हौषमिति (*tad vyacikitset juhavāni mā hauṣam iti*, Taittiriya Samhita 6.3.9.1)
**Vidhi:** यजमानेन सम्मितांडुम्भारी भवति (*yajamānena sammitāṇḍumbhāri bhavati*, Taittiriya Samhita 6.2.7.4)
**Parakriyā:** माषानेव मह्यं पचन्ति (*māṣān eva mahyaṃ pacanti*)
**Purākalpa:** पुरा ब्राह्मणा अभैषुः (*purā brāhmaṇā abhaiṣuḥ*, Taittiriya Samhita 1.5.2.4)
**Vyavadhāraṇa-kalpanā:** यावतोऽश्वान् प्रतिगृह्णीयात्तावतो नारायणांश्च तुष्टशालान्निर्वपेत् (*yāvato'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt tāvato nārāyaṇāṇ ca tuṣṭa-śālān nirvapet*, Taittiriya Samhita 2.1.10.1)

Many more examples like these could be given.

**But such marks cannot, on their own, serve as brahmana's true defining characteristic** — one cannot simply say brahmana consists of statements bearing hetu, nirvacana, and similar features while excluding mantra-portions, nor that brahmana is defined purely as whatever differs from hetu/nirvacana-type statements. Why not? Because mantras themselves also contain such hetu, nirvacana, and similar features:

**Hetu:** इन्दवो वामुशन्ति हि (*indavo vām uṣanti hi*, Rigveda 1.2.5.1[?])
**Nirvacana:** उदानीषुर्महीरिति तस्मादुदकमुच्यते (*udānīṣur mahīr iti tasmād udakam ucyate*, Ashvamedha 3.1.2.1[?])
**Nindā:** मोघामन्नं विन्दतेऽप्रचेताः (*moghām annaṃ vindate apracetāḥ*, Rigveda 10.117.6)
**Praśaṃsā:** अग्निर्मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (*agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut*, Rigveda 8.44.16)
**Saṃśaya:** अधः स्विदासीदुपरि स्विदासीत् (*adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt*, Rigveda 10.129.5)

**Vidhi:** वसन्ताय कपिञ्जलानालभत (*vasantāya kapiñjalān ālabhata*, Vajasaneyi Samhita 24.20)
**Parakriyā:** सहस्रमयुता ददत् (*sahasram ayutā dadat*, Rigveda 8.20.19)

Many such statements exist. What about defining brahmana as "statements using the word 'iti'"? This too fails — many mantras themselves contain "iti"-words ("ityadada," "ityayajatha," "ityapacatha," and similar) that priests must recite during yajna — creating ativyāpti. What about defining brahmana as "narrative content, story-form"? This fails too — Rigveda Sukta 10.10, containing the dialogue between Yama and Yami, is itself a mantra-portion, yet narrative in form — again ativyāpti. Therefore, it must be concluded that no faultless definition of brahmana, free from avyāpti/ativyāpti, exists. (This concludes the objection.)

**The true resolution:** not so — here is the correct answer. Brahmana does indeed have a valid definition. Since disciples accept that the Veda comprises exactly two portions — mantra and brahmana — and since mantra's own defining characteristic has already been established, it follows correctly that all remaining Vedic content, not being mantra, is brahmana. Jaimini himself states this precisely through two sutras:

> तच्चोदकेषु मन्त्राख्या । शेषे ब्राह्मणशब्दः ।
> *tac codakeṣu mantrākhyā |* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.32) — *śeṣe brāhmaṇa-śabdaḥ |* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.33)
>
> "In [passages containing] exhortation, the designation 'mantra' applies; 'brahmana' is the term for the remainder."

That is: the Veda contains certain exhortatory statements, to which those versed in tradition give the designation "mantra" — "we study the mantras," they say. The rest of the Veda they call brahmana.

And we have laid down how the mantra part is to be known. Well, whatever is not mantra, that is our definition of a brahmana."
>
> This very definition is given by Jaimini in the two sutras "tach chodakeshu mantrakhya" and "seshe brahmanasabdha." That is to say, In this Veda there are certain exhortatory sentences to which the name mantra part is given by those who know tradition. We study the "mantras" they say. The rest of the Veda they call brahmana.

...as stated in the Bhashya (2.1.33). Disciples familiar with the tradition call such exhortatory statements "mantras," saying "we study the mantras" — and every Vedic portion so designated is indeed mantra; every remaining portion is called brahmana.

**A new objection:** in the Brahmayajna chapter, don't we find portions distinct from both mantra and brahmana — itihāsas and similar? As stated: "yad brāhmaṇetihāsān purāṇāni kalpān gāthā nārāśaṃsīḥ" (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.9) — "whatever brahmanas, itihasas, puranas, kalpas, gathas, narashamsis..."

> "Not so. This is simply a case of naming distinct sub-varieties of brahmana under their own separate designations — itihāsa, purāṇa, and the rest — just as with the wandering-monk-priest analogy. Statements like 'devāsurāḥ saṃyattā' ('the gods and demons were in conflict') are itihāsas. Passages beginning from the world's pre-creation state and describing cosmic origination, like 'idaṃ vā agre naiva kiṃcanāsīt' ('in the beginning, there was truly nothing at all'), constitute purāṇa. 'Kalpa' refers to procedural passages found within sections like the Arunaketuka fire-altar rite. 'Gāthās' are specific mantra-types, as in 'agni-cayane yugma-gāthābhiḥ parigāyati' (Taittiriya Samhita 5.1.6.1). 'Nārāśaṃsī' verses (ṛc) narrate human affairs. Therefore, since no portion exists beyond mantra and brahmana, the Veda's full scope, once mantra and brahmana are properly defined, remains soundly and completely accounted for by these two categories alone."

### Page 486

"Feed the parivrajakas inside" doesn't mean parivrajakas aren't brahmins — they are brahmins, simply a distinct sub-group within the class. In the same way, calling something "brahmana" (the Veda's brahmana-portion) includes all its natural sub-classifications — itihasa, purana, kalpa, and similar content. Examples:

**Itihāsa:** देवासुराः संयत्ता आसन् (*devāsurāḥ saṃyattā āsan*, Taittiriya Samhita 3.3.10.1) and similar.
**Purāṇa:** इदं वा अग्रे नैव किंचनासीत् (*idaṃ vā agre naiva kiṃcanāsīt*, Taittiriya Brahmana 2.2.9.1) and similar — describing the pre-creation state and the act of creation itself, just as in Purana literature.
**Kalpa:** इति मन्त्रः, कल्पोऽत ऊर्ध्वम्, यदि बलिं हरेत् (*iti mantraḥ, kalpo'ta ūrdhvam, yadi baliṃ haret*, Taittiriya Aranyaka 1.13.1), occurring in the Arunaketuka-chayana section.
**Gāthā:** युग्मगाथाभिः परिगायति (*yugma-gāthābhiḥ parigāyati*, Taittiriya Samhita 5.1.6.1), in the Agnichayana rite.
**Nārāśaṃsī:** Riks narrating human affairs.

**Therefore, all these itihasa-and-similar statements are sub-classifications of the brahmana-portion, and are themselves brahmanas.** It follows that the Veda comprises exactly two portions — mantra and brahmana — with no third category existing anywhere. **The Veda is thus definitively established as consisting precisely of mantra and brahmana.**

---

What "kalpa" means is told in the Arunakesukachayana chapter. The mantras "iti mantrah," "kalpo 'ta urdhvam" and "yadi balim haret," prescribed in the Agnichayana chapter by the text "yamagathabhih parigayati," are gathas. Verses that tell of the deeds of men of old time are narasansis. There are therefore besides mantra and brahmana no other parts of the Veda. And we have shown how these two are to be severally defined. That definition of the Veda itself then, according to which it is the sum of the mantras and the brahmanas, is established.

## Chapter 13. Vedic Mantras Are of Three Kinds: Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda Mantras
*Original title: "Vēdamantragaḷu Ṛgvēda, Yajurvēda, Sāmavēdamantragaḷendu mūruvidhavu"*
**Printed pages 487–489 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter — p.489 repaired during Phase B: the cross-Veda mantra example and Jaimini's three-sutra Rik/Sama/Yajus classification now carry full Devanagari.)*

### Page 487

> मन्त्राणां तर-विशेषस्य तस्मिन्न् एव पाद इत्य् अं विचारितः ।
> mantrāṇāṃ tara-viśeṣasya tasminn eva pāda ity aṃ vicāritaḥ | (Jaimini-nyaya-mala 2.1.10)

**The differences between the three kinds of mantras (rik, sama, yajus) are considered in this same pada, as follows:**

> नकार्यम् अयसम्बाधं लक्ष साङ्कर्याद् इति शङ्किते । पादेश् च गीतिः प्रोक्षिष्ट-पाठ इत्य् एष्यैः सङ्करकः ॥
> nakāryam ayasambādhaṃ lakṣa sāṅkaryād iti śaṅkite | pādeś ca gītiḥ prokṣiṣṭa-pāṭha ity eṣyaiḥ saṅkarakaḥ || (Jaimini-nyaya-mala 2.1.10)
>
> "Some say that on account of the way in which they are mixed up, there is no characteristic mark distinguishing rik, sama, and yajus verses; but there is really no confusion, because we have the pada [word-form], the gīti [chant-form], and the praśliṣṭapāṭha [continuous-recitation form] by means of which we can discriminate the three."

**It is thus stated in the Veda:**

> अहे बुध्निय मन्त्रं मे गोपाय यम् ऋषयस् त्रैविदा विदुः । ऋचः सामानि यजूंषि चेति । त्रैविदा इत्य् उच्यते । त्रीणि वेदान् अवगत्वानि यस्य स त्रैविदः । तेषां शिष्याः सामानि यजूंषि चेति त्रैविदाः । त्रिविधं मन्त्र-भागं वेदस्य यं गायन्ति तं गोपायेत्य् अन्वयः ॥
> ahe budhniya mantraṃ me gopāya yam ṛṣayas traividā viduḥ | ṛcaḥ sāmāni yajūṃṣi ceti | traividā ity ucyate | trīṇi vedān avagatvāni yasya sa traividaḥ | teṣāṃ śiṣyāḥ sāmāni yajūṃṣi ceti traividāḥ | trividhaṃ mantra-bhāgaṃ vedasya yaṃ gāyanti taṃ gopāyety anvayaḥ ||
>
> "'O Serpent of the Deep, guard my mantra which the sages, versed in the three [Vedas], know — riks, samans, and yajus.' 'Traividā' means one who has thoroughly comprehended the three Vedas. Their disciples — [taught] riks, samans, and yajus — are likewise called 'traividas.' The construction: 'protect the threefold mantra-portion of the Veda which they recite.'"

This opens a new technical discussion: since rik, sama, and yajus mantras appear intermixed throughout the Veda, how can one reliably tell them apart? The resolution draws on three distinguishing forms of textual presentation — pada, gīti, and praśliṣṭapāṭha.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> The differences between the three kinds of mantras are considered in the same pada as follows:—
>
> "Some say that on account of the way in which they are mixed up there is no characteristic mark of rik, sama and yajur verses: but there is really no confusion, because we have the pada, the giti and the prashtahtapatha by means of which we can discriminate the three."
>
> There is the text "ahe budhniya mantram me gopaya yam rishayas traivida viduh richah samani yajunshi." By "trivid" is meant a man who knows the three vedas. Pupils of such an one called traividas. "The threefold mantra portion of the Veda which they recite—protect it," that is the construction here.


### Page 488

> गीत-रूपा मन्त्राः सामानि । वृत्ते गीति-वर्जितत्वेन प्रश्लिष्ट-पठिता मन्त्रा यजूंषीत्य् एते न क्वाप्य् अस्ति सङ्करः । तेषां त्रिविधं जैमिना सूत्र-त्रेण लक्षितम् । तेषाम् अग्र्यार्थ-वशेन पाद-व्यवस्था । गीतिष् सामाख्या । शेषे यजुः-शब्दः (पुर्व मिमम्स २.१.३५–३७) इति । एकम् एव मन्त्राणां तर-विशेषम् उपजीव्य वेदानाम् अग्र्यादिर् यो यजुर्-वेद साम-वेद इति त्रैविध्यं संसिद्धम् ॥
> gīta-rūpā mantrāḥ sāmāni | vṛtte gīti-varjitatvena praśliṣṭa-paṭhitā mantrā yajūṃṣīty ete na kvāpy asti saṅkaraḥ | teṣāṃ trividhaṃ jaiminā sūtra-treṇa lakṣitam | teṣām agryārtha-vaśena pāda-vyavasthā | gītiṣ sāmākhyā | śeṣe yajuḥ-śabdaḥ (Purva Mimamsa 2.1.35–37) iti | ekam eva mantrāṇāṃ tara-viśeṣam upajīvya vedānām agryādir yo yajur-veda sāma-veda iti traividhyaṃ saṃsiddham ||
>
> "Sung-form mantras are sāmans. Metered mantras recited continuously without song-form are yajuṣes — thus, no confusion at all remains. Jaimini himself defines these three types through three [distinct] sutras. Their pada-arrangement is determined by their primary meaning; their being sung is the mark of 'sāman'; the remainder bears the term 'yajus' (Purva Mimamsa 2.1.35–37). Relying on this one specific distinguishing feature of mantras, the Veda's own threefold division — into Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda — stands firmly established."

Among Vedic mantras, there are exactly three principal types — Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda — intermixed throughout the Veda, with no obvious single mark distinguishing them at first glance. Mimamsa-shastra resolves this in its own dedicated pada: a mantra built from metrical **padas** (verse-feet, matching meters like Gayatri and similar — one pada for "ekapada" meter, two for "dvipada," three for Gayatri, four for Trishtubh/Jagati, five for Saptanta, and so on) is called **Rigveda**. Mantras in musically-tuned, sung form (**gīti**) are called **Sāmaveda**. Prose collections with no metrical constraint are called **Yajus**. This way, distinguishing them individually is possible, and no confusion arises in principle.

**But a genuine difficulty now surfaces:** the mantra "ahe budhniya mantraṃ me gopāya yaṃ ṛṣayas traividā viduḥ | ṛcaḥ sāmāni yajūṃṣi" (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.3.9) invokes "traividas" — those learned in all three Vedas. But the three mantra-types (rik, yajus, sāma) as defined above turn out to lack a *stable* defining mark after all — because certain mantras appear within the Veda in ways that cut against this clean threefold scheme...

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Now it is said here that there is no characteristic mark peculiar to each of the three Vedas in their mantra portion, Rig Sama and Yajur. Why? Because of the difficulty of avoiding confusion. The only satisfactory mark would be that the teacher, to whom all three are familiar should say, This mantra is part of the Rig or Sama or Yajur Veda as the case might be. But there the confusion comes in. The mantra devo vah savitotpunatvachchhidrena pavitrena vasoh suryasya rasmibhih occurs in the Yajur Veda, and is recited with the other texts there. But it is not a Yajur text. Because in the brahmana of that Veda it is spoken of as a text of the Rig Veda "Savitryarcha." In the same way a Sama text is...

---

*(To be continued.)*

### Page 489

They become genuinely intermixed with one another, making them difficult to separate cleanly. One might propose that teachers simply say "this mantra belongs to Rigveda" and so on — but it turns out that mantras properly belonging to Rigveda occur within Yajurveda texts too, and Samaveda mantras get incorporated into Yajurveda as well, causing real confusion (sāṅkarya). For example:

> देवो वः सवितोत्पुनात्वच्छिद्रेण पवित्रेण वसोः सूर्यस्य रश्मिभिः ।
> *devo vaḥ savitotpunatv acchidreṇa pavitreṇa vasoḥ sūryasya raśmibhiḥ |* (Taittiriya Samhita 1.1.11.1)

occurs within the Yajurveda Samhita, among other Yajurveda mantras — yet it's stated (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.3.9.3) that this mantra is not truly a Yajurveda text at all, but a Rigveda mark, called there "**सावित्र्यर्चा**" (*Sāvitryarcā*, "a rik dedicated to Savitr"). Such Rigveda-mantras and Samaveda-mantras thus appear woven throughout Yajurveda's own liturgy.

**Yet this is resolved:** each of the three Vedas' mantras does carry its own distinct, statable mark. Mantras composed with metrical padas (verse-feet, per meters like Gayatri and similar) belong to **Rigveda**. Mantras used specifically for singing/chanting are **Samaveda**. The remaining mantra-portions — unmetered, not suited for singing, in plain prose — are classified as **Yajurveda**. Stated this way, no genuine confusion remains.

**Jaimini himself formulates this threefold scheme through three sutras:**

> तेषां ऋग्यथार्थवशेन पादव्यवस्था । गीतिषु सामाख्या । शेषे यजुःशब्दः ।
> *teṣāṃ ṛg-yathārthavaśena pādavyavasthā | gītiṣ sāmākhyā | śeṣe yajuḥ-śabdaḥ |*
>
> "Their pada-arrangement follows from their primary meaning [in Rigveda]; being sung is the mark of 'sāman'; the remainder bears the term 'yajus.'"

**It is precisely on this difference among the three mantra-types that the distinct classification of the three Vedas — Rigveda, Sama, and Yajur — rests.**

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> sung in the Yajur Veda with the prelude "etat sama gayannaste." The Sama Veda contains three Yajur texts "akshitam asi" "achyutam asi" and "pranasansitam asi." The verses of the Rig Veda, too, are the basis on which the chanted Sama Veda rests. Therefore there is no mark by which we can discriminate between these three. Not so. The three marks mentioned in the verse pada, giti and prashlishtapathah avert all confusion. Mantra in metre that are divided into padas and half verses, are riks. Mantras in the form of song are samans. Mantras that are neither metrical nor adopted for singing, but are in plain prose, are Yajur texts. Thus there is no confusion.
>
> This threefold character of the mantras is set out by Jaimini in the three sutras "tesham rig yatrarthavasena padavyavastha," "gitishu samakhya" and "seshe yajuhsabdh." And it is on this difference between the three kinds of mantras that the distinction between the three Vedas—Rig, Sama and Yajur—rests.




## Chapter 14. The Matter That Vedic Study, Together with Its Meaning, Is an Obligatory Duty
*Original title: "Arthasahitavāgi vēdādhyayanavu kartavyavemba vicāra"*
**Printed pages 490–519 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter — all previously-flagged pages repaired during Phase B. One note carried forward: p.514's sutra citation was a reconstruction from an earlier-established IAST reading rather than a fresh confident transcription, and is worth a source-image check during any future verification pass; everything else in this chapter is a confident transcription.)*
> - p.518 (no Devanagari found — likely paraphrased instead of quoted)

### Page 490

The great sage Jaimini establishes this threefold mantra-classification through three sutras: "teṣāṃ pṛthag-artha-vaśena pādavyavasthā" (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.35), "gītiṣ sāmākhyā" (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.36), "śeṣe yajuḥ-śabdaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.37). Distinguishing these sub-classifications within Vedic mantras as Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Samaveda appropriately yields the term "traividhya" (threefold-ness).

### A Discussion, with Consideration of Fruit, Establishing Vedic Study as an Obligatory Duty

> तेषां च वेदानां सर्वेषाम् अप्य् एकतमस्य वा स्व-स्व-ज्ञानुसारेणाध्ययनम् उपवीतेन कर्तव्यम् । तथा च याज्ञवल्क्यः स्वयं वेदान् अधीत्य वेदौ वा वेदं वापि यथा-क्रमं । एक-वेदेऽपि पित्र्ये तं पैत्र्यवं वेदम् इत्य् उच्यते । एक-वेदस्ये पितृ-सम्प्राप्तागतं स्वं वेदोऽत्र श्रुत्युक्तः । प्रधीयीत स्वकं वेदम् इति । श्रुतिश् च नियमोऽयं काम्यं किं तु नित्यम् । अत एव पुरुषार्थानुशासने सूचितम् ॥
> teṣāṃ ca vedānāṃ sarveṣām apy ekatamasya vā sva-sva-jñānusāreṇādhyayanam upavītena kartavyam | tathā ca yājñavalkyaḥ svayaṃ vedān adhītya vedau vā vedaṃ vāpi yathā-kramaṃ | eka-vede'pi pitrye taṃ paitryavaṃ vedam ity ucyate | eka-vedasye pitṛ-samprāptāgataṃ svaṃ vedo'tra śrutyuktaḥ | pradhīyīta svakaṃ vedam iti | śrutiś ca niyamo'yaṃ kāmyaṃ kiṃ tu nityam | ata eva puruṣārthānuśāsane sūcitam ||
>
> "Study of these Vedas — all of them, or any one, according to one's own intellectual capacity — is obligatory for every person invested with the sacred thread. As Yajnavalkya himself states: 'Having studied the Vedas — all of them, two, or even one, in proper order.' Even when only a single Veda is studied, it should be the one handed down through one's paternal lineage — this is what 'one's own' means in the scriptural statement, 'let him study his own Veda.' This obligation is a Shruti-injunction — not merely optional (kāmya) but obligatory (nitya). This very point is indicated in the Purusharthanushasana [treatise on human duty]—"

This opens a substantial new discussion: is studying the Veda a matter of personal choice, or an unconditional religious duty? And if a person's capacity permits only one Veda, which one should it be? The answer given here is striking — it must be the specific Veda transmitted through one's own paternal family line, not simply any Veda of one's choosing.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> The study of these Vedas, all of them or any one of them according to the measure of the student's intelligence, is incumbent on every one who has put on the sacred thread. Listen to what the holy Yajnavalkya says, "Learning the Vedas, or any two of them, or any one." In the case where one Veda only is studied, it should be that handed down from father to son as the Veda of the family. This is what is meant by the word "own" in this text of Scripture, "A man should study his own Veda." And this study is imperative, not optional. This is what is meant in the sutra of the Purusharthanusasana.—


### Page 491

> तथापि गृहस्थार्थाध्ययनम् अन्तरेण ब्रह्मचर्यज्ञा सम्भवात् तदीय-फलम् अपि सम्पद्येत ।
> tathāpi gṛhasthārthādhyayanam antareṇa brahmacaryajñā sambhavāt tadīya-phalam api sampadyeta | 
>
> **"The study of the Veda is imperative, because if you do not study it you will become an outcast."**
>
> This outlawry is thus referred to in Scripture: "The study of one's own Veda delivers from sin. It purifies the gods. He who abandons that study has no lot or part in Speech, has no lot or part in Heaven." As it has been said:
>
> "He who abandons his friend who loves him — the Veda in the form of a companion — he has no lot or part in Speech: what he hears, he hears amiss; he does not know the path of virtue."
>
> "Therefore one should study one's own Veda." (Manu Smriti 2.168)

A dvija (twice-born) purified through upanayana must, according to his intellectual capacity, study all three Vedas as above; if unable, at least one. Yajnavalkya states: "A householder-dvija should study three Vedas — or two, or, failing that, at least one." Here, "one Veda" specifically means the Veda transmitted through one's own paternal, ancestral lineage — hence the word "sva" (own) appears in the injunction. "Svādhyāya" means study of one's own [family's] shakha specifically — and this obligation is **nitya** (obligatory), not **kāmya** (optional): one cannot simply choose whether to undertake it, on pain of forfeiting one's dvija-status entirely. On this matter, the text Purusharthanushasana states this very sutra—

### "Vedasvādhyāyanaṃ nityam anadhyayane pātād iti" — "Vedic Study is Obligatory; in Non-Study, There Is Fall"

Vedic study is a nitya-karma (obligatory duty) for the dvija; failing to study causes one to fall from one's own dharma, becoming "patita" (fallen). Regarding this "fall," the Taittiriya Aranyaka states:

One who studies removes all his sins and becomes purified — study purifies even the deities. One who fails to study loses his connection with speech, and thereby loses heaven's joy too; he is not called learned, mantras don't come under his command, and he has no fluency in speech. As Shruti states:

> यस्य स्थाज् सखिविदं सखायं न तस्य वाच्यपि भागो अस्ति । यद् ईदं शृणोत्य् उलकं शृणोति न हि प्रवेद सुकृतस्य पन्थाम् ॥
> yasya sthāj sakhividaṃ sakhāyaṃ na tasya vācyapi bhāgo asti | yad īdaṃ śṛṇoty ulakaṃ śṛṇoti na hi praveda sukṛtasya panthām || (Taittiriya Aranyaka 9.2.3)
>
> "He who abandons his friend who knows companionship — for him, there is no share even in speech; whatever he hears, he hears crookedly; he does not know the path of righteous action."

One who fails to study the Veda — his genuine friend — becomes devoid of eloquence; whatever he says or hears is flawed, and he does not know the path to salvation (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.15). Therefore, a dvija must undertake study of his own family shakha specifically. Here "sacivit" (companion) means: the Veda, understanding the difficulty the student undergoes, protects him like a friend — even the fruit of yajnas requiring vast expenditure and effort can be obtained through mere Vedic study alone. Shruti confirms this directly:

> "यं यं क्रतुम् अधीशे केन केनाष्टेष्ट भवत्य् अग्नि-वाय्व्-आदित्यस्य सायुज्यं गच्छति"
> "yaṃ yaṃ kratum adhīśe kena kenāṣṭeṣṭa bhavaty agni-vāyv-ādityasya sāyujyaṃ gacchati" (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.13)
>
> "Whatever ritual-portion one studies, that very rite becomes [ritually] accomplished for him — he attains companionship (sāyujya) with the deities Agni, Vayu, and Aditya."

Shudra-status befalls even one's descendants. As many such statements as needed could be cited.

**A technical clarification on karma-types:** karmas are of three kinds — **nitya** (obligatory), **naimittika** (occasional), and **kāmya** (optional/desired). Nitya-karma is duty that must be performed, not optional — Sandhyavandana and similar rites, per the rule—

> अहरहः स्वाध्यायमुशासीत ।
> *ahar ahaḥ svādhyāyam uśāsīta |*
> "One should perform daily recitation each day"

—abandoning such duty makes one fallen. Naimittika-karma is performed on a specific occasion — marriage rites, funerary rites, and similar — obligatory when the occasion arises, though views differ on some details. Kāmya-karma is performed from personal desire for a specific fruit — vows, yajnas, and similar; the shastras state that a given act yields a given fruit, and one desiring that fruit may perform it, but there is no compulsion to do so, and no fault in abstaining.

**A genuinely difficult doubt now arises:** must Vedic study occur *before* one knows the shastric rule "one should study one's own shakha," or only *after* knowing it? Does one study first and thereby come to learn the rule — or must one first know the rule and only then study? This difficulty may be admitted. On this very question rests the difference of opinion between those who follow Prabhākara, and those, such as Prakāśātma, who follow the different doctrine of Kumārila—

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Here a doubt arises. Does this study of the Veda precede or follow knowledge of that precept which is in the Veda, and according to which a man should study his own Veda? Do you study and so learn the precept? Or do you know the precept and therefore study? The difficulty may be admitted. On it is based the difference between those who follow Prabhakara, and those, such as Prakasatma, who follow the different doctrine of Kumarila—


### Page 495

A genuine doubt arises: to know the rule that Vedic study must be performed, one would seemingly need to have already studied the Veda and learned what it states — yet the desire to study only arises *after* knowing this rule. So which comes first? This creates a mutual-dependence flaw (anyonyāśraya-doṣa), like saying one cannot marry until born, and cannot be born until married. Since this doubt has genuine grounds, we accept it as worth resolving.

**Two resolutions emerge.** Followers of "**गुरुमत** (*Guru-mata*)" hold that teachers, through great effort, instill in boys the very inclination to undertake study. Followers of Prakāśātma's differing doctrine argue instead: just as the notion "one should perform Sandhyavandana" is instilled in boys by their father *before* study even begins, so too the desire to study itself comes from one's father, elder brother, or other elders — not from the Veda's own text. Either way, whether the study-obligation is learned through Vedic study itself or through one's elders beforehand, one thing remains beyond dispute: a person who has undergone upanayana must undertake Vedic study.

**Historical note:** among the Mimamsakas, two teachers — **कुमारिल भट्ट** (*Kumārila Bhaṭṭa*) and **प्रभाकर** (*Prabhākara*) — lived around the time of Shankaracharya, each establishing an independent doctrine. Kumārila's school is called "**भाट्टमत**" (*Bhāṭṭa-mata*); Prabhākara's is called "**गुरुमत**" (*Guru-mata*). As referenced above, "followers of Guru-mata" means followers of the Prabhākara doctrine specifically.

Since it's established that upanayana-invested persons must undertake Vedic study, this study consists of memorizing the syllables — reciting the Vedas by heart without error — stated in the Purusharthanushasana as the observable fruit. The following sutras and their commentary are presented here. The objection is formulated to establish that study has merely an observable purpose:

> "adṛṣṭārthā kṣtiḥ vidhy-arthikatvāc coditeti || 1 ||" — dṛṣṭa-phala-sādhane bhojanādau vidhy-adarśanād vidhy-anvitam adhyayanam adṛṣṭārtham avagatavyam | adṛṣṭa-viśeṣo na śruta iti cet, tatrāha—
>
> "The study of the Veda must have some unseen [spiritual] object, because that study is a matter of positive injunction. Since no injunction exists for observable-fruit acts like eating (we simply eat when hungry, and the fruit is directly visible), while an actual injunction *does* exist for Vedic study, it must be understood that this study carries an unseen purpose."

**Sutra's meaning:** since it comes about through a proper injunction, Vedic study has only an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose — not a visible one. Eating and drinking produce directly observable fruit — no shastric command exists saying "one should eat" — we eat simply when hungry, and the fruit (satisfied hunger) is plainly visible. But regarding the Veda, shastras explicitly command study. Observing this command, one must conclude that mere study alone produces an unseen fruit — puṇya (merit) — invisible to ordinary perception.

**A counter-objection:** but nowhere does Shruti explicitly state that such unseen fruit results from study! The resolution follows in the next sutra:

> "घृत-कुल्याद्य्-अतिदेशः स्वर्ग-कल्प्यं वेति ॥ २ ॥"
> "ghṛta-kulyādy-atideśaḥ svarga-kalpyaṃ veti || 2 ||"
>
> "Extend to this case the promise of rivers of butter and the like; or understand heaven to be the reward."

**A sharp counter-objection now arises:** since study already has two observable (dṛṣṭa) fruits — ritual refinement (saṃskāra, correct recitation) and acquisition of learning — why posit an unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit like heaven at all? The next sutra answers this.

### "Amyukte saṃskāra-prāptiḥ" (Sutra 3)

> संस्कारार्थ्ये कृत्वे च्युञ्जसिम् अपि विसर्गयोगादर्श्हनात् य्वे स्यात् क्वस्थां च गां प्रयुक्ते न गां प्रयुजीतेति फलाफलत्वे स्वोज्जं फलान्तर कल्प्येत । अध्ययनस्य तु पुरुषार्थत्वाभावात् पुरुषार्थ-फलं स्वर्गादिकं कल्प्येय एव ।
> saṃskārārthye kṛtve cyuñjasim api visargayogādarśhanāt yve syāt kvasthāṃ ca gāṃ prayukte na gāṃ prayujīteti phalāphalatve svojjaṃ phalāntara kalpyeta | adhyayanasya tu puruṣārthatvābhāvāt puruṣārtha-phalaṃ svargādikaṃ kalpyeya eva |
>
> "**Ceremonial perfection and a mastery of the text are not appropriate rewards.** For it is nowhere said that a ceremonially perfect text is to be used at such and such a sacrifice, but only a text; while, as for the mastery of the text, that is not in itself an object of human desire at all, and so cannot be the reward which is contemplated by the injunction to study the Veda."

**Sutra's meaning:** the two supposed fruits — correctly grasping the letters (reciting without variation) and mastering the recitation — are not genuinely proper fruits of study. Nowhere does scripture say one must recite *with* refinement in a yajna, only that one must recite; recitation-scholarship in itself is not a genuine human aim (puruṣārtha), so the study-injunction cannot intend this as its purpose.

**A further defense is anticipated and answered:** but surely text-mastery aids meaning-comprehension, and thereby becomes a genuine human aim? Against this, Sayana points out that mantras belonging to the jyotiṣṭoma and similar yajnas, when recited merely as part of this prescribed study, carry no authority regarding their own meaning — exactly like the mantras used for expelling snake-venom, which are recited instrumentally without their literal sense needing independent justification.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Ceremonial perfection and a mastery of the text are not oppropriate rewards.
>
> For it is nowhere said that a ceremonially perfect text is to be used at such and such a sacrifice, but only a text; while, as for the mastery of the text, that is not in itself an object of human desire at all, and so cannot be the reward which is contemplated by the injunction to study the Veda.
>
> But, it may be said, the mastery of the text of the Veda, though not in itself an object of human desire, is the cause of our apprehending the meaning, and in that way becomes an object of human desire. Against this he urges the plea that the Vedic texts about the jyotishtoma and other sacrifices, being, as they are, used merely as part of this prescribed study of the text of the Veda, are not authoritative as regards their meaning any more than are the mantras which are used for expelling the poison of serpents and the like.


### Page 500

Even while reciting mantras used in jyotiṣṭoma and similar rites, understanding their meaning is unnecessary — reciting them at the proper time is simply custom, with no requirement to grasp their sense. Given this, whether Vedic study carries fruit beyond mere refinement-and-recitation is addressed next.

### "Anyāṅgaṃ nārthapramāṇakam iti" (Sutra 4)

> अध्ययन-विधायकं तु वाक्यं स्वयम् इतः स्वाध्ययनस्यैवाङ्गम् इति कृत्वा स्वार्थे प्रमाणम् इष्यात ॥
> adhyayana-vidhāyakaṃ tu vākyaṃ svayam itaḥ svādhyayanasyaivāṅgam iti kṛtvā svārthe pramāṇam iṣyāta ||
>
> "**What is part of something else is not authoritative as regards its meaning.** If you retort that in that case this very text which enjoins the study of the Veda will lose all its authority, he rejoins that that text is part of the study which it itself enjoins, and of nothing else, and that it therefore is authoritative as regards its meaning."

**Sutra's meaning:** something that is a mere component of one act is not authoritative regarding a *different* act's meaning, since it cannot independently establish sense outside its own proper context. One might object that the study-enjoining statement, being itself just one part of the Veda, cannot be authoritative regarding study — but this fails: that statement belongs to the Veda, not to some other text, and discusses precisely its own proper subject matter (study itself), not anything foreign to it — hence it remains fully authoritative.

### "Adhyayana-vākyam anyāṅgam iti" (Sutra 5) — "The Text About the Study of the Veda Is Not Part of Some Other Third Thing"

> नैवम् अदृष्टार्थस्य कर्म-कारक-भूतस्याध्ययन-गत-फलाभावाद् अध्येतव्य इति कर्मणा च श्रुत्या विरुध्येतेति आह ॥
> naivam adṛṣṭārthasya karma-kāraka-bhūtasyādhyayana-gata-phalābhāvād adhyetavya iti karmaṇā ca śrutyā virudhyeteti āha ||
>
> "Well, let us concede that the purpose of the study of the Veda is a spiritual one: there remains a grammatical difficulty. The affix 'tavya' in the word 'adhyetavyah' denotes the object [in the accusative case]; and the result of the action should accordingly be connected with the object, and not with the agent. But we do not see that any spiritual reward accrues to the Veda itself, which is the object of the act of studying. To this the opponent replies—"

This raises a genuinely subtle grammatical objection: since Sanskrit's own karaka-theory (case-role grammar) directs the fruit of an action toward its grammatical *object* — and "the Veda" is grammatically the object of "should be studied" — how can the spiritual fruit of study accrue to the *student* (the agent) rather than to the Veda itself (the object)?

---

>
> If you retort that in that case this very text which enjoins the study of the Veda, will lose all its authority, he rejoins that that text is part of the study which it itself enjoins, and of nothing else, and that it therefore is authoritative as regards its meaning.
>
> The text about the study of the Veda is not part of some other third thing.
>
> Well, let us concede that the purpose of the study of the Veda is a spiritual one: there remains a grammatical difficulty. The affix 'tavya' in the word 'adhyetavyah' denotes the object: and the result of the action should accordingly be connected with the object, and not with the agent. But we do not see that any spiritual reward accrues to the Veda itself, which is the object of the act of studying. To this the opponent replies—


### Page 501

One might argue the statement carries authority, and thereby an unseen fruit results for it too. But a grammatical doubt arises: since the "tavya" affix in "adhyetavyaḥ" expresses the object-role (karma-kāraka), it requires a grammatical object — "of what?" — answered by "the Veda" (accusative). This word doesn't state who must study; one might conclude the fruit of study accrues to the *Veda itself* rather than to the studying person. But the sutra actually means to establish that the fruit belongs to the person, not the Veda. The objector replies:

### "साक्तुवत्करणपरिणाम इति" (Sutra 6)
*"Sāktuvat karaṇa-pariṇāma iti"*

> "**You must take the object to stand for the instrument here, as in the case of the grain used at the sacrifice.**
>
> Take the sentence 'saktun juhoti.' Here the matter in hand is the ceremonial perfection to be acquired by means of the Homa offering. But there is no further use for grain made ceremonially perfect at the Homa sacrifice; it is reduced to ashes. The accusative here then must be made to give up its primary reference, and be taken as standing for the instrumental. 'Saktun juhoti,' 'he offers grain,' stands for 'saktubhir juhoti,' 'he makes his offering with grain.' So here the rewards you suggest, ceremonial perfection and a..."

**Sutra's meaning:** just as with the word "saktu" (ground grain), here too the accusative (object-case) word must be reinterpreted as an instrumental. In—

> सक्तून् जुहोति ।
> *saktūn juhoti |*
> "He offers grain-as-oblation"

—"**saktūn**" is grammatically the object — yet since the offered grain is consumed to ash and has no further use, this accusative cannot literally mean the grain *receives* the ritual's fruit. Instead, it must be read as—

> सक्तुभिर्जुहोति ।
> *saktubhir juhoti |*
> "He performs the offering by means of grain"

— (instrumental). By this same grammatical reinterpretation, "the Veda" in "adhyetavyaḥ" — though grammatically accusative — should be understood as the *instrument* through which the fruit is attained, not its recipient; the actual recipient of the fruit remains the studying person.

---

But there is no further use for grain made ceremonially perfect at the Homa sacrifice; it is reduced to ashes. "Saktun juhoti," "he offers grain," stands for "saktubhir juhoti," "he makes his offering with grain." So here the rewards you suggest, ceremonial perfection and a...

**Sayana now establishes his own view: a directly observable, temporal reward already attends Vedic study, so no unexpressed unseen/spiritual reward need be supplied.**

### "दृष्टे तु नादृष्टमिति" (Sutra 7) — "Where There Is a Visible Reward You Must Not Supply an Invisible One"
*"Dṛṣṭe tu nādṛṣṭam iti"*

What is this visible reward? He states it:

### "दृष्ट्वा प्राप्तिसंस्कारावीति" (Sutra 8) — "The Visible Rewards Are the Mastery of the Text and Ceremonial Perfection"
*"Dṛṣṭvā prāpti-saṃskārāv iti"*

He further declares that mastery of the syllables is, mediately, a genuine human purpose (puruṣārtha)—

**Sutra's meaning:** prāpti (acquisition/mastery of the syllables) and saṃskāra (ritual refinement) are indeed the directly observable fruits [of study]. Of these, the first — prāpti, in the sense of grasping and memorizing the syllables — becomes, progressively [through a chain of practical uses], a genuine means to human ends.

### "Prāptārtha-bodha iti" (Sutra 9) — "By Mastering the Text, Knowledge of the Meaning [Is Produced]"

> जायते इति शेषः । न च भोजनादिवद् अस्त्य् अयुत्ति-विशेष-विधिस् त्व् अर्थ्यम् इति शङ्कनीयम् । अवश्याकादिवन् नियमाद् अव्यय विध्य-वस-त्व् इत्य् आह ॥
> jāyate iti śeṣaḥ | na ca bhojanādivad asty ayutti-viśeṣa-vidhis tv arthyam iti śaṅkanīyam | avaśyākādivan niyamād avyaya vidhya-vasa-tv ity āha ||
>
> "Supply 'is produced.' You will perhaps say, why should it not be with studying the Veda as it is with eating food? We eat food because we know that if we eat, we shall be satisfied, and if we do not eat, we shall be hungry. So with the Veda. Why not say that we study it because only so can we understand it, and, understanding it, perform the sacrifices commanded, and reap the reward? Why insist on the study of the Veda being in itself matter of Scriptural injunction? In answer to this he shows that the injunction referred to looks to the spiritual reward which accrues from the thing being done in the way prescribed, and in no other. As in the case of the rice for the sacrifice, which must be pounded in a mortar and not husked in any other way."

**Sutra's meaning:** prāpti (mastering the text through memorization) aids understanding of the Veda's meaning — "arthabodha" here means "artha-jñāna" (knowledge of meaning), with "jāyate" (arises) elliptically understood.

**A genuinely sharp counter-objection follows:** just as with eating — we eat because we know it satisfies hunger, with no separate injunction needed to eat — why isn't Vedic study the same? Why not simply say we study *because* it lets us understand the Veda, and understanding it, we perform the commanded yajnas and reap their reward — without needing to treat the *study itself* as independently commanded by scripture? Since this fruit (understanding, leading to yajna, leading to reward) is not directly observable at the moment of study itself, and study proceeds under specific rules and constraints, why should it need separate scriptural authority at all?

**Sayana's answer:** where a fruit is directly observable, no injunction is needed; no one desires an unseen fruit for its own sake. Therefore, an injunction becomes necessary precisely to establish an unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit — and for no other reason. A parallel example: pounding rice for a yajna with the specific mantra-accompanied method (avaghāta) is itself a case of unseen-fruit dependency — the rice could be dehusked in any number of ways to serve merely as food, but rice prepared other than by this exact prescribed method cannot be used in the yajna. The prescribed method itself carries the unseen fruit; ordinary efficient dehusking does not.

### "विधिर्नियोज्य इति" (Sutra 10) — "Because the Injunction Must Needs Have Fulfilment"
*"Vidhir niyojya iti"*

As for the objection to ceremonial perfection as study's visible result — that no ritual text ever explicitly calls for a *ceremonially perfect* recitation, only this-or-that specific text — the answer follows:

### "संस्कारसिद्धिः कृताध्ययनविध्युद्योगसाधनादिति" (Sutra 11)
*"Saṃskāra-siddhiḥ kṛtādhyayana-vidhy-udyoga-sādhanād iti"*

> "**Ceremonial perfection is established as one visible immediate result of the study of the Veda by reading together the injunctions about sacrifice, and this one which enjoins the study of Scripture.**
>
> The injunctions about sacrifices are not complete without knowledge of the circumstances of each, such as the particular fruit to be gained by each, and the like. For this knowledge they refer to the sacred text. On the other hand, the injunction to learn that..."

**Sutra's meaning:** since the yajna-injunctions and the study-injunction are jointly connected through their shared practical application, ceremonial refinement (saṃskāra) stands firmly established as study's own observable fruit — because sacrificial injunctions themselves remain incomplete without knowledge of their surrounding circumstances (which specific fruit each rite yields, and similar details), and this required knowledge is precisely what the sacred text, properly and refinedly mastered through study, supplies.

---

>
> As for the objection taken to ceremonial perfection as one visible immediate result of the Veda, namely, that a ceremonially perfect text is nowhere called for in the ritual, but only this or that text, his answer is in the next sutra.
>

### Page 505

...text by repetition, expressly excluding, as it does, such other methods as reading from a written text, clearly indicates that a certain ceremonial perfection must attach to the text which the student must know if he is to fully understand the application of the sacrifices. Take the two sets of injunctions together, and it becomes clear that the Scripture, which every man born again is bound to possess, must be a ceremonially perfect Scripture.

**A genuinely important twist now emerges:** ceremonial perfection turns out to be, in its own way, a *spiritual* reward — and one that accrues not to the text studied, but to the person studying. Because the affix "tavya" itself denotes spiritual merit attaching to an act, further specified by its root — here, "studied." How, then, can this be mere ceremonial perfection of the text?

### "तव्यः कर्मण्यदृष्टवाची" (Sutra 12)
*"Tavyaḥ karmaṇy adṛṣṭa-vācī"*

> "**'Tavya' denotes spiritual merit attaching to the object of the sentence.**
>
> The affix 'tavya' denotes the object studied as well as the act of studying, and the former is the nearer meaning, and accordingly the affix denotes here a spiritual result attaching to the Veda itself."

**Sutra's meaning:** knowing the injunctions for yajnas and similar rites in full detail — timing, manner, correct mantras, and their respective fruits — requires studying them directly, heard sequentially from a guru's own mouth (never from a written text, per the study-injunction's own restriction, which is what "svādhyāya" specifically requires). Combining these heard injunctions makes clear that a genuine saṃskāra results. **But this saṃskāra is itself an unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit — and it belongs to the person who studies, not to the text studied.** This is because the "tavya" affix denotes a special quality (apūrva) generated in the agent through the act, not in the object. (For a fuller technical treatment of "apūrva," see the Jaimini-nyaya-mala-vistara, third adhyaya, first pada, sutras 1–3.) The next sutra answers the implication that follows from this.

That being so, how can there be this ceremonial perfection of the text you speak of? He answers in the next sutra.

>

### Page 506

**Sutra's meaning:** the "tavya" affix expresses the unseen entity (**अपूर्व** *apūrva*) attaching to the object (karma), not the agent. Though "tavya" grammatically expresses both the object and the studying agent, its primary sense points toward the object's side — hence this affix indicates an apūrva connected specifically to the Veda (as object), not to the person. One might object that agent-connected apūrva could equally arise from the verbal root itself — but no rule forbids it arising from the affix instead, so it may indeed arise from "tavya."

**Resolving the earlier "part of another thing" objection:** this principle doesn't apply here — mantras' own apūrva-quality arises independently, needing no separate justification. The apūrva indicated here belongs to the Veda itself. A fruit already exists for the studying person (understanding the text's meaning) — but positing apūrva as a further additional fruit only strengthens, rather than weakens, the text's overall authority, as the next sutra explains.

That study has itself an immediate visible result in the shape of the understanding of the meaning,—an understanding which flows out of the words. But when a result is present it is against the general principle to supply one. The spiritual benefit therefore must be held to further, not prevent, that understanding of Scripture which is the direct result of the study here enjoined. This is the meaning of the next sutra.

**A remaining question:** couldn't the same "saktu-analogy" grammatical move (giving up the object-role for the instrumental) apply here too?

### "यथाप्राप्तोपपत्त्यर्ये सक्तुन्यायं इति" (Sutra 14)
*"Yathāprāpta-upapattarye saktu-nyāya iti"*

> "**The natural meaning gives a good sense, and there is therefore no occasion to force the construction as in the sentence referred to.**

**Sutra's meaning:** since the plain, natural meaning already works perfectly well, there's no need to posit an alternative interpretation as was necessary in the saktu-example. In "saktūn juhoti," the natural (accusative) sense simply didn't work grammatically, forcing an instrumental reinterpretation. But here, no such forcing is required — the natural sense already yields a coherent result.

### "Vyathamartha-nirṇayaṃ bhaṭṭa-gurū vidheḥ puruṣārtha-sānād iti" (Sutra 15)

> sarvatra vidhiḥ puruṣārtha-paryavasāyi ceti niyamād ity api puruṣārtha-bhūtaṃ phalavad-artha-niścayam adhyayana-vidhi-prayuktaṃ bhaṭṭa-guror manyete | nanu sakṛd-adhyayanasyāḍāvṛtti-saṃhitārtha-niścaye sojjhalabhye ity āśaṅkya sati taj-jñānaṃ phalāntarādhyayana-vidhy-artha-niścayaṃ vicāraṃ kalpayiṣyāha ||
>
> "Having thus proved that the study of the text of the Veda has an immediate, visible result in view, namely, the mastery by the pupil of that text, he now goes on to confute the idea that the authority of the Scripture injunction, in virtue of which the student enters upon the study of the text, extends to the interpretation thereof. And first he sets out the view to be controverted.
>
> **Both the Bhatt and the Guru hold that the determination of the meaning is contemplated by this injunction of Scripture, for the reason that all such injunctions must stretch up to some object of human desire.**
>
> Kumarilabhatta and Prabhakaraguru agree in thinking that, inasmuch as each and every injunction of Scripture must extend to some object of human desire, the determination..."

**Sutra's meaning:** injunction exists precisely to bring about a person's well-being — this is its very purpose, and the benefit ultimately reaching the person is what should govern its stated meaning. Both Kumārila Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara Guru hold that the study-injunction's own purpose isn't merely mechanical memorization of the Veda — it extends to actually understanding the text's meaning and thereby obtaining the well-being that flows from that understanding. On this specific point, the two rival schools (Bhāṭṭa and Guru-mata) genuinely agree.

...of the meaning of the Veda, to which, and not to the text, the fruit of the blessings obtained by performing the commanded sacrifices is attached, must be held to be contemplated by the injunction to study the text.

But, it will be said, merely going over the text of Scripture, once or repeatedly, need not by itself result in knowledge of its meaning. Both schools grant this, and therefore hold that the study-injunction must, to be properly fulfilled, be understood to include study of the **Mimamsa shastra** itself, by which the Veda's meaning is actually determined.

### "स विचारमाक्षिपेत्" — "Let the Injunction Include the Mimamsa"
*"Sa vicāram ākṣipet"*

But isn't it a universal rule that a scriptural injunction incites only to what it expressly enjoins, or what is immediately subservient to that? If so, how can the study-injunction be said to include studying the Mimamsa shastra — which is neither the thing itself enjoined, nor subservient to it?

**Sutra's meaning:** the injunction, regarding understanding the Veda's meaning, implicitly requires the Vichara (Mimamsa) shastra too. "Vidhi" (injunction) means: do exactly what is stated, connected to its own specific act — so why should a wholly separate text (Mimamsa) be required, since it is neither the Veda nor even part of it? The resolution follows.

### "अविधीयानुषकार्याक्षेपोऽवघातावृत्तिवत्" (Sutra 3)
*"Avidhīyānuṣakāryākṣepo'vaghātāvṛttivat"*

> "**An injunction may include something which is neither expressly enjoined nor subservient to what is expressly enjoined, as, for example, the repetition of the act of striking the rice.**
>
> The text—

> व्रीहीनवहन्ति ।
> *vrīhīn avahanti |*
> "One strikes the rice"

—enjoins striking the rice with a pestle, but not the repetition of that act. For that is no part of the meaning of the root. Nor can the repetition of the act be described as subservient to the thing expressly enjoined. For without any such repetition the striking of the rice, which is all that is expressly enjoined, can be accomplished by a single blow of the pestle. Nevertheless, since the rice cannot be husked—the result..."

**A genuinely illuminating example:** the injunction "one should strike the rice" literally requires only a single pestle-blow to satisfy its words — yet since a single blow can never actually husk the rice (the real goal), *repetition*, though never explicitly commanded, is implicitly required by the injunction's own practical purpose. By this same logic, though "study the Veda" doesn't explicitly mention Mimamsa-shastra, since genuine understanding of the Veda's meaning (the injunction's real purpose) is practically unreachable without it, studying Mimamsa is implicitly included.
