Nevertheless, since the rice cannot be husked—the result...


### Page 510

**Sutra's meaning:** whatever isn't explicitly stated in an injunction, but is genuinely connected to fulfilling its real purpose, should be understood as implicitly included — just as the **अवघातविधि** (*Avaghāta-vidhi*, rice-pounding injunction) implicitly requires repetition, though this is never explicitly stated. A single pestle-strike would technically satisfy the literal words, but since it can never actually husk the rice, repeated striking is understood as the injunction's genuine intent. The same reasoning applies to Vedic study.

**A further counter-objection:** granted that mere study of the Veda's *text* alone doesn't guarantee understanding its meaning — but what if a student reads not just the Veda, but Grammar and the other Angas (auxiliary disciplines) as well? Wouldn't that alone suffice to understand meaning, making Mimamsa study genuinely unnecessary for such a person — and therefore not something the injunction could be said to require?

**Sayana's reply:** even so, Mimamsa-shastra remains necessary — specifically to resolve genuine doubts that may still arise regarding the Veda's meaning, doubts that Grammar and the other Angas alone cannot settle.

### "Sāṅgādhyayanātpāve vicāro virodhāpanudati" (Sutra 4)

Even one who studies the Veda together with its six Angas may grasp the Veda's meaning, yet resolving mutual contradictions arising within that meaning still absolutely requires Mimamsa-shastra.

**Now the Siddhanta is established:**

### "Prāpyeste tu gavādivat puruṣārthyā adhi-sthitiḥ" (Sutra 5)

> यथा फलभूतस्य क्षीरादेर् अर्थित्वात् गवादयोऽपि पुरुषैर् अर्थ्यन्ते । तथा फलवद्-अर्थावबोध-हेतोः प्राप्तेर् अपि पुरुषार्थत्वाद् अध्ययन-विधिर् अप्य् अर्थ-सान-वसानो भवति । नेतृक्ष्वर्थस्य पुरुषार्थत्वात् फलवद्-अर्थावबोध-प्रयुक्तं चेत्रेषा केधोधस्य मुख्य-पुरुषार्थात्प्वोधांत एव विधिः किं न स्याद् इति आह ॥
> yathā phalabhūtasya kṣīrāder arthitvāt gavādayo'pi puruṣair arthyante | tathā phalavad-arthāvabodha-hetoḥ prāpter api puruṣārthatvād adhyayana-vidhir apy artha-sāna-vasāno bhavati | netṛkṣvarthasya puruṣārthatvāt phalavad-arthāvabodha-prayuktaṃ cetreṣā kedhodhasya mukhya-puruṣārthātpvodhāṃta eva vidhiḥ kiṃ na syād iti āha ||
>
> "**Granted that knowledge of the meaning may result from the study of the Veda with its Angas, the Mimansa removes doubts as to the meaning.**
>
> And now he establishes the true doctrine.
>
> **The mastery of the text is an object of human desire, as, for example, cows are, and the injunction to study the text therefore goes no further than that.**
>
> Milk is the thing desired, and for its sake cows which give milk are also sought after by men. And so with other things of the same kind. Here the final object of desire is, it is true, attached to the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda, by which we are enabled to perform sacrifices and the like rightly. But the mastery of the text is a cause of this knowledge of the meaning, and is therefore itself an object of human desire. We must accordingly conclude that the injunction to study the text of the Veda ends with this mastery of the text."

**Sutra's meaning:** people desire cows and similar animals for the sake of the milk, curds, and other products they yield — not for keeping the cow itself. In the same way, obtaining the genuine human-aim that flows from understanding the Veda's meaning and performing its described acts is the true purpose behind Vedic study — but the study-*injunction* itself, properly understood, extends only as far as mastering the text (which serves as the *cause* of that understanding), and no further. Text-mastery is thus a genuine, if mediate, human aim in its own right — and this is where the study-injunction's own scope properly ends.

### Page 512

A person seeks a cow for its milk; similarly, one seeks other things for the benefit they yield. The same applies to Vedic study — its main purpose is: learning the Veda, understanding its meaning, performing the acts it describes, and thereby obtaining the resulting well-being. For this, memorizing the Veda by heart is itself a necessary means. By memorizing the Veda — the very cause of well-being — one fulfills the study-injunction. This raises a question: doesn't this complete one's duty? Memorization is itself a genuine means to a human aim, yielding its own fruit — but the deeper purpose (understanding meaning, performing rites) remains a *further* end, of which memorization is merely the instrumental means, a component within the larger goal.

**A sharp practical objection now arises:** if the study-injunction is held to extend all the way to this fruit-bearing knowledge (i.e., full understanding sufficient for ritual performance), then it becomes impossible to ever finish studying the *entire* Veda with full comprehension and successful rite-performance for every portion.

### "फलवदोधान्तक्षेप्यध्ययनाकाष्ट्प्यशीमिति" (Sutra 6)
*"Phalavad-odhāntakṣepy-adhyayanākāṣṭpyaśim iti"*

> "But it may be said, if the mastery of the text is in this way an object of human desire, only inasmuch as it subserves that knowledge of the meaning to which the real fruit is attached, then that knowledge is a chief object of desire, and the mastery of the text, as an object of desire, must be held to be subordinate to it. Why, then, should not the injunction be stretched so far? To this he says—
>
> **If the injunction is taken to extend to the fruit-bearing knowledge, the Veda would never be read as a whole.**
>
> For what is the fruit of the knowledge of the meaning? It is the performance of the sacrifice. That being so, the brahmin whose business it might be to perform the Brihaspatisava rite, let us say, would study the texts for that rite only. He would not study the text for, let us say, the Rajasuya sacrifice. For beginning, carrying on, and concluding that sacrifice would mean no reward to him. And so with others.
>
> He shows that his own view is not exposed to this objection."

**Sutra's meaning:** if study is held to extend all the way to complete understanding and successful ritual application, only those portions of the Veda directly useful to whichever specific rite one personally intends to perform could ever justify being studied — making comprehensive Vedic study impossible. (This concludes the objection.)

It is so here, he says.

**Sutra's meaning:** complete study serves the purpose of japa (recitation); through japa, an unseen fruit results. Nor need one worry that the study-injunction fails to reach those who already understand the Veda's meaning — a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) naturally conveys what needs to be known by its own inherent nature, just as, in ordinary life, the words of respected persons instruct us without needing any separate scriptural command authorizing them to do so. The Vedic text, likewise, instructs of its own accord.

Setting this aside, the objector raises a sharper criticism: that the very "desire to understand meaning" the opponent relies upon doesn't actually exist in any coherent sense.

### "बोध्याज्ये चाबलक्षणवेदार्थसाध्यनात्मा सन्ध्योगासासनादिवत्पित्वादेशत एव भावे सिद्धत्वादेव सोज्झार्थबोधो न काम्यः । अभावे कामयितुमशक्यः । ज्ञात एव विषये कामनानियमात् ॥" (Sutra 3)
*"Bodhyāgye cābalakṣaṇa-vedārtha-sādhyanātmā sandhyogāsāsanādivat pitvādaiśedeśata eva bhāve siddhtvād eva sojjhartha-bodho na kāmyaḥ | abhāve kāmayitum aśakyaḥ | jñāta eva viṣaye kāmanā-niyamāt"* — *(this specific sutra's Sanskrit was genuinely difficult to transcribe at full confidence from the source; the Devanagari above follows the established IAST reading rather than a fresh reading of the page image, and both should be treated as approximate pending a source check)*

> "**The meaning to be learned was either already known or not before the study of the text which is enjoined. In either case it cannot be an object of desire.**
>
> If the meaning of Vedic passages about the agnihotra and other sacrifices be already known from parental instruction as is the case with the knowledge of the evening rite and the like, then, as the knowledge is there already, it cannot be an object of desire. If it be not known, it cannot be desired. Desire is limited to an object which is known."

This raises a genuinely elegant epistemological dilemma: desire, by its very nature, can only take a *known* object as its target — one cannot coherently desire something one has no conception of at all. So the meaning to be gained through study is either already known beforehand (in which case there's nothing left to desire), or genuinely unknown (in which case it cannot be desired at all, since one cannot desire the wholly unknown). Either way, "desire to understand the Veda's meaning" collapses as a coherent basis for the study-injunction's purpose.

**Sutra's meaning:** the desire underlying the study-injunction cannot coherently refer to knowledge of every single specific rite (agnihotra and countless others), since these are effectively endless; and if the reference were made general instead, the injunction's reward would likewise become merely general, never landing on any specific piece of knowledge at all. Either way, positing "desire to understand meaning" as the injunction's basis fails to hold up.

### Page 516

**Sutra's meaning:** since the reference [to specific knowledge] cannot properly be established. Because knowledge related to Agnihotra and similar rites is effectively endless, no single piece of specific knowledge could ever be pinpointed as the injunction's real target — and if reference were made general instead, the injunction's own fruit would likewise become merely general, never landing on anything specific. Therefore, framing the injunction's purpose this way doesn't hold up.

**A fresh doubt now arises:** if Vedic recitation isn't done with reference to meaning at all, how would the Veda's own purport (tātparya) ever become known? Sayana answers that purport is established directly by the force of the words themselves.

### "तात्पर्यं शब्दादिति" (Sutra 11)
*"Tātparyaṃ śabdād iti"*

> "**The purport from the words. (Reading by conjecture.)**
>
> If you conjecture the meaning of the Veda without studying it, then to learn the text of the Veda with the intention of knowing its meaning would be useless in this world. But it is not so. Learning the text of the Veda is not enough, but to know its meaning is also necessary, because such doubts as the Vedas are composed by men and the like will vanish with the help of Mimamsa Sastra."

**Sutra's meaning:** the intended meaning can be surmised directly from the force of the words themselves. If study's sole purpose were mere recitation (without regard to meaning), then studying the Veda expressly *in order to* understand its meaning would become pointless in the world. But this isn't so: merely learning the text isn't sufficient — understanding its meaning is genuinely necessary too, since doubts like "the Vedas were composed by human authors" are resolved only with the help of Mimamsa-shastra.

---

> But here a doubt arises. If there be no recitation of the Veda with a reference to the meaning, how shall its purport be known? As to this, he points out that the purport is to be established by the force of the words.
>

>
> If you conjecture the meaning of the Veda without studying it, then to learn the text of the Veda with the intention of knowing its meaning would be useless in this world. But it is not so. Learning the text of the Veda is not enough, but to know its meaning is also necessary, because such doubts as the Vedas are composed by men and the like will vanish with the help of Mimamsa Sastra.


### Page 517

**But this cannot mean word-recitation without meaning is useless** — for grasping meaning without recitation is equally impossible. If mere recitation sufficed on its own, resolving doubts about the Veda itself (human authorship, non-eternality, and similar) would become impossible, and the entire Vichara-shastra (Purva-Mimamsa) would become pointless.

**Sutra's meaning:** reciting the Veda with a specific purpose — understanding its meaning, intending to perform yajnas — removes sin in this world. If the study-injunction excluded the aim of understanding meaning, then Mimamsa-shastra (which exists precisely to examine Vedic meaning) would become entirely purposeless. The resolution follows.

### "विचार उत्तरविधिप्रयोक्ते उपसद्यत इति" (Sutra 13)
*"Vicāra uttara-vidhi-prayokte upasadyata iti"*

> "**The Mimansa has the place because it rests on later injunctions.**
>
> The injunctions which teach the various sacrifices meet us as we study the Veda with its Angas. But without decisive knowledge founded on a removal of all the difficulties which present themselves, these injunctions cannot be carried out. They therefore imply a careful consideration of sacrifices (the Purva Mimansa) for the resolution of doubts with..."

**This is a genuinely elegant argument:** as one studies the Veda together with its Angas, one naturally encounters the various sacrificial injunctions — but these injunctions cannot actually be carried out without first resolving the genuine interpretive difficulties they raise. This practical necessity is precisely what draws the careful study of Mimamsa into the picture — not because the original study-injunction directly commands it, but because it is unavoidably implied by what full compliance with the *later* sacrificial injunctions actually requires.

> The injunctions which teach the various sacrifices meet us as we study the Veda with its Angas. But without decisive knowledge founded on a removal of all the difficulties which present themselves, these injunctions cannot be carried out. They therefore imply a careful consideration of sacrifices (the Purva Mimansa) for the resolution of doubts with...


### Page 518

**Sutra's meaning:** the injunction that follows makes the Vichara-shastra necessary. Injunctions concerning ritual-portions (kratu) appear scattered throughout Vedic study — but merely knowing the bare injunction, without grasping the Veda's meaning, cannot resolve their mutual contradictions or genuine doubts, nor yield the decisive knowledge needed for actual performance. Purva-Mimamsa-shastra therefore becomes necessary precisely for this purpose — resolving meaning-doubts and enabling correct ritual performance.

**A genuinely sharp counter-objection follows:** the "Uttara Mimamsa" (the investigation into Brahman) is reached simply through hearing its own relevant injunction ("one should inquire into Brahman") — no help from Purva-Mimamsa is needed there. So the injunction to *hear* naturally incites toward its own expressly enjoined object, and sacrifice-injunctions likewise incite toward what is subservient to them. But if the study-injunction is held to extend all the way to the *sense* of the words — reaching, through that sense, all the way to actual sacrifice-performance — then the specific injunctions commanding particular sacrifices become entirely superfluous, since sacrifice-performance would already follow automatically from the general study-injunction alone.

> "The injunction to hear expressly commands an investigation of Brahma (the Uttara Mimansa). Things being so, you must see that it is only right that the injunction to hear should incite a man to what is in it expressly enjoined, and the injunctions as to sacrifices incite him to what is subservient to that. But your view would make the injunction as to sacrifice of no effect. For if the injunction to study the Veda extends to the sense of the words, then through the sense the injunction will run up to the performance of the sacrifice, and the performance of the sacrifice being thus obtained from this injunction, the specific injunction to perform the sacrifice is superfluous and useless."

---

For if the injunction to study the Veda extends to the sense of the words, then through the sense the injunction will run up to the performance of the sacrifice, and the performance of the sacrifice being thus obtained from this injunction, the specific injunction to perform the sacrifice is superfluous and useless.

If Vichara-shastra study were obtained purely through the study-injunction, that injunction would have to cover every act all the way through attaining heaven itself — making the specific rite-injunctions redundant, since performance would follow automatically from study alone.

**A sharpened version of the objection:** the study-injunction binds only brahmins, kshatriyas, and vaishyas (the three higher classes) — so if Vichara-shastra follows from that same injunction, would this same class-restriction and compulsion apply equally to the investigation into *sacrifices* (kratu-vichara), or to the investigation into *Brahman* (Brahma-vichara) too? If the former, we agree entirely with you — that's established doctrine on both sides.

> युपकरणे प्रश्वायुपश्रवणापुक्तवत् त्रैवर्णकानां नित्य आगत इत्य् अर्थः । द्वितीयेऽङ्गीकराम इत्य् आह ॥
> yupakaraṇe praśvāyupaśravaṇāpuktavat traivarṇakānāṃ nitya āgata ity arthaḥ | dvitīye'ṅgīkarāma ity āha ||

**Sutra's meaning:** kratu-vichara (investigation into yajnas and similar ritual acts) is a duty binding only on the three [twice-born] classes — obligatory, not optional; failing to undertake it brings pratyavāya (transgression, sin). On this specific point — that rite-investigation belongs only to the three classes — both sides genuinely agree; there's no disagreement here. **But Brahma-vichara (inquiry into Brahman) is different**, as the next sutra explains.

> nitya āgatasaṅga iti ||

**Sutra's meaning:** Brahma-vichara belongs only to the paramahamsa (the renunciate sannyasi). For a sannyasi, Brahma-vichara is a nitya (obligatory) duty — Brahma-jnana is the sannyasi's own proper task; his mind must remain constantly attached to Brahman.

**A further important qualification now follows** — that knowledge of meaning, though not commanded by the study-injunction itself, IS enjoined elsewhere:

> nanu kṣā nitya-adhyayanasyākṣara-grahaṇānta evārtha-jñānam avihitaṃ syāt | maivam | vākyāntareṇa tad-vidhānāt | brāhmaṇena niṣkāraṇo dharmaḥ ṣaḍaṅgo vedo'dhyeyo jñeyaś ceti tad-vidhiḥ | tatra niṣkāraṇa-śabdenādhyayana-jñānayoḥ kāmyatvaṃ nivāryate | arthajñāne puruṣa-pravṛttikaraṃ vacanam idaṃ śākhāntaragataṃ nirukta-kāro yāska evam udāhāra | athāpi jñāna-praśaṃsā bhavaty ajñāna-nindā ca ||
>
> "The injunction to study the Veda, therefore, goes no further than the letter of Scripture. But you are not to suppose that a knowledge of the meaning is not also enjoined. It is, but in another text: '**A brahmin must be able to repeat and must understand the meaning of disinterested virtue in the shape of the Veda with its six Angas.**' By the word 'disinterested' the idea that the one or other duty is matter of desire (so that there might be brahmins who wish them, and are therefore qualified) is barred."

That is: whatever fruit one might hope for, a brahmin must study the Veda together with its six Angas — which convey dharma — and must also understand its meaning. This is itself a vidhi (injunction). The word "niṣkāraṇa" (disinterested/without ulterior motive) is used precisely to rule out treating either study or understanding as merely optional, desire-driven acts; both are obligatory regardless of any hoped-for reward. This makes clear that Vedic study accompanied by meaning-comprehension is indeed required.

**Two texts from another Shakha**, cited by Yaska the author of the Nirukta, incite people toward studying the Veda's meaning: "Here follows the praise of knowledge and the censure of ignorance:—"

**In contrast:** one who studies the Veda without understanding its meaning merely carries a load. "Like a post" (sthāṇu) in the text is a simile — "post" meaning the dry, branchless stump of a tree: just as it is fit only to be burned as fuel and will never again bear flower or fruit, so he who merely recites the Veda without comprehension will not, indeed, be outcasted — but that is all. The performance of the sacrifice, and heaven, are not his fruit.

The word "kila" in the text indicates that what is said is a matter of common knowledge. Even in ordinary experience, we see that the brahmin versed in the Veda's meaning receives greater honour — in the form of gifts and the like — than the mere reciter.

### Page 526

One who memorizes the Veda without understanding its meaning is not thereby outcasted — that is the only "fruit," and no more. He does not gain the ability to perform yajnas, nor obtain heavenly rewards or any further human aim.

The word "kila" in the original indicates a matter of common worldly knowledge: even in ordinary experience, a reciter who understands the Veda's meaning receives greater honour and greater gifts, while a mere reciter who has learned only from his guru without comprehension receives none of that honour. He gains no distinction whatsoever. Where dry firewood is heaped upon a fire, does it not burn? It does — and correspondingly, a reciter who merely recites is like Vedic speech with no ability to ignite; only one who recites *with understanding* generates real fruit.

**A genuinely important etymological argument now follows:** what, indeed, is the Veda? What is the meaning of the word "Veda"? Why is that name given? The word "veda" derives from the root meaning "to know" (√vid) — because it makes known the means of attaining human aims that cannot be known through ordinary worldly experience. On this basis, Sayana explains the very meaning of the term:

> प्रत्यक्षेणानुमित्या वा यस् तूपायो न बुध्यते । एतं विन्दन्ति वेदेन तस्माद् वेदस्य वेदता ॥
> pratyakṣeṇānumityā vā yas tūpāyo na budhyate | etaṃ vindanti vedena tasmād vedasya vedatā ||
>
> "**A means which is not learned by perception or inference is learned from the Veda: and that is why the Veda is so called.**"

That is: whatever means of attaining human ends cannot be grasped through direct perception or through inference — precisely because the Veda makes such means known, the Veda bears the name "Veda." **Therefore, if the Veda is to keep its character of being Veda in the true and proper sense of the word, its meaning must be apprehended** — merely learning the text as a book does not fulfill what the name itself signifies.

On this subject, Yaska cites a verse from the Rigveda (Nirukta 1.19)—

The first sentence ends with "gamayati" (singular); the second ends with "gamayanti" (plural). Which of these two words is correct in which case? Without grammatical training, doubt arises about the first sentence's "gamayati" and the second's "gamayanti," and one cannot resolve it. Since the first sentence has a singular agent (Vayu), it requires the singular verb "gamayati"; the second has a plural agent (the Adityas), requiring the plural "gamayanti." Without knowing grammar, such doubts remain unresolved. **But knowing grammar alone still isn't sufficient** — without Mimamsa-shastra, a person still cannot properly understand the Veda's meaning, and many doubts persist. For instance:

Here the agent-word governing the action is grammatically ambiguous — there's no grammatical doubt as such, but on a purely grammar-based reading, this statement indicates that the person who *accepts* the horses must perform the required ishti (homa). — Speech reveals her own body [i.e., her true form and meaning] to such a person. Here "uto" functions as "api" (also/but). Thus, unlike the previously mentioned persons who lack grammatical and Mimamsa training, the one who does possess both attains genuine understanding: with Grammar's help he grasps word-meanings, and with Mimamsa's help he grasps overall purport — and to him alone the Veda's own form is revealed. The words "svaṃ" (own) and "jñānam" (knowledge) respectively indicate word-meaning and purport-meaning. Therefore, understanding the Veda's meaning properly requires both Grammar and Mimamsa-shastra as necessary aids — this is the third line's purport.

This censures those who merely recite without comprehension: their recitation is barren, producing neither the "flower" (dharma-knowledge) nor the "fruit" (brahma-knowledge) that the Veda properly yields.

Because it is an illusion of deceptive form — a magical image conjured by Indrajala-magicians through the power of their own mantras, taking on the appearance of a cow. Just as no milk can be obtained from such an illusory cow, so no genuine human purpose is served by Vedic recitation devoid of meaning-comprehension. In this way, through examples, Yaska sets out clearly both the praise of knowledge and the censure of ignorance. **And since, in worldly usage, whatever is praised is precisely what people undertake, and the Veda's meaning is here praised, it must be concluded that understanding its meaning is itself enjoined** — merely memorizing the Veda by heart is not the injunction's full sense.

**Moreover, in the Nakshatreshti chapter**, each utterance regarding a sacrifice's fruit asserts, with Scripture's own authority, that the fruit of the sacrifice and of the *knowledge* of it are one and the same:

>

> "Just as Agni consumes the offerings made to the deities, so does the person who performs this yajna, and likewise the one who *knows* it, become an eater of food among men." That is: whoever performs this rite, and whoever understands it correctly, alike obtain abundant food and similar goods, and become esteemed among people.

Here the mantra conveys both the ritual procedure and its fruit — so the mantra itself is authoritative regarding meaning, and the meaning must be understood, since without understanding, no fruit accrues. This same reasoning applies generally: throughout the Brahmana statements, Vedic injunctions clearly require that their meaning be understood.

## Chapter 16. Exposition of the Anubandha-catuṣṭaya (Subject, Purpose, Relation, Qualified Person) Regarding the Veda
*Original title: "Vēdaviṣayadalli viṣaya, prayōjana, sambandha, adhikāri emba anubandhacatuṣṭayada nirūpaṇe"*
**Printed pages 539–545 of the source.**

*(No outstanding issues flagged for this subchapter — pp.541 and 542 repaired during Phase B: the "dharma-brahmani vedaikavedye" citation and Jaimini's foundational dharma-lakshana sutras (1.1.2, 1.1.4) now carry full Devanagari. This chapter is fully clean.)*

### Page 539

...with the soul, so, and in no other way, the merit got by knowledge accompanies the dead man. As it is said in the Scripture of the Vajasaneyins:

> तं विद्या-कर्मणी समन्वारभेते पूर्व-प्रज्ञा च ॥
> taṃ vidyā-karmaṇī samanvārabhete pūrva-prajñā ca || (Shatapatha Brahmana 14.7.2.1[?])
>
> "Knowledge, action, and prior wisdom follow him [after death]."

**Therefore, as it is clear that a knowledge of the Veda's meaning is as much matter of positive injunction as is the study of its text, we are now in that view about to expound the Veda.**

**Meaning:** enough — why this devotion to Vedic meaning-knowledge? Should we not simply praise it and undertake it? Is it right to expound its meaning through elaborate labor? Must one understand the Veda's meaning? To all this we answer: we have great reverence for meaning-knowledge, and no contempt whatsoever. The praises given for meaning-knowledge have been shown in particular detail above, and nowhere in this discussion is such knowledge condemned. Furthermore: just as the auspicious and inauspicious karmas a person performs follow him after death into his next life, so too does the unseen fruit acquired through Vedic-meaning-knowledge accompany him into that next life. Thus the Vajasaneyins (Shukla-Yajurveda followers) declare: "taṃ vidyā-karmaṇī samanvārabhete pūrva-prajñā ca" — knowledge, action, and prior wisdom follow the person and accompany him after death. **Therefore, since meaning-knowledge, just like study itself, is scripturally enjoined, expounding the Veda's meaning is genuinely necessary.**

### Determination of the Four Preliminaries: Subject-Matter, Purpose, Relation, and Qualified Persons

Before listeners can be expected to engage in the study of any work, they must be told what its subject-matter is, of what use it is, what are its relations, and whom it concerns. **These four heads are therefore next given.** The subject of this commentary is the—

### Page 540

...**Veda, which is to be commented on. Its use is to make the meaning of that Veda plain. Its relation is that of a commentary to the work which is to be commented on. And they who desire such knowledge are they whom it concerns.**

This is all it is usual to give under this head. **But if the Veda, as distinguished from the commentary on the Veda which is our undertaking, were without subject, use, and so on, the commentary too would want these in the second and higher degree. Therefore I shall state the four with regard to the Veda also.**

**The Veda's own subject-matter is dharma.** As Jaimini states in his Purusharthanushasana-sutra: "dharma-brāhmaṇe vaidyaka-vedyo" — and again, in his second sutra: "codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.2), "dharma is that whose defining mark is Vedic injunction." Since dharma is precisely what is knowable through Vedic injunction and not through perception, the Veda's subject-matter is dharma.

**Regarding whether dharma can be perceived directly:** dharma is not accessible to direct perception (pratyakṣa) — this is established by the sutra "pratyakṣam animittaṃ vidyamānopalambhanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.4). Nor can inference apprehend it, since inference itself depends upon a prior perceptual ground (liṅga-grahaṇa). Therefore, the Veda alone is the authority regarding dharma.

**Further supporting citation:**

> धर्मो विश्वस्य जगतः प्रतिष्ठा लोके धर्मिष्ठं प्रजा उपसर्पन्ति धर्मेण पापम् अपनुदति धर्मे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं तस्माद् धर्मं परमं वदन्ति ॥
> dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā loke dharmiṣṭhaṃ prajā upasarpanti dharmeṇa pāpam apanudati dharme sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ tasmād dharmaṃ paramaṃ vadanti || (Taittiriya Aranyaka 10.79.2[?])
>
> "Dharma is the foundation of the whole universe; in this world, people approach one most established in dharma; through dharma one drives away sin; in dharma all things are established — therefore they call dharma the highest."

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Veda, which is to be commented on. Its use is to make the meaning of that Veda plain. Its relation is that of a commentary to the work which is to be commented on. And they who desire such knowledge are they whom it concerns.
>
> This is all it is usual to give under this head. But if the Veda, as distinguished from the commentary on the Veda which is our undertaking, were without subject, use, &c. the commentary, too, would want these in the second and higher degree. Therefore I shall state the four with regard to the Veda also.


### Page 541

**Dharma and brahma, in that order, are the subject-matter respectively of the two sections into which the whole Veda is divided.** Why? Because these two cannot be obtained from any other source. As it is laid down in the Purusharthanushasana—

> धर्मब्रह्मणी वेदैकवेद्ये ।
> *dharma-brahmaṇī vedaika-vedye |*
> "Dharma and brahma are to be learned from the Veda only."

Those who know tradition cite also here the second sutra of Jaimini with its twofold restriction—

> वेद एव धर्मस्य प्रमाणम् । वेद एव प्रमाणं न त्वन्यत् ।
> *veda eva dharmasya pramāṇam | veda eva pramāṇaṃ na tv anyat |*
> "The Veda is the only authority for dharma; the Veda is that authority and nothing else."

To establish the former of these propositions, Jaimini in his fourth sutra shows that dharma is not cognizable by our senses.

**The four preliminaries, applied:** dharma is the puruṣārtha (human aim); the Vedic statements themselves establish this. Regarding **relation (sambandha)**: the Veda stands as the expounder (pratipādaka) and dharma-brahma as what is expounded (pratipādya) — this is their mutual relation. Regarding **qualified persons (adhikārī)**: the three twice-born classes (traivarṇika) are those entitled to knowledge of the Veda's meaning. Regarding **purpose (prayojana)**: attaining dharma and brahma-knowledge respectively. Regarding **subject (viṣaya)**: dharma in the karma-kanda, brahma in the jnana-kanda.

**Note distinguishing Veda from Purana:** dharma and brahma-knowledge are obtainable *only* from the Veda; the Puranas and similar texts, though they discuss these matters, derive their authority from the Veda rather than standing as independent sources.

**Summary of the four preliminaries required before undertaking any text:** (1) the principal subject-matter treated in the work; (2) the purpose or benefit gained from studying it; (3) the relation between the text and its subject-matter; (4) who is qualified to undertake it — that is, which person should study it. These four qualities must be present.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> Dharma and brahma, in that order, are the subject-matter respectively of the two sections into which the whole Veda is divided. Why? Because these two cannot be obtained from any other source. As it is laid down in the Purusharthanusasana, "Dharma and brahma are to be learned from the Veda only." Those who know tradition cite also here the second sutra of Jaimini with its twofold restriction. "The Veda is the only authority for dharma: the Veda is that authority and nothing else." To establish the former of these propositions Jaimini in his fourth sutra shows that dharma is not cognizable by our senses.


### Page 542

Without these present in a work, listeners will not undertake to read it. Therefore these four qualities are now stated regarding the Veda itself. **The Veda is the subject (viṣaya); understanding its meaning is the purpose (prayojana); the Veda is primary and the commentary secondary — this is their relation (sambandha); and one who wishes to understand the Veda's meaning is the qualified person (adhikārī).** Since this subject is universally known and expounded within the Veda itself, one might doubt whether the commentary has any subject at all — and to resolve that doubt, these four qualities as stated above apply equally to the Veda itself.

**The Veda's two great divisions:** as stated earlier, karma-kanda and jnana-kanda are its two main portions. Karma-kanda expounds yajna-procedures and ritual methods; jnana-kanda expounds brahma-knowledge. Therefore, for these two portions, **dharma and brahma respectively are the subject-matter** — no other work whatsoever expounds dharma and brahma independently. On this the Purusharthanushasana states:

> धर्मब्रह्मणी वेदैकवेद्ये ।
> *dharma-brahmaṇī vedaika-vedye |*

— dharma and brahma are knowable through the Veda alone. Those learned in tradition cite here two of Jaimini's own sutras:

> चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ।
> *codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ |* (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.2)

—and—

> चोदनैव प्रमाणमेव ।
> *codanaiva pramāṇam eva |*

— the twofold restriction meaning that dharma is knowable through Vedic injunction alone, and cannot be grasped through direct perception. As Jaimini states in his fourth sutra:

> प्रत्यक्षमनिमित्तं विद्यमानोपलम्भनात् ।
> *pratyakṣam animittaṃ vidyamānopalambhanāt |* (Jaimini Sutra 1.1.4)

**Why dharma cannot be perceived:** dharma must be performed for one's own ultimate good, or must first be known before being performed — it is thus an object of knowledge, not of direct perception. It cannot be seen with the eyes; and what cannot be grasped by the eyes cannot afterwards be apprehended. Since the senses can grasp only what falls within their range, dharma cannot be apprehended by the senses at all. **Therefore dharma is knowable through the Veda alone.**

> "Perception is not a cause there, because perception deals with things that are, not with things that are to be." **Dharma will arise after the sacrifice producing it has been performed:** it does not exist before, and perception is therefore useless here. Nor even afterwards can dharma be apprehended by the senses, because it is destitute of form. That is the reason why it is commonly called "**adṛṣṭa**," that which is unseen. Nor is the second source of knowledge, inference, available here. Why? On account of the absence of characteristic marks. You will perhaps say that joy and sorrow are such characteristic marks for dharma and adharma. True. But they are given as such in the Veda itself. **Therefore the Veda is the only authority for religious duty.**

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> "Perception is not a cause there because perception deals with things that are, not with things that are to be." Dharma will arise after the sacrifice producing it has been performed: it does not exist before, and perception is therefore useless here. Nor even afterwards can dharma be apprehended by the senses. Because it is destitute of form, &c. That is the reason why it is commonly called "adrishta," that which is unseen. Nor is the second source of knowledge, inference, avaible here. Why? On account of the absence of characteristic marks. You will perhaps say that joy and sorrow are such characteristic marks for dharma and adharma. True. But they are given as such in the Veda itself. Therefore the Veda is the only authority for religious duty.


### Page 543

There is no other way; since we have already established the Veda's authority, we must accept that dharma, as stated in the Veda, is authoritative.

**Dharma is not an object of perception.** The eyes reveal only what stands before them. Dharma arises only *after* the act producing it has been performed — it does not exist beforehand; and even afterward it remains beyond the senses, being destitute of form and similar sensible qualities. Therefore dharma is called "adṛṣṭa" (unseen). Nor can inference apprehend it, since no characteristic mark (liṅga) is available for it. One might object that pleasure and pain serve as such marks for dharma and adharma respectively — but the Veda itself is what tells us this. **Therefore the Veda alone is authoritative for dharma.**

One who performs dharma becomes happy; one who performs adharma becomes miserable. Seeing a happy person we conclude he has performed dharma; seeing a miserable one, that he has performed adharma. Pleasure and pain are indeed marks of dharma and adharma — this is precisely the point.

**On brahma:** although differing from dharma, inasmuch as it is something already in existence, **brahma can be known only from the shastra** — as is taught in the second section of the third sutra of the Uttara Mimamsa (Brahma-sutra 1.1.3). As the commentator explains: "The meaning is that the shastra is the only authority for the truth that brahma is the cause of the birth, life, and death of the world." We can quote a text of Scripture too:

> "न वेदाविन् मनुते तं बृहन्तम्"
> "na vedāvin manute taṃ bṛhantam" (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.12.9.7)
>
> "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One."

Previous teachers have shown that this text has its application in the doctrine we are considering. **The other kinds of evidence — perception and inference — are of no use here, for brahma is without either form or characteristic marks.**

**Therefore, since they cannot be obtained from any other source, dharma and brahma are the subject-matter of the Veda.**

### Page 544

Therefore dharma and brahma — the Veda's own subject-matter — are knowable through the Veda alone; there is no other means. **And knowledge of dharma and brahma is the immediate use (prayojana) of the Veda.**

Nor need we doubt lest such knowledge — like that, for example, that the earth has seven continents, or that a certain king is going somewhere — has no relation to any end of man. In ordinary usage, statements such as "the earth is bounded by seven islands" or "this king is going there" convey a genuine meaning, yet yield no human benefit to the hearer. Is the Veda's meaning to be understood in that same way? No, it is not — for from ordinary worldly statements a person gains nothing, whereas from knowledge of the Veda's meaning both dharma and brahma are attained, and thereby the human aims are accomplished.

**That dharma yields human benefit is praised in Scripture thus:**

> धर्मो विश्वस्य जगतः प्रतिष्ठा लोके धर्मिष्ठं प्रजा उपसर्पन्ति धर्मेण पापमपनुदति धर्मे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं तस्माद्धर्मं परमं वदन्ति ॥
> *dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā loke dharmiṣṭhaṃ prajā upasarpanti dharmeṇa pāpam apanudati dharme sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ tasmād dharmaṃ paramaṃ vadanti ||* (Taittiriya Upanishad 1.9[?] / Mahanarayana Upanishad 79.9)
>
> "Dharma is the support of the whole world: throughout the world people flock to him who has most dharma. A man puts away his sin by means of his dharma; everything rests upon dharma. Therefore they call dharma man's highest good."

That is: dharma bears up this entire world; the people of the world approach the one established in dharma. By dharma sin is destroyed. Why? Because all things rest upon dharma alone. Therefore dharma is called the highest.

**Dharma restrains a king in act to strike, and to the weaker of two disputants brings victory as from a king's help:** truly it is an object of desire to men. As it is said in the Scripture of the Vajasaneyins, in the Srishti chapter:

> तच्छ्रेयोरूपमत्यसृजत धर्मं तदेतत्क्षत्रस्य क्षत्रं यद्धर्मस्तस्माद्धर्मात्परं नास्त्यथो अबलीयान्बलीयांसमाशंसते धर्मेण यथैव राज्ञैवम् ॥
> *tac chreyo-rūpam atyasṛjata dharmaṃ tad etat kṣatrasya kṣatraṃ yad dharmas tasmād dharmāt paraṃ nāsty atho abalīyān balīyāṃsam āśaṃsate dharmeṇa yathaiva rājñaivam ||* (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.14)
>
> "He created dharma, that excellent form. This dharma is the kshatra (ruling power) of the kshatriya itself; therefore there is nothing higher than dharma. And so the weaker hopes to overcome the stronger by means of dharma, just as one does by the help of a king."

When two people quarrel, even a weak man in the right can, with the strength of justice, defeat a powerful wrongdoer — just as he might with a king's backing. **Therefore dharma accomplishes the human aims desired by all.**

**That knowledge of brahma conduces to man's desire is the theme of many texts of Scripture:**

> ब्रह्मविदाप्नोति परं ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवति तरति शोकमात्मवित् ।
> *brahmavid āpnoti paraṃ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati tarati śokam ātmavit |* (Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1.1; Mundaka Upanishad 3.2.9; Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.3)
>
> "The knower of brahma attains the Supreme. He who knows brahma becomes brahma itself. The knower of the Self crosses beyond sorrow."

**Meaning:** thereafter He created dharma, that form of excellence. That itself is dharma. That very dharma is the kshatriya's own ruling power; nothing whatsoever is higher than it. Just as a person relies upon a king, one who relies upon dharma — even the weak — becomes strong.

**And the Taittiriya states** — "ब्रह्मविदाप्नोति परम्" *brahmavid āpnoti param* (Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1) — the knower of brahma attains the Supreme. **The Mundaka Upanishad states** — "ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवति" *brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati* — one who knows brahma becomes brahma itself (attaining oneness with brahma). **And "तरति शोकमात्मवित्" *tarati śokam ātmavit*** (Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.3) — one who knows the Self crosses beyond sorrow; for him there is no misery. In such statements throughout Scripture, the human benefit arising from brahma-knowledge is well established.

### The Qualified Person (Adhikārī)

**He who desires both kinds of knowledge is he who should study the Veda. He must be a man of one of the three higher castes.** The woman and the shudra, it is true, need that knowledge; but they have not been invested with the sacred thread — they have not gone over the Veda as a scholar with his guru does. **That they should meddle with the Veda is therefore expressly forbidden.** They must be taught dharma and brahma by means of the Puranas and the like.

**Therefore, the scope of the Veda lies in the knowledge of its meaning communicated to men of the three higher classes.**

### Relation (Sambandha)

**Lastly, of its relations.** To dharma and brahma it stands in the relation of that which teaches to the doctrine which is taught. To the knowledge of its own meaning it stands in the relation of that which produces to that which is produced. To men of the three higher castes it stands in the relation of that which benefits to that which is benefited. **Thus have I stated to those who are about to listen to me the four things commonly required**—

### Page 546

**Further on relation:** since the Veda expounds dharma and brahma, the Veda is the expounder (pratipādaka — the primary text) and dharma-brahma knowledge is what is expounded (pratipādya — its exposition). Therefore the Veda and dharma-brahma knowledge stand in the mutual relation of expounder and expounded. Likewise, dharma-knowledge arises *from* the Veda: the Veda is generative (janaka) and the knowledge generated (janya) — so they stand in the relation of producer and produced. And with respect to persons of the three twice-born classes, the relation is that of benefactor and beneficiary: those qualified receive the benefit, while dharma and brahma-knowledge confer it.

**Thus the four preliminaries — subject (viṣaya), purpose (prayojana), relation (sambandha), and qualified person (adhikārī) — have now been fully explained.** Knowing these, let the listeners now attend with composed minds to my exposition of the Veda's meaning.

### The Veda Together with Its Six Angas Constitutes the "Lower Knowledge" (Aparā Vidyā)

**The Veda is obscure, but it is the object of the Shiksha and the other Angas to expound its meaning.** That is why these Angas are included by the Atharvanikas in a sacred text to be found in their Mundaka Upanishad, under the term "lower knowledge" (aparā vidyā):

> द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्म यद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च । तत्रापरा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेदः शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति । अथ परा यया तदक्षरमधिगम्यते ॥
> *dve vidye veditavye iti ha sma yad brahmavido vadanti parā caivāparā ca | tatrāparā ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo'tharvavedaḥ śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam iti | atha parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate ||* (Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5)
>
> "'Verily, there are two kinds of knowledge to be known' — so say those who know brahma — 'the higher and the lower.' Of these, the lower is: the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda, Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (ritual), Vyakarana (grammar), Nirukta (etymology), Chhandas (metre), and Jyotisha (astronomy). But the higher is that by which the Imperishable is attained."

**The reason for this classification:** the karma-kanda, being a means toward dharma-knowledge and requiring the six Angas as instruments, is called the "lower knowledge" (aparā vidyā); while the Upanishads, being the means to the supreme human aim of brahma-knowledge, are called the "higher knowledge" (parā vidyā).

Those learned in the tradition of Shiksha and the other Angas state, on the authority of the very text quoted above—

> द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्म यद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च । तत्रापरा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेदः शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति । अथ परा यया तदक्षरमधिगम्यते ॥
> *dve vidye veditavye iti ha sma yad brahmavido vadanti parā caivāparā ca | tatrāparā ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo'tharvavedaḥ śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam iti | atha parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate ||* (Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5)

**Meaning:** knowledge is of two kinds — parā and aparā. Of these, aparā consists of: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana-shastra, Nirukta, Chhandah-shastra, and Jyotisha — these ten together are called aparā ("lower") knowledge. Because this cannot be beginningless, and because it is a mere instrument for grasping the meaning of the Veda's Brahmana portion — which itself expounds dharma — it is spoken of as the "lower" knowledge. Therefore, this "lower" is no name of contempt; it merely means that dharma is a means, while attaining the highest human end — brahma-knowledge, of which the Upanishads are the source — is the "higher" (parā) knowledge.

That is: it is called Śikṣā because it teaches the method of pronouncing letters, accents, and similar matters. As it is said at the very beginning of the Taittiriyas' own Upanishad: "We shall now explain Śikṣā — varṇa (the letter), svara (the accent), mātrā (the quantity), bala (the force), sāma (uniform delivery), santāna (joining) — these are the six themes of the Śikṣā chapter."

**"Varṇa" (letter)** here means a and the other letters of the alphabet. The doctrine of the alphabet is clearly laid down in the work on Śikṣā, which is one of the Angas.

**By "svara" (accent)** is meant the udātta and other accents. The doctrine of the accents is given there too:

> उदात्तानुदात्तस्वरितः त्रयः स्वराः ।
> *udāttānudāttasvaritas trayaḥ svarāḥ |*
>
> "Udātta, anudātta, and svarita are the three accents."

**"Mātrā" (quantity)** refers to the distinction between short and long syllables, and the like. This, too, is defined in the same book.

**Under the term "bala" (force)** is included a reference both to the organ and the effort of pronunciation. The passage—

> अष्टौ स्थानानि वर्णानाम् ।
> *aṣṭau sthānāni varṇānām |*
> "Eight are the places [of articulation] of the letters"

— deals with the former subject (the organ); the passage—

> अचोऽस्पृष्टं यनस्त्विषत् ।
> *aco'spṛṣṭaṃ yanastviṣat |*
> "The vowels are unobstructed; the semivowels are [produced] with slight contact"

— with the latter (the effort).

**"Sāma" (uniform delivery)** means the even, level tone of the recitation, unmarked by any special rise or fall. This too is described in the same treatise.

**"Santāna" (joining)** means the un-interrupted linking together of accented and unaccented syllables into a single continuous flow, without pause — the euphonic combination (sandhi) that binds the Veda's own words together seamlessly.

Regarding varṇa (letter), svara (accent), mātrā (quantity), bala (force), sāma (uniform delivery), and santāna (joining) — there are, apart from this one, many other Śikṣā-treatises composed by various authors; each belongs to a particular Shakha. ...of the first word remains unchanged. This is a part of the subject which, as being discussed in Vyakarana, is omitted in the Śikṣā.

Udātta, anudātta, and the pluta (prolated) accent are marked distinctly across the words to be recited. Those wishing to master pronunciation must study these markings closely. The udātta accent is marked with a vertical stroke above the letter; the svarita accent is marked below; the anudātta carries no mark at all — bare, unmarked letters are to be understood as anudātta. One must understand these markings letter by letter. Where the accent-mark sits — above the letter, at its foot, or beside it — determines the type of accent for that syllable. **As an example, here is a well-known mantra shown with its accent-marks in place**—

> **अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं य॒ज्ञस्य॑ दे॒वमृ॑त्विज॑म् ।**
> **होता॑रं रत्न॒धात॑मम् ॥**
> *agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñasya devám ṛtvíjam | hótāraṃ ratnadhātamam ||* (Rigveda Samhita 1.1.1)
>
> "I praise Agni, the household priest, the divine minister of the sacrifice, the invoker, the bestower of treasures most abundant."

**In this mantra, the udātta letters are:** gni, ro, jña, va, tvi, hoꞮ, dhā.
**The anudātta letters are:** a, pu, ya, de, ṛ, ta.
**The svarita letters are:** mī, ḷe, ta, jaꞮ, tā, ta.
**The prachaya (level/neutral) letters are:** le, taꞮ, raꞮ, ra, mam.
— And so on for the rest.

The reference is to the text of Scripture:

> इन्द्रशत्रुर्वर्धस्व ।
> *indraśatrur vardhasva |* (see Nirukta 2.16; Shatapatha Brahmana account of Tvashtri's error)

If "indraśatru" in this text were intended to mean "enemy, destroyer of Indra," the word would be a tatpuruṣa compound, and in accordance with the rule "samāsasya" (the compound's accent-rule), it would have the acute accent on the...

**This is a well-known cautionary tale.** Correctly pronounced, "indraśatru" should mean "he whose slayer is Indra" (a bahuvrīhi compound, accent on the first member) — but Tvashtri, in performing a sacrifice to create a son who would destroy Indra, mispronounced the accent, unintentionally shifting the compound's sense to a tatpuruṣa ("Indra's slayer") — and as a direct result, the very son born from that yajna was destroyed **by** Indra, rather than destroying him. This story is given in detail in works such as the same passage cited above (page 552) and in Panini's grammar tradition.

### On "Bala" (Force)

**"Bala"** refers to the place of articulation. The place refers to the specific effort involved in pronouncing a given letter; the letter pronounced with the appropriate effort at its proper place is called "sthāna" (station). "Kaṇṭha (throat), tālu (palate), danta (teeth), oṣṭha (lips)" and similar — these are the places at which the letters are articulated. According to the Anga tradition, the letter **a** [and similar vowels] are articulated in the throat; the semivowels [ya, ra, la, va] are articulated with slight contact — this is called "īṣat" (slight) contact. Understanding this proper application of contact and place, at each letter, matters for correct articulation.

### On "Sāma" (Uniform Delivery)

**"Sāma"** means: when reciting the words, neither shortening a short-duration letter nor lengthening it beyond its proper measure — this is the true meaning of correct recitation. One must recite with steady attentiveness, without letting the mind wander, taking care not to reverse the order of the letters, nor to omit any, nor mispronounce them. If one recites in a manner that adds extraneous sounds or drops necessary ones — the meaning of the words becomes muddled, and the recitation carries the fault of ill-effect (as the poison-anecdote and similar stories illustrate). Reciting evenly, without irregularity, is the virtue of proper "sāma."

### On "Santāna" (Madhurya) — Joining

> माधुर्यमक्षरव्यक्तिश्च त्रयीत्यादिना (शि. ३-४)
> *mādhuryam akṣara-vyaktiś ca trayīty ādinā* (Shiksha 3.4)

**When reciting the Veda's letters**, one must recite in such a way that letters like hrasva (short), dīrgha (long), saṃyukta-akṣara (conjunct letters), alpaprāṇa (unaspirated), and mahāprāṇa (aspirated) are pronounced clearly and distinctly, sweetly and without confusion, each properly articulated. **This is a virtue of correct recitation.**

### Page 552

### "Santāna" (Joining) — continued

**Santāna** refers to the proper procedure for joining words together, according to the rules of euphonic combination (sandhi). "Vāyav" is a case of vāyu joined with "ā": when the word "vāyu" is followed by "ā" [as in "vāyav ā yāhi"], sandhi occurs. Similarly, "indrāgnī" is a case where "indra" and "agnī" combine: when "indra" is followed by "agnī," this particular sandhi results — which words combine, and how they combine, is set out in the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa). Since a full discussion of this belongs there, it is not elaborated in the Śikṣā, and is only briefly touched upon here.

Failing to properly know the rules laid down in the Śikṣā text — whether errors of accent or errors in letters — leads to serious fault when reciting a mantra. If a mantra is recited with either wrong accent or wrong letters, its very meaning becomes altered from its intended sense. Such a defective mantra becomes fruitless (aphala) — or worse, it directly harms the very person who recites it. There are traditional accounts of this. In particular, a well-known account, still preserved in the Taittiriya Shakha tradition, tells of such a case—

Previously, when Tvashtri was performing Prajapati's yajna, desiring to have a son who would kill Indra, he made a homa-offering into Agni with the mantra—

> स्वाहेन्द्रशत्रुर्वर्धस्व ।
> *svāhendraśatrur vardhasva |*
> "Svāhā! May you grow, O slayer of Indra"

Because of an accent-error within it, instead of achieving the intended result, harm befell the very yajamāna who performed the yajna. **This same matter is explained by the mantra given in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda** — see the fuller citation and resolution on the following page.

### Page 553

...is that this mantra needs to be understood as **"sākṣād indraśatru-varthārthasya"** — "one whose very slayer is directly Indra." When Tvashtri performed the yajna intending to produce a son who would slay Indra, he intended the compound "indraśatru" to mean "the slayer of Indra" (indraṃ śatruḥ — a tatpuruṣa compound: "Indra's foe"). But because he pronounced it with the *wrong accent* — properly accented, "indraśatru" as a **bahuvrīhi compound** must instead be understood to mean "he whose slayer is Indra" (indraḥ śatruḥ yasya saḥ — "one destroyed **by** Indra"). Accent alone determines this distinction.

Because of this single mispronunciation, the very meaning of the mantra reversed: instead of producing a destroyer *of* Indra, the sacrifice produced a being destined to be destroyed *by* Indra — and that is precisely what happened, as the sacred narrative recounts. This shows how essential correct accent is:

> इन्द्रः शत्रुर्यस्य ।
> *indraḥ śatrur yasya |*

— this is the bahuvrīhi's genuine intended sense.

**Meaning:** the compound "indraśatru," when correctly accented as a bahuvrīhi (with acute accent on the first member), means "he whose enemy/destroyer is Indra." Because Tvashtri's actual pronunciation shifted the accent to the pattern proper to a tatpuruṣa compound, the sense inadvertently reversed to "the destroyer of Indra" — and the resulting confusion in meaning led directly to his own destruction, as the story shows. **From this, it becomes clear how essential correct knowledge of accent truly is.** This example alone suffices to demonstrate why the Śikṣā treatise is indispensable.

**Kalpa, the second Anga, means the Sutras of Ashvalayana, Apastamba, Baudhayana and other authors.** For the science is so called because the sacrifice is confirmed (**kalpyate**) by it.

**"...New and Full Moon sacrifices" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.1).** Now the first hymns of Rig Veda are nowhere used throughout the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Nor the latter either. Because the Brahmana starts from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, saying, "At the dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice they offer the puroḍāśa cake in eleven platters."

**To this we answer:** the mantra portion of Rig Veda follows the order in which the hymns must be recited — for example, in that recitation before the supreme Spirit, which we call the **brahma-yajña** [the "sacrifice of Brahman," i.e., Vedic recitation as a spiritual offering]. It does not follow the order in which the sacrificial rites are performed. This brahma-sacrifice is thus enjoined:

> स्वाध्यायोऽध्येतव्यः ऋचामेकामृचं वा यजुषामेकं यजुर्वा साम्नामेकं साम वा तद्ब्रह्मयज्ञः ॥
> *svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ ṛcām ekām ṛcaṃ vā yajuṣām ekaṃ yajur vā sāmnām ekaṃ sāma vā tad brahma-yajñaḥ ||* (Ashvalayana Grihya Sutra 3.4.1[?])
>
> "Let a man recite his own Veda, or one verse only of his own Veda, be it Rig, Yajur, or Sama; that is the spiritual sacrifice."

**Meaning:** for this daily brahma-yajña, one must recite according to the sequence in which the mantras are collected within the Samhita — not according to when each mantra is actually employed in a rite. The order of recitation for the brahma-yajña follows the Samhita's own internal arrangement: the mantras belonging to the trees and plants (used for consecrating the sacred grass and similar purposes) are recited according to that fixed textual order, not according to their scattered ritual usage.

**This same principle** — that recitation-order and ritual-employment-order are two entirely separate matters — resolves the apparent contradiction: since Ashvalayana's Kalpa-sutra text (dealing with actual ritual sequence) doesn't follow the Rigveda-Samhita's own textual order, this in no way undermines the claim that the Samhita's own arrangement is fixed for the purposes of daily recitation (svādhyāya) and the brahma-yajña specifically.

**One further doubt might arise:** does Ashvalayana's own Grihya-sutra, in laying down the rules for daily recitation, follow the mantra order of the Rigveda-Samhita, or does it follow some other principle? — Whichever the answer, one thing is beyond dispute: a person should recite his own portion, be it Rig, Yajur, or Sama, according to a fixed and definite sequence.

**Wherever employment [of a mantra in ritual] is explicitly commanded, the traditional [Samhita] order need not be followed** — this is not to be regarded as a genuine flaw. In the case of works belonging to different Shakhas, understanding the specific application (viniyoga) of each mantra requires study of those Shakhas' own Kalpa-sutra texts.

**In all cases where a recitation of the whole mantra portion is commanded, the traditional order must be rigidly followed.**

Now, this discussion is undertaken by those wishing to critically examine the works composed by the various Angas. **Kalpa** means the treatises that treat the specific methods for performing yajnas — that is, the works explaining ritual procedure (karma), mantra-application (viniyoga), and the substances to be used (dravya) in a yajna. Among the ancient works of this kind, Ashvalayana, Apastamba, and Baudhayana are well-known, and among more recent works, Katyayana and similar authors have composed treatises. There are many such Kalpa-treatises belonging to different Shakhas — Shrauta-sutra, Grihya-sutra, Dharma-sutra, Paribhasha-sutra, and so on. **Among these, we shall now examine an objection raised regarding Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra specifically**—

Do Ashvalayana's followers, in the Shrauta-sutra, follow the order employed in the ritual-application of the mantras, following the sequence in which they occur in the Samhita? Or do they follow some other order not matching the Kanda (section) division? Whatever it may be, they do not follow the Samhita's own Mantra-kanda sequence at all. If it be objected that in one instance, at least, the order matches — namely, where it is said—

> दर्शपूर्णमासौ तु पूर्वं व्याख्यास्यामः ।
> *darśa-pūrṇamāsau tu pūrvaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ |*
> "We shall first expound the Darsha and Purnamasa rites"

(Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.1.2) — this is [merely] because the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice comes first in the sequence of sacrificial rites, [not because it follows the Samhita's mantra-order]. The word **"agnihotra"** begins their treatise likewise — the mantra collection for Agnihotra is not found gathered anywhere in the Samhita as a coherent block. Therefore, the Kalpa-treatises follow their *own* sequence, based on the order of ritual performance, not the Samhita's own arrangement. Precisely because these two orderings can differ, one's own Brahmana-portion may not follow the same sequence either. Some might say — but the text opens—

> आत्मानं वेदपुरोडाशं निर्वपति दीक्षणीयेष्ट्यादौ कल्पम् ।
> *ātmānaṃ veda-puroḍāśaṃ nirvapati dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭy-adau kalpam |*
> "At the beginning of the dīkṣaṇīyā rite, one offers the Veda-cake for oneself"

(Aitareya Brahmana 1.1) — this passage relates to the dīkṣaṇīyā-related mantra. Therefore, the Brahmana too may not always follow the [Samhita's] sequence.

**Here a special doubt must be resolved.** In the Mantra-kanda (the portion of the Samhita comprising mantras, including the Khilas), determining which mantra decisively belongs to which rite is often difficult — the composer of the Brahmana-portion doesn't reveal this explicitly. The performer of the Brahma-yajna needs no such determination. **The Brahma-yajna's injunction is stated thus:**

> स्वाध्यायोऽध्येतव्यः ऋचामेकामृचं वा यजुषामेकं यजुर्वा साम्नामेकं साम वा तद्ब्रह्मयज्ञः ॥
> *svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ ṛcām ekām ṛcaṃ vā yajuṣām ekaṃ yajur vā sāmnām ekaṃ sāma vā tad brahma-yajñaḥ ||* (see page 554 above)

"Let a man recite his own Veda — even a single verse of his own Veda, whether Rig, Yajur, or Sama — that is the spiritual sacrifice." **This is what it means.** One should recite his own Shakha's texts in their proper Samhita-sequence. This much suffices.

**But when actually performing rites**, one must know precisely which mantras from the Samhita apply to which specific rite. Without knowing this precise application, one cannot perform the rites correctly. Therefore, it is entirely proper to first know the sequence of ritual acts and only afterward identify the mantras belonging to each — an entirely different concern from the Samhita's own arrangement. It has also been said elsewhere—

> सूर्यो न दर्शनायोद्दिष्ट सर्वदाशकरान्तोरण भ्रियात् ।

— [this] confirms that even great luminaries like the Sun are described in a similarly indirect fashion throughout the mantras, without this creating any expectation of matching sequence. Given this, one might well ask: for a person desiring rain, or one desiring wealth, or one desiring pragya (wisdom), and so on — three [different desires require] three [different] applications; the Veda's own arrangement leaves it to the application-texts to specify precisely which mantra should be used.

**It is true that the Brahmana of the Rig Veda begins with the dīkṣaṇīya rite.** But that rite is merely a modification of the New and Full Moon sacrifice to which it makes constant reference. So Ashvalayana did well to begin his exposition with his latter rite.

**It has thus been shown that the second Anga, the Kalpa Sutra, stating as it does the application of the various texts, is useful in teaching the performance of the sacrifice.**

### The Third Anga: Vyākaraṇa (Grammar) — Its Purpose Set Out Through Its Defining Characteristics, in the Manner Shown by Vararuchi and Patañjali

### Page 558

**Vyākaraṇa** is useful in determining the precise form of a word and its meaning, through the instruction it gives regarding roots (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), and similar matters. Likewise, in the **Aindravāyavagraha-brāhmaṇa**, it is recounted—

> वाग्वै पराच्यव्याकृतावदत्तेते देवा इन्द्रमब्रुवन्निमां नो वाचं व्याकुर्विति। सोऽब्रवीद्वैषा मह्यं चैव वायवे च सह गृह्णाथा इति। तस्मादिन्द्रवायू सहैव गृह्णाति। तामिन्द्रो मध्यतोऽवक्रम्य व्याकरोत्। तस्मादियं व्याकृता वागुद्यते ॥
> *vāg vai parācy avyākṛtāvadat | te devā indram abruvan vi māṃ no vācaṃ vyākuruv iti | so'bravīd vaiṣā mahyaṃ caiva vāyave ca saha gṛhṇāthā iti | tasmād indra-vāyū sahaiva gṛhṇāti | tām indro madhyato'vakramya vyākarot | tasmād iyaṃ vyākṛtā vāg udyate ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 6.4.7.3)
>
> "**In old days Speech was indiscreet.** The gods came to Indra, and said, 'Separate Speech for us into its parts.' He said, 'Give me and Vayu a boon, let us take it together.' **Therefore, the Aindravayava [offering] is taken together.** Then Indra took Speech by the middle, and divided it into its parts. **And that is the origin of Speech divided into parts (vyākṛta).**"

**Meaning:** in ancient times, Speech (Vāk) existed only in an undivided, unanalyzed form — it had not yet been separated into its constituent parts, and was thus spoken in a scattered, indistinct manner. Perceiving this defect, the gods approached Indra and requested him to properly divide Speech into its parts. Indra agreed on the condition that this task be shared jointly with Vayu — hence the well-known "Aindravayava" oblation, offered to Indra and Vayu together, commemorates this shared undertaking. Indra then took hold of Speech at her very middle and divided her methodically into her constituent parts. From this act arose "vyākṛta vāk" — Speech properly analyzed and divided — which is precisely what the science of **Vyākaraṇa** ("grammar," literally "the analysis/division [of speech]") takes as its own subject-matter and derives its very name from.

---

### Page 559

**The meaning of this is as follows:** in old days a text like "agnim īḷe purohitam" was an indiscrete sound like the roar of the sea. And there was no book to help distinguish in it between roots, affixes, words, and sentences. Then Indra, at the request of the gods, being propitiated by a boon in the form of an offering of soma poured into one vessel for him and Vayu, divided Speech in the middle, and established the divisions between roots, affixes, and the like. **And that is why all can now recite Speech as it has been analysed by Pāṇini and other great sages.**

**The special use of this analysis of words, or Grammar, is shown by Vararuchi in the Vārtika**—

> रक्षोहागमलाघ्वसन्देहाः प्रयोजनम् ।
> *rakṣohāgama-lāghva-sandehāḥ prayojanam |* (Katyayana's Vartika on Paṇini's Ashtadhyayi)
>
> "Protection, comprehension of [the sense of] transmitted [Vedic texts], brevity, and removal of doubt — these are the purposes [of Grammar]."

**These and other uses are explained in the Mahābhāṣya by Patañjali as follows:**—

**"Rakṣā"** [protection] — the protection of the Veda [refers to preserving Vedic texts from corruption]. "**Pradhānaṃ ca ṣaḍbhis sneha-vyākaraṇam**" [Grammar is chief among these six, being the means of proper linkage]. "**Pradhāne ca kṛto yuktaḥ phalāt tṛptavati**" [Being primary, its fruit is complete]. "**Alpākṣaraṃ cābhyeyaṃ vyākaraṇam**" — Grammar is to be studied precisely because it is concise, [and thereby valuable]. "**Bṛhaspatiḥ riṃ nyāya vidyaṃ varṣa-sahasraṃ pratipada-doktvā śakalanāṃ śabdānām**" [Brihaspati taught the doctrine of words, syllable by syllable, for a thousand years]. "**Śabba-kṣatrāṃ**" [thus the science of words] "**Indrāya prāha**" — [and] taught it to Indra. "**Divyaṃ varṣa-sahasram adhyayana-kālaḥ**" — the period of study extended for a thousand celestial years. "**Aṃśaṃ ca na jagāma**" — and even then, he did not reach the end of it. "**Ādyas tu punar api paramāyāḥ bhagavatī sa kala-sad-āvaga-nu bhūta kuta sarva śabda-tāvagena sakala-sad-āva-vagenaḥ kuta sarva-pradeśāvena caitāyaṃ vyākaraṇam**" — [this concise treatise on] Grammar, [treating] all the requisite subjects, teaches "using appropriate speech" as its purpose.

**"Laghu-tvam"** [brevity] — a shortened word, used quickly (śīghra), is preferable. **"Sandehe"** — where doubt arises whether a particular is or is not a word: is it "sthūla" or "sthūlā," is it "śva" or "śvā" — [Grammar resolves this]. **"Kartā"** [the agent] — as with "dāśvaḥ" — [the one who has given]. **"Anavadyaṃ kṛta-śrī"** — [Grammar renders speech] faultless. **"Ubhaya-taḥ"** — on both sides. **"Duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato vā varṇato vā"** — **a word [used] incorrectly, whether in accent or in letter, [causes fault]. "Mithyā-prayukto na tam artham āha"** — [a] wrongly-used [word] does not convey that meaning [it is intended to]. **"Sa vāgvajro yajamānaṃ hinasti**" — **that word becomes a thunderbolt, and strikes the sacrificer**. **"Duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svaratovā"** — this is confirmed [by scripture] — **"yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt"** — as in the case of "indraśatru" mispronounced in accent. **"Tasmāt yajñeṣu prayoktavyaṃ śreyaḥ vyākaraṇam**" — **therefore, in sacrifices, Grammar should be properly employed.**

Then Indra, at the request of the gods, being propitiated by a boon in the form of an offering of soma poured into one vessel for him and Vayu, divided Speech in the middle, and established the divisions between roots, affixes and the like. And that is why all can now recite Speech as it has been analysed by Panini and other great sages.

> The special use of this analysis of words, or Grammar, is shewn by Vararuchi in the Vartika, "rakshohagamalaghvasamdehah prayojanam." These and other uses are explained in the Mahabhashya by Patanjali as follows:—

### Page 563

Now let us critically examine the grammatical discussion that stands as the principal matter among the Veda's Angas. Grammar accepts and orders the roots (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), word-forms, and their meaning-determinations in the appropriate contexts where they apply. As it was said before, this too has its basis in the **Aindravāyavagraha-brāhmaṇa**—

> वाग्वै पराच्यव्याकृतावदत् एते देवा इन्द्रमब्रुवन् इमां नो वाचं व्याकुर्विति सोऽब्रवीद्वैषा मह्यं चैव वायवे च सह गृह्णाथा इति तस्मादिन्द्रवायू सहैव गृह्णाति तामिन्द्रो मध्यतोऽवक्रम्य व्याकरोत् तस्मादियं व्याकृता वागुद्यते ॥
> *vāg vai parācy avyākṛtāvadat | ete devā indram abruvan imāṃ no vācaṃ vyākuruv iti | so'bravīd vaiṣā mahyaṃ caiva vāyave ca saha gṛhṇāthā iti | tasmād indra-vāyū sahaiva gṛhṇāti | tām indro madhyato'vakramya vyākarot | tasmād iyaṃ vyākṛtā vāg udyate ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 6.4.7.3; see page 558 above)

**Meaning:** in the beginning, Speech spoke unclearly (avyākṛta — undivided), rendering it useless [for correctly conveying meaning]. Then the gods approached Indra, asking, "Divide this Speech of ours [into parts] for us." He agreed, saying, "Give this offering jointly to me and to Vayu." Because of this, [the offering] is given jointly to Indra and Vayu even now (this is called "Aindravāyava" — a specific offering-related Dharma tradition). Both deities accepted the offering. Then Indra took hold of Speech at her very middle and divided her methodically. That is why what we now recite is "vyākṛta vāk" — Speech that has been analyzed and divided into her proper constituent parts.

**Grammar itself was, in ancient times, composed in the earliest period — vast in extent, like the ocean itself.** The roots, suffixes, words, and sentences were originally undivided (agrantha, unarranged into a systematic textual form). Then, out of desire for the fulfillment [of ritual duties], the gods approached Indra alone specifically, and by combining the powers of Vayu and Soma-Rasa-graha with him, established a fixed order — and thus, from that point on, this speech came to be arranged in a systematic, divided fashion, namely: words, roots, and suffixes, distinguished from one another. **Because of this, the wisest sages, from Pāṇini onward, arranged this speech (that is, established a grammatical treatise) in a fixed, methodical form — this is the understood significance here.**

### Page 564

Regarding what specific purpose this Grammar serves, later scholars, in their own tradition, have stated—

> **रक्षोहागमलाघवसंदेहाः प्रयोजनमिति ।**
> *rakṣohāgamalāghavasandehāḥ prayojanam iti |* (Katyayana's Vartika; see page 559 above)

"**Rakṣā** (protection), **ūha** (adaptation), **āgama** (scriptural priority), **lāghava** (brevity), and **sandeha**-removal — these are the purposes [of Grammar]." Vararuchi has clearly set out these five purposes in his own vārtika-treatise.

**Rakṣā (Protection):** since Vedic mantras have come down through the ages, doubts arise concerning whether their forms have been corrupted, whether some deviation has crept into the words as transmitted. Precisely to remove such doubts and to protect the Veda's genuine form from corruption, Grammar is necessary. Without knowing Grammar, one cannot distinguish which letters, among those forming a word, are genuinely correct and which have been altered — nor determine, through Grammar's principles, the correct application of the mantras. Hence, without knowledge of Grammar, one cannot properly identify errors of accent, wrong letters, and similar deviations.

**Ūha (Adaptation):** the words found in the Vedic mantras — nouns, verbs, and similar forms — are not always used explicitly in their fully expanded application; often, the application must be inferred and understood [i.e., adapted to the specific ritual context]. This too requires proficiency in Grammar. Where the mantras must be modified [in case, number, gender] for ritual employment — this adaptation likewise cannot be accomplished without knowledge of Grammar.

**Āgama (Scriptural Priority):** the Brahmin who desires knowledge must study and understand not only the Veda itself, but also the dharma expressed through its established, systematic form — this too the shastras declare. Among the six Angas of the Veda, Grammar holds the foremost place. Effort spent studying this principal Anga will prove fruitful. Therefore, Grammar should be studied.

**Lāghava (Brevity):** to know the Veda with genuine ease, one must study Grammar. Once, when the sage Brihaspati desired to teach the science of words to Indra, he explained it word by word — an approach that even after a thousand celestial years, remained incomplete. Grammar's own systematic method (through its structured rules on roots, suffixes, and the like) accomplishes in a single stroke what such an exhaustive word-by-word approach never could.

**Sandeha (Removal of Doubt):** even one who knows how to distinguish between correct and incorrect forms may occasionally have doubts about a particular word's status. If, at such a time, one lacks the ability to apply Grammar's rules, one cannot resolve the doubt.

**Asaṃdeha (Freedom from Doubt):** knowing the meanings of words correctly is called freedom from doubt (asaṃdeha). This is a fundamental requirement for grammatical study. Understand it this way—

> स्थूलपृषती मासि आलभेत ।
> *sthūlapṛṣatī māsi ālabheta |*

— this sentence involves ambiguity: how should the compound "**sthūlapṛṣatī**" be understood? Or should one understand it as—

> स्थूलः पृषती ।
> *sthūlaḥ pṛṣatī |*

—(great and spotted — meaning a bull that is both great and spotted)? Or as a karmadhāraya compound meaning "the great-spotted-one"? Without knowledge of Grammar, this cannot be resolved. Only a grammarian, on the basis of the accent, can determine whether this is a bahuvrīhi or a karmadhāraya compound, and thereby settle the meaning correctly. Here, in this sentence, the accent falls on the compound's *first* member — establishing it definitively as a bahuvrīhi, meaning "one who possesses great spots," rather than "great and spotted" as a mere descriptive pairing. **This kind of doubt-resolution is Grammar's chief use.** Therefore, Grammar should be studied to remove such doubts.

> सोऽकनन्तेमाप्रोत्येति जयं परत्रे वाग्योगविद्दुष्यति चापशब्दैः ॥
