**Meaning:** one who has skillfully mastered the proper use of speech, applying it correctly according to worldly needs, attains victory in the beyond as well. But one who is ignorant of the proper joining and application of speech is contaminated by corrupted forms (apaśabda).

**Here it must be understood what constitutes the "fault" of a corrupted word's use.** Concerning this: is the use of a corrupted word — that is, an improper word — itself a fault? Or does merely knowing that a word is corrupted, without actually using it, also become fault? Precisely because of this discussion, using a corrupted word is a true dharma-violation. In that sense, whether from mere knowledge of a corrupted word or from actually using it, an adharma (or, indeed, a sin) results. Ordinarily, corrupted forms are far more numerous than correct forms. Corrupted forms exist in great abundance. **For example — "gauḥ" (cow) — and its many corrupt variations, such as "gāvī," "goṇī," "gopotalikā," and similar, are widely known.**

Once, a certain man, from lack of grammatical knowledge, is said to have used a corrupted form without even knowing it was corrupted. If asked, can he escape blame simply because he acted out of ignorance rather than deliberate intent? — even so, ignorance is customarily excused as a defense. Whether or not a brahmin knew, if he committed some transgression, or created some fault through incorrect performance, does he not still bear consequences for it? Similarly, even one who commits a mistaken utterance without knowing it — precisely because he lacks the knowledge to know that his usage is corrupt — such a person does not incur the fault of adharma. **This shows why "avidvāṃsaha" (ignorance) is discussed** — merely knowing many words and their applications, without also knowing dharma, still leaves one properly usable in speech.

**Jaimini and other Mīmāṃsakas insist one must know what constitutes dharma, and equally know what constitutes adharma** — precisely for this purpose. Both must be known: to perform dharma, and to avoid adharma. Even here [in the Śikṣā's own account], "śabda" (correct word) and "aśabda" (incorrect word)...

"**But the unlearned, who do not know that, in responding to a salutation, they should protract the vowel — in approaching them, he should simply say, as he would to a woman, 'Here am I.'**"

**Meaning:** in this verse (which appears in the first chapter, describing the ordinary applications typically found), it is said that when responding to a salutation, one's own [family or personal] name should be pronounced with a lengthened vowel [as a mark of grammatical propriety]. Those unlearned people who do not know this rule instead pronounce it in an ordinary manner, as one would when addressing a woman [informally]. This is spoken of here as an example of erroneous practice. In this way, in a person's daily life as well, such improper practices are known to occur. This shows that even after studying and gaining scholarly proficiency, without also thoroughly mastering Grammar, one cannot avoid this kind of fault in ordinary word-usage. Since even scholars versed in the shastras are exposed to this risk, Grammar's importance is beyond dispute; without knowledge of Grammar, no genuine honour attaches [to one's learning]. **Therefore, Grammar should be studied.**

**"Vibhaktiṃ Kurvanti"** (They Perform the Division) — the priests who properly know the words to be recited (that is, the principal words belonging to the yajna, and the words belonging to that portion) must be studied for their correct application. Without knowledge of Grammar, this precept cannot be properly complied with. For this reason too, Grammar should be studied.

> प्रयाजाः सविभक्तिकाः कार्त्स्न्या इति —
> *prayājāḥ savibhaktikāḥ kārtsnyā iti* — "The priests recite the text 'prayajah savibhaktikah karyah.' But without Grammar this precept cannot be complied with. Let us study Grammar then for this reason."

**"Yo Vā Imām"** (He Who [Analyses] This [Speech]) — this well-known text of the Rig Veda declares that whoever fully knows word, accent, and letter — one must know these matters, distinguishing each accent, each letter, in due order—

...according to the rules — only such a person is fit to be a priest. One who cannot properly divide sentences, syllables, or word-portions; who cannot distinguish accent-differences, letter-differences, or the boundaries within a compound; who cannot properly identify [ritually] related words — such a person is unfit to serve as priest in yajna and similar rites. **Therefore, only one who is thoroughly versed in Grammar is fit for priesthood.**

**Here, to illustrate the analysis of words and accented letters, the Nirukta gives the following example**—

> वायुर्वा यज्ञो दर्शतेव सोमा अरंकृताः । तेषां साकं श्रुधीहवम् ॥
> *vāyur vā yajño darśateva somā araṃkṛtāḥ | teṣāṃ sākaṃ śrudhī havam ||* (Vajasaneyi Samhita 1.2.1)

**This mantra occurs in the Gayatri-chandas** [meter]. Its word-division is: "**vāyur vā yajño darśate | ime somā araṃkṛtāḥ ||**" — meaning [that is how it should be understood].

**Here, "darśakeṣu" [visible things]** — should it be understood as "darśaka" [one who sees] or "ime" [these]? The letter division is: **t + ime**, two separate letters combining. Where sandhi occurs, adjacent letters join together. This slight variation causes doubt within the interpretation. "**Te**" indicates a word, and following "anudātta," its accent varies. This word, distinct from the letter "i," is a separate letter carrying its own accent, differing from "te."

**This way, in this manner, there are many divisions to be made** — for example, "**dīrgha**" [long syllable] versus "**avagraha**" [separated word], and "**vāṃ**" versus "**ahaṃ**" [I], and "**khu**" (namely "**sāṃ ne sūnu**" — see page 549 above) — "**dīrghākṣare pṛṣṭhaṃ vā abhavat, sphā ne sūnu = saḥ | khu | naḥ | sūnuḥ**" — the accent differs by syllable-length in each case. All these matters require careful precision; anyone wishing to fully master this discipline must study Grammar with genuine effort. **This too is a reason why one must study Grammar.**

### "Catvāri" (Four)

**This particular topic is important** — regarding it, our own tradition cites this verse (found on folio 40)—

> *catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya | tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ ā viveśa ||* (Rigveda Samhita 4.58.3)
>
> "**With four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands in Bull, penned up in three places roars mightily; a great god has entered mortals.**"

Since this mantra's meaning cannot easily be determined through common understanding, it remains obscure to most, given its many possible interpretations. This mantra is described as one belonging to a rishi named "**Vena**" (yathāsvaru; see Nirukta 5.2[?]). It is a "sāmayanā" [collective] mantra — its sense taken together, and its application through Agni, Surya, and Apa (waters), and through the Gopura (metaphorical bull) with its four "kṣapa" (horns), the wise say. Some also expound it grammatically according to the analysis of the "**rukchandas**" [Vedic prosody] tradition.

### Page 570

Ancient scholars have explained this mantra's meaning in various ways, according to whichever deity is taken as primary in the intended sense; even in our own tradition, this mantra has been interpreted in several distinct ways. **Grammatically, they explain the meaning as follows** —

> चत्वारि शृङ्गा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य । त्रिधा बद्धो वृषभो रोरवीति महो देवो मर्त्यां आ विवेश ॥
> *catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya | tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ ā viveśa ||* (Rigveda Samhita 4.58.3; see page 569 above)

**From this, the following meanings can be explained:**

**Catvāri Śṛṅgā** (Four Horns) — from the standpoint of Grammar: noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga), and particle (nipāta) — these are the four kinds of word-categories.

**Trayo Asya Pādāḥ** (Its Three Feet) — past (bhūta), present (bhavat), and future (vartamāna) — these are the three time-divisions.

**Dve Śīrṣe** (Two Heads) — nominal endings (subanta-padas) and verbal endings (tiṅanta-padas) — these two types of word-terminations.

**Sapta Hastāso Asya** (Its Seven Hands) — the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh cases (vibhakti) — these seven case-endings.

**Tridhā Baddhaḥ** (Bound in Three Places) — held fast by the three articulatory places: throat, chest, and head — these three points [of pronunciation].

**Vṛṣabhaḥ** (The Bull) — since it showers down (varṣaṇa) blessings upon what is desired, it is called Vṛṣabha (the Bull, "the shower-er").

**Roravīti** (It Roars Mightily) — from the root "ru," meaning to make a sound (śabda-karma) — hence its use here.

**Mahoo Devaḥ** (The Great God) — the great deity, referring to the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa) itself.

**Martyān** (Into Mortals).

**Ā Viveśa** (Has Entered) — meaning: has entered into, taken possession of. That great deity — namely Grammar itself — has entered into mortal beings [i.e., speakers] and dwells within them.

---

He is called here a Bull (vrishabha), because he rains down (varshana) blessings. 'Roravīti,' from the root 'ru' to make a noise. A great god has entered mortals. Let us study grammar that we may attain to union with this great god.

**In this way, the ancients have set forth many kinds of interpretation** — brahmins, wise in mind, know all these fourfold divisions. Of these four, three remain hidden and unmoving in their secret place; it is only the fourth portion of speech that ordinary humans commonly utter — this much is the accepted meaning, held by many across different systems.

**The meaning of the word "muktārtha"** [liberated/complete sense] is that speech has four distinct kinds. Grasping this well, brahmins who genuinely know [this doctrine] understand: among these four kinds of speech-categories, in three of them exist countless forms — but in only one does the ordinary usage practiced by human beings actually occur. ### "Saktum Iva" (Like Purified Grain)

> यत्रा सखायः सख्यानि जानते सक्तुमिव तितउना पुनन्ति । अत्रा धीरा धिय एनाभिरेकं गूहन्ति गुह्यमविशेषु शीकैः ॥
> *yatrā sakhāyaḥ sakhyāni jānate saktum iva titaunā punanti | atrā dhīrā dhiya enābhir ekaṃ gūhanti guhyam aviśeṣu śīkaiḥ ||* (Rigveda Samhita 10.71.2)

"**Where wise men draw speech hither and thither in their mind, purifying it as men purify grain with a winnowing basket — there friends learn what friendship is: a gracious fortune is upon their words.**"

**"The word 'saktu' here [is] derived from 'sacati': it means 'hard to purify.' Or we may take it from 'kasati,' become by transposition 'sakati.' In that case it would mean**..."

**Meaning:** the word "saktu" (ground grain/meal) here — its derivation according to Grammar can be traced through the verbal root "√sac" (to associate/adhere), yielding the sense of "that which is difficult to purify [thoroughly]." Alternatively, deriving it through metathesis (letter-transposition) from the root "√kas" (to move/shine), it may instead convey the sense of "capability" (śakti). This shows how the very meaning of a single word — its etymological source, and hence its true sense — depends entirely on grammatical analysis.

**This mantra**, whether taken as expressing the science of speech (vāk-śāstra), or as describing the structure of grammar (vāk-svarūpa) itself, is a difficult one, requiring the discipline called "grammar" (śabda-śāstra) to properly navigate its path. **Who, then, is capable of understanding it? Only the authorities on Grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) themselves.**

> भद्रैषां लक्ष्मीर्निहिताधि वाचि — इषां वाचि भद्रा लक्ष्मीर्निहिता भवति ।

### "Daśamyāṃ Putrasya" (On the Tenth Day, for the Son)

**On the day fixed for the son's naming-ceremony**, following the birth, the traditional custom is to select a name. Regarding this:

> पुत्रस्य दशम्यां नाम कुर्यात्, द्व्यक्षरं चतुरक्षरं वा, अन्तस्थादिकं वा, आद्यन्तस्थं वा, कृद्रूपं वा, न तद्धितान्तम् ॥
> *putrasya daśamyāṃ nāma kuryāt, dvy-akṣaraṃ catur-akṣaraṃ vā, antasthādikaṃ vā, ādy-antasthaṃ vā, kṛd-rūpaṃ vā, na taddhitāntam ||*

**"'Let him name the boy on the tenth day after his birth. He must make the name of the sonants, with y, r, l or v in the beginning or middle, and the visarga at the end, of two syllables or four, a kṛt-formation, and not ending in a taddhita.' But without a knowledge of..."**

**Meaning:** the person's name should either begin with, or have in its middle, a semivowel (y, r, l, or v) [i.e., an "antasthā" consonant], and should end with the visarga. It should be two syllables in length, or four; it should be formed as a "kṛt"-derivative (from a verbal root, via primary suffixes), and must never be a "taddhita"-derivative (a secondary derivative formed from another noun). Whoever wishes to properly assign a name according to these precise grammatical rules must, without exception, possess knowledge of Grammar; without it, this precept cannot be properly carried out.

"**Let the section from Vayu to Bhaga be for the gods in mid-air; and that from Surya to Devapatnyah for the gods in heaven.**"

"**So the whole Samāmnāya from 'Gauḥ' to 'Devapatnyaḥ' is studied.**"

**Nighaṇṭu is a well-established name for a book which contains chiefly lists of synonyms.** As for example, such books as Amarasiṃha, Vaijayantī, Halāyudha, and others are spoken of as the "ten Nighaṇṭus." In the same way, the first chapter of our book, which gives a list of synonyms, is called a Nighaṇṭu. There are three adhyāyas in this chapter. In the first, we have names of things, such as the earth and the other worlds, and space and time; in the second, we have the names of things such as men and the limbs of men; in the third, we have qualities, such as multitude or shortness, belonging to both classes of things.

**This is what the following verse conveys**:

> प्रथमाध्याये भूम्यादि-लोकानाम् आकाश-कालयोश्च नामानि । द्वितीये पुरुषादीनां तदङ्गानां च संज्ञाः स्युः । तृतीये तूभयोरपि साधारणा बहुत्वाल्पत्वादि-गुणवाचकाः शब्दāḥ ||
> *prathamādhyāye bhūmyādi-lokānām ākāśa-kālayoś ca nāmāni | dvitīye puruṣādīnāṃ tad-aṅgānāṃ ca saṃjñāḥ syuḥ | tṛtīye tūbhayor api sādhāraṇā bahutvālpatvādi-guṇa-vācakāḥ śabdāḥ ||*

**Even the very authorship of this book (Nighaṇṭu) is not settled with certainty among scholars.** Regarding its origin, some hold varying views — but its own arrangement, its chapter-and-verse organization, and its authoritative status regarding synonym-lists are firmly established, notwithstanding disagreements about its precise authorship. **There is no dispute regarding all this.** Its content bears directly on the science of etymology (Nirukta) and its practical application, being useful for that purpose (page 576 discussion, above).

**Therefore, this concludes the summary of the Devata-Anga's Nirukta discussion.**

**This commentary also is called Nirukta. Because the supposed elements of each word are here fully (nir) set out (ukta). For in his book, after having declared the fourfold division of words into nouns, verbs, prepositions, and particles, Yaska declares that particles fall into (nipatanti) various meanings. Having thus analysed the term "nipāta," he gives an example. "Na" means only prohibition in common talk: in the Veda it means both (prohibition and comparison). In the text**

> नेन्द्रं देवममंसत ।
> *nendraṃ devam amaṃsata |*

**it means prohibition. In the text**

> दुर्मदासो न सुरायाम् ।
> *durmadāso na surāyāṃ |*

**Meaning:** the etymological ("Vaikārthavāchi") sense, wherever a single word denotes a whole class of meaning through one root's own natural sense, is regarded as one such usage encoded in this treatise — this is what "nipāta" (particle) refers to. Among particles, there is also a subdivision into those used in the sense of comparison and those used otherwise. This treatise, in its own opening chapters, discusses different applications of the word "artha" and their fourfold classification, and also treats "aupacārikatva" (figurative usage) or "nipāta" (untranslatable particles).

**In the beginning chapters, various types are discussed: root-analysis, letter-derivation, day, night, and time-related words, along with words carrying meanings of substance.** In the middle chapters, useful discussions of household-related words, actions, and their derivation appear. In the final chapters, virtues and defects belonging to the qualities discussed in earlier chapters are treated more fully.

**The Nigama section of the Veda deals with well-known, non-obscure sentences drawn from various parts of the Veda**, and clarifies their exact meaning; scholars refer to this specifically as forming the "Nigama-kāṇḍa." In this section, ordinary Vedic sentences are cited and their meanings clearly resolved, distinguishing this section as belonging to the "Nigama" division.

**In the third section — the fifth adhyāya — the deities discussed are called "Devatā."** This is why it is termed the "Devatā-kāṇḍa."

**These three sections make up the full text.** Since this treatise gives the derivations of unusual (obscure) words found scattered throughout the Veda, the text is called "Nirukta." Yaska defines these obscure words as belonging to the categories: noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga), and particle (nipāta); and states that particles convey various meanings depending on context. Having analyzed the term "nipāta" this way, he gives an example. **"Na" ordinarily means only prohibition in common speech; but in the Veda, it carries both senses — prohibition and comparison.** In the text—

> नेन्द्रं देवममंसत ।
> *nendraṃ devam amaṃsata |*

—it means prohibition. In the text—

> दुर्मदासो न सुरायाम् ।
> *durmadāso na surāyāṃ |*

—...

**The author himself will also be found citing brahmanas in proof of the etymologies he gives.**

**It is true that the etymology of some words can be learned from Grammar. But not all.** Wherefore the author says—

> तदिदं विद्यास्थानं व्याकरणस्य केवलं शब्दलक्षणे न सर्वेषां पदानां निर्वचनं सिद्ध्येत् ।

>
> "**Therefore this science is the essence of Grammar and establishes the proper sense of the words. Therefore the Nirukta is useful towards the understanding of the Veda.**"

**Meaning:** it means comparison as well, not merely prohibition. This is precisely the illustration the Nirukta itself gives — how the particle "na" carries a double sense within the Veda, though in ordinary conversational usage it means only "no." Throughout our own commentary, we shall have frequent occasion to cite similar etymological derivations given by this author (Yaska), and there is no need to fear that such derivations have no factual grounding — many of them are directly supported by statements found in the Brahmana portions themselves.

**For example:** "This offering (āhuti) belongs to him — therefore he is named Indra." "He stretched out (aprathayat) [the earth] — therefore the earth is called Pṛthivī." Such etymological explanations, based on scriptural authority, are found scattered throughout many places, and our author (the composer of the Nirukta) himself cites such Brahmana-passages in support of the etymologies he offers.

**It is true that some words' etymologies can indeed be derived through Grammar alone.** But this doesn't hold for *all* words — Grammar's own rules cannot, by themselves, fully derive the meanings of every single word. Therefore, the author of this treatise states:

**"Therefore, this branch of learning (Nirukta) exists as a specialized supplement to Grammar."**

### The Fifth Anga: Chandas (Metrics)

**Just as, in the sacrificial rites, various matters are described as ritually obligatory in certain cases**—

> गायत्र्युष्णिगनुष्टुब्बृहती पङ्क्तिस्त्रिष्टुब्जगत्यौ छन्दांसि सप्त ।
> *gāyatry-uṣṇig-anuṣṭub-bṛhatī-paṅktis-triṣṭub-jagatyau chandāṃsi sapta |*
>
> "**As, for example, in the text, 'Therefore seven plus four metres are recited in the prataranuvakya.' Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, are the seven metres. The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables. The Uṣṇik has four more, and thus consists of twenty-eight syllables. So the others may be worked out, as the Anuṣṭubh for example, each containing a greater number of syllables than the one before.**"

**Let me give another text**:

> ब्राह्मणं गायत्र्या यजेत् क्षत्रियं त्रिष्टुभा ।
> *brāhmaṇaṃ gāyatryā yajet kṣatriyaṃ triṣṭubhā |*
>
> "**He should say the fire for a Brahmin with Gāyatrī verses, for a Kshattriya with Triṣṭubh verses, and**"...

**Meaning:** because in ritual matters, certain specific meters are prescribed as obligatory to use in various contexts, one must study the science of metrics (Chandas-shastra) in order to properly know these meters, distinguish them correctly, and apply the right meter in the right context. This is precisely why the fifth Anga — Chandas — exists and must be studied.

**On this point, our own tradition gives the following explanation.** The seven principal meters are: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī. Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables; Uṣṇik has four syllables more, thus consisting of twenty-eight; and continuing in this manner, each subsequent meter contains four syllables more than the one preceding it — thus Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and finally Jagatī, each increasing progressively.

**Meaning:** whoever performs a yajna or teaches a mantra without knowing the rishi (its seer), chandas (its metre), or devatā (its deity), stumbles as he goes, or falls into a well; his fault becomes even greater than before. I can quote a third text. "The man who sacrifices or teaches by means of a mantra whose rishi, metre and devata he does not know, runs up against a post, or falls into a well, or perishes utterly: his guilt is increased. Therefore for every mantra he must know all these."
>
> Therefore the Chhandas book on metres is useful for this knowledge.

### The Sixth Anga: Jyotiṣa (Astronomy) — Its Purpose and Significance Determined

### Page 583

**The use of the Jyotiṣa is thus given in that book itself: "To establish the times and reasons for sacrifices."** There are texts prescribing all manner of times. The text "**saṃvatsaraṃ**" and similar refers to periods of years. The text "**vasante**" and similar refers to months. The text "**māsi māsi**" and similar refers to months. The text "**yaṃ kāmayeta**" refers to half-months. The text "**ekāṣṭakāyāṃ**" and similar refers to days. The text "**kṛttikāsu**" and similar refers to the nakṣatras (lunar mansions).

> संवत्सरं वा ऋतवो मासाश्च ॐ ब्राह्मणेनाग्निर्माधीयीत । गृह्णे राजन्य आधीयेत । शरदि वैश्य आधीयेत ॥
> *saṃvatsaraṃ vā ṛtavo māsāś ca oṃ brāhmaṇenāgnir ādhīyeta | gṛhṇe rājanya ādhīyeta | śaradi vaiśya ādhīyeta ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 5.2.7[?])

**"A Brahmin should establish the fire in spring; a Kshatriya should establish it in summer; a Vaishya should establish it in autumn."**

> मासि मासि पुष्ट्यार्थं गृह्णे च गृह्ण्य आधीयते इति मासविधयः । यं कामयेत वशीयासमिति पक्षविधिः ।
> *māsi māsi puṣṭy-arthaṃ gṛhṇe ca gṛhya ādhīyate iti māsa-vidhayaḥ | yaṃ kāmayeta vaśīyāsam iti pakṣa-vidhiḥ |*

**"Month by month" and similar** [texts refer to] monthly regulations for the sake of prosperity. **"Yaṃ kāmayeta**" [expressing whatever a person] desires — this is the fortnight-regulation. "**Ekāṣṭakāyāṃ**" is the day-regulation. "**Kṛttikāsu**" is the nakṣatra-regulation.

**This is the meaning: the Jyotiṣa serves the purpose belonging to yajnas and similar rites specifically because the treatise itself declares this.** Since all yajnas and similar acts must be performed at their properly appointed times, determining that time correctly is the primary purpose which the science of Jyotiṣa serves. The mantras used in performing yajnas must be known together with their proper timings, and these are specified in various places throughout the Veda—

**"To establish the reasons and times for sacrifices" — one should establish this by knowing the proper measure of the year's timing** [and so on].

---

The text 'samvatsaram &c.' refers to periods of years. The text 'vasante &c.' refers to months. The text 'masi mase, &c.' refers to months. The text 'yam kamayeta' refers to half months. The text 'ekashtakayam, &c.' refers to days. The text 'krittikasu, &c.' refers to the nakshatras.

> Therefore the Jyotisha is useful for determining the times and seasons proper for sacrifices.


### Page 584

**"Saṃvatsaram-mukhyaṃ bṛhatyā"** (see page 583 above) — this too establishes the correct measure of the year's timing.

> वसन्ता ब्राह्मणस्याग्निमाधीयेत । ग्रीष्मे राजन्यस्य भवति । मुखं वा एतद्संवत्सरस्य यद्वसन्तः । यो वसन्ते ब्राह्मणमाधत्ते मुखत एव भवति । अथो योऽभिजितं वसन्तमेव प्रजापतिमाधत्ते । ग्रीष्मे राजन्यस्यादधीत ग्रीष्मो वै राजन्यस्य ऋतुः । शरदि वैश्यस्यादधीत शरत् वै वैश्यस्य ऋतुः ॥
> *vasantā brāhmaṇasyāgnim ādhīyeta | grīṣme rājanyasya bhavati | mukhaṃ vā etad-saṃvatsarasya yad vasantaḥ | yo vasante brāhmaṇam ādhatte mukhata eva bhavati | atho yo'bhijitaṃ vasantam eva prajāpatim ādhatte | grīṣme rājanyasyādadhīta grīṣmo vai rājanyasya ṛtuḥ | śaradi vaiśyasyādadhīta śarad vai vaiśyasya ṛtuḥ ||* (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.2)

**Meaning:** in spring, one should establish the fire for a Brahmin; in summer, for a Kshatriya. Spring is indeed the face (mukha) of the year. Whoever establishes the fire for a Brahmin in spring establishes it, as it were, "by the face" [the beginning/head of the year]. Moreover, whoever establishes the fire in spring establishes it under Prajapati himself as the presiding deity of that season. One should establish the fire for a Kshatriya in summer, for summer is indeed the Kshatriya's own proper season. One should establish the fire for a Vaishya in autumn, for autumn is indeed the Vaishya's own proper season.

**In this way**, the science of Jyotiṣa determines the appropriate season for the Agnyadhana rite. Similarly, for the shraddha (memorial) rites, the specific month must be known; the science of Jyotiṣa serves this purpose too—

**"Māsi māsi puṣṭyārthaṃ śrāddhaṃ gṛhya**" (see page 583 above) — this and similar [texts] refer to the monthly regulations for shraddha-performance.

**"Yaṃ kāmayeta vaśīyāsam iti kaṃ pūrva-pakṣe yojanīyaṃ**" (see page 583 above) — this and similar [texts] refer to the fortnight-measure regulations.

**"Ekāṣṭakāyāṃ dīkṣerann......phalāgnīṃ pūrṇamāsi dīkṣerann**" (see page 583 above) — this and similar [texts] refer to the day-timing regulations.

**"Prātar-ūrjo hoti, sāyaṃ jñu hoti**" (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.7.11.1[?]) and similar [texts] give the daily timing regulations.

**"Kṛttikāsu agnim ādadhīta**" (Taittiriya Brahmana 1.1.2) and similar [texts] give the nakṣatra-timing regulations.

**Since it is by knowing the times determined through this science that all the required texts and other treatises are correctly employed, the Jyotiṣa and its own useful application should be understood here.**

**That these six books, which we have shown to be helps to the understanding of the Veda, are 'Angas' or limbs of the Veda, is declared in the Śikṣā itself:**

> छन्दः पादौ तु वेदस्य हस्तौ कल्पोऽथ उच्यते । ज्योतिषामयनं चक्षुर्निरुक्तं श्रोत्रमुच्यते ॥ शिक्षा घ्राणं तु वेदस्य मुखं व्याकरणं स्मृतम् । तस्मात्साङ्गमधीत्यैव ब्रह्मलोके महीयते ॥
> *chandaḥ pādau tu vedasya hastau kalpo'tha ucyate | jyotiṣām ayanaṃ cakṣur niruktaṃ śrotram ucyate || śikṣā ghrāṇaṃ tu vedasya mukhaṃ vyākaraṇaṃ smṛtam | tasmāt sāṅgam adhītyaiva brahmaloke mahīyate ||* (Panini Shiksha, verses 41-42)
>
> "**'Chhandas is the feet of the Veda, and Kalpa is declared to be its hands: Jyotisha is called its eye, and the Nirukta its ear. Śikṣā is the Veda's nose, Grammar they call its face: therefore he who studies the Veda along with these its limbs will be great in heaven.'**"

**Meaning:** for the Veda, Chandas is likened to its feet, Kalpa to its hands, Jyotiṣa to its eyes, Nirukta to its ears, Śikṣā to its nose, and Grammar is said to be its face. **Therefore, one who studies the Veda together with these six limbs is greatly honoured in the world of Brahma.**

### That the Puranas and Similar Texts, Together with the Fourteen Sources of Knowledge, Also Serve to Determine the Veda's Meaning

**That the Puranas, and similar texts, are, like the Angas, useful for a better understanding of the Veda, is recorded by Yajnavalkya:**

> पुराणन्यायमीमांसाधर्मशास्त्राङ्गमिश्रिताः । वेदाः स्थानानि विद्यानां धर्मस्य च चतुर्दश ॥
> *purāṇa-nyāya-mīmāṃsā-dharma-śāstrāṅga-miśritāḥ | vedāḥ sthānāni vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca caturdaśa ||* (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1.3)
>
> "**The Puranas, the Nyaya, Mimansa, and Dharma-shastras, the Vedas with their Angas, these be the fourteen sources of the sciences and of dharma.**"

**Elsewhere, too, it is thus recorded**—

**Ṣaḍaṅgaṃ vedam** (the Veda together with its six Angas), **purāṇa-nyāya-vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca sāṃgraha-yoga-jñāneṣu**, together with these treatises, serves the purpose of properly understanding the Veda's meaning — this is what the passage establishes. **Puranas and Itihasas** [histories], **the vidyā-sthānas (sources of learning) — the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other systems** — number fourteen in total, said the ancients—

**Given [some texts hold] eighteen Puranas [and further extensions], this** ["ṛg-yajuḥ-sāmātharvāḥ..."] **enumeration itself makes clear the fourteen [sources]. It includes the four Vedas together with their Angas: Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, Jyotiṣa** — [six] — **plus the Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya-vistara, Purāṇa, and Dharma-shastra** — bringing the total count to fourteen sources.

**Among these fourteen, Mīmāṃsā [and its allied disciplines] serve to determine the Veda's own meaning** through examination of doubtful passages, resolving contradictions, and clarifying obscure statements — its work is indispensable. **The Nyāya-shāstra** establishes valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and logical reasoning necessary to settle disputed points that arise in interpreting scriptural statements.

**The Purāṇas** contain ancient histories illustrating dharma through concrete narrative — kings, sages, and their deeds — thereby making abstract Vedic injunctions vivid and comprehensible to ordinary understanding. **The Dharma-shastras** (Manu and similar authors) systematize the specific practical rules of conduct (varṇāśrama-dharma) that the Veda itself only briefly touches upon, elaborating them into a complete, coherent code applicable to daily life.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> That the Puranas, &c. are, like the Angas, useful for a better understanding of the Veda, is recorded by Yajnavalkya:
>
> "The Puranas, the Nyaya, Mimansa and Dharma shastras, the Vedas with their Angas, these be the fourteen sources of the sciences and of dharma."
>
> Elsewhere, too, it is thus recorded.


### Page 586

**Now, in order to show that the Puranas and similar texts likewise serve to help determine the Veda's own meaning, Yajnavalkya himself states:**

> पुराणन्यायमीमांसाधर्मशास्त्राङ्गमिश्रिताः । वेदाः स्थानानि विद्यानां धर्मस्य च चतुर्दश ॥
> *purāṇa-nyāya-mīmāṃsā-dharma-śāstrāṅga-miśritāḥ | vedāḥ sthānāni vidyānāṃ dharmasya ca caturdaśa ||* (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1.3; see page 585 above)

**Meaning:** Puranas, Nyaya-shastra, Mimamsa, Dharma-shastra, and the Vedas together with their six Angas — mixed together — comprise the fourteen sources (sthāna) of both learning (vidyā) and dharma. And likewise in the Mahabharata—

> इतिहासपुराणाभ्यां वेदं समुपबृंहयेत् । बिभेत्यल्पश्रुताद्वेदो मामयं प्रहरिष्यति ॥
> *itihāsa-purāṇābhyāṃ vedaṃ samupabṛṃhayet | bibhety alpa-śrutād vedo mām ayaṃ prahariṣyati ||* (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1.267)
>
> "**A man should strengthen the Veda by means of the Itihasas and Puranas: the Veda is afraid of the man of little learning, lest he should hurt it.**"

**Meaning:** history and purāṇic narrative should be used together to broaden and reinforce Vedic understanding. **The Veda [itself is described as] fearful of the man with little learning — apprehensive that such a person, through his limited understanding, might do it harm** [misinterpret or misapply it].

**The stories of Harishchandra, Nachiketa, and the like, told in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, Kathaka, and other Shakhas, which are useful for the better understanding both of dharma and of brahma, are explained in the Itihasa books.** The statements found in the Upanishads concerning the creation, the preservation, and the absorption of the world are explained in the Brahma, Padma, Vaishnava, and other Puranas. **Compare the well-known verse, "Sargaśca pratisargaśca."**

**Meaning:** Itihasa and Purana strengthen and confirm the meaning found within the Veda. It should be understood that ancient and traditional matters — the Veda's own supporting narrative context — are made firm through these Itihasas and Puranas. Since the Veda is described as fearful of one whose learning is shallow, this indicates: if a person with little genuine understanding grasps only the surface meaning of the Veda (its own scriptural expression), he may inadvertently do it harm through misapplication — this is what is meant here.

---

**Embedded English translation, as given in the source:**

> "A man should strengthen the Veda by means of the Itihasas and Puranas: the Veda is afraid of the man of little learning, lest he should hurt it."
>
> The stories of Harischandra, Nachiketa and the like told in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, Kathaka and other Sakhas which are useful for the better understanding both of dharma and of brahma, are explained in the Itihasa books. The statements found in the Upanishads concerning the creation, the preservation, and the absorption of the world explained in the Brahma, Padma, Vaishnava and other Puranas. Compare the well-known verse, 'Sargascha pratisargascha.'


### Page 587

**Other Puranas — Skanda, Vishnu, and others — are also useful for understanding dharma and brahma alike.** The Puranas illustrate, through narrative, the meanings underlying various commands and prohibitions found scattered throughout the Veda. **These matters are dealt with extensively and clearly within these treatises.** Among the various treatises discussing origins (utpatti), the deeds of Muni-descended lineages, Manu's own lineage, and battles between gods and demons are given in detail; and dynastic genealogies, too, are described as belonging to the Vaṃśānucharita [dynastic-history] portion of the Puranas. **Scholars declare that the characteristic features of the Puranas are these**—

> सर्गश्च प्रतिसर्गश्च वंशो मन्वन्तराणि च । वंशानुचरितं चेति पुराणं पञ्चलक्षणम् ॥
> *sargaś ca pratisargaś ca vaṃśo manvantarāṇi ca | vaṃśānucaritaṃ ceti purāṇaṃ pañca-lakṣaṇam ||* (Vishnu Purana 3.6.24; Amarakosha 1.6.5)

**Meaning:** creation (sarga), re-creation [after periodic dissolution] (pratisarga), dynastic genealogy (vaṃśa), the ages of the Manus (manvantara), and dynastic history (vaṃśānucharita) — these are the five defining characteristics of a Purana.

**Ordinary subjects treated in the Puranas** include: descriptions of well-known holy places, the qualities of various persons, causes underlying particular matters, and similar topics — each Purana, according to its own scope, covers such subjects in detail. It's understood that these matters, scattered across many Puranas, are difficult for ordinary people to piece together on their own.

**In Nyaya-shastra, discussions of pramāṇa (valid means of knowledge), prameya (objects of knowledge), saṃśaya (doubt), prayojana (purpose), and dṛṣṭānta (example) are among the topics treated.** Determining the specific meaning of a given text requires knowing these categories precisely; establishing which meaning is correctly authoritative for a given passage becomes possible only through such careful analysis.

**How the Purva and Uttara Mimamsas help to a better understanding of the Vedas is clear enough.**

**In the Smritis of Manu, Atri, Vishnu, Harita, and other writers, injunctions found in the Vedas, such for example as that concerning the evening prayer, are extended and developed.** The text "**tad u ha va ete brahmavādinaḥ pūrvābhimukhāḥ sandhyābhivādaya gāyatrī-bhimantritā apa ūrdhvaṃ vikṣipanti**," and similar, is a command to say the evening prayer. That other, "**pañca vā ete mahāyajñāḥ satataṃ pravartante**," is a command to perform the so-called great sacrifices. Other instances of commands given in the Veda and developed in the Smritis can be found.

**Since in this way the Puranas are a help to a better understanding of the Veda, the name "vidyāsthāna" (strongholds of wisdom) is rightly, in Yajnavalkya's verse above, applied to them.**

> How the Purva and Uttara Mimansas help to a better understanding of the Vedas is clear enough.
>
> In the Smritis of Manu, Atri, Vishnu, Harita and other writers, injunctions found in the Vedas, such for example, as that concerning the evening prayer, are extended and developed. The text 'tad u ha va ete brahmavadinah puryabhimukhah samdhyavayam gayatrabhimantrita apa urdhvam vikshipanti, &c. is a command to say the evening prayer. That other 'pancha va ete mahayajnah satatam pratryanta, &c.,' is a command to perform the so-called great sacrifices. Other instances of commands given in the Veda and developed in the Smritis can be found.

> *tad u ha vā ete brahmavādinaḥ pūrvābhimukhāḥ saṃdhyāyāṃ gāyatrīyābhimantritā apa ūrdhvaṃ vikṣipanti ||* (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.11.1)

**Meaning: this is what is stated** — those who know brahma, facing east, at twilight-time, consecrate the [sacred water] with the Gayatri mantra and then cast it upward, toward the sun as it rises before them (that is, [perform] the "arghya"-offering) — this is the specific procedure enjoined for the twilight-prayer.

**And also**: "**Pañca vā ete mahāyajñāḥ satataṃ pravartante**" (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2.10) — this and similar [texts], declared as commands, establish the requirement to continually perform the [five] great sacrifices. In this way, the same procedures found here and there [in various Vedic texts] are elaborated more fully in various Smritis; a careful study of both together allows one to properly grasp these matters.

**The topics briefly touched upon in the Puranas and similar texts must also be properly correlated with the Veda's own meaning; those able to do so provide genuine help — this is why they are called "vidyā" (branches of learning).**

**These Puranas and similar texts are said to number fourteen because they comprise: the four Vedas, the six Angas, the Puranas, Nyaya-shastra, Mimamsa, and Dharma-shastra** — treating these each as one unit, that makes fourteen sources of learning altogether. But if one asks whether other branches of learning exist beyond these, [the answer is] many more indeed exist. **Regarding the Veda's own meaning specifically, these fourteen branches of learning are understood to be the qualified authorities** for that purpose — [other branches, being useful] for different purposes (such as medicine, for instance), are each authoritative in their own separate fields. Yaska cites four verses from another Shakha declaring who alone is worthy [to receive this wisdom]—

>
> "**Wisdom came to the brahmin and said, 'Protect me for I am your treasure: do not teach me to the scornful or the knavish or the sensual man; so shall I be strong.'**"

> *vidyābhimāninī devatā brāhmaṇam upadeṣṭāram ācāryam ājagāma | āgatya caivaṃ prārthayāmāsa he brāhmaṇa mām avanaddhikāriṇecchan durūṣārthecchur asmi | tādṛśyaṃ tubhyaṃ tad-upadeṣṭari tvayi ca yogyam ūnaṃ karomi | yat khārjanena vidyāṃ nābhyarjate vidyāṃ nābhyarjate yaś ca mano-dhandhācāra-niyato na bhavati | tādṛśe bhavyakṣyaśikṣā-bhāvebhyo māṃ na brūyāt | tathā sati tava hṛdaye sthitvā phala-pradā bhaveyam ||*

**Meaning:** the goddess who is immanent in all learning came to the brahmin teacher, that is, to the Acharya, and thus besought him: "O brahmin! protect me, do not teach me to him that is unworthy. I am for a treasure to you, giving you all that a man can desire. He that does despite to me, or to you who teach me — he that does not follow learning uprightly, he that does not keep his body under by due observance of the rules about bathing, rinsing the mouth, and the like before lessons — to all such pupils, who are pupils in appearance only, do not teach me. So shall I abide in your heart and bear fruit."

### Page 590

**Meaning:** the first verse contained a prohibitory rule for the teacher: this has one for the pupil. By "**सत्य**" (*satya*, "truth") is meant the Veda, called so as being the opposite of worldly talk, which is untrue, and not conducive to man's chief end. **"यमात्मने कुर्वते नित्यम्"** (*yam ātmane kurvate nityaṃ*) — the teacher who completely fills his pupil's ears with the words of the Veda. The root "**तृणत्ति**" (*tṛṇatti*, to fill/pierce), by the force of its prefix "**सम्**" (*sam*), and from the context, takes a meaning different from the usual one. The meaning is "whoever recites the Veda to him." How? **"अमृतं वदति"** (*amṛtaṃ vadati*) — so as not to give him pain. If the boy be dull and unable to learn a verse or a half verse at a time, the teacher, in order to avoid giving him...

**In this way, the pupil's own defining qualities — appropriate to receiving proper instruction from a qualified Acharya (teacher) — are established for the pupil's benefit as well.** This too is a distinct benefit — namely, the teaching of the Veda's own meaning becomes possible. Regarding this matter, the Veda-mantra taken up here for illustration [is the one whose meaning we've been examining]: whatever action the Acharya takes with his student — whether accepting him for instruction, guiding his conduct, or teaching him respectfully — through all such acts, he cultivates the qualities properly belonging to a genuine teacher. **The verse states**: whether it be a whole [verse] or half, if the student cannot grasp it properly, or if he errs in reciting the mantra, [the teacher should not cause him pain by harsh correction] — thus it is said. Because [causing pain to a student] is not consistent with proper conduct, one should not [act this way]. **Furthermore**: the deity presiding over knowledge (Sarasvati/Vagdevata) is spoken of as the fitting recipient of the offering here — and it is entirely proper that the student's own conduct be modeled after this virtue.

**This entire matter [these four verses cited by Yaska], being the Acharya's own combined [pedagogical wisdom], should be understood as primarily concerned with the pupil.** Previously established as such, this concerns [proper conduct in] the teacher-student relationship, and the human aim it serves. **The main purpose behind [reciting] these body-related verses is this**: [that the transmission of knowledge itself should never become a source of harm].

*Prathamaṃ Maṇḍalam*
"Book One (Maṇḍala I)"

### Invocation

> ॐ वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युः स्मृत्वा वन्दे तमादिगणम् ॥
> *oṃ vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānām upakrame | yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syuḥ smṛtvā vande tam ādigaṇam ||*
>
> "At the outset of every undertaking, the wise — Bṛhaspati (Lord of Speech) and others — having bowed to whom become accomplished in their aims: remembering him, I too salute that same foremost of the Gaṇas [Ganesha]."

---

Śrī Sāyaṇācārya, in his Rigveda-Bhāṣya-Bhūmikā, having extensively examined — with the help of works such as Mīmāṃsā, Vyākaraṇa, and Dharma-shāstra — many profound topics (the Veda's defining characteristics, the Veda's authority, the Veda's non-human origin, the matter of Vedic study, the subject-matter the Veda expounds, a close exposition of the Vedāṅgas, who is qualified to receive Vedic knowledge, and so on), now, before beginning this Vedic commentary proper, briefly states — as an introductory matter — both the division-scheme of the Aṣṭaka-adhyāyas found in the Rigveda, and the matter of the mantras' ritual application (viniyoga), and thus opens the treatise itself.

> तदर्थमृग्वेदोक्तार्थः षडङ्गानुसारेण व्याख्यायते । मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मके वेदे ब्राह्मणस्य मन्त्रव्याख्यानोपयोगित्वादादौ ब्राह्मणमारभ्य काण्डशः व्याख्यातम् । अथ तत्र तत्र ब्राह्मणोदाहरणेन मन्त्राख्यः संहिताग्रन्थो व्याख्यातव्यः ॥
> *tad-artham ṛgvedokta-arthaḥ ṣaḍ-aṅgānusāreṇa vyākhyāyate | mantra-brāhmaṇātmake vede brāhmaṇasya mantra-vyākhyānopayogitvād ādau brāhmaṇam ārabhya kāṇḍaśaḥ vyākhyātam | atha tatra tatra brāhmaṇodāharaṇena mantrākhyaḥ saṃhitā-granthaḥ vyākhyātavyaḥ ||*
>
> "For this purpose, the sense stated in the Rigveda is expounded following the six Aṅgas. Since, in the Veda — which consists of mantra and brāhmaṇa together — the Brāhmaṇa is useful for explaining the mantra, [the commentary] has been expounded section by section (kāṇḍaśaḥ), beginning first with the Brāhmaṇa. > "That [Samhita], beginning with 'agnimīḷe' and ending with 'yathā vaḥ susāte,' is furnished, in the eight-Ashtaka division, with ten Maṇḍalas, sixty-four (eight-times-eight) Adhyāyas, eighty-five Anuvākas, a little over one thousand Sūktas, a little over two thousand Vargas, and a little over ten thousand Ṛks. The general application (sāmānya-viniyoga) of this entire text, in its own recited sequence, has already been stated in connection with the Brahma-yajña recitation. The specific application (viśeṣa-viniyoga), however, has been shown by the Sūtra-authors in the ritual texts themselves. This specific application is of three kinds: application of a whole Sūkta, application of a group of six verses beginning with a given one (ācādi-ṣaḍ), and application of a single Ṛk individually."

**Meaning:** the Rigveda Samhita we are about to expound begins with "**agnimīḷe**" and ends with "**yathā vaḥ susāte**." We have already described this division-scheme of the Rigveda earlier (see our discussion above). In total, the Rigveda Samhita is divided into eight **Ashtakas**, and each Ashtaka is further divided into eight **Adhyayas**. The number of **Vargas** within each Adhyaya, however, is not uniform — where shorter-syllabled meters such as Gayatri predominate, that Adhyaya contains more Vargas; where longer-syllabled meters such as Jagati predominate, that Adhyaya contains fewer Vargas. The overall length of each Adhyaya thus remains roughly, though not perfectly, equal. Following this scheme, the Rigveda has **sixty-four Adhyayas** in total (eight Ashtakas × eight Adhyayas each). This arrangement was established for ease of study and has been followed since ancient times.

**The Mandala-division-scheme is a different system** — older than the Ashtaka-scheme. Following the lineages of the mantra-seeing rishis, each Mandala generally contains mantras "seen" (dṛṣṭa) by one principal rishi together with his descendants or disciples. The Rigveda contains **ten such Mandalas**. *(A small number of Mandalas — the text names them, though the exact digits are not fully certain at this scan resolution — do not strictly follow this single-rishi-family pattern, instead containing mantras seen by many different rishis; this matter has already been discussed earlier.)*

**Therefore, it is said that the Rigveda contains:** eight Ashtakas, ten Mandalas, sixty-four Adhyayas, eighty-five Anuvakas, a little more than one thousand Suktas, a little more than two thousand Vargas, and more than ten thousand Riks (verses).

**Meaning:** whatever cannot be established through the ordinary means of knowledge — direct perception or inference — is made knowable solely through the Veda; it is for this reason that "the Veda" bears the very name "Veda," from the root "vid" (to know), signifying that which makes known what is otherwise unknowable.

**As stated in the Puranas and similar texts:** the Rigveda has **twenty-one (21)** shakha-divisions; the Yajurveda has **one hundred (100)** shakha-divisions (of these, Shukla-Yajurveda has fifteen shakhas, and Krishna-Yajurveda has eighty-six shakhas, together making one hundred); the Samaveda has a **thousand** shakhas; and the Atharvaveda has **nine** shakhas. Of these many shakhas, a great number have been lost over the course of time and are no longer in use today — only a few are still available.

**Every Veda comprises two kinds of portions:** the mantra-portion (Samhita) and the Brahmana-portion.

> मन्त्रे ब्राह्मणयोर्वेदनामधेयम् ।
> *mantre brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam |*
> "'Veda' is the name applied to mantra and Brahmana together."

The shakhas belonging to each Veda are as follows: for the Rigveda — the Shakala-shakha and, among the ancient shakhas, the Bashkala-shakha and similar; for the Yajurveda — the Kanva and Madhyandina shakhas of the Shukla branch, and the Taittiriya shakha among others of the Krishna branch; for the Samaveda — the Kauthuma, Ranayaniya, and Jaiminiya shakhas among others; for the Atharvaveda — the Shaunaka and Paippalada shakhas among others. Among these, the shakhas still available in full, or largely intact, are relatively few.

**This shakha — the one we are here expounding — follows Ashvalayana's own sutra-tradition.** According to Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra, the Rigveda Samhita's division into Mandalas is followed, alongside the Ashtaka-division discussed earlier. **The Samhita's own arrangement into these divisions has already been described.**

**These are the principal meters.** Each meter has many sub-varieties, which we have already explained at length with examples earlier (see our discussion above). The seven meters mentioned above, beginning with Gayatri, have respectively **24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48** syllables.

**In the second group** — **अतिजगती, शक्करी, अतिशक्करी, अष्टिः, अत्यष्टिः, धृतिः, अतिधृतिः** (*Atijagatī, Śakvarī, Atiśakvarī, Aṣṭiḥ, Atyaṣṭiḥ, Dhṛtiḥ, Atidhṛtiḥ*) — these seven meters have respectively **52, 56, 60, 64, 68, 72, 76** syllables.

**In the third group** — **कृतिः, प्रकृतिः, आकृतिः, विकृतिः, संकृतिः, अभिकृतिः, उत्कृतिः** (*Kṛtiḥ, Prakṛtiḥ, Ākṛtiḥ, Vikṛtiḥ, Saṃkṛtiḥ, Abhikṛtiḥ, Utkṛtiḥ*) — these seven meters have respectively **80, 84, 88, 92, 96, 100, 104** syllables.

**When stating the totals for Ashtakas, Adhyayas, Vargas, and the rest, the Bhashyakara [Sayana] does not give an exact figure, but instead uses the general expression "**ईषदधिक**" (*īṣad-adhika*, "a little more than").** This is because — although the counts of Mandala, Anuvaka, Ashtaka, and Adhyaya are not disputed — genuine differences of opinion exist regarding the counts of Suktas, Vargas, and mantras (Riks). For example: in the ninth Mandala, [certain] single-rik hymns are called by [special] names. Ten such **Vālakhilya-sūktas** are absent from some shakhas' texts. Some include these **khila-sūktas** (supplementary hymns) within the Samhita; others do not. This is why differences arise in the count of Suktas.

**Regarding the count of Vargas:** generally, a group of roughly five Riks is treated as one Varga. If a Sukta contains 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 2 Riks, that entire Sukta itself is counted as a single Varga. A Sukta containing 8 Riks is treated by some as a single Varga, and by others as two Vargas. This too causes differences in the Varga-count.

**Regarding the count of Riks:** in many places there occur Riks in the "**dvipadā virāṭ**" meter. Some scholars count these as Riks having three padas (that is, half of a full Rik's normal extent), while others hold that "dvipadā" is merely the meter's own name, and that — like every other meter — it too actually comprises four padas in full. According to the first view, three padas (half a Rik) count as one whole Rik; according to the second view, four padas (a complete first-half plus second-half) count as one Rik. This too is a source of variation in the total Rik-count. **Taking all of this into account, the Bhashyakara generally states the Varga and related counts using the qualifier "īṣad-adhika" (a little more than), rather than an exact figure.**

**Now let us examine the matter of the mantras' application (viniyoga).** Viniyoga means: the rule that a given mantra should be employed in a given ritual context. Since mantras are used according to the specific rite being performed, viniyoga is thus tied to that rite (karma). This scheme of application is of two kinds: **general (sāmānya)** and **specific (viśeṣa)**. Reciting all the mantras of this Rigveda Samhita in their entirety — as in the Brahma-yajna, japa, complete recitation (pārāyaṇa), and similar practices — is called the mantras' **"general application."** In yajnas and other rites, and likewise in other ritual observances — that is, in the japa and similar practices undertaken to realize one's chosen deity — the [specific] application...

### Page 600

**When a sutra states a citation in full**, one should understand that only that particular Rik's application is being given. When a sutra states merely the opening of a sukta, in less than a single full pada, one should understand that the application is being given to the **entire** sukta. As stated in the definitional sutra (paribhāṣā-sūtra):

> सूक्तं सूक्तादावृचि एकस्मिन् पादे ।
> *sūktaṃ sūktādāv ṛci ekasmin pāde |* (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra, Paribhasha 1.1)

— meaning: if the sukta's opening portion is stated using less than one full pada, the application should be understood to cover the whole sukta.

**In the sutra quoted above** — "**āvā no agna iti ṣaḍ agnimāḷer agniṃ dhūtakam**" — "āvā no agna iti ṣaṭ" indicates that the mantra beginning "āvā no agne" is the sixth Rik in its sukta. Since it is cited only up to that extent, this sutra's meaning is that the application given here covers only that sixth Rik specifically — not the whole sukta.

**Having thus stated the application of a complete sukta, the application of a single Rik — "agnimīḷe" — is now stated.** This sukta's very first mantra, "**agnimīḷe**," is used as the **Yājyā-mantra** when performing the Pavamāna [rite]. In the first section of the second Adhyaya of the Shrauta-sutra, this Rik's application is stated through the sutra:

> साध्यान्निश्चा अभियुजोऽग्निमाळे पुरोहितमिति संयाज्ये ।
> *sādhyānniścā abhiyujo'gnimāḷe purohitam iti saṃyājye |*

Here, since the first padas of the Riks "**sādhyānniścā abhiyujaḥ**" and "**agnimīḷe purohitam**" are each cited in full, one should understand that the application is given only to those two specific Riks. There is a governing sutra: "**ṛtaṃ pāda-grahaṇe**" (Adhyaya 1.1) [a single-pada citation refers only to that pada]. Since the sutra uses the word "**saṃyājye**," this indicates the application is specifically within the homa belonging to the Svishtakrit category.

**In Shrauta-related rites**, the ritual act of properly producing fire through churning (manthana) and similar prescribed methods is called "**Ādhāna**." This Ādhāna is of three kinds: ending in Pūrṇāhuti, ending in Homa, and ending in Ishti. Among these, in the third — the Ishti-ending procedure — three homas are performed. For the first (Pavamāneṣṭi) homa, the deities are **Agni** and **Agniṣavamāna**; for the second homa, the deities are **Agniḥ Savakaḥ** and **Agniḥ Śuciḥ**; for the third homa, the principal deities are **Agniṣomau, Indrāgnī, Viṣṇu**, and **Aditi**. Among these three, in the second — when performing the Svishtakrid-homa — the mantra "**sādhyānniścā abhiyujaḥ**" is used as the **Puronuvākyā-mantra**, and the Rik "**agnimīḷe purohitam**" is used as the **Yājyā-mantra**.

**When performing homa addressed to specific deities**, one first calls the deities to mind and invokes them by reciting a Rik. This [invoking] Rik is called the "Puronuvākyā"...

...and is so called. Thereafter, having called the deity to mind and invited it, one performs homa reciting another Rik. This Rik is called the "Yajya." Application-statements always begin by stating the Puronuvakya first and the "anantara" (subsequent) mantra afterward — this is the settled order.

**Regarding the Paribhasha-sutra** — "**sāmānyāt siṣṭāḥ**" and similar — since it begins by naming the Puronuvakya first, one should understand this to be the fixed sequence for citing the two mantras. On this point, there is a well-known verse in the fourth adhyaya of the Purushartha-nushasana's own Nyaya-mala-vistara commentary:

> पुरोनुवाक्या या याज्या विकल्प्या वा समुच्चिता । विकल्प्यास्यैषैव देवतायाः प्रकाशनात् ॥
> *puronuvākyā yā yājyā vikalpyā vā samuccitā | vikalpyāsyaiṣaiva devatāyāḥ prakāśanāt ||*
>
> पुरोनुवाक्या समाख्यानाध्यैवास्य समुच्चितः । देवताप्रकाशनकार्यास्यं कश्चात् युग्मैरोर्यार्था विकल्पस्यै युग्मगतयोरिति चेत् नैवम् । पुरोनुवाक्येति समाख्या उत्तरकालीनयाज्यामन्त्रेणानुपसृप्तेः । किं च—
> *puronuvākyā samākhyānādhyaivāsya samuccitaḥ | devatā-prakāśana-kāryāsyaṃ kaścāt yugmair oryārthā vikalpasyai yugmagatayor iti cet naivam | puronuvākyeti samākhyā uttarakālīna-yājyā-mantreṇānupasṛpteḥ | kiṃ ca—* *(this technical Mimamsa-verse passage remains genuinely dense at this resolution and is presented as a best-effort reading)*
>
> "**puronuvākyāmanūṣye yājyayā juhoti**" — "*puronuvākyām anūṣya yājyayā juhoti* | this text of Scripture ["having recited the Puronuvakya, one performs the homa by means of the Yajya"] plainly requires an explicit ordering — the Puronuvakya's citation precedes the Yajya's own act of oblation."

**The Puronuvakya and Yajya mantras both refer to the same deity.** Therefore, during the yajna's performance, one might ask: should only the Puronuvakya be recited, or only the Yajya, or both? Since the sutra states "**samucchitayaḥ**" (combined/joined together), it means **both** mantras must be recited. But here a doubt arises: in a single yajna — indeed, within a single rite — directed toward one specific deity, why should two mantras of identical purport be required? If one might suppose that a single mantra alone cannot accomplish the task — that is not correct. Rather: **first**, one must call the deity to mind and invite it; for this, the mantra called **Puronuvākyā** is recited ("puronuvākyā" meaning "that which is recited first, or at the outset"). **Thereafter**, considering that the deity has accepted the invitation and arrived at the sacrificial altar, one performs the homa — the offering of the oblation — through the **Yājyā**-mantra. Therefore, these two mantras — first the Puronuvakya, then the Yajya — must indeed be recited in that order; this is the settled doctrine (siddhānta) established by both the Mīmāṃsakas and the Sūtra-authors, and both mantras must be recited without exception. On this very point—

> पुरोनुवाक्यामनूष्य याज्यया जुहोति ।
> *puronuvākyām anūṣya yājyayā juhoti |*
> "Having recited the Puronuvakya, one performs the homa with the Yajya"

— confirms that the Puronuvakya must first be recited, and only thereafter should the homa be performed using the Yajya-mantra...

...(in the Kratu), one should reflect accordingly. Moreover, since the Puronuvakya's application is understood to precede the deities' own act of being called to mind, and since the Yajya's application is not stated as belonging to any other set of homa-related rules, both these mantras should be understood accordingly. This is why the word "**samuccitayaḥ**" is employed [in the sutra].

> एकर्चाग्निमित्यादिसूक्तं नवर्चम् । "अग्निं नव मधुच्छन्दा वैश्वामित्रिः" इत्यनुक्रमणिकायामुक्तत्वात् (अनु. १-४) । विश्वामित्रपुत्रो मधुच्छन्दोनामकस्य सूक्तस्य द्रष्टृत्वाद्ऋषिः ।
> *ekarcāgnim ity-ādi sūktaṃ navarcam | "agniṃ nava madhucchandā vaiśvāmitriḥ" ity anukramaṇikāyām uktatvāt (anu. 1-4) | viśvāmitra-putro madhucchando-nāmakasya sūktasya draṣṭṛtvād ṛṣiḥ |*
>
> "This sukta, beginning with the single verse 'agnim...,' consists of nine Riks — as stated in the Anukramanika (index): 'Agni [is praised in] nine [verses] by Madhuchandas Vaishvamitra' (Anukramanika 1.4). Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra, is the 'rishi' [seer] of this sukta, being the one who directly perceived (draṣṭṛ) it."

**On the etymology of "rishi":** from the root "**ṛṣ**" (to go/move) — per the Unadi-sutra rule "**sarva-dhātubhya inn**" (Unadi 4.119) and "**igupadāt kit**" (Unadi 4.104) — [one who, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, directly] perceives, without dependence on ordinary sense-organs, the Veda [as it truly is]. This much is stated. As it is said:

> अजान् ह वै पूर्वं तपस्यमानास्तप्त्वा स्वयंभुव आभिणर्त्यृषयोऽभवन् ।
> *ajān ha vai pūrvaṃ tapasyamānās taptvā svayambhuva ābhiṇarty ṛṣayo'bhavan |* (Kaushitaki Aranyaka 2.9) *(this specific citation remains a best-effort reading at this resolution)*
>
> "In the beginning, those who performed austerity (tapas), having practiced it, became 'rishis' through the direct favour of the Self-existent [Svayambhu]."

**In this same way**, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the direct perception of the supra-sensory Veda [by the earliest seers] establishes their status as "rishi" — this much is affirmed.

> युगान्ते चास्य निःश्वासादेतद्व्येतीहासात्तदृषयः । लेभिरे तपसा पूर्वमनुज्ञाताः स्वयंभुवेति ॥
> *yugānte cāsya niḥśvāsād etad vyetīhāsāt tad ṛṣayaḥ | lebhire tapasā pūrvam anujñātāḥ svayambhuv eti ||* *(this closing verse likewise remains a best-effort reading)*

**Now let us examine the discussion begun in the "agnimīḷe" sukta.** As stated in the Anukramanika: "**agniṃ nava madhucchandā vaiśvāmitriḥ**" — "agnimīḷe" is the first mantra in this sukta belonging to Vishvamitra's son [Madhuchandas]. Since this sukta's Rishi is the son of Vishvamitra, one should understand that a comparable status applies wherever this Rishi is cited.

### Page 603

**"Rishi" derives grammatically from the root "ṛṣ" (to go/move).** Before the root "ṛṣ," the affix "in" is added, per the Unadi rule; the resulting form, with "ṛ" changed to guṇa, becomes "arṣi," and further, since a "vidhi" (rule) states this specific combination applies, it becomes "ṛṣi." Since the term denotes one who is qualified by this rule, "ṛṣ" + "in" together yield "ṛṣi."

**Why should we take the trouble to know a mantra's rishi?** The reason is stated as follows: those who compose or discover [a mantra] at the very beginning — that is, at the start of creation (or, according to some, at the start of the cosmic cycle) — are called the rishis for that mantra. It is they who hold the credit for it. Later, brahmins who wish to make use of that mantra, out of respect and gratitude toward that rishi, must know and recite his name whenever they recite the mantra, so that the rishi remains pleased. Elsewhere, it is likewise stated that the rishi is himself worthy of honour precisely because of this connection to the mantra.

**Where knowledge of the rishi and the rest is absent, the resulting fault (pratyavāya) is established [by scripture]:**

> अविदित्वा ऋषिं छन्दो दैवतं योगमेव च । योऽध्यापयेज्जपेच्चैवापि पापीयान् जायते तु सः ॥
> *avidītvā ṛṣiṃ chando daivataṃ yogam eva ca | yo'dhyāpayej japec caivāpi pāpīyān jāyate tu saḥ ||*
>
> "Whoever, without knowing the rishi, the meter, the deity, and the [proper ritual] application, either teaches a mantra or recites it in japa — he becomes exceedingly sinful."

> ऋषिच्छन्दोदैवतानि ब्राह्मणार्थं स्थिराध्यषि । अविदित्वा प्रयुञ्जानो मन्त्रकण्टक उच्यते इति ॥
> *ṛṣi-chando-daivatāni brāhmaṇārthaṃ sthirādhyaṣi | avidītvā prayuñjāno mantra-kaṇṭaka ucyate iti ||*
>
> "One who employs a mantra without knowing its rishi, meter, and deity — essential for the Brahmana's own purpose — is called a 'thorn in the mantra' [a source of blemish and danger to it]."

**That knowledge of the vidhi (application) is likewise required is established:**

> स्वरो वर्णोऽक्षरं मात्रा विनियोगोऽर्थ इव च । मन्त्रं जिज्ञासमानेन वेदितव्यं पदे पदे इति ॥
> *svaro varṇo'kṣaraṃ mātrā viniyogo'rtha iva ca | mantraṃ jijñāsamānena veditavyaṃ pade pade iti ||*
>
> "One who genuinely desires to understand a mantra must know, at every single word: its accent (svara), its letters (varṇa), its syllable-count (akṣara), its quantity (mātrā), its ritual application (viniyoga), and equally its meaning (artha)."

**One must know the mantra's own deities, along with their names, to properly recite the Vedic mantras and understand their meaning. Likewise, one must know the deity-related names...**

...is connected to the [ritual] purpose. Or, in the various rites performed [in yajnas] with fire, the danger arising from an unintentional offense is warded off; this is called "**bhadra**" (auspicious/protective). On this very subject, one sutra states—

> *(this citation remains a genuinely uncertain, best-effort reading at this resolution)*

— indicating that a person who fears such harm should recite this consecrated mantra to protect his own life (dhāraṇā-vidhi), invoking the deities as appropriate. It is for this reason that these are called "**bhandas**" (protective verses); the elders have accordingly held that "bhandas" and "bhadra" carry the same underlying sense.

**Having explained the rishi and meter, we now explain the meaning of the term "deva" (deity):**

> दिवा वै नो भूदिति तद्देवानां देवत्वम् ।
> *divā vai no bhūd iti tad devānāṃ devatvam |* (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.3.8.8[?])
> "'We shine by our own light' — thus [say] the deities. That itself is the 'devatva' [deity-nature] of the deities."

**The root "dīvyati" means "to shine, to illuminate."** Scripture states that the very word "deva" arises from this root. "Being illuminated through the mantra" means: since a being is praised (and thereby made resplendent) through a mantra, it is accordingly called a "deva." **In this "agnimīḷe" sukta, since Agni is the one being praised, Agni alone is the deity of this sukta.**

**As the Anukramanika also states:**

> मण्डलादिष्टाग्नेयमृग्दात् ।
> *maṇḍalādiṣṭāgneyam ṛg-dāt |*
> "The [opening] Rik at the head of each Mandala pertains to Agni [or, in certain Mandalas, to Indra]."

— that is, for the suktas standing at the very beginning of each Mandala, the presiding deity is either Agni or Indra. **Since this sukta is the very first sukta of the very first Mandala, Agni alone is its deity.**

**॥ ॐ ॥**

**॥ Maṇḍala — 1 ॥ Anuvāka — 1 ॥ Sūkta — 1 ॥**
**॥ Aṣṭaka — 1 ॥ Adhyāya — 1 ॥ Varga — 1–2 ॥**
**॥ Rik-numbers contained in this sukta: 1–9 ॥**

**Ṛṣi — Madhucchandā Vaiśvāmitraḥ** (Madhuchandas, son of Vishvamitra)
**Devatā — Agniḥ** (Agni)
**Chandaḥ — Gāyatrī** (the Gayatri meter)

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ (the accented continuous-recitation text) ॥**

> अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं य॒ज्ञस्य॑ दे॒वमृ॑त्विज॑म् ।
> होता॑रं रत्न॒धात॑मम् ॥१॥

> *agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñásya devám ṛtvíjam |*
> *hótāraṃ ratnadhā́tamam ||1||*

> होतारम् । रत्न-धातमम् ॥१॥
>
> *agnim | īḷe | puraḥ-hitam | yajñasya | devam | ṛtvijam ||*

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam (Sāyaṇa's Sanskrit commentary) ॥**

> अग्निनामके देवम् ईळे । स्तौमि । ईड स्तुतौ । धा. २४-४ । इति धातुः, डकारस्य ळकारो बह्वचि आर्धधातुके सम्प्रदायप्राप्तेः । तथा च प्रकृतौ अज्झ्यधस्थडकारस्य ळकारं बह्वचा जगुः । अज्झ्यधस्थभकारस्य ळकारं वा यथाक्रमम् इति । निरुक्ते हॊता प्रियोज्यात् पदं होता स्वा इति लभ्यते । ईड्यम् अग्निम् । यज्ञस्य पुरोहितम् । यथा राज्ञः पुरोहितस्तद्भृत्यं संपादयति तथाग्निरपि यज्ञस्वाभीष्टिकं होमं संपादयति । यद्वा । यज्ञस्य संबन्धिनि पूर्वभागे आहवनीयरूपेणास्थितम् । पुनः ईदृशम् । देवं दानादिगुणयुक्तम् । पुनः ईदृशम् । होतारम् ऋत्विजम् । देवानां यज्ञेषु होतृनामक ऋत्विगेव । तथा च श्रूयते । अग्निर्वै...
>
> *agni-nāmake devam īḷe | staumi | īḍa stutau | dhā. 24-4 | iti dhātuḥ, ḍakārasya ḷakāro bahvaci ārdhadhātuke sampradāya-prāpteḥ | tathā ca prakṛtau ajjhyadhastha-ḍakārasya ḷakāraṃ bahvacā jaguḥ | ajjhyadhastha-bhakārasya ḷakāraṃ vā yathākramam iti | (nirukte) hotā priyojyāt padaṃ hotā svā iti labhyate | īḍyam agnim | yajñasya purohitam | yathā rājñaḥ purohitas tad-bhṛtyaṃ sampādayati tathāgnir api yajña-svābhīṣṭikaṃ homaṃ sampādayati | yadvā | yajñasya sambandhini pūrva-bhāge āhavanīya-rūpeṇāsthitam | punaḥ īdṛśam | devaṃ dānādi-guṇa-yuktam | punaḥ īdṛśam | hotāram ṛtvijam | devānāṃ yajñeṣu hotṛ-nāmaka ṛtvig eva | tathā ca śrūyate | agnir vai...* *(the two brief grammatical citations on the ḍa-to-ḷa shift are best-effort readings given their compressed technical form)*

**Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary:** "I praise (*īḷe*) the deity named Agni. [The verb] 'īḷe' derives from the root 'īḍ,' meaning 'to praise' (Dhatupatha 24.4); by grammatical convention, the root's 'ḍ' becomes 'ḷ' before a vowel-beginning ārdhadhātuka affix. Correspondingly [certain sutras confirm this]: '...the letter ḍ standing between vowels becomes ḷ before a vowel-initial [affix]... the letter bh standing between vowels similarly becomes ḷ in due sequence.' In the Nirukta, the word 'hotā' [priest/invoker] is derived from a root meaning 'to call' — 'hotā' is thus obtained as meaning 'one who calls' [i.e., invokes the gods].

'**Īḍyam agnim**' — the praiseworthy Agni. '**Yajñasya purohitam**' — just as a king's Purohita (chief priest/minister) accomplishes tasks on the king's behalf, so too Agni accomplishes the yajna's own desired oblation. Alternatively: [Agni] stands established in the front portion connected with the yajna, in the form of the Āhavanīya fire. Again, of this same [Agni]: '**devam**' — endowed with qualities such as generosity and the like. Again, of this same [Agni]: '**hotāram ṛtvijam**' — among the gods' own priests at sacrifices, [Agni] is indeed the one bearing the name 'Hotṛ,' [acting as] their ritual-priest. And thus it is heard in scripture: 'Agnir vai...'"

> देवानां होता । ऐ. ब्रा. ३-७ । इति ।
> *devānāṃ hotā | ai. brā. 3-7 | iti |*
> "'[Agni is] the Hotr of the gods' (Aitareya Brahmana 3.7)."

**"Ratna-dhātamam"** — the one who, most abundantly (atiśayena), bestows or holds (dhārayitāram) the treasures (ratnāni) that take the form of a yajna's own fruits — that is, "the bestower of treasures most abundant."

**Here, the word "Agni" is shown to admit of many derivations**, following Yāska's own established method in the Nirukta. *(The extended etymological passage that follows here — deriving "Agni" variously from roots meaning "to lead," "to shine," "foremost," and similar, in the classical Nirukta multi-derivation style, along with several further Vedic citations supporting each derivation — is presented in the source in a very tightly compressed technical register. **The overall sense of this first Rik, as conveyed by the mantra itself, is this:** "I praise Agni — the household-priest (purohita) of the sacrifice, its divine ritual-priest (ṛtvij), its invoking-priest (hotṛ), the one who most abundantly bestows treasures."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (word-by-word meaning) ॥**

**अग्निम् (agnim)** — Agni **ईळे (īḷe)** — I praise **पुरोहितम् (purohitam)** — the household-priest [of the sacrifice] **यज्ञस्य (yajñasya)** — of the yajna **देवम् (devam)** — the divine one **ऋत्विजम् (ṛtvijam)** — the ritual-priest **होतारम् (hotāram)** — the invoking-priest **रत्नधातमम् (ratna-dhātamam)** — the one who most abundantly bestows treasures.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ (overall sense) ॥**

I praise Agni, who serves as the household-priest of the sacrifice, its own divine ritual-priest, its invoking-priest, and who most abundantly bestows treasures [upon the sacrificer].

### Page 608 — Grammatical Analysis (Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā) of Verse 1

*This page continues Sāyaṇa's etymological support for "ratna-dhātamam" and then opens the formal grammatical derivation (prakriyā) of the verse's individual words. Working through it carefully below: recognizable roots, well-known citations, and the overall logical structure of the argument are given with confidence; specific numeric sūtra-citations that could not be independently confirmed against my own knowledge of the Aṣṭādhyāyī are marked with "[sūtra-ref uncertain]" rather than presented as verified — this is a deliberately more cautious register than the rest of this translation, given how easily a single misread digit here becomes a fabricated citation.*

> धनानां दातृतमम् । नि. २-१५ । इति ।
> *dhanānāṃ dātṛtamam | ni. 2.15 | iti |*
> "'The greatest giver of wealth' (Nirukta 2.15)."

**This further supports "ratna-dhātamam" through an independent Nirukta citation** — Yaska himself glosses a closely related term as "dhanānāṃ dātṛtamam" ("the greatest bestower of riches"), lending etymological support to Sayana's own gloss of "ratna-dhātamam" above.

**Turning now to the grammatical derivation itself:** the root "**īḍ**" (from which "īḷe" derives) belongs to a verb-class where its meaning is "praise" (stuti) — this sense is well-established (prasiddha). Although the root admits multiple senses even where well-known, by the governing convention (nyāya), the specific senses of "asking/requesting" (yācanā) and "invoking with reverence" (adhyeṣaṇā, closely tied to pūjā, worship) are the ones appropriate here, and the word is explained accordingly.

**On "purohitam":** the word is analyzed as a compound — "puraḥ" (in front) + "hitam" (placed) — meaning "one placed in front" [i.e., stationed before the sacrificer as his priest/protector], following the standard krit-formation for such compounds. *[The specific sutra-citations governing this compound's exact formation, visible in the source at this point, could not be confirmed with full confidence and are not reproduced as numbered citations here.]*

**On "devam":** derived from the root "div" (to shine/sport/play), with the appropriate primary affix, yielding "deva" in the sense of "the shining/resplendent one."

**On "hotāram":** derived from the root "hu" (to call/invoke, or, in ritual context, to offer oblation), with the agentive affix "tṛc" (or an equivalent krit-affix), yielding "hotṛ" — "one who invokes/offers" — here declined in the accusative "hotāram."

**On "ṛtvijam":** analyzed as a compound of "ṛtu" (season/proper time) and a form of the root "yaj" (to sacrifice) — "one who sacrifices at the proper/appointed time" — the standing grammatical explanation for this well-established ritual term.

**On "ratna-dhātamam":** "ratna" (treasure) + "dhā" (to hold/bestow, the same root seen in "dhātṛ") + the superlative affix "tamap," yielding "dhātamam" — "most abundantly bestowing" — hence "the one who most abundantly bestows treasures," as already given in the Pratipadartha above.

*(A number of further short technical notes on accent-placement (svara) for each derived form appear interspersed in the source at this point; these follow standard rules for the placement of udātta accent on krit and taddhita formations, but the specific accent-mark-by-syllable detail is not reproduced here with full confidence, consistent with the same caution noted for the Shiksha Anga's accent-classification passages earlier in this project.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (word-by-word meaning, given here in fuller form) ॥**

**यज्ञस्य (yajñasya)** — for the yajna (of the yajna) | **पुरोहितम् (purohitam)** — who acts as the ācārya who conducts the yajna, or as its purohita | **देवम् (devam)** — the resplendent one, or the one generous in giving | **होतारम् ऋत्विजम् (hotāram ṛtvijam)** — who is the principal ritvij called "Hotṛ" among those performing the yajna for the gods | **रत्नधातमम् (ratna-dhātamam)** — who bestows upon the sacrificer, as the yajna's fruit, jewels and other excellent things | **अग्निम् (agnim)** — the deity named Agni | **ईळे (īḷe)** — I praise.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ (overall sense) ॥**

I praise the deity named Agni — who stands in the foremost place within the yajna as its Purohita; who is present in the yajna as its own directly-embodied deity; who, among the four principal ritvijs — **Brahmā, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu**, and **Udgātṛ** — serves specifically as the **Hotṛ**-priest; and who graciously bestows upon the performing yajamāna wealth in the form of jewels and similar treasures.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> I praise (with hymns) Agni, the chief priest of the sacrifice, the bright one, the invoking priest, the greatest giver of reward.

**॥ Viśeṣārthaḥ (special topics) ॥**

**In this Rik**, the one who says "I shall praise" is the priest called the **Hotṛ**. In praising Agni here, only matters connected with the yajna are described — the qualities properly belonging to those who bear the principal roles within a yajna are here attributed to Agni himself. The word "**purohitam**" signifies either the chief ācārya who officiates the yajna, or, [more generally,] a brāhmaṇa [in that role]...

### Page 611

**...or, alternatively, it refers to the Adhvaryu** — the priest who accomplishes the majority of the practical tasks within the yajna — because "purohitam" (puraḥ + hitam) means: one who, during the yajna's performance, sits foremost, ahead of everyone else, and carries out the yajna's own tasks. "**Yajñasya devam**" means: Agni alone is the directly-visible deity within the yajna. The other deities are not visible to us. Moreover, since the oblations meant for other deities are all offered through Agni himself as the medium, there is no greater giver within the yajna than Agni. "**Ṛtvijam**" may refer to any one of the four principal ritvijs, beginning with Brahmā. "**Hotāram**" means the ritvij associated with the invoking/Homa-offering — but since it is well established that Agni himself brings the other deities to the sacrificial altar (**sa devān eha vakṣati**, "he shall bring the gods here," as stated explicitly in the very next Rik), he is accordingly called "**hotāram**." "**Ratna-dhātamam**" means: one who bestows, as the fruit of the yajna, jewels and similar things upon the yajamāna. There is an established usage whereby "ratna" refers not only to gems such as diamonds, but to any excellent or superior object generally. Hence the meaning: one who gives the yajamāna wealth, grain, cattle, jewels, and other such excellent things, as needed.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**For this first sukta of the first Mandala**, it is stated that the rishi is **Madhuchandas**, son of **Vishvamitra**. From this sukta through the tenth sukta — that is, across a total of ten suktas — this same Madhuchandas remains the rishi. This rishi Madhuchandas is one of the sons of the rishi Vishvamitra. That Vishvamitra was himself the son of Gadhi is stated both in the Aitareya Brahmana (2.12) and the Jaiminiya Brahmana (1.317[?]). In the Rigveda's own comprehensive index (Sarvanukramanika), he is said to be the son of Kushika's son Gadhi. Only in the Panchavimsha Brahmana (21.12.2[?]) is Vishvamitra instead described as a king born in the lineage of a king named Jahnu.

**For the Rigveda's third Mandala, this same Vishvamitra, son of Gadhi, is the rishi** — that Mandala contains 71 suktas. Logically, these ten suktas belonging to Vishvamitra's son Madhuchandas ought to have been included within the third Mandala. Why they were not so included, and instead came to stand at the head of the first Mandala, remains unknown.

**This sukta contains a total of nine Riks, all having Agni as their deity.** Ordinarily, a single sukta has only one rishi; yet it is occasionally found that a single sukta has several. The same holds for deities — a sukta may have one deity, or many. Likewise, a sukta's verses may all share one meter, or differ. **For the present sukta we are expounding — "agnimīḷe" — across all nine of its Riks, there is a single rishi (Madhuchandas), a single deity (Agni), and a single meter (Gayatri).**
