### Page 612

**Should it not be "agnimāḍe" rather than "agnimīḷe"?** [This is explained:] per the sutra "**īḍa stutau**" (Dhatupatha 24.4), the form "īḷe" arises from the root "**īḍ**." In place of the letter "ḍa," the major grammarians employ the letter "ḷa" in certain contexts. This is a long-established, traditional convention—

> अज्झ्यधस्थडकारस्य ळकारं बह्वचा जगुः । अज्झ्यधस्थढकारस्य ळ्हकारं वै यथाक्रमम् ॥ इति ॥
> *ajjhyadhastha-ḍakārasya ḷakāraṃ bahvacā jaguḥ | ajjhyadhastha-ḍhakārasya ḷhakāraṃ vai yathākramam || iti ||*
>
> "The letter 'ḍa,' standing between vowels, is pronounced as 'ḷa' before a vowel-beginning [affix]; the letter 'ḍha,' standing between vowels, likewise becomes 'ḷha,' in the same manner."

**That is:** when "ḍa" occurs between two vowels ("aj" here meaning the class of vowel-sounds), it is pronounced as "ḷa." Here, when "īḍe" is to be spoken: ī + ḍa + e = "īḷe" results. Since the "ḍa" falls between the two vowels "ī" and "e," it becomes "ḷa," and the whole word becomes "**īḷe**." Correspondingly, wherever "ḍha" occurs in the same position, it becomes "ḷha." For example:

> आषाळ्हं यां प्रतनासु पश्वम् ।
> *āṣāḷhaṃ yāṃ pratanāsu paśvam |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.100.3[?])

---

**Many commentators construct many different derivational analyses for the word "Agni."** Generally, following grammatical sutras, they devise various component-meanings that happen to fit with Agni's own well-known qualities. But it cannot be said with certainty that these are the word's actually intended meaning, or the original poet's own sense. In Sanskrit, with the aid of grammar and verbal roots, it is far from impossible to construct *some* meaning in almost any direction one wishes. Yet it is difficult to simply accept that the many words used throughout the Veda — deity-names especially — actually contain such elaborate component-meanings, achievable only through such intricate grammatical machinery. The Veda's own language tends toward simplicity, stating its intended sense directly; a compound of more than two elements is itself a rarity there. Given this, some scholars decline to set aside a word's natural sense in favor of derivations achievable only through comparatively late-arising grammatical apparatus.

**However, it is no fault of the Bhashyakara [Sayana] that "Agni" has been explained in so many ways** — for, following precisely what is already stated regarding this word in the Brahmanas and in the Nirukta, the meaning has been worked out with grammar's assistance. We shall now explain some of the principal derivations among these.

> अथातोऽनुक्रमिष्यामोऽग्निः प्रथमस्थं प्रथमं व्याख्यास्यामोऽग्निः कस्मादग्रणीर्भवत्यग्रं यज्ञेषु प्रणीयतेऽग्रं यज्ञं नयति सन्नमानो वा क्रोशनो भवतीति स्थौलाष्ठीविः । क्रोशनयति न स्नेयति तृप्तेराख्यातेभ्यो जायत इति शाकपूणिः ।
> *athāto'nukramiṣyāmo'gniḥ prathama-sthaṃ prathamaṃ vyākhyāsyāmo'gniḥ kasmād agraṇīr bhavaty agraṃ yajñeṣu praṇīyate'graṃ yajñaṃ nayati sannamāno vā krośano bhavatīti sthaulāṣṭhīviḥ | krośanayati na sneyati tṛpter ākhyātebhyo jāyata iti śākapūṇiḥ |* (Nirukta 7.14) *(the remainder of this Nirukta passage on this page continues with further, highly compressed etymological reasoning — deriving pieces of "Agni" variously from roots connected with "aṅga," "nī," and "dah" — which is not reproduced further here with full confidence, consistent with the cautious approach adopted for this register of text)*
>
> "Now, hereafter, we shall proceed [to explain the deity-names in order]. Since Agni stands first [in the list], we explain him first. Why is Agni called 'agraṇī' (foremost-leader)? Because he is led at the forefront in sacrifices, or because he leads the sacrifice forward. Or — he becomes so through bending low, or through crying out — thus says **Sthaulāṣṭhīvi**. [Regarding the sense 'krośana,' crying out, as against 'na sneyati,' not becoming smooth:] it is born from verbal roots (ākhyāta) — thus says **Śākapūṇi**."

**Meaning:** Yaska, in his Nirukta, having decided to explain the deity-names in the order they occur, takes up Agni first, since Agni stands first among them. Two ancient authorities are cited for the etymology of "agraṇī" (one who leads at the forefront) — Sthaulashthivi holding one view, Shakapuni offering a related but distinct grammatical explanation...

### Page 613

**The meaning of this is:** it is generally customary to state defining marks for all deities alike; accordingly, we shall now provide a special explanation of "Agni" from the standpoint of its component-meaning. Since Agni the deity is said to exist both on earth and in heaven, we first explain his form as present on earth. In explaining how the word "Agni" came to bear this name, the answer "**agraṇe**" may be given. "Agraṇe" means: one who himself leads the divine army, or who serves as its foremost leader (nāyaka). This is one reason for the name.

**Moreover, a Brahmana passage states:**

> अग्निर्देवानां सेनानीः ।
> *agnir devānāṃ senānīḥ |*
> "Agni is the general (senānī) of the gods' army."

**Following this, the Aitareya scholars state in their own Mantra-Brahmana:**

> अग्निर्मुखं प्रथमो देवतानाम् ।
> *agnir mukhaṃ prathamo devatānām |* (Aitareya Brahmana 1.4)
> "Agni is the face — the foremost among the deities."

**Elsewhere in the same Brahmana:**

> अग्निर्वै देवानामवमः ।
> *agnir vai devānām avamaḥ |* (Aitareya Brahmana 1.1)
> "Agni is indeed the nearest of the deities [to men]."

**And in the Taittiriya Brahmana:**

> अग्निरग्रे प्रथमो देवतानाम् ।
> *agnir agre prathamo devatānām |* (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.4.2.1[?])
> "Agni, at the forefront, is the first among the deities" — and also "**agnir avamo devatānām**" ["Agni is the nearest of the deities"].

**From these examples, Agni is established as first among the deities, standing at the forefront, serving as their leader.**

**Because of this**, in the sacrificial rites generally, fire is first carried from the Gārhapatya fire-pit onward to the Āhavanīya fire-pit standing in the eastern direction — and it is from this "carrying forward" (**agra**-nayana) that Agni comes to bear his name; this is the **second** reason.

**Furthermore**, since Agni, offering up his very own body, burns kindling and similar fuel, and likewise cooks the oblation in homas and similar rites — through this self-consuming, self-propelling action — Agni comes to bear his name; this is counted among the **third** such reasons.

**The Nirukta-scholar Sthaulāṣṭhīvin**, son of the great sage Sthaulāṣṭhīva, holds that Agni's very nature — burning continuously, without pause or restraint — accounts for the name: from a root meaning "to behave harshly" (krośa) comes "krośayati"; "**na krośayati**" gives "**akroṣaṇaḥ**" — that is, [Agni] burns wood and similar material mercilessly, without the gentleness [that quality's absence implies].

**Another Nirukta-scholar, Śākapūṇi** (son of Śakapūṇi, also known by the name Rathītara), holds that the word "Agni" arises from **three separate roots**:

> इण् गतौ इति धातुः (धा. २४-२५) ।
> *iṇ gatau iti dhātuḥ (dhā. 24.25) |* — "'iṇ,' in the sense of 'going'" —

> अक्ष्णोतेर्वा तृप्रक्षणकाङ्क्षिषु इति धातुः ।
> *akṣṇoter vā tṛpra-kṣaṇa-kāṅkṣiṣu iti dhātuḥ |* — [a root connected with desiring/aspiring] —

> दघ्नोतेर्वा दह भस्मीकरणे इति धातुः ।
> *daghnoter vā daha bhasmīkaraṇe iti dhātuḥ |* — "'dah,' in the sense of 'reducing to ash [by burning]'" —

*(the precise Dhatupatha reference-numbers for the second and third roots, and a fourth root the passage appears to introduce at the very bottom of this page, remain uncertain at this resolution and are not asserted as verified citations)*

### Page 614

**The word "Agni" is thus formed from the sounds "a," "g," and "ni":** the "a" comes from "ayana" (a form derived from the root "iṇ," "to go," via "eti"); the "g" comes either from the root "ac" (whose "k" becomes "g" by substitution) or from "dagdha" (a form of "dah," "to burn, reduce to ash"); and the long "nī" — from "nayati," a form of the root "nī" ("to lead/obtain") — is shortened to "ni." These three — **ā + g + ni = Agni** — combine, formed from the three roots discussed above. Since Agni comes to the sacrificial ground and, by offering up his own body, burns the kindling and similarly causes the oblation to be cooked, this deity accordingly bears the name "Agni" — this is the overall sense.

**Since the praise of this deity Agni — bearing this full range of meaning — is the principal subject of this Rik, this mantra is well known by the name "agnimīḷe."** The sage Yāska himself explains this very Rik in his Nirukta, as follows:

> अग्निमीळेऽग्निं याचामीळिध्येषणकर्मा पूजाकर्मा वा पुरोहितो व्याख्यातो यज्ञस्य देवो दानाद्वा दीपनाद्वा द्योतनाद्वा द्युस्थानो भवतीति वा यो देवः सा देवता होतारं ह्वातारं जुहोतेर्होतेर्वाभोरत्नधातमं रमणीयानां धनानां दातृतमम् ॥ इति (नि. ७-१५)
> *agnim īḷe'gniṃ yācāmi īḍi-adhyeṣaṇa-karmā pūjā-karmā vā purohito vyākhyāto yajñasya devo dānād vā dīpanād vā dyotanād vā dyu-sthāno bhavatīti vā yo devaḥ sā devatā hotāraṃ hvātāraṃ juhoter hoter vā abhoḥ ratna-dhātamaṃ ramaṇīyānāṃ dhanānāṃ dātṛtamam || iti* (Nirukta 7.15)
>
> "'Agnim īḷe' — 'I entreat Agni'; [the root 'īḍ'] carries the sense of asking (adhyeṣaṇa) or of worship (pūjā). 'Purohita' has already been explained. 'Devaḥ' [of the yajna] — [Agni is called 'deva'] either from 'dāna' (giving), 'dīpana' (illuminating), or 'dyotana' (shining) — or because he abides in the region of the sky (dyu-sthāna); whoever is thus 'deva' constitutes 'devatā.' 'Hotāram' — the one who calls (hvātāram), from the root 'hu' (to invoke or to offer). 'Ratna-dhātamam' — the greatest giver (dātṛtamam) of desirable riches (ramaṇīyānāṃ dhanānām)."

**Meaning:** the root "īḍ" is well known to carry a sense connected with praise. Following the accepted principle that roots may carry multiple senses, the meanings "entreaty" (yācñā), "asking/invocation" (adhyeṣaṇā), and "worship" (pūjā) have all been assigned to the root "īḍ," and the verse is explained accordingly here.

**The word "purohita" was already explained in the Nirukta's second chapter** (2.13), in the course of commenting on the Rik "**yeṣṭe vāpiḥ śaṃ kenāve purohitaḥ**" (Rigveda Samhita 10.14.2[?]) — that is, "**puraḥ hitaṃ dadhāti purohitaḥ**": one who stands in front, [specifically] in front of the sacrificer [facing him] during the yajna. The Yajurvedins too gloss it as "**puro hitaṃ dadhate**" — one standing in front, that is, in the foremost position. The word "purohita" carries the established sense of the principal ācārya who properly conducts yajnas and similar rites according to shastric injunction. In this Rik, since the qualities of the Hotr and other ritvijs are attributed to Agni in this praise, "purohita" may equally be understood here as "chief ācārya." **This word "purohita" occurs only in a few places within the Rigveda itself.** Though the Bhashyakara [Sayana] clearly explains this word's sense as "chief ācārya" there, in the Krishna-Yajur[veda]...

### Page 615

**In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda:**

> विश्वरूपो नै त्वाष्ट्रः पुरोहितो देवानाम् ।
> *viśvarūpo nai tvāṣṭraḥ purohito devānām |* (Taittiriya Samhita 2.5.1[?])
> "Vishvarupa, son of Tvashtri, was the purohita of the gods."

**And:**

> बृहस्पतिर्देवानां पुरोहित आसीच्छन्दःसाराणां कार्षणसुराणाम् ।
> *bṛhaspatir devānāṃ purohita āsīc chandaḥsārāṇāṃ kārṣaṇa-surāṇām |* (Taittiriya Samhita 3.4.10[?])
> "Brihaspati was the purohita of the gods; Shanda and Marka were the purohitas of the demons (daityas)."

**In these instances, "purohita" is used in the sense of the chief ācārya who conducts ritual performances (High Priest).**

**On "devam":** the word "deva" expresses senses connected with giving (dāna), illuminating (dīpana), and shining (dyotana). It derives from the root "**div**," "to shine." "Devam" thus means "one who shines, one who illuminates" — that is, "a deity." Alternatively, taken as "giver [of vigor] to the yajna," it means one who plays the principal role within it — since the yajna cannot be accomplished without Agni at all, this is the sense. Since "deva" and "devatā" are synonymous terms bearing identical meaning ("deva" masculine, "devatā" feminine), the deity meant in this mantra need not be thought to be anyone other than Agni himself.

**On "ṛtvijam":**

> ऋतौ युज्यते इति ऋत्विक् ।
> *ṛtau yujyate iti ṛtvik |* (cf. Panini Ashtadhyayi 3.2.59)
> "One who is engaged/employed at the proper season [or appointed time] is called 'ṛtvik.'"

Though "ṛtvij" is used generally for anyone engaged in reciting mantras and similar duties during a ritual, it more specifically denotes one of the four who bear the principal roles in a yajna: **Brahmā, Hotṛ, Adhvaryu**, and **Udgātṛ**. Since the word "hotāram" immediately follows "ṛtvijam" in this Rik, the Bhashyakara and many other commentators hold that the specific reference here is to the ritvij called **Hotṛ**.

**On "hotāram":** the word "hotṛ" derives from the root "**hve**" (to invoke, to call) — hence "one who invokes the deities." This sense is reinforced by the very next Rik, which states "**sa devān eha vakṣati**" ("he shall bring the gods here"). The sage **Baurṇavābha** holds the alternative view that "hotṛ" instead derives from "**juhoti**" (to perform homa). For the word "hotṛ," this [alternate derivation]...

### Page 616

**Both meanings apply.** In connection with Agni, the word "hotāram" has frequently been used alongside "ṛtvijam" in many places across the Rigveda:

> नि त्वा यज्ञस्य साधनमग्ने होतारमृत्विजम् । नि त्वा होतारमृत्विजम् । त्वां यज्ञेष्वृत्विजमग्ने होतारमीळते । मन्द्रं होतारमृत्विजं चिकित्वांसं विभावसुम् ।
> *ni tvā yajñasya sādhanam agne hotāram ṛtvijam | ni tvā hotāram ṛtvijam | tvāṃ yajñeṣv ṛtvijam agne hotāram īḷate | mandraṃ hotāram ṛtvijaṃ cikitvāṃsaṃ vibhāvasum |* *(this cluster of formulaic parallel citations, and their specific chapter-verse locators, remain a best-effort reading at this resolution)*

— and so on. **As shown above, many rishis, in praising Agni, use the two words "hotāram" and "ṛtvijam" together.** Since the Hotṛ's role in a yajna is especially prominent, the custom of calling Agni himself "Hotṛ" may well have arisen from this frequent pairing.

**On "ratna-dhātamam":** Yaska, in the Nirukta's second chapter, explains "ratna" alongside other words denoting wealth. Anything pleasing or delightful is called "ratna"; it may also mean simply "an excellent object." Here, primarily, "ratna" carries the sense of wealth (aiśvarya). "**Dhātamaḥ**" is used in the sense of "giving." In the Rigveda, it is generally found that where the sense "to give" (dadāti) is intended, the root "**dadhāti**" is used instead. For example:

> प्रातर्रत्नं प्रातरित्वा दधाति ।
> *prātar ratnaṃ prātaritvā dadhāti |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.125.1[?])

**In this verse, the rishi Kakṣīvān describes a donation made by a king named Svanaya.** Here "ratna" clearly means gold and similar wealth, or cattle and other excellent possessions, as becomes evident from the words used in the following verses. "Dadhāti" here means simply "giving" (dadāti). Similarly, in passages such as:

> रायस्पोषं यजमानेषु धत्ते । प्रजां पुष्टिं भूतिमस्मासु धत्ते ।
> *rāyas poṣaṃ yajamāneṣu dhatte | prajāṃ puṣṭiṃ bhūtim asmāsu dhatte |* (Rigveda Samhita 7.48.2[?])

— "**dhatte**" is likewise used in place of "dadāti." All of this draws upon Yaska's own explanation, as the Nirukta's author, of this mantra.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (Grammatical Process) ॥**

> हयास्तूपरङ्गेन्द्रा नत्वा तत्वार्थदौ ब्रुवे । ऋतिं देष्या पाणिनीयमाक्ष्णोशो मार्गपोक्तः ॥
> *(this brief opening verse to the grammar section remains a best-effort reading, its precise sense unclear even after careful re-examination)*

**The word "Agni" arises from the root "ag," meaning "to go"** — per the Unadi rule "**aṅger ṇa-lopaś ca**" (Unadi Sutra, precise number uncertain): before the root "ag," the affix "ni" is added; moreover, [a rule governs] the loss of the nasal "n" [in the root]...

### Page 617

**...the elision also occurs; by this rule, the affix "ni" comes after the root "ag."** Since the "i" in the root "ag" bears the designation "it" (a marker later dropped), by the rule "**idito nuṃ dhātoḥ**" (Panini 7.1.58) — a nasal "n" is added after the final vowel of a root so marked — the resulting nasal then undergoes its own elision by a further rule. "**Aṅgati iti agniḥ**" — "he who moves/goes forth" is "Agni" — that is, because he carries the oblation up to the deities in heaven, he bears this name.

*(Several further accent-rule citations follow, working out that the resulting word "Agni" has its "a" as anudātta and its "i" as udātta — this is confirmed by the accent marks already seen on "agním" in the Saṃhitā-pāṭha itself. The specific chain of Ashtadhyayi sutra-numbers cited here — governing root-accent, affix-accent, and the eventual "ekādeśa" [single-substitute] accent rule for the accusative "agnim" — is presented with the same caution as elsewhere in this section, though the overall grammatical logic and its conclusion are clear and consistent with the verse's own printed accentuation.)*

**Here the discussion turns to a foundational methodological question in Sanskrit grammar itself:**

> नामान्याख्यातजानीति शाकटायनस्य नैरुक्ते समये । न सर्वाणीति गार्ग्ये वैयाकरणानां चैके ।
> *nāmāny ākhyāta-jāneti śākaṭāyanasya nairukte samaye | na sarvāṇīti gārgye vaiyākaraṇānāṃ caike |* (Nirukta 1.13)
>
> "'All nouns are born from verbs' — this is Śākaṭāyana's own view, within the Nirukta's own convention. 'Not all [nouns are so derived]' — this is Gārgya's view, and that of some grammarians as well."

**Śākaṭāyana, himself a Nirukta-author, holds that every nominal stem (prātipadika) derives from a verbal root (dhātu).** In **Gārgya's** own view, however, the word "Agni" is "**akhaṇḍa**" — that is, an underived, indivisible nominal stem, admitting no division into root and affix. In this [Gargya's] view...

### Page 618

> उदात्तं (फिट् सू. १) ।
> *udāttaṃ (phiṭ sū. 1) |*
> "'Phiṭ' [denotes] a nominal stem (prātipadika); its final [syllable] takes the udātta accent."

**By this rule, "agni" as a prātipadika likewise has udātta accent on its final syllable.** When the accusative ending "am" is applied, the same grammatical process as before should be understood to apply.

**Yaska himself favors three derivations of the word "Agni":**

> अग्रं नयतीत्यग्रणिः, अग्रं प्रति प्रीयत इत्यग्निः, अङ्गं नयतीत्यग्निः ।
> *agraṃ nayatīty agraṇiḥ, agraṃ prati prīyata ity agniḥ, aṅgaṃ nayatīty agniḥ |*
>
> "'He who leads forward' is Agraṇi; 'he who inclines with delight toward the forefront' is Agni; 'he who leads the body/limb onward' is Agni."

**The great sage Sthaulāṣṭhīvi instead offers:** "**akṣṇo'payatīty agniḥ**" — "he who removes affliction from the eye is Agni." In these derivations, the division into root and affix must be constructed as appropriate in each case.

**On this very point, Yaska states one of the Nirukta's own foundational methodological statements:**

> अथ निर्वचने तेष्वेषु पदेषु स्वरसंस्कारौ समर्थः प्रादेशिकेन गुणेनान्वितौ स्यातां तथा तानि निब्रूयात्, अप्रादेशिके विकारीर्थनि परीक्षिते केनचिद् दृष्टिसामान्येन, असिध्यमाने सामान्ये स्वक्षरवर्णसामान्यान् निब्रूयाच्चैव न निब्रूयात् ॥
> *atha nirvacane teṣv eṣu padeṣu svara-saṃskārau samarthaḥ prādeśikena guṇenānvitau syātāṃ tathā tāni nibrūyāt, aprādeśike vikārīrthani parīkṣite kenacid dṛṣṭi-sāmānyena, asidhyamāne sāmānye svākṣara-varṇa-sāmānyān nibrūyāc caiva na nibrūyāt ||* (Nirukta 2.1)
>
> "Now, in etymological explanation: in whichever words the accent and grammatical processing prove capable [of derivation] and are found connected with a rootward (prādeśika) sense-quality, one should explain them accordingly. Where such a root-connection is absent, but some general resemblance can still be discerned through a certain manner of observation, [one may explain by that resemblance]. Where even that general resemblance cannot be established, one may resort to mere resemblance of individual letters and sounds — or else one need not attempt an explanation at all."

**Meaning:** where a word's accent and grammatical derivation (via root and affix) can be properly connected to its intended sense through standard grammatical procedure, one should explain it that way — this is the strongest kind of explanation. Where this isn't available, a general resemblance of sense, discernible by some means, may serve instead. Where not even that can be shown, mere resemblance of individual sounds may be invoked as a last resort. **Taking "Agni" as the example: the derivation "aṅgati ity agniḥ" — where root, affix, and accent-pattern are all fully established through grammar — satisfies this strongest, first kind of explanation.**

**Where the root's own sense does not directly apply to the intended meaning**, one may instead follow a Brahmana-passage's own usage, or an intended qualifying sense applied to a deity, adapting the general action-sense (kriyā-sāmānya) of the root so that the intended meaning still emerges from the word. In "**agraṃ nayati ity agni**" [as above], the general notion of "leading" is what grounds the word "Agni" here. Where even this general action-sense proves unavailable, one should form the etymology on the basis of mere resemblance of syllables or letters (akṣara-sāmānya / varṇa-sāmānya). When "**akṣṇo'payatīty agniḥ**" is analyzed this way, "**akṣṇaḥ**" — per the lexicon's sense "akṣo nānā-pratiṣedhe" — carries a negating sense with an initial "a"-sound; since the word "Agni" likewise begins with the sound "a," this derivation rests on mere sound-resemblance (akṣara-sāmya). "**Akṣara**" here means a meaning-bearing sound. **Śākapūṇi's own derivation proceeds by mere letter-resemblance (varṇa-sāmya)** — noting only that both words happen to share the sound "g." **Thus, an etymological explanation should never be abandoned outright, by whichever of these means it can be achieved** — this is the sense of Nirukta 2.1.

**This is a genuinely significant piece of classical Indian linguistic philosophy**, and it's satisfying to see it appear organically as Sayana works through the very first word of the Rigveda's very first verse.

**This confirms that the word "īḷe" is properly svara-accented as derived above.** Continuing with "**timbū**" and similar forms [a brief transitional note], the same accent process applies.

**On "purohitam" — its grammatical derivation:**

> आयं पुरो भुवः ।
> *āyaṃ puro bhuvaḥ |* (Taittiriya Samhita 4.3.2.1[?])

— here "puraḥ" is accented on its final syllable (antodātta). The word "puraḥ" itself derives from "pūrva," per the rule:

> पूर्वाधरावरादिभ्यो दिक्देशकालेष्वस् ।
> *pūrvādhara-avarādibhyo dik-deśa-kāleṣv asa* (cf. Panini Ashtadhyayi 5.3.39)

— the taddhita affix "as," expressing direction, place, or time, is added after words such as "pūrva," "adhara," and "avara." When this affix is applied, "pūrva" takes the substitute "pur," yielding "pūrva + as = puras" — and with visarga, "**puraḥ**." Since the vowel here belongs to the affix "as," by the rule "**ādyudāttaś ca**" (Panini 3.1.3) — the affix's own initial letter takes udātta — "puraḥ" becomes antodātta [accented on its final syllable].

**On "hitam":** from the root "**dhā**" (ḍudhāñ, "to hold, to nourish") — before the affix "kta," per the rule "**dadhāter kit**" (Panini 7.4.42), the substitute "hi" replaces "dhā." The resulting "hita" thus takes udātta accent on its final syllable.

**When "puraḥ" and "hitam" combine as a compound** — per the general rule that a compound's final member ordinarily governs accent, with the specific exception applying here for this type of tatpurusha formation — the compound "**purohitam**" results, accented accordingly on the vowel following the combination.

*(Several further specific citation-chains on this page — governing sandhi between the visarga of "puraḥ" and the initial "h" of "hitam," and the precise accent-retention rule for this particular tatpurusha type — involve highly compressed technical shorthand that could not be independently confirmed at full confidence and are not reproduced as specific numbered sutras here.)*

**On "yajñasya":** derived from the root "**yaj**," meaning "devapūjā" (worship of the deities) — through the standard krit-affix process yielding the noun "yajña" ("sacrifice, act of worship"), here declined in the genitive "yajñasya" ("of the sacrifice").

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**अग्निः (agniḥ)** — the deity Agni | **पूर्वेभिः ऋषिभिः (pūrvebhiḥ ṛṣibhiḥ)** — by many ancient rishis, such as Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and others | **ईड्यः (īḍyaḥ)** — is praised | **उत (uta)** — and | **नूतनैः (nūtanaiḥ)** — by present-day [rishis] such as us, and by other rishis who are our contemporaries | **ईड्यः (īḍyaḥ)** — is worthy of being praised, that is, is [likewise] praised | **सः (saḥ)** — that Agni | **देवान् (devān)** — the deities invoked in the yajna | **इह (iha)** — here, that is, to the yajna-ground | **आ वक्षति (ā vakṣati)** — brings, [may he] bring.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

This Agni, whom I now praise, has been praised by many great sages in ancient times. In the present age too, I myself, along with other rishis who are my contemporaries, praise Agni. May this Agni — thus worthy of praise by rishis of both past and present ages — bring here the deities whom we invoke, so that they may accept their portion of the oblation in the yajna we now perform.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> Agni is a god to be praised by sages ancient and by sages modern. May he bring the gods hither.

**॥ Viśeṣārthaḥ ॥**

**This Rik's meaning is straightforward** — it contains nothing difficult or ambiguous. Since it is said that Agni exists both on earth and in heaven, the principal rishi here prays that Agni bring the deities dwelling in heaven down to the sacrificial altar.

### Page 624

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**Since this Rik states "pūrvebhiḥ ṛṣibhiḥ" (by ancient rishis), it becomes clear that suktas even more ancient than this one existed, composed by rishis even more ancient than the present one.** This "agnimīḷe" sukta, though standing at the very head of the Rigveda, is by no means itself the most ancient composition. Suktas evidently far older than this one were already current in this rishi's own time, and appear — from the way they were handed down — to have been taught traditionally from a considerably earlier period still. Even examined purely from the standpoint of linguistic style, a good many suktas can be found that are more archaic, more ambiguous in sense, and built from more obscure word-combinations than this one.

**Some rishi-names earlier than the present one may be given as follows:**

**In the lineage of the rishi Bhṛgu** — Bṛhaspati, Ayāsya, Ajarvan(?), Dadhyañc, Vyaśva(?), Saṃvarta, Ucithya(?), Ucathya, Bharadvāja, Dīrghatamas, Sudhanvan, Ṛbhu, Vibhvan(?), Vāja, Kavandhya(?), Vicāra, and others.

**In the lineage of the rishi Aṅgiras** — Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others, as well as those of the present rishi's own family: Kuśika, Gādhin, Viśvāmitra, and others.

**Since the names of these rishis appear within the Veda itself, all of them are established as having directly perceived (draṣṭṛ) their respective mantras in praising Agni.** Among such rishis, there may well have been many others whose very names are unknown even to me [the commentator, Venkatarao himself is speaking here]; the suktas they composed are no longer available to us today. They may have composed many suktas not now found within the Rigveda at all — but since these fell out of use, they remain inaccessible to us. Since only the suktas actually preserved within the Rigveda have come down to us, it is only the matters contained in these that we are able to examine.

> अ॒ग्निना॑ र॒यिम॑श्नव॒त् पोष॑मे॒व दि॒वेदि॑वे ।

> *agnínā rayím aśnavat póṣam evá divé-dive |*
> *yaśásaṃ vīrávattamam ||3||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> अग्निना । रयिम् । अश्नवत् । पोषम् । एव । दिवेऽदिवे ।
> यशसम् । वीरवत्तमम् ॥३॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> यो'यं होत्रा स्तुत्योऽस्य नाग्ना निमित्तभूतेन यजमानो रयिं धनम् अश्नवत् प्राप्नोति । पोष्यं रयिम् । दिवे दिवे पोषणेव प्रतिदिनं पुष्यमानतया वर्धमानम् एव, न तु कदाचिद् अपि क्षीयमानम् । यशसं दानादिना यशोयुक्तम् । वीरवत् अतिशयेन पुत्रपौत्रादि-वीरपुरुषोपेतम् । अति हि धने पुरुषाः संपद्यन्ते । रयिशब्दो माघमित्यादिधननामसु पठितः । तत्र फिट् स्वरः । अश्नवत् अशेर्मा-...
> *yo'yaṃ hotrā stutyo'sya nāgnā nimitta-bhūtena yajamāno rayiṃ dhanam aśnavat prāpnoti | poṣyaṃ rayim | dive dive poṣaṇeva pratidinaṃ puṣyamānatayā vardhamānam eva, na tu kadācid api kṣīyamānam | yaśasaṃ dānādinā yaśo-yuktam | vīravat atiśayena putra-pautrādi-vīra-puruṣopetam | ati hi dhane puruṣāḥ sampadyante | rayi-śabdo māgham ity-ādi-dhana-nāmasu paṭhitaḥ | tatra phiṭ svaraḥ | aśnavat aśer mā-...*

'Poṣyam rayim' — wealth that is [continually] nourished. 'Dive dive' — day by day, ever growing through such continual nourishment, never at any time diminishing. 'Yaśasam' — endowed with fame, through generosity and similar virtues. 'Vīravat[-tamam]' — endowed, in the highest degree, with heroic men such as sons and grandsons; for indeed, men [descendants] are what truly complete [and enrich] wealth. The word 'rayi' is listed among the terms for wealth, such as 'māgham' and similar; for it, the Phit-sutra's own accent rule applies. 'Aśnavat' derives from the root 'aś'..."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(यजमानः)** — (the sacrificer) | **अग्निना (agninā)** — by Agni, who has been praised by the Hotṛ | **दिवेदिवे (dive-dive)** — day by day | **पोषमेव (poṣam eva)** — that which is continually nourished/increasing | **रयिम् (rayim)** — wealth, or prosperity | **यशसम् (yaśasam)** — the renown that comes through generosity and similar virtues | **वीरवत्तमम् (vīravattamam)** — brave sons, servants, and similar men, in the highest measure | **अश्नवत् (aśnavat)** — may [he] obtain.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

When the Hotṛ praises Agni, may Agni, pleased by this praise, bestow upon the sacrificer who performs the yajna: wealth and prosperity, renown, and valorous sons together with servants and other members of his household. The wealth Agni bestows should not merely last for some time and then dwindle away — rather, it should keep increasing day by day, bringing the sacrificer continual joy. This is the intended sense.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> Through Agni, may the worshipper obtain wealth and prosperity which increases day by day accompanied by renown and a host of brave followers.

**॥ Viśeṣārthaḥ ॥**

**The Hotṛ, having praised Agni, prays that Agni may graciously grant the sacrificer wealth and prosperity, fame, and brave sons, servants, and the like.** The sense is that whatever wealth Agni gives should increase day by day, and never diminish. Alternatively, through the specific phrase "**dive-dive**" (on every single day), the further sense emerges: may Agni continue giving such wealth on each and every day, without interruption.

### Page 630

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Rayim" means wealth, as the Nirukta itself states.** The word "**rāyaḥ**" expresses this same sense. "Rāyaḥ" is commonly paired with the word "**poṣa**" throughout the Vedas. For example:

> रायस्पोषं यजमानेषु धत्तम् । रायस्पोषेण सचीय सुवीरः ।
> *rāyas poṣaṃ yajamāneṣu dhattam | rāyas poṣeṇa sacīya suvīraḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita 7.43.3[?]; 1.151.1[?])

— and so on. **Here, the Bhashyakara explains "poṣa" as "abhivṛddhi" (increase).** This meaning fits well here, though "poṣa" often carries a somewhat distinct sense elsewhere in the Rigveda:

> भूरि पोषं स धत्ते वीरवद्गृहः । दधद् रयिं मयि पोषम् । पोषं रयीणामरिष्टिं तनूनाम् ।
> *bhūri poṣaṃ sa dhatte vīravad gṛhaḥ | dadhad rayiṃ mayi poṣam | poṣaṃ rayīṇām ariṣṭiṃ tanūnām |* (Rigveda Samhita 8.23.21[?]; 7.66.11[?]; 3.51.8[?])

**In these verses, "poṣa" primarily means "nourishment, plumpness," though the sense of "increase" is also implied.**

**"Aśnavat"** is explained as "obtains." Though this root can also mean "to eat, to enjoy," it is likewise commonly used in the sense "to obtain" even in present-day literature. **The word "eva" here indicates that "rayi" and "poṣa" refer to two distinct things**, not a single repeated notion.

**"Dine-dive"** — "on every single day": when the same word is repeated in this manner, it conveys the sense "in each and every instance." Compare: "**ahar-ahaḥ**" (day after day), "**pade-pade**" (at every step), "**bhare-bhare**" (in every battle), and similar forms — **a usage pattern that was first employed precisely within the Vedas themselves.**

**"Yaśasam"** — fame, standing, reputation. **It became customary in the Veda that when a rishi prays to a deity for desired things, he typically asks for exactly these: fame, wealth, nourishment, and "vīravat" — brave men.** In an era when battles were frequently fought, the need for brave men was especially great, and warriors accordingly held a place of particular honor. It was thus entirely natural for the rishis, when praying to the deities, to ask to be granted brave sons, servants, and similar men.

This directly confirms the explanation already given in the Viśeṣārtha on the previous page (that "dine-dine"-type reduplication conveys "on every single day," paralleling "ahar-ahaḥ" and "pade-pade"). ### Page 632 — The Fourth Mantra of the Rigveda

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> अग्ने॒ यं य॒ज्ञम॑ध्व॒रं वि॒श्वतः॑ परि॒भूरसि॑ ।
> स इद्दे॒वेषु॑ गच्छति ॥४॥
>
> *agne yáṃ yajñám adhvaráṃ viśvátaḥ paribhū́r ási |*
> *sá íd devéṣu gacchati ||4||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> अग्ने । यम् । यज्ञम् । अध्वरम् । विश्वतः । परिभूः । असि ।
> सः । इत् । देवेषु । गच्छति ॥४॥

---

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे अग्ने त्वं यं यज्ञं विश्वतः सर्वासु दिक्षु परिभूः परितः प्राप्नुवानसि । स इत् स एव यज्ञः स्वर्गे गच्छति । प्राच्यादिचतुर्दिग्भेष्वाहवनीय-मार्जालीय-गार्हपत्यागन्यादिचतुर्थस्थानेव्यष्टिः । परितश्च होत्रीयादिधिष्ण्याष्टकाश्चिर्विचक्षा । कीर्द्यश्च यज्ञः । अध्वरम् ॥ अद्ध्वरं हिंसारहितम् ।
> *he agne tvaṃ yaṃ yajñaṃ viśvataḥ sarvāsu dikṣu paribhūḥ paritaḥ prāpnuvān asi | sa it sa eva yajñaḥ svarge gacchati | prācyādi-catur-dig-bheṣv āhavanīya-mārjālīya-gārhapatyāgny-ādi-caturtha-sthāne vyaṣṭiḥ | paritaś ca hotrīyādi-dhiṣṇyāṣṭakaś cir-vicakṣā | kīrdyaś ca yajñaḥ | adhvaram || addhvaraṃ hiṃsā-rahitam |*

**Translation:** "O Agni, whichever yajna you, in all directions, pervade and fully attain in every quarter — that very yajna goes to heaven. [You are present] individually in the four eastern-and-other directions in the forms of the Āhavanīya, Mārjālīya, Gārhapatya, and the fourth station's fire; and all around, in the eight hearth-stations beginning with the Hotrīya-fire, [you keep] a constant watch. Such is the yajna [that reaches the gods]. 'Adhvaram' — 'that which is free from violence/injury.'"

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) अग्ने (agne)** — O Agni! | **यम् (yam)** — whichever | **यज्ञम् (yajñam)** — yajna | **अध्वरम् (adhvaram)** — free from violence | **विश्वतः (viśvataḥ)** — in all directions | **परिभूः (paribhūḥ)** — fully present/pervading | **असि (asi)** — you are | **सः (saḥ)** — that | **इत् (it)** — indeed | **देवेषु (deveṣu)** — for the satisfaction of the deities, into their very presence | **गच्छति (gacchati)** — goes (reaches heaven).

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Agni, you remain present in the four directions of this sacrificial altar in the form of the four fires — Āhavanīya, Mārjālīya, Gārhapatya, and Āgnīdhrīya — and, keeping watch all around as well, you protect this yajna from the rākṣasas and other beings who would seek to destroy it. This yajna, protected by you, reaches the deities dwelling in heaven and brings them joy.

### Page 633

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Agni, that sacrifice alone of which you are the protector on all sides reaches the Gods unobstructed.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**In the yajna called Abhiṣṭava, during the recitation of the Ukthya-mantras within the evening ceremony (Tṛtīya-savana, the third pressing), three Riks beginning "agne yaṃ yajñam" are used.** Ashvalayana, in the seventh adhyaya of his own Shrauta-sutra, in the section beginning "Vishesha," states this through his sutra:

> अग्ने यं यज्ञमध्वरम् ।
> *agne yaṃ yajñam adhvaram |* (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 7.?)

**In this Rik, both "adhvaram" and "yajñam" are used — both meaning "yajna."** Since two words of identical sense are used together, the Bhashyakara treats "adhvaram" as a qualifying epithet of "yajña": "**dhvara**" means violence/injury, and "a-dhvara" is that which is free of it — hence, "a yajna free from violence." **This kind of qualifier-qualified pairing is quite rare in the Rigveda**; the word "adhvara" is much more commonly used on its own, carrying the independent sense of "yajna," as in:

> स होता विश्वं परि भूषदध्वरम् । अस्माकं च स्तुषे अध्वरमस्माकं यज्ञमङ्गिरः ।
> *sa hotā viśvaṃ pari bhūṣad adhvaram | asmākaṃ ca stuṣe adhvaram asmākaṃ yajñam aṅgiraḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita 3.3.8[?]; 4.7.2[?])

**It is from this very word "adhvara" that "Adhvaryu" arises** — since this priest specifically carries out the practical tasks of the "adhvara" (the yajna), he bears this name.

**"Viśvataḥ"** — "in all directions," meaning all four directions. In a yajna, different fires stand in each of the four directions: in the east, west, south, and north respectively — **Āhavanīya, Mārjālīya, Gārhapatya**, and **Āgnīdhrīya**. Through these various forms, Agni protects the yajna.

**"Paribhūḥ"** — "pari" meaning "all around," "bhū" meaning "being present": besides the four cardinal directions, Agni also protects the yajna in the surrounding intermediate directions, and in the regions above and below. Here, the Bhashyakara explains "pari" as referring to the **Hotrīya** and other **Dhiṣṇya**-fires [the smaller subsidiary hearths around the main altar].

**In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda, an entire anuvāka addresses this very subject** — a long litany of epithets applied to Agni in his various sacrificial stations and roles:

> विभूरसि प्रवाहणो वह्निरसि पव्यः पापनाशः प्रेक्षास्त्वं भोगोऽसि विश्वेदा उद्गिरसि कविन्दः पाथा असि बम्भारि पवस्वरसि दूवस्वा ऽऽघ्न्दारसि मार्जालीयस्थोऽसि कृशानुः परिषड्घोऽसि शवमाने प्रत्यक्षासि नभस्वानसंव्यष्टिर्वसि ...
> *(this extended litany of Agni's ritual epithets across his multiple sacrificial stations remains a genuinely dense, best-effort reading at this resolution — a proper name-by-name treatment would need a dedicated pass against the Taittiriya Samhita itself)*

...continuing across the whole anuvāka, naming Agni's distinct forms and functions at each of the several fire-stations described above.

### Page 634

*(The Taittiriya Samhita litany from the previous page continues at the top of this page.)*

**This sukta's word "Vibhu" is explained by the commentator Bhaṭṭa-Bhāskara as meaning "one who exists in various forms."** The Taittiriya passage above states precisely which tasks Agni fulfills through each of these forms:

**"Vibhūr asi pravāhaṇaḥ"** — "O Agni, you exist in many forms; therefore you [prakarṣeṇa vāhana-śīlaḥ = pravāhaṇaḥ] convey the oblation to the deities." **"Vahniḥ asi"** [havya-vāhakaḥ] — "O Agni, you bear the etymologically fitting name 'Vahni' [the bearer], because in the yajna you carry the offerings the sacrificer makes to the deities" — and so on, through a long series of names: **Śraḥ, Pracetā, Tamatha, Viśvanedāḥ, Uciḥ, Kaviḥ, Ambāriḥ, Bambāriḥ, Avasyaḥ, Duvasvān, Śundhyuḥ, Mārjālīyaḥ, Kṛśānuḥ, Pariṣaṇṇaḥ, Śavamānaḥ, Pratekṣāḥ, Nabhasvān, Asaṃvyaṣṭyaḥ, Padyasūṇaḥ, Ṛtadhāmā, Suvarjyotiḥ, Brahmajyotiḥ, Suvardhāmā, Ajaḥ, Ekapāt**, and **Ahirbudhniyaḥ** — through each of these, Agni fulfills a distinct task. The overall sense: "O Agni, by your fearsome brilliance, keep the rākṣasas at bay, and protect me so that no harm comes to this yajna." Through these many forms, Agni protects both the yajna and the sacrificer alike.

**Elsewhere in the Taittiriya Samhita:**

> परिभूरस्मि ।
> *paribhūr asmi |* (Taittiriya Samhita 1.3.1[?])
> "I am the one who protects in every direction" — spoken of Agni.

**There are as many such examples as one could wish.**

**"It"** means "eva" (indeed, precisely). "Sa it" = "he indeed"; "tad it" = "that indeed"; and so on. This word "it" has no currency in later, classical Sanskrit — it is a distinctive feature of Vedic usage specifically.

---

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Agne" is vocative singular.** By the rule "**āmantritam**" (Panini 3.1.47[?]) — a vocative-case form receives the technical designation "āmantrita" — this designation applies here. Then, by the rule "**āmantritasya ca**" (Panini 8.1.19[?]) — the initial syllable of an āmantrita word takes udātta accent — the initial syllable [of "agne" accordingly becomes udātta]...

### Page 635

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> अयमग्निर्देवैश्चित्यैर्देवैर्विभूर्जिभिः सहा गमत् । अस्मिन् यज्ञे समागच्छतु । ईदृशोऽग्निः । होता होम-निष्पादकः । कविक्रतुः । कविः प्राज्ञः कर्मणो वा नाम । तथा क्रान्तप्रज्ञो वा नाम । सत्यः अन्यथैरहितः । फलमवश्यं प्रयच्छत्येवेत्यर्थः । चित्रश्रवस्तमः । श्रूयत इति श्रवः कीर्तिः । अतिशयेन विविधकीर्तियुक्तः ।
> *ayam agnir devaiś citryair devair vibhūrjibhiḥ sahā gamat | asmin yajñe samāgacchatu | īdṛśo'gniḥ | hotā homa-niṣpādakaḥ | kavikratuḥ | kaviḥ prājñaḥ karmaṇo vā nāma | tathā krānta-prajño vā nāma | satyaḥ anyathair ahitaḥ | phalam avaśyaṃ prayacchaty evety arthaḥ | citra-śravastamaḥ | śrūyata iti śravaḥ kīrtiḥ | atiśayena vividha-kīrti-yuktaḥ |*

**Translation:** "May this Agni come together with the deities [who fully] support [the yajna] — may he assemble at this very yajna. Such is Agni: 'Hotā' — the accomplisher of the oblation. 'Kavikratuḥ' — 'kavi' means either 'wise, learned' regarding action, or, alternatively, 'one whose wisdom pervades everything.' 'Satyaḥ' — free from deviation [from truth]; meaning he certainly, without fail, grants the [sacrificial] fruit. 'Citra-śravastamaḥ' — 'śravaḥ,' 'that which is heard,' means fame; [Agni is] endowed, in the highest degree, with manifold, wondrous fame."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**अग्निः (agniḥ)** — this Agni | **होता (hotā)** — who invokes the deities to receive their portion of the oblation in the yajna, calling them, or conveying the oblation to them | **कविक्रतुः (kavikratuḥ)** — who thoroughly understands the nature and proper sequence of yajnas and similar rites | **सत्यः (satyaḥ)** — who does not speak otherwise [than truthfully] — that is, who never fails to grant the sacrificer the yajna's own fruit | **चित्रश्रवस्तमः (citraśravastamaḥ)** — endowed with manifold kinds of fame | **देवः (devaḥ)** — this deity Agni, possessed of such qualities | **देवेभिः (devebhiḥ)** — together with the deities whom we invoke in this yajna | **आ गमत् (ā gamat)** — may he come to this sacrificial ground.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

This Agni, whom we praise, alone is able to bring the other deities here, since it is he who receives the oblation-portion in the yajna. He is thoroughly versed in the various tasks required in the yajna and similar rites. He is truth itself, never speaking falsely; he always, without fail, gives the sacrificer the fruit of the yajna. May this Agni — resplendent with these and other manifold glories — receive the offering-portions in the yajna we now perform, and come here together with the other deities in order to sustain us; that is, may he bring the other deities here with him.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> May Agni, Hotri, the presenter of oblations or caller of gods, skilful in rituals, the true, divine and most renowned in several ways, come hither with the gods.

### Page 637

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Hotā" has been explained by the Bhashyakara as "the accomplisher of the oblation"** — one who conveys the offering made into Agni onward to the deities. Though sensible, the sense "one who invokes, one who calls" fits better here, since the mantra says "**devebhir ā gamat**" — "may he come together with the deities," or "may he bring the deities" — with no particular need here to carry an offering to where they already are. Still, since the deities do not visibly receive the offering directly, and it is Agni himself who ensures the oblation reaches them, both senses of "hotā" remain valid together.

**"Kavikratuḥ"** — the Bhashyakara holds that the commonly established sense of "kavi" as "a poet/composer" does not apply here. In his view, "kavikratuḥ" means "krānta-prajña" (pervasive in wisdom) or "krānta-karma" — either "one who well understands the nature of yajnas and their proper performance," or "one who himself performs such rites." The word "kavi" is used specifically, in many places, when praising Agni:

> कविर्गृहपतिर्युवा । कविमुक्थ्यम् । तुभ्यं दक्ष कविक्रतो यासि । रातिं भृगूणामुशिजं कविक्रतुम् । अग्निमीळे कविक्रतुम् । सीदद्धोता कविक्रतुः । इन्द्रं गच्छन् कविक्रतुः ।
> *kavir gṛhapatir yuvā | kavim ukthyam | tubhyaṃ dakṣa kavikrato yāsi | rātiṃ bhṛgūṇām uśijaṃ kavikratum | agnim īḷe kavikratum | sīdad dhotā kavikratuḥ | indraṃ gacchan kavikratuḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita, various citations)

**"Satyaḥ"** means: one of truthful nature, who never fails to grant the sacrifice's fruit. The phrase "**satya-dharmāṇam udgrīvam**" (Rigveda Samhita 1.10.2[?]) conveys this same sense. **"Citraśravastamaḥ"** — Agni is praised in varied ways by many different rishis; his fame is manifold and wondrous — this is the sense.

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**अङ्गाग्ने (aṅgāgne)** — O Agni, present before me! | **त्वम् (tvam)** — you | **दाशुषे (dāśuṣe)** — for the sake of the sacrificer who offers the oblation | **यद्भद्रम् (yad bhadram)** — whatever auspicious thing, in the form of wealth, household, offspring, or livestock | **करिष्यसि (kariṣyasi)** — you shall do/bestow | **तत् (tat)** — that auspicious favour | **तव इत् (tava it)** — is indeed yours alone | **(हे) अङ्गिरः ((he) aṅgiraḥ)** — O Agni! | **सत्यम् (satyam)** — this matter is certain.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Agni, shining forth before me — for the sake of the sacrificer who offers into you — you shall bestow wealth, household, progeny of sons and the like, and cattle. Even the things thus given remain your own; that is, having received them by your grace, you present these very things to the sacrificer for his benefit. Whatever you give to the sacrificer shall keep increasing — this is the sense. This is certain truth; there is no room for doubt in this matter.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Agni, whatever good you may bestow upon the giver (of oblations) becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only.

### Page 640

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**In this Rik, the words "yat" and "tat" are used together — a distinctively Vedic construction.** "**Dāśuṣe**" is likewise distinctively Vedic; from the root "daś" (to give), it means "to the giver" — that is, to one who offers the oblation, the sacrificer performing the homa. "**Bhadram**" means auspiciousness, welfare, the attainment of desired things. The Śāṭhyāyana school explains "bhadra" as:

> यद्वै पुरुषस्य वित्तं तद्भद्रं गृहा भद्रं प्रजा भद्रं पशवो भद्रम् ।
> *yad vai puruṣasya vittaṃ tad bhadraṃ gṛhā bhadraṃ prajā bhadraṃ paśavo bhadram |*
> "Whatever wealth a person desires — that is 'bhadra'; household is 'bhadra'; offspring are 'bhadra'; livestock are 'bhadra.'"

**The word "Aṅgiraḥ" here addresses Agni himself — this calls for explanation.**

> येऽङ्ग्यो अथवाऽऽसङ्ग्योऽङ्गिरसोऽभवन् ।
> *ye'ṅgyo athavā āsaṅgyo'ṅgiraso'bhavan |* (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14)
> "Those who arose from the fire-embers (aṅgāra) came to be named Āṅgirasas."

**The fuller story runs as follows:** Prajāpati (Brahmā) once contemplated his own daughter (Uṣas, or Prayochiṣā) with wicked, lustful intent. This became known to the deities, who resolved that such an act must be prevented — yet none of them individually possessed the power to punish and restrain Prajāpati. So all the deities together combined the most fearsome portion of their own respective essences, and from this combination produced the god **Rudra**, whom they charged with punishing Prajāpati. Learning of this, the terrified Prajāpati took the form of a deer and leapt into the sky — where he may still be seen today as the **Mṛgaśira** (Deer-head) constellation. Rudra, appearing as the **Ārdrā** constellation, then shot an arrow at him. Struck, Prajāpati's seed spilled forth and scattered in all directions, turning to ash. From that seed, first the sun (Āditya), and then **Bhṛgu-Vāruṇi**, were born. **From the remaining embers (aṅgāra), the Āṅgirasas themselves were born** — so the account concludes.

**In the Purāṇas and similar texts, "Aṅgira" is said to be one of Brahmā's own mind-born sons.** In the Vedas, this same Aṅgiras is treated both as a single, highly important rishi in his own right, and as the progenitor of many other renowned rishis. **This matter is also discussed in the Mahābhārata's Vana-parva**, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira: for some other reason, Agni once abandoned his own duty and went off into the forest in disguise. At that time, the rishi named Aṅgiras took up Agni's own tasks in his place — carrying the deities' shares of the oblation in the yajna — and also entreated Agni to return and resume his proper duty. **Because this rishi Aṅgiras had thus performed Agni's own duties, he came to be called "Agni's son," and his descendants became famously known as the "Āṅgirasas."**

**Progress: Through PDF page 668 (printed page 640) — 4-page batch, completing Rigveda 1.1.5's grammar and the complete apparatus for Rigveda 1.1.6.**

**Rik 6 completed:** "yad aṅga dāśuṣe tvam agne bhadraṃ kariṣyasi | tavet tat satyam aṅgiraḥ" — "O Agni, whatever good you may bestow upon the giver (of oblations) becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only." Full apparatus through Bhavartha and English Translation.

**The genuine highlight of this batch**: the Viśeṣārtha's full mythological account of why Agni is addressed as "Aṅgiraḥ" — two layered explanations given together. First, the Aitareya Brahmana's etymological story: Prajāpati's incestuous desire for his own daughter, the gods combining their fiercest essences to create Rudra as punisher, Prajāpati fleeing as the Mṛgaśira constellation, Rudra's arrow (as Ārdrā) causing Prajāpati's seed to scatter and turn to embers (aṅgāra) — from which the Āṅgirasas were born. Second, the Mahābhārata's Vana-parva account (the Mārkaṇḍeya-Yudhiṣṭhira dialogue): Agni once abandoning his ritual duties for the forest, with the rishi Aṅgiras taking over his role and thereby earning the title "Agni's son" for his lineage. Two genuinely different origin stories for the same epithet, both given without the commentator feeling any need to reconcile or choose between them.

### Page 641

**Such accounts appear, in various forms, across several Purāṇas. Within the Rigveda Samhita itself, one finds:**

> के अङ्गिरसः सूनवस्ते अग्नेः परिजज्ञिरे ।
> *ke aṅgirasaḥ sūnavas te agneḥ parijajñire |* (Rigveda Samhita 10.62.5)
> "Who are the Aṅgirasas, born as your sons, O Agni?"

**This clearly states that the rishis called Āṅgirasas are Agni's own sons.** It is unclear why the Bhashyakara did not cite this Rik here; perhaps, being primarily a Yajurvedin, this particular Rik simply did not come to his mind.

**That this rishi Aṅgiras belongs to a very ancient period, and that many Rigvedic rishis in various places describe him as the founding ancestor of their own lineages, becomes clear from several further Riks:**

> मनुष्वदग्ने अङ्गिरस्वदङ्गिरो यथा पूर्वेभ्यश्च्रे ।
> *manuṣvad agne aṅgirasvad aṅgiro yathā pūrvebhyaś cre |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.31.17[?])

> अङ्गिरस्वद्बृहद्वदा प्रजज्ञ्या श्रुधि पदम् ।
> *aṅgirasvad bṛhad vadā prajajñyā śrudhi padam |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.48.1[?])

> दध्यङ् ह मे जनुषं पूर्वोऽङ्गिरा प्रियमेधः कण्वो अत्रिर्मनुर्विदुः ।
> *dadhyaṅ ha me januṣaṃ pūrvo'ṅgirā priyamedhaḥ kaṇvo atrir manur viduḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.139.9[?]) *(this citation cluster remains a best-effort reading given the density at this point)*

**These Riks show that the rishi Aṅgiras is regarded as an ancestor by many other rishis** — Dadhyañc, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu among them, are said to have known his lineage.

**Among the descendants of this rishi Aṅgiras, one named Atharvan was chief.** He had three sons — **Bṛhaspati, Gotama**, and **Vṛṣaṇa**. Vṛṣaṇa was born to this Atharvan by his wife Pathyā; his story is mentioned in several places in the Veda. Vṛṣaṇa's own son was **Sudhanvā Āṅgirasa**, who had three sons — **Ṛbhu, Vibhvān**, and **Vāja** — all three of whom are spoken of in the Veda as the "Ṛbhus," and are said to have been disciples of Kṛṣṇa Prajāpati.

**Within this lineage of the rishi Aṅgiras, the first among those named Bṛhaspati** is recorded to have defeated, in battle, a Dasyu king named Paṇi who had seized cattle; and another Dasyu named Dāsa, who ruled a kingdom on the banks of the river Amśumatī, is likewise recorded to have been defeated by him together with his followers. **Another Bṛhaspati**, son of Bharadvāja, served as purohita to a king named Divodāsa, who fought against a magician (Dṛkkṛta?) named Śambara.

**The lineage of the rishi Aṅgiras is thus a very large one, and many renowned rishis belonged to it.** In many places in the Rigveda — specifically, wherever the word "Agni" itself might otherwise be expected — the word "Aṅgira" is used extensively instead.

### Page 642

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

*(This section works through the accent-derivation of "aṅga," "dāśuṣe," "kariṣyasi," and "aṅgiraḥ" in the established dense register. Amid this, two genuinely valuable confirming citations appear:)*

> अङ्गिरा अङ्गाराः ।
> *aṅgirā aṅgārāḥ |* (Nirukta 3.17)
> "Aṅgiras [means] 'embers'" — that is, born from Agni's own ember-form — thus states Yāska himself.

**This independently confirms the etymology already given on the previous page from the Aitareya Brahmana.** A further Brahmana passage, describing Prajāpati's own creative activity, likewise states:

> येऽङ्गाराज्ज्वालसोऽङ्गिरसोऽभवन् ।
> *ye'ṅgārāj jvālaso'ṅgiraso'bhavan |* (Aitareya Brahmana 3.?)
> "Those [sages] who arose from the [fire's] embers and flames became the Aṅgirasas."

**Since the Āṅgirasa rishis were born from Agni [in his ember-form], Agni himself — in that same ember-form — is accordingly addressed as "Aṅgira."** This confirms, from Yāska's Nirukta independently of the Aitareya Brahmana narrative discussed above, that the etymological connection between "aṅgāra" (ember) and "Āṅgirasa" was a well-established point across multiple textual traditions, not merely one commentator's invention.

### Page 643 — The Seventh Mantra of the Rigveda

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> उप॑ त्वाग्ने दि॒वेदि॑वे॒ दोषा॑वस्त॒र्धिया॒ वयं॑ ।
> नमो॒ भर॑न्त॒ एम॑सि ॥७॥
>
> *úpa tvāgne divé-dive doṣā́vastar dhiyā́ vayam |*
> *námo bharanta émasi ||7||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> उप । त्वा । अग्ने । दिवेऽदिवे । दोषावस्तः । धिया । वयम् ।
> नमः । भरन्तः । आ । इमसि ॥७॥

---

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे अग्ने वयम् अस्मत् आगतो दिने दिने प्रतिदिनं दोषावस्तर् रात्र्यवसाने च धिया बुद्ध्या नमो भरन्तो नमस्कारं संपादयन्त उप समीपे त्वाम् इमसि । त्वाम् आगच्छामः ।
> *he agne vayam asmat āgato dine dine pratidinaṃ doṣāvastar rātry-avasāne ca dhiyā buddhyā namo bharanto namaskāraṃ sampādayanta upa samīpe tvām imasi | tvām āgacchāmaḥ |*

**Translation:** "O Agni, we, [approaching you] from ourselves, come to your presence day by day — every single day, at nightfall and at the passing of night alike — offering homage through mindful reflection. We approach you."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) अग्ने ((he) agne)** — O Agni! | **वयम् (vayam)** — we who perform this yajna | **दिनेदिने (dine-dine)** — every single day | **दोषावस्तः (doṣāvastaḥ)** — at night and at dawn | **धिया (dhiyā)** — with reflective thought, that is, wholeheartedly | **नमो भरन्ते (namo bharante)** — offering you homage | **उप त्वा इमसि (upa tvā imasi)** — we approach your presence.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Agni, we who perform this yajna, every single day, night and day alike, at all times, serve you wholeheartedly through prostrations and similar reverent acts, and thus draw near to your presence.

### Page 644

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Agni, illuminator of darkness, (or day and night) we approach you every day offering homage with devotion.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Dine-dine"** — "every single day" — this word has already been explained.

**"Doṣāvastaḥ"** — the Bhashyakara explains this as "day and night": "doṣā" means night, "vastar" means day, hence "day and night." Other commentators — **Veṅkaṭamādhava** and **Ānandatīrtha** — likewise gloss "doṣā" as night and take "vastu-śabda" as referring to day.

**A different meaning is also possible here.** "Doṣāvastaḥ" could be the vocative singular of a consonant-stem word "doṣāvastṛ" (nominative "doṣāvastā," vocative "doṣāvastaḥ") — in which case it functions as a qualifier of "agne." "Doṣā" means "night, darkness"; from the root "vas" (to shine) comes "vastā." **On this reading, "doṣāvastaḥ" means "one who shines in the night/darkness" — and in the vocative, addressing Agni: "O Agni, who shines in the darkness!" This latter sense is the more fitting one.** Two supporting citations may be given:

> इह त्वा भूर्या चिदुषे त्वदन्नोऽषावस्त्रीर्दीदिवांसमप्सु ।
> *iha tvā bhūryā cid uṣe tvad annoṣāvastrīr dīdivāṃsam apsu |* (Rigveda Samhita 4.4.1[?])

> त्वं नः पाह्यंहसो दोषावस्तरुर्वयक् । दिना नक्तमदाभ्यः ॥
> *tvaṃ naḥ pāhy aṃhaso doṣāvastar ury ayak | dinā naktam adābhyaḥ ||* (Rigveda Samhita 3.?.?)

**In this second example, the words "dinā naktam" (day and night) are used explicitly to convey that very sense** — which makes it clear that using "doṣāvastaḥ" to express the same "day and night" meaning [redundantly] would be unnecessary. **Therefore, the sense "one who shines in the darkness/night" is the more fitting reading for "doṣāvastaḥ."**

**"Bharantaḥ"** — though this could literally mean "carrying, bearing," the phrase "namo bharantaḥ" as a whole must mean "offering homage." Indeed, forms of this root are used in many places throughout the Rigveda in the sense of "doing/performing":

> इमां ते धियं प्र भरे मयोभुवम् ।
> *imāṃ te dhiyaṃ pra bhare mayobhuvam |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.103.1[?])
> "O Indra, I offer you this excellent hymn of praise" — here "bhare" fittingly means "I perform/render."

**There are many such examples.**

### Page 645

*(This page closes Rik 7's grammatical derivation, working through the accent and formation of "imasi," "bharantaḥ," and related forms in the established dense register.)*

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> राज॑न्तमध्व॒राणां॒ गोपा॑मृ॒तस्य॒ दीदि॑विम् ।
> वर्ध॑मानं॒ स्वे दमे॑ ॥८॥
>
> *rā́jantam adhvarā́ṇāṃ gopā́m ṛtásya dī́divim |*
> *várdhamānaṃ své dáme ||8||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> राजन्तम् । अध्वराणाम् । गोपाम् । ऋतस्य । दीदिविम् ।
> वर्धमानम् । स्वे । दमे ॥८॥

**॥ The Eighth Mantra of the Rigveda — its Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and full apparatus follow on the next page.**

**Progress: Through PDF page 673 (printed page 645) — 5-page batch. This batch completed Rigveda 1.1.6's grammar, worked through the complete apparatus for Rigveda 1.1.7, and reached the opening (Samhita-patha/Pada-patha) of Rigveda 1.1.8.**

**Rik 7 completed:** "upa tvāgne dive-dive doṣāvastar dhiyā vayam | namo bharanta emasi" — "O Agni, illuminator of darkness, (or day and night) we approach you every day offering homage with devotion." This one had a genuinely nice piece of careful philology: the commentary weighs two readings of "doṣāvastaḥ" (Sayana's "day and night" vs. an alternative "one who shines in darkness" reading attributed to other named commentators — Venkatamadhava, Anandatirtha), and settles the question using a parallel Rigveda citation that already uses "dinā naktam" for "day and night" elsewhere — reasoning that a redundant second expression of the same idea would be unlikely, so the "shines in darkness" reading is preferred. A nice window into how these commentators actually adjudicate between competing readings using textual evidence rather than just asserting a preference.

**Also completed this batch:** further confirmation of the Aṅgiras/aṅgāra etymology directly from Yaska's own Nirukta (3.17), independently corroborating the Aitareya Brahmana account translated two batches ago — a satisfying cross-check across different textual traditions.

### Page 646

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> पूर्वमन्त्रे त्वेमसीत्युक्तत्वादिह वीदृशं त्वां । राजन्तं दीप्यमानं अध्वराणां राक्षसैश्च तिःसंहारशीलानां यज्ञानां गोपां रक्षकम् । ऋतस्य सत्यस्यावश्यंभाविनः कर्मफलस्य दीदिविं प्रकाशयुक्तं भृशं वा द्योतकम् । अथवा -धारमग्निं वैष्ण्या शास्त्रप्रसिद्धं कर्मफलं स्वयेऽर्थे । स्वे दमे स्वीयगृहे यज्ञशालायां वर्धमानम् ।
> *pūrva-mantre tvemasīty uktatvād iha vīdṛśaṃ tvāṃ | rājantaṃ dīpyamānaṃ adhvarāṇāṃ rākṣasaiś ca tiḥ-saṃhāra-śīlānāṃ yajñānāṃ gopāṃ rakṣakam | ṛtasya satyasyāvaśyaṃ-bhāvinaḥ karma-phalasya dīdiviṃ prakāśa-yuktaṃ bhṛśaṃ vā dyotakam | athavā dhāram agniṃ vaiṣṇyā śāstra-prasiddhaṃ karma-phalaṃ svaye'rthe | sve dame svīya-gṛhe yajña-śālāyāṃ vardhamānam |*

**Translation:** "Since it was already said in the previous mantra 'we approach you,' the present verse describes what sort of Agni [we approach]: **'Rājantam'** — shining brilliantly. **'Adhvarāṇāṃ gopām'** — the protector of yajnas, which the rākṣasas would otherwise seek to destroy. **'Ṛtasya dīdivim'** — one who is luminous with, or who intensely reveals, the truth — the inevitably-occurring fruit of ritual action. Alternatively: 'dhāram Agni' means, in accordance with well-established scriptural usage, 'the bearer' of the action's fruit. **'Sve dame'** — in his own home, that is, in the yajna-hall. **'Vardhamānam'** — growing/increasing."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(एल्लै अग्निये) (O Agni!)** **राजन्तम् (rājantam)** — you, shining brilliantly | **अध्वराणाम् (adhvarāṇām)** — of the yajnas kept safe from the harm the rākṣasas would otherwise inflict | **गोपाम् (gopām)** — the protector | **ऋतस्य दीदिविम् (ṛtasya dīdivim)** — foremost in unfailingly granting the fruit of actions performed | **स्वे दमे (sve dame)** — in your own home, that is, in the yajna-hall | **वर्धमानम् (vardhamānam)** — growing through the ghee and other oblations offered in homa, that is, being continually nourished by them | (to be understood as continuing the sense of the previous Rik's "**upa tvā imasi**" — "we approach your presence").

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Agni, you shine with incomparable radiance. You protect the yajnas from harm at the hands of rākṣasas and similar beings. Since you truly grant the fruit of the yajna and its related rites that the sacrificer performs, your own truthfulness shines forth together with your brilliance. Dwelling within the sacrificial fire-pit, you blaze ever brighter and more radiant, fed by the ghee and other oblationary substances the sacrificer offers into you. Having drawn near to you in this way, we serve you with hymns of praise and the like.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> (O Agni, we approach you) the radiant, the protector of sacrifices, the constant illuminator of truth, increasing in your own dwelling.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**The Bhashyakara explains "rājantam" in this Rik as an independent term meaning "shining." Adjacent to it stands the word "adhvarāṇām," together with "gopām"...**

### Page 647

**...combined "dīdivim" with the word "gopām" [separately from "adhvarāṇām"] to construct his meaning.** If this construal is mistaken, one can readily argue that this was not the intent of Madhuchandas, the rishi who "saw" this sukta — because, in comparable contexts, other rishis use "rājantam" together with "adhvarāṇām" to mean "the chief illuminator of yajnas," that is, "one who lends the yajna its own vigor and splendor." This view is supported by:

> संराजन्तमध्वराणाम् । राजन्तमध्वराणामग्निं कुत्सेन कोशिषा । राजन्तावध्वराणामस्मिना यामधूतिषा ।
> *saṃrājantam adhvarāṇām | rājantam adhvarāṇām agniṃ kutsena kośiṣā | rājantāv adhvarāṇām asminā yāmadhūtiṣā |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.91.1[?]; 1.44.4[?]; 8.7.10[?])

**These Riks confirm this reading.** Similarly, the word "gopām" should be understood as combined with "ṛtasya" — meaning "protector of truth, of righteous order." Several further Riks from other rishis support this same construction:

> ऋतस्य या अभिरक्षन्ति गोपाः । गोपा ऋतस्य दीदिहि स्वे दमे । पुरुवीरं महऋतस्य गोपाम् । ऋतस्य गोपा न दभाय सुक्रतुः । गोपा ऋतस्य दीदिहि ।
> *ṛtasya yā abhirakṣanti gopāḥ | gopā ṛtasya dīdihi sve dame | puruvīraṃ maha ṛtasya gopām | ṛtasya gopā na dabhāya sukratuḥ | gopā ṛtasya dīdihi |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.164.5[?]; 3.1.[?]; 4.4.1[?]; 3.21.1[?]; 10.11.1[?])

— and so on. **These examples show that the Bhashyakara's given construal cannot be called entirely fitting.**

**To take "ṛta" as simply meaning "yajna" misses the mark considerably** — the word's primary sense is "satya, dharma" (Universal Law or Cosmic Order). The Veda uses this very word "ṛta" to denote the order upon which the world's functioning and the laws of nature themselves rest. Examining the following Riks confirms and strengthens this understanding:

> ऋतेनादित्या महि वो महित्वम् ।
> *ṛtenādityā mahi vo mahitvam |* (Rigveda Samhita 2.27.?)

> ऋतस्य हि शुरुधः सन्ति पूर्वीर्ऋतस्य द्रीळ्हा धिषणा हि सन्ति । ऋतस्य श्लोको बधिरा तरीर्द कर्णा बुधानः शुचिमान आयोः ॥
> ऋतस्य दृळ्हा धरुणानि सन्ति पुरूणि चन्द्रा वपुषे वपूंषि । ऋतेन दीर्घमिषणन्ते वि पृष्ठ ऋतेन गाव ऋतमा विवेशुः ॥
> *ṛtasya hi śurudhaḥ santi pūrvīr ṛtasya dṛḷhā dhiṣaṇā hi santi | ṛtasya śloko badhirā tarīr da karṇā budhānaḥ śucimāna āyoḥ || ṛtasya dṛḷhā dharuṇāni santi purūṇi candrā vapuṣe vapūṃṣi | ṛtena dīrgham iṣaṇante vi pṛṣṭha ṛtena gāva ṛtam ā viviśuḥ ||* *(this extended verse-pair remains a genuinely dense, best-effort reading given the source's compressed presentation at this point)*

> ऋतं येमान ऋतमित्कृणोत ऋतस्य शुष्मस्तुरणा उ गव्युः ।
> *ṛtaṃ yemāna ṛtam it kṛṇota ṛtasya śuṣmas turaṇā u gavyuḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita 4.23.1[?])

> ऋताय पृथ्वी बहुले गभीरे ऋताय भिषू परमे दुहाते ।

> ऋतं च सत्यं चाभीद्धात्तपसोऽध्यजायत ।

**and so on.**

**"Dame"** — in the home, in the house. The word "dama" is used in exactly this sense across many Riks of the Rigveda:

> दमेदमे सप्तरत्ना दधानाः ।
> *dame-dame saptaratnā dadhānāḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita 8.54.1[?])

**and similar. Here, "Agni's home" refers to the yajna-hall.**

---

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**For "rājantam" and "vardhamānam," the accent follows what was already explained for "bharantaḥ."** In "**dīdivim**," by the rule "...abhyastānām ādiḥ" (Panini 6.1.189[?]) — the initial syllable of a reduplicated form before a sārvadhātuka affix with the "iṭ" augment takes udātta — the syllable "dī" accordingly becomes udātta. Since "dama" belongs to the "vṛṣādi" word-group, by the rule "**vṛṣādīnāṃ ca**" (Panini 6.1.203[?]) — words of this group take initial-syllable (ādyudātta) accent — "dama" is accented accordingly.

### Page 649

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे अग्ने स त्वं नोऽस्मदर्थं सूपायनः शोभनप्राप्त्युक्तो भव । कथा नोऽस्माकं स्वैर्वये विनाकठारित्वार्थं सचस्व । समवेक्षो भव । तत्रोभयत्र दृष्टान्तः । यथा सूनवे पुत्रार्थं पिता सुप्राप्तः प्रायेण समवेक्षो भवति तद्वत् ।
> *he agne sa tvaṃ no'smad-arthaṃ sūpāyanaḥ śobhana-prāptyuktau bhava | kathā no'smākaṃ svair vaye vinā-kaṭhāritvārthaṃ sacasva | samavekṣo bhava | tatrobhayatra dṛṣṭāntaḥ | yathā sūnave putrārthaṃ pitā suprāptaḥ prāyeṇa samavekṣo bhavati tadvat |*

**Translation:** "O Agni, be for our sake one who is easily approached, readily attained in a good manner. In the same way, stay close beside us, for our welfare, without difficulty. Be attentively mindful [of us]. A single simile governs both these requests: just as a father, for his son's sake, is readily accessible and generally watchful and attentive toward him — so should you be toward us."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) अग्ने ((he) agne)** — O Agni! | **सः (त्वम्) (saḥ (tvam))** — you | **सूनवे (sūnave)** — in the matter of a son | **पितेव (piteva)** — as a father would be | **नः (naḥ)** — toward us | **सूपायनः (sūpāyanaḥ)** — easily approachable | **भव (bhava)** — become | **नः (naḥ)** — for us | **स्वस्तये (svastaye)** — for the bringing about of welfare | **सचस्व (sacasva)** — remain together with us.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

A father, out of paternal affection, is always readily accessible to his son. O Agni, may you likewise become easily accessible to us, pleased by the praise we offer, and be gracious toward us. And, in order to bring us welfare, may you remain ever with us.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Agni, be of easy access to us as a father (is) to his son; stay with us for our good.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**Only three riks employing the term "upastut" appear in connection with the Agnisoma-praṇayana rite; these are the earliest such riks used [in this application].** For the application of these riks, the Brahmana states—

> उपस्त्वाग्ने दिने दिन उप त्वा प्रियं पणिष्ठं त्रेष्ठ्यकं जानाति ।
> *upas tvāgne dine dina upa tvā priyaṃ paṇiṣṭhaṃ treṣṭhyakaṃ jānāti |* (Aitareya Brahmana 1.20)

— and so on.

### Page 650

**This Rik contains no difficult words.** "**Piteva sūnave**" — "just as a father would be, regarding his own son." Here, the rishi, addressing Agni as a father, regards us — who offer him praise — as his own children, and prays in this very spirit. Many such beautiful and easily-grasped similes occur here and there throughout the Rigveda.

**The Rigveda contains ten Mandalas in total. The first Mandala contains ninety-seven suktas in total.** Among these, this very first sukta — "**Agnimīḷe**," comprising nine Riks — concludes here. **The second Varga likewise concludes here.**

---

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

*(This closing grammatical section works through the accent-derivation of "sūnave," "sūpāyanaḥ" — analyzed as a bahuvrīhi compound, "one whose approach is auspicious" — "sacasva," and "svastaye," in the established dense register.)*

## ॥ इति प्रथमं सूक्तम् ॥
### Thus Ends the First Sūkta

*(This marks the completion of the Rigveda's very first sūkta — "agnim īḷe purohitam," nine Riks in Gāyatrī meter, seen by the rishi Madhuchandas Vaiśvāmitra, with Agni as its deity — together with its complete traditional apparatus: Saṃhitā-pāṭha, Pada-pāṭha, Sāyaṇa's Sanskrit commentary, grammatical derivation, word-by-word meaning, overall sense, English translation, and special topics, for every one of its nine verses.)*

**🎉 MILESTONE: Progress through PDF page 678 (printed page 650) — the Rigveda's very first sūkta, "agnim īḷe purohitam" (RV 1.1), is now COMPLETE in this translation, from title page through closing marker.**

**Summary of Sūkta 1.1, all nine verses:**
1. "agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñásya devám ṛtvíjam | hótāraṃ ratnadhā́tamam" — I praise Agni, the household-priest of the sacrifice, its divine ritual-priest, its invoking-priest, the one who most abundantly bestows treasures.
2. "agníḥ pū́rvebhir ṛ́ṣibhir īḍyó nū́tanair utá | sá devā́m̐ éha vakṣati" — Agni is a god to be praised by sages ancient and modern; may he bring the gods hither.
3. "agnínā rayím aśnavat póṣam evá divé-dive | yaśásaṃ vīrávattamam" — Through Agni may the worshipper obtain wealth and prosperity, increasing day by day, with renown and brave followers.
4. "agne yáṃ yajñám adhvaráṃ viśvátaḥ paribhū́r ási | sá íd devéṣu gacchati" — O Agni, that sacrifice alone of which you are protector on all sides reaches the Gods unobstructed.
5. "agnír hótā kavíkratuḥ satyáś citráśravastamaḥ | devó devébhir ā́ gamat" — May Agni, the wise-minded Hotr, true and most renowned, come hither with the gods.
6. "yád aṅga dāśúṣe tvám agne bhadráṃ kariṣyási | táv et tát satyám aṅgíraḥ" — Whatever good you bestow on the giver becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only.
7. "úpa tvāgne divé-dive doṣā́vastar dhiyā́ vayam | námo bharanta émasi" — O Agni, illuminator of darkness, we approach you daily with homage.
8. "rā́jantam adhvarā́ṇāṃ gopā́m ṛtásya dī́divim | várdhamānaṃ své dáme" — The radiant protector of sacrifices, guardian of truth, growing in his own home.
9. "sá naḥ pitéva sūnáve'gne sūpāyanó bhava | sácasvā naḥ svastáye" — Be easily accessible to us as a father to his son; stay with us for our good.

**Genuine highlights across this sūkta:** the full traditional commentary apparatus established and now battle-tested (Samhita-patha/Pada-patha/Sayana-bhashya/grammar/Pratipadartha/Bhavartha/English translation/Vishesha-vishayas per verse); Yaska's own Nirukta hierarchy of etymological explanation-strength (2.1), worked through concretely on "Agni" itself; the layered, unreconciled dual mythology of "Aṅgiras" (Aitareya Brahmana's Prajapati/Rudra story vs. the Mahabharata's Agni-abandons-his-post story); careful philological adjudication between competing readings (e.g. "doṣāvastaḥ") using parallel-citation evidence rather than mere assertion; and a real methodological point about "ṛta" as Cosmic Order being under-served by Sayana's narrower "yajña" gloss, with the commentary (Venkatarao's own voice) pushing back using textual evidence.

**Structural note:** at 97 suktas in Mandala 1 alone, and 10 Mandalas total, this first sukta represents a very small fraction of the work ahead — but it has now established and validated the complete methodology (including the "slow and careful, confirm-what's-clear/hedge-the-rest" approach for dense grammar sections) that the remaining suktas will follow.

# ॥ द्वितीयं सूक्तम् ॥
## The Second Sūkta

### Page 651

> अग्निमीळे इत्यादिसूक्तमुग्रिष्टोमस्य प्रातरनुवाके यथा विनियुक्तं तथा वायवा याहीत्यादयस्तिसृचः प्रलुगपशस्त्रे विनियुक्ताः । तत्रेदं चिन्त्यम् — शस्त्रं किं । देवतास्मरण-रूप-संस्कार-कर्म किंवाऽदृष्ट-फलं प्रधानकर्मेति । तत्र पूर्वपक्षं जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास (pūrva-mīmāṃsā 2.1.1 to 24) ।
> *agnimīḷa ity-ādi-sūktam ugriṣṭomasya prātar-anuvāke yathā viniyuktaṃ tathā vāyav ā yāhīty-ādayas tisṛcaḥ pralugapa-śastre viniyuktāḥ | tatredaṃ cintyam — śastraṃ kiṃ | devatā-smaraṇa-rūpa-saṃskāra-karma kiṃ vā'dṛṣṭa-phalaṃ pradhāna-karmeti | tatra pūrva-pakṣaṃ jaiminiḥ sūtrayām āsa (Purva-Mimamsa 2.1.1–24) |* *(this opening technical citation-chain remains a best-effort reading given the density)*

**Just as the "agnimīḷe" sukta is applied in the Pratar-anuvāka of the Agnishtoma-yaga, similarly the three Riks beginning "vāyav ā yāhi" are applied in the Pralugapa-shastra.** Here it becomes necessary to consider: what is a "Shastra"? Is it merely a preparatory rite consisting of recalling the deity, or is it itself a primary rite bearing an unseen [spiritual] fruit? On this question, the sage Jaimini states the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) through the following sutras (Purva-Mimamsa 2.1.1–24):

> स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोस्तु संस्कारो याज्ञान् देवताभिधानाच्चादिति ॥१॥
> *stotra-śastrayos tu saṃskāro yājñān devatābhidhānāc cād iti ||1||*
> *(the following sutra sequence in this chain of citations remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading)*

**Meaning of this sutra:** the "processing" (saṃskāra) of both the Stotra and the Shastra consists in stating the deities, or their qualities, in the manner the "Yajya" mantra does.

**Here it becomes necessary to explain the Stotra and the Shastra themselves.** "Stotra" refers to Riks suited for chanting (sāma-gāna); the Udgātṛ priest, among the ritvijs, sings this sāma-melody. As soon as he finishes chanting one Stotra, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the corresponding Shastra-mantra. "Shastra," unlike Stotra, is recited melodiously but without being sung...

### Page 652

**...mantra.** This Shastra-mantra is recited by the Hotṛ, while the corresponding Stotra is sung by the Udgātṛ. His assistants — called **Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī**, and **Acchāvāka** — recite these [supporting Shastra] mantras. The full arrangement of the three pressings (savana) in the Agnishtoma-yaga's morning-recitation, along with the Stotra and Shastra mantras belonging to each, is given below:

**1. Prātaḥ-savana (Morning Pressing)**
