| 1. Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra | 1. Ājya-śastra |
| 2. Ājya-stotragaḷu | 2. Pṛuhugala-śastra |
| 3. " | *(these two recited by the Hotṛ)* |
| 4. " | 1. Ājya-śastragaḷu |
| 5. " | 2. " |
| *(these five Stotras sung by the Udgātṛ)* | 3. " |
| | *(these four Shastras recited by the Hotṛ's assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, and Acchāvāka)* |

**2. Mādhyandina-savana (Midday Pressing)**

| Stotra-mantras | Shastra-mantras |
|---|---|
| 6. Mādhyandina-savana-stotra | 6. Marutstrīya-śastra |
| 7. Pṛṣṭha-stotra | 7. Niṣkevalya-śastra |
| 8. " | *(these two recited by the Hotṛ)* |
| 9. " | 8. Niṣkevalya-śastra |
| 10. " | 9. " |
| *(these five sung by the Udgātṛ)* | *(these recited by the Hotṛ's three assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa and others)* |

**3. Tṛtīya-savana (Evening/Third Pressing)**

| Stotra-mantras | Shastra-mantras |
|---|---|
| 11. Ārbhava or Tṛtīya-savana-stotra | 11. Vaiśvadeva-śastra |
| 12. Agniṣṭoma-sāma (Yajñāyajñīya) | 12. Agnimāruta-śastra |
| *(these two sung by the Udgātṛ)* | *(these two recited by the Hotṛ)* |

**The Bhashyakara [in his earlier discussion above] identifies:** "**ājyaḥ stuvate**" — that the Udgātṛ sings the Stotra using the Ājya-stotra mantras (in the morning pressing); "**pṛṣṭhyaḥ stuvate**" — that the Udgātṛ sings the Pṛṣṭha-stotra...

### Page 653

**...(in the Midday Pressing); "pṛhugaḥ śaṃsati"** — the Hotṛ recites the Pṛhuga-shastra mantras (in the Prataḥ-savana); **"niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati"** — the Hotṛ recites the Niṣkevalya-shastra mantras (in the Madhyandina-savana). That is: as soon as the Udgātṛ finishes chanting the Ājya-stotras in the morning pressing, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the Pṛhuga-shastra mantras; similarly for the Pṛṣṭha-stotra and Niṣkevalya-shastra in the midday pressing, and so on.

**Here it must be shown that "Stotra" and "recitation" (śaṃsana) describe the deities' own qualities.** For example, in the mantra:

> इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्र वोचम् ।
> *indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocam |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.32.1)
> "I shall now proclaim Indra's heroic powers"

**— since this describes Indra's own heroic deeds, the mantra (whether Stotra or Shastra) is thereby describing the deity's qualities. Therefore, just as with Yajya-mantras, since Stotra and Shastra mantras describe the deities (or their specific qualities), these mantras are themselves preparatory (saṃskāra) to some other primary rite — that is, they are subordinate parts (aṅga) of it, not independent rites in their own right.** Because, by singing the deities' praises, the Stotra-Shastra mantras bring the deities' names and qualities to mind. Therefore these mantras carry no independent primacy of their own; they must be understood as subordinate to the deity-invoking act itself. The word "**tu**" in the sutra signals precisely this — that Stotra and Shastra lack independent primacy.

**The full details concerning the Yajya-mantra's own nature are treated in the sutras of the tenth Adhyaya, fourth Pada, of the Mimamsa-sutras** (Jaimini Sutra 10.4.6–41) — that discussion may be consulted there. *(This concludes the Pūrva-pakṣa — the objector's prima facie position.)*

### Page 654

**Sutra's meaning:** since the mantra states the deities' names in the relevant context, the mantra thereby describes the deities' qualities — that is, it becomes a subordinate part of the deity-invoking act. Therefore, mantras should be used, according to their sense, only in the specific contexts matching their known [deity-]position.

**The Siddhāntins [proponents of the established view] do not accept the pūrva-pakṣa stated in the preceding sutra**, because the word "tu" actually negates the notion that Stotra and Shastra are merely preparatory (saṃskāra). If one insisted they were preparatory, it would follow that a mantra must always be matched strictly to its literal deity-reference — meaning mantras naming a specific deity like Indra could only be used in rites addressed to that exact deity, disrupting the established, ordered sequence of mantras actually used in yajna practice. **For example:** in the Mahendra-graha rite, the mantra:

> अथ त्वा शूर नोनुमोऽदुग्धा इव धेनवः । ईशानमस्य जगतः स्वर्यशसमीशानमिन्द्र तस्थुषः ॥
> *atha tvā śūra nonumo'dugdhā iva dhenavaḥ | īśānam asya jagataḥ svar yaśasam īśānam indra tasthuṣaḥ ||* (Rigveda Samhita 2.13.13[?])

— is used as a Pragātha [paired hymn]. This mantra speaks of Indra specifically, not of Mahendra. On the strict view, this mantra should thus be usable only in a rite addressed specifically to Indra — meaning the established, ordered sequence of mantras used across the whole yajna would need constant disruption to match each mantra's literal deity-reference. **To refute this objection, the Pūrva-pakṣin now offers a further sutra:**

> वशावद्या गुणार्थं स्यादिति ॥२॥ (जै. सू. २-१-४)
> *vaśāvadyā guṇārthaṃ syād iti ||2||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.4)

**"The particle 'vā' here prevents strict one-to-one matching for each individual Pragātha. Whatever deity-name the mantra states may, where it carries general qualities, serve merely as an illustrative pointer (upalakṣaṇa) rather than a strict specification."** For example:

> सा वा एषा सर्वदेवत्या यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभेत ।
> *sā vā eṣā sarva-devatyā yad ajā vaśā vāyavyām ālabheta |* (Taittiriya Samhita 1.4.6.1[?])
> "That indeed is universally-deity-related — in that one should offer a barren she-goat consecrated to Vāyu."

**Here the word "ajā" (she-goat) and similar generic terms, in an enjoined rite, illustratively point toward the general quality [of a suitable animal] rather than a specific one — and the same reasoning applies to the Indra-example above.** Why? Because when a rite already carries its own specific qualifying details, there is no contradiction in also using a general term like "Indra" as a mere illustrative reference, even where the rite is really directed elsewhere. **Even in ordinary worldly usage, we observe the general term "king" applied even to a specific great king (Mahārāja).** Therefore, the Siddhāntin's proposed objection is itself refuted [by this further Pūrva-pakṣa argument].

### Page 655

**The word "vā" in the sutra resolves the difficulty of having to displace the Pragātha-mantra from its established position** — because the qualities stated in the mantra regarding Indra apply equally to Mahendra. If two mantras genuinely described different deities, the flaw the Siddhāntin raised would need to be accepted. But since one names "Indra" and the other "Mahendra," and there is no real difference between them, the flaw of disrupting the established sequence does not actually arise. **The word "Mahā" in "Mahendra" is merely a qualifying epithet of Indra himself** — just as, in ordinary usage, we call a Mahārāja simply "Rāja" (king): "Mahā" is only a qualifier, and "Mahārāja" and "Rāja" both refer to the same person. Likewise, "Indra" and "Mahendra" name the same single deity; the presence of the qualifier "Mahā" alone does not make Mahendra a different deity.

**For example:**

> यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभीत ।
> *yad ajā vaśā vāyavyām ālabhīta |*
> "A barren goat should be offered to the Vāyu-deity"

— this explicitly requires that the goat offered to Vāyu be barren. In other passages connected with Vāyu, only the plain word "ajām" (goat) may appear without this qualifier — yet even there, "ajām" must still be understood as meaning specifically "the barren goat." **Whether one says "ajā" or "ajā vaśā," the meaning is identical; in just the same way, "Indra" and "Mahendra" name a single deity** — this is the Pūrva-pakṣin's resolution. **The Siddhāntin now refutes this very resolution in the next sutra:**

> न श्रुतिसमुदायात्वादिति ॥४॥ (जै. सू. २-१-९)
> *na śruti-samudāyatvād iti ||4||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.9)

**"Even granting that 'vaśā' or 'rāja' might generally admit flexible reference, the deity of this particular Graha-offering is Indra, and Indra alone — fixedly established. Because a term's deity-affiliation must be determined by taking the whole expression together as a single unit (śruti-samudāya), not piecemeal. In the phrase 'Māhendra-graha' itself, the word 'Mahendra' —**

> महेन्द्राद् घोश्च ।
> *mahendrād ghaś ca |* (Panini 4.2.39[?])

**— is, by this very affixation rule, established as a deity-denoting term in its own right, distinct from 'Indra' alone. Therefore this is not simply Indra; in this specific instance, the general 'mahā-as-mere-qualifier' principle is overridden."**

**Progress: Through PDF page 683 (printed page 655) — 5-page batch opening Sūkta 2 of the Rigveda (RV 1.2, "vāyav ā yāhi").**

**This batch is different in character from Sukta 1**: rather than moving straight into the verses themselves, the commentary opens with an extended Mimamsa-sutra discussion (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.1–9) on the metaphysical status of Stotra and Shastra mantras — genuinely sophisticated philosophical argument conducted through a real back-and-forth: Pūrva-pakṣa (Stotra/Shastra are merely preparatory, subordinate to a primary rite, since they just describe deities' qualities) → Siddhānta objection (this would force disrupting the established mantra-sequence to match literal deity-references) → Pūrva-pakṣa's counter (the "vā" particle allows general/illustrative reference, so "Indra" and "Mahendra" can be treated as the same deity) → Siddhānta's refutation (no — "Mahendra" is grammatically its own distinct deity-term by Ashtadhyayi 4.2.39, so the general principle doesn't apply here). This dialectical structure — thesis, objection, counter, refutation — is a genuinely good window into how Purva-Mimamsa argumentation actually proceeds, worked through on a concrete ritual example (the Mahendra-graha offering) rather than in the abstract.

**Also included**: a genuinely valuable structural table laying out the Stotra and Shastra mantras across all three Savanas (Prataḥ, Mādhyandina, Tṛtīya) of the Agnishtoma Soma-yaga, showing which priest (Udgātṛ vs. Hotṛ and his three assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, Acchāvāka) performs which recitation at each stage.

**Target for next session:** continue forward from PDF page 684 / printed page 656 — likely the conclusion of this Mimamsa discussion, then the actual verses of Sukta 2 themselves.

### Page 656

**To take "the word describing a quality of Indra" as equivalent to "Mahendra" is not correct.** Even though mantras describe deities' qualities, where a distinct deity-name is specified, it must be treated as a genuinely different deity. Some scholars offer this etymology: "**mahān + indraḥ = mahendraḥ**" — "the great Indra"; and correspondingly, "**mahendro devatā asya saḥ = māhendraḥ**" — [the rite] "whose deity is Mahendra." On this view, since Indra is described as exceedingly great, this would merely describe a quality of Indra himself. **But this is incorrect. In the word "Mahendra," "Mahā" is not a qualifier of "Indra" — "Mahendra" is a single, complete word in its own right**, referring to a single deity called Mahendra alone. That is: Indra is one deity, Mahendra another.

**One might object: since Indra slew the demon Vṛtra, shouldn't he be called "Mahendra" specifically to honor that deed?** No — this is not so. It would then have to be said that Indra was merely "Indra" before slaying Vṛtrāsura, and became "Mahendra" only afterward, based on a temporal distinction — but the Veda admits no such usage, where a deity's very name shifts over time according to deeds performed. **Therefore, Indra never "became" Mahendra. From the very beginning, Indra has always been Indra, and Mahendra has always been Mahendra — two genuinely distinct deities.**

> गुणश्चानर्थक इति ॥३॥ (जै. सू. २-१-८)
> *guṇaś cānarthaka iti ||3||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.8)

**"If Indra alone were the intended deity, then in expressions such as 'dāsīr vaindra-graha' and 'Māhendra-graha,' the qualifying term 'mahat' (great) would become entirely purposeless. The word 'ca' indicates that this reason joins the one already given."**

**Sutra's meaning:** furthermore, beyond the reason already given, the quality-term itself would become purposeless. **Whether a deity's quality is permanent or transient, if a text merely praises a quality without conveying anything about the deity's own essential identity, the quality-word "mahān" in "Mahendra" would serve no function.** When performing a rite connected to a given deity, the rite must proceed in its proper sequence regardless of whether that deity's qualities happen to be restated. If the quality-term carried no genuine function here, then in a yajna already connected with Indra, restating his "greatness" would accomplish nothing. **If Indra alone were truly the deity for this yajna, it would simply be called the "Aindra-graha," not the "Māhendra-graha."** The very fact that it is called Māhendra-graha shows that "Mahendra" functions as its own genuinely distinct deity-name.

**The word "ca" in the sutra signals that this reason joins the one stated previously. A further reason now follows—**

### Page 657

> तथा याज्यापुरोरुचोरिति ॥५॥ (जै. सू. २-१-५)
> *tathā yājyā-purorucor iti ||5||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.5)
>
> **"For Indra and Mahendra, being distinct deities, the quality-word 'mahat' becomes meaningfully purposeful — just as their Puronuvakya-mantras themselves differ: 'endra sānasiṃ' (Rigveda Samhita 1.4.1) and similar are Indra's own Yajyā-Puronuvākyā; 'mahāṃ indro ya ojasā' (Rigveda Samhita 8.6.1) and similar belong to Mahendra."**

**Sutra's meaning:** just as with the Yajyā and Puronuvākyā mantras [already discussed]. We have already explained these two mantra-types earlier: **Puronuvākyā** invokes the primary deity first, at the time of offering the oblation; **Yajyā** is the mantra used to actually make the offering into the fire, addressing the deity already invoked. Both kinds are required to complete an offering dedicated to a given deity, and both — directly or indirectly — express precisely the intended deity. **In the present case, the Yajyā-Puronuvākyā mantras connected with Indra differ entirely from those connected with Mahendra** — that is, Indra has his own set of mantras, and Mahendra has his own, distinct set. For example: "endra sānasiṃ" belongs to Indra; "mahāṃ indro ya ojasā" belongs to Mahendra. **Therefore, Indra and Mahendra are established as genuinely distinct deities.**

**Regarding the word "purorucaḥ" used in this sutra, some examination is warranted.** Ashvalayana, in his own Shrauta-sutra, names seven Riks called "Purorucaḥ" — these are not found within the Rigveda Samhita itself, but are given in a supplementary chapter called "Vividhyantāpa," and have no direct connection to the Yajyā-mantras at all. Yet the sutra here uses "purorucaḥ" in place of "puronuvākyā." **Either this word was used here by mistake, or this variation arose through the sutra's own transmission across different lineages** — [an honest acknowledgment of a genuine textual puzzle rather than a forced resolution].

**The Pūrva-pakṣin now raises a further objection, regarding the earlier "vaśā" (barren goat) example:**

> वशायामर्थसमुदायादिति ॥६॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१०)
> *vaśāyām artha-samudāyād iti ||6||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.10)
>
> "The 'vaśā' heard in the injunction-passage — regarding that very passage's own usage, through the generic term (bhāga-śabda), in the offering-context..."

### Page 658

> न विरुध्यते । भागत्वलक्षणार्थस्य वशायां समुदायात् । तच्च प्रत्यक्षेण गोचरम् इभ्यते । इन्द्रमहेन्द्रयोस्तु भेदे उपपादिते । तस्माद्विषमो दृष्टान्तः । एवं संस्कारपक्षे प्रगाथस्येन्द्रकर्मण्यनर्थक्य-समापत्त्यादार्षिकं स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोः प्रधानकर्मत्वमिति सिद्धान्तिनो मतम् ।
> *na virudhyate | bhāgatva-lakṣaṇārthasya vaśāyāṃ samudāyāt | tac ca pratyakṣeṇa gocaram ibhyate | indra-mahendrayos tu bhede upapādite | tasmād viṣamo dṛṣṭāntaḥ | evaṃ saṃskāra-pakṣe pragāthasyendra-karmaṇy anarthakya-samāpattyād ārṣikaṃ stotra-śastrayoḥ pradhāna-karmatvam iti siddhāntino mataṃ |*

**Meaning:** there is no contradiction. **Because the generic sense of "vaśā" is established as encompassed within the perceptibly-visible object [the goat] itself** — whereas the distinction between Indra and Mahendra has already been established as genuinely real. **Therefore the analogy with "vaśā" does not hold in this case.** Given this — since treating Stotra/Shastra as merely preparatory would render the Indra-Pragātha useless in its own rite — **it becomes the Siddhāntins' considered position that Stotra and Shastra are themselves primary rites**, established through the rishis' own [authoritative] tradition.

**Yet the Pūrva-pakṣin once more attempts to refute this very conclusion:**

> यत्रेति पार्थक्येन पृक्षमिति ॥८॥ (जै. सू. २-१-११)
> *yatreti pārthakyena pṛkṣam iti ||8||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.11) *(this final sutra in the sequence remains a genuinely dense, best-effort reading given the compressed technical shorthand here)*

*(The commentary now proceeds to state the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion of this entire discussion.)*

### Page 659

**The statement in this sutra is used to refute the Siddhāntin's own view.** Wherever a rite connected with Indra takes place, reciting the Pragātha (Stotra-Shastra) is fitting — because that mantra pertains specifically to Indra. Mantras stating a sense pertaining to Indra should indeed be used in rites connected with Indra — this much the Siddhāntin grants. **But correspondingly**, the mantra connected with Indra is only capable of expressing Indra specifically; the mantra connected with Mahendra is capable only of expressing Mahendra. For this very reason — since Stotra-Shastra mantras have the capacity to directly express their own intended deities — they may be used in that particular deity's rite.

**The main point:** whatever mantra is capable of expressing a particular deity, that mantra is used in that deity's own rite — that is, a mantra's application (viniyoga) follows from its own meaning. If a mantra's sense varies such that it is *not* capable of directly expressing the intended deity, it is not fit for use in that deity's rite. **A mantra's application thus follows precisely from its own capacity to express its deity** — this remains the continuing Pūrva-pakṣa.

**Now the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion — is stated:**

> अस्ति वा श्रुतिसंयोगात्त्वेकेन स्यातिशंसती क्रियोक्त्यिं विदध्यातामिति ॥९॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१३)
> *asti vā śruti-saṃyogāt tv ekena syāti-śaṃsatī kriyoktyiṃ vidadhyātām iti ||9||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.13) *(this concluding sutra remains a best-effort reading given its compressed technical form)*

### Page 660

> तिस्ऋचे । यदि देवतास्मरणरूपं दृष्टं प्रयोजनं न लभ्येत तर्ह्य्ऋषमस्तु । प्रधानकर्मत्वे हेत्वन्तरमाह ॥
> *tisṛce | yadi devatā-smaraṇa-rūpaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ na labhyeta tarhy ṛṣam astu | pradhāna-karmatve hetv-antaram āha ||*

**Meaning:** if the visible [worldly] purpose of deity-recollection alone cannot be established, then let there be an unseen purpose instead. [The Siddhāntin] now states a further reason for Stotra-Shastra's status as a primary rite.

**Sutra's meaning:** the words "stauti" and "śaṃsati," being stated directly within the Vedas themselves, are used as primary [acts] in the relevant ritual context, and thereby produce an "apūrva" (unseen fruit) for the rite. **The words "asti vā" indicate that Stotra and Shastra are not merely preparatory** — that is, they are not subordinate parts of some other primary rite. Since these terms are used directly within the Vedas, their stated meaning is itself Veda-related — they are themselves a portion of the Vedic mantras, and thus connected directly to the primary rite. **That is: reciting the Stotra-Shastra is not a subordinate part of some other rite — it is itself the primary rite.** This is now established as the Siddhānta.

**A further point now follows: what actually constitutes genuine "praise" (stuti)?** Setting aside the possessor of qualities (a deity or person) and simply stating the qualities as the principal, identifying matter — that constitutes genuine praise. For example: "**yo devaśabdī sa caturvedābhidhyaja**" — "one skilled in the four Vedas, among the deva-party" — here, since the statement's qualities actually identify a specific person, people come to know who is meant. But if a quality is stated without thereby identifying anyone specific, that does not constitute genuine praise. For example: "**yaś ca turvedābhijña stvākāraya**" — "call forth whoever here knows the four Vedas" — since "knowing the four Vedas" here doesn't pick out any one specific person, no one's quality has actually been praised; the sentence's true intent is simply "call such a person," not a description of anyone's qualities.

**In the same way, in mantras: where a mantra states that whichever deity possesses certain qualities is meant by it — giving the quality genuine identifying primacy — then the root "stu" functions in this quality-denoting sense, and the mantra properly counts as a Stotra.**

**Since Stotra and Shastra thus have genuine, direct connection to the Veda itself, they are primary rites.** Some individual mantras may not explicitly name a deity — but since the sukta containing them is devoted to one specific deity throughout, an unnamed mantra within it should still be understood as addressing that same deity, since the preceding and following Riks make this clear. **Therefore: if a mantra containing merely the plain word "Indra" occurs amid mantras otherwise connected with Mahendra, it should be understood as referring to Mahendra himself — not to Indra alone.** Context and sequence, taken together...

> *śabda-pṛthaktvāc ceti ||10||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.23)

Since these Ājya-stotras and similarly-named Stotras are distinct among the primary rites, their individual connection to deities becomes well-founded — and the same applies equally to the Shastras."**

**Sutra's meaning:** because the word [twelve] is used separately [for Stotra and for Shastra], indicating a distinct primary rite in each case.

**There is a Vedic statement:** "**dvādaśāgniṣṭomasya stotrāṇi**" — that the Agnishtoma-yaga has twelve Stotras and twelve Shastra-mantras (see page 652 above). Here, the word "**dvādaśa**" (twelve), stated separately, indicates twelve *distinct* Stotras. Had all twelve addressed a single deity collectively, there would have been no need to specify "twelve" at all — one would simply have said "such mantras," not given an exact count. **Since "twelve" is stated as a precise number, it is established that there are twelve genuinely distinct Stotras — and, correspondingly, twelve distinct Shastra-mantras** (their names were already given on page 652). Nor does this create the opposite problem of needing twelve *separate deities* — stating a bare number carries no such implication.

**Meaning:** on the objector's view, this second statement becomes purposeless. **In the Veda: "āgneyā grahā bhavanti"** — "Agni-related substances become the Grahas here" — meaning one should praise Agni. **Elsewhere, addressing the same matter: "āgneyāḥ stuvate" and "āgneyāḥ śaṃsanti"** — meaning one should perform Stotra using specifically Agni-related mantras or suktas. If the sole purpose were simply to establish that Agni should be praised, wouldn't the first statement alone have sufficed? What does the second add? **On the Siddhānta's own reading, however, both statements serve genuine, distinct purposes**: the first establishes *that* Agni is the deity here; the second establishes *which specific mantras* should be used to praise him. Both scriptural statements thus receive a coherent, non-redundant reading. **A further reason follows:**

> अन्यश्चार्थः प्रतीयत इति ॥१२॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२१)

On the primary-rite view, however, the distinction is naturally established: whatever is accomplished through a sung mantra is called Stotra; whatever is accomplished through an unsung, recited mantra is called Shastra."**

**Sutra's meaning:** [the terms] convey genuinely distinct meanings from one another.

**In the Veda: "sambaddhe vai stotra-śastre"** — Stotra and Shastra mantras are mutually connected...

### Page 663

**...it is said.** "Connection" here means holding between *two* distinct things, not existing for one thing alone — and to speak of genuine connection, the two objects must be distinct while sharing some point of commonality. **This shows that the words describing Stotra and Shastra as "preparatory" must carry genuinely different meanings for each** — a single "preparatory" description could not otherwise sustain any real distinction. Because if both merely supported one single deity-illuminating rite, they would in effect be the same rite, with no mutual difference possible. **But when Stotra and Shastra are understood as primary rites, their meanings genuinely diverge.** Though the underlying roots share a common basic sense, "**Stotra**" refers specifically to a mantra capable of being sung/chanted, while "**Shastra**" refers to a mantra recited melodiously but *without* singing. **This is itself stated directly in the Veda, requiring no further proof. A further reason follows:**

> अभिधानं च कर्मण इति ॥१३॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२६)
> *abhidhānaṃ ca karmaṇa iti ||13||* (Jaimini Sutra 2.1.26)

### Page 664

> देवताप्रयुक्तं फलमाम्नातं । अतो न देवतासंस्कारः किंतु प्रधानकर्मेति स्थितं ।
> *devatā-prayuktaṃ phalam āmnātaṃ | ato na devatā-saṃskāraḥ kiṃtu pradhāna-karmeti sthitaṃ |*

**Meaning:** the fruit stated here is not one merely accruing via the deity — therefore Stotra-Shastra are not preparatory to deity-worship, but are established as primary rites in their own right.

**The fuller sense:** it is well known that certain mantras within suktas yield desired fruits through their recitation. For fruit to genuinely accrue, mantras must be independent and primary — this could not hold if they were merely preparatory, subordinate parts. In ordinary life, when pursuing an important task, we rely on the chief person capable of accomplishing it, not on his servants, who lack that capacity themselves. **In the same way, since Stotra-Shastra mantras are primary within their own rite, they are capable of yielding both seen and unseen fruits.** The Vedic statement "**stutasya stutam asi**" itself states the fruit obtained through Stotra; likewise "**indriyāvanto vanāmahe ghṛtenāktim ajim iṣam**" states Stotra's own fruit specifically — not a fruit given by the deity directly. **Therefore Stotra and Shastra are not subordinate to deities — they are primary rites.**

**Given this, in variant/subordinate rite contexts, the fruit must be inferred accordingly.** On the rival "preparatory" view, one would also have to infer, in such variant contexts, some other deity's name-term even where absent from the mantra — which is untenable. **To avoid this, Stotra-Shastra's status as primary rites has been established.** This same matter is confirmed in the tenth Adhyaya of Jaimini's own Sutras:

> ग्रहाणां देवतास्तुत्ये स्तुतशस्त्रयोः कर्मत्वाद्विकारः स्यात् ।
> *grahāṇāṃ devatā-stutye stuta-śastrayoḥ karmatvād vikāraḥ syāt |* (Purva-Mimamsa 10.4.46)

**On this matter, summary verses from the Nyāya-mālā-Vistara commentary are cited:**

**"In 'pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati' and similar expressions, what is stated through the qualifying accusative term is itself the primary matter; the visible recollection of the deity that results is merely a secondary quality of Stotra and Shastra. ### Page 665

**This is said. These two verses condense and summarize everything discussed so far.** The statements "pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati, niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati, ājyaṃ stuvate, pṛṣṭhyaṃ stuvate" are simply instructions used within the Agnishtoma-yaga. **"Pṛhuga" and "Nishkevalya" name Shastra-mantras; "Ajya" and "Prishtha" name Stotra-mantras.** Riks used to praise deities without being sung are called "Shastra"; mantras suited to chanted praise are called "Stotra." **These Stotra-Shastra mantras are themselves primary, each bearing its own distinct fruit.**

**If it were said instead that these mantras are merely preparatory, this would force the roots "stu" and "śaṃs" to be understood as describing only a deity's quality — with no primary sense of their own.** But a sentence like "Devadattaḥ caturvedābhijñaḥ" (Devadatta, knower of the four Vedas) constitutes genuine praise precisely because it identifies a specific person; if no such connection existed, no genuine praise would be possible. **Therefore, Vedic injunctive statements such as "ājyena devaṃ prakāśayet" (one should illuminate the deity through Ajya) would lose their primary sense entirely on the rival view. To avoid contradicting scripture, one must accept that Stotra and Shastra are themselves primary rites** — bearing, if not visible purpose, then certainly an unseen one (adṛṣṭa-phala).

**In the Agnishtoma, the Hotṛ, commanded before sunrise, should recite the Prātar-anuvāka.** This is stated in a single chapter of the Aitareya Brahmana:

> देवेभ्यः प्रातर्यावभ्यः प्रेषितोऽनुब्रूयाद्धृतीचारणायृगादि ब्राह्मणम् ।
> *devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyaḥ preṣito'nubrūyād dhṛtī-cāraṇāya ṛg-ādi brāhmaṇam |* (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14)

**Within this Prātar-anuvāka, the "agnimīḷe" sukta forms a part** — this has already been explained [in Sukta 1]. **In the morning pressing, following the Vaishvadeva-Grahana, the Hotṛ is to recite the Pralugat-Shastra — which consists of the sukta beginning "vāyunā yāhi" [Sukta 2 itself].** This is confirmed both in the relevant Brahmana section and in Ashvalayana's own Shrauta-sutra (5.10[?]).

**The Anukramaṇikā [index] entry for this sukta reads:**

> वायो नायहि । इन्द्रवाय्वादित्यमैत्रावरुणाश्च त्रयो देवताः, पालुगत-देवता इति ।
> *vāyo nāyahi | indra-vāyu-āditya-maitrāvaruṇāś ca trayo devatāḥ, pālugata-devatā iti |*
> "'Vāyav ā yāhi' — with Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, and Mitra-Varuṇa as its three deities — a Prāluga-deity sukta."

**Its meaning:** "vāyunā yāhi" and so on is a nine-versed sukta.

**On the day of the Agnishtoma when the Soma juice is crushed and extracted — called "Sutya-dina" or "Stutya-dina"** — on that morning, before sunrise (after the previous midnight has passed, but before dawn), **the Adhvaryu speaks the directive (Praiṣa-mantra) to the Hotṛ: "devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyaḥ hotar anubrūhi,"** and the Hotṛ then immediately recites the Prātar-anuvāka mantras. This is stated in the Aitareya Brahmana itself:

> देवेभ्यः प्रातर्यावभ्यो होतरनुब्रूहीत्यध्वर्युः ।
> *devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyo hotar anubrūhīty adhvaryuḥ |* (Aitareya Brahmana 3.14)

**These Prātar-anuvāka mantras include the "agnimīḷe" mantras and others** [i.e., all of Sukta 1] — their application has already been explained.

**We shall now describe, in careful detail, the sequence the Hotṛ follows when reciting the Prātar-anuvāka.** In the yajna, the Adhvaryu — who directs the Hotṛ, the primary ritvij — must periodically instruct the other ritvijs to perform their respective tasks; such directive statements are called "**Praiṣas**." Here, the Adhvaryu addresses the Hotṛ: "O Hotṛ! Recite the Prātar-anuvāka mantras, addressing the deities." **Upon this, the Hotṛ proceeds to the vicinity of the Āgnīdhra fire-pit and, for the sake of a mantra-linkage, offers one Ājya-oblation into the Āhavanīya fire and two into the Āgnīdhra fire, following the prescribed mantras. He then enters the Havirdhāna-hall (where the Soma-cart is kept) through its eastern doorway, sits near the yoke of the carts there, and recites this mantra first—**

### Page 667

> आप्रे रेवतीक प्रयज्ञा हि वसुक क्रतुं च भद्रं बिभृथामृतं च । रायश्च स्था स्वश्च शंख्रिके सरस्वती कद्वणके वयो धात् ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-११०-१)
> *(this opening mnemonic verse remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading given its compressed form)*

**Following this, the Hotṛ addresses Agni, Uṣas, and the Aśvin-deities in turn, reciting the Prātar-anuvāka mantras — in three portions.** Mantras addressing Agni belong to the "**Āgneya-kratu**"; those addressing Uṣas, to the "**Auṣasya-kratu**"; those addressing the Aśvins, to the "**Āśvina-kratu**." **Within each of these kratus, there are seven distinct sections, each in a different meter** — Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇik, Jagatī, and Paṅkti. These mantras — not fewer than a hundred in total — must be recited continuously from midnight until dawn. Depending on context, they are recited in one of seven accent-registers, including **upāṃśu-svara** and **mantra-svara**. **Among these Prātar-anuvāka mantras, within the Āgneya-kratu's own portion, the "agnimīḷe" sukta is included** — already expounded above.

**Now, in the morning pressing, following the Vaishvadeva-grahaṇa, the Hotṛ must recite the Shastra-mantra called the "Pralugat-shastra."** This Shastra-mantra includes the mantras of this present, second sukta, beginning "vāyunā yāhi."

---

**It is worth explaining here what "Prātaḥ-savana" (the morning pressing) actually means.** In the Soma-yaga, the Soma creeper's juice is crushed out with stones, and, following prescribed mantra-procedures, homa and similar rites are performed with that juice for the deities' satisfaction — after which the sacrificer and his ritvijs drink the Soma juice. **There are seven varieties of Soma-yaga**, traditionally called by the seven "Soma" designations: **Agnishtoma, Atyagnishtoma, Ukthya, Shodashi, Atiratra, Aptoryama**, and **Vajapeya**. Among these, the **Agnishtoma-yaga is the foundational form** — that is, it serves as the base from which the remaining six Soma-yagas derive, through certain modifications.

**We shall summarize the Agnishtoma-yaga's procedure here.** Its full, prescribed treatment is given at length in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda, Kanda 6, Adhyayas 1–8. **Since explaining this rite's own form requires clarifying many technical terms — and since doing so fully would make this work excessively long — only the Sanskrit verses summarizing the rite's structure are given here, together with a Kannada explanation of only those points genuinely useful for the present context:**

**A concise summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure:**

> अथाग्निष्टोमसंज्ञेन ज्योतिष्टोमेन याजयेत् । स पूर्वमृत्विजो वृत्वा देवभावमिनिश्चये ॥
> *athāgniṣṭoma-saṃjñena jyotiṣṭomena yājayet | sa pūrvam ṛtvijo vṛtvā deva-bhāvam iniścaye ||*

### Page 670

**A Soma-yaga may have a single sacrificer, or as many as sixteen ritvijs.** In some Soma-yagas, many sacrificers together, along with an even larger number of ritvijs, participate. **Such a Soma-yaga, performed jointly by many people together, is called a "Sattra."** This Sattra-yaga is of two kinds: one performed continuously over twelve days, and another performed over a full year. The year-long Sattras are themselves of many kinds — **Ganamayana, Adityanamayana, Angirasamayana**, and others — of which Ganamayana serves as the foundational form underlying all the rest.

**"Abhiplava"** is the name given to a Soma-yaga performed over six days. This too is of two kinds: **Abhiplava** and **Prishthya**. The great sage Ashvalayana describes the defining character of both: "**ubhayato-jyotiḥ ṣaḍahakam**" and "**antarataś-jyotiḥ ṣaḍahakam**." That is: in a six-day Soma-yaga where the first and last days are performed like the Agnishtoma-yaga, and the remaining four days like the Ukthya Soma-yaga, that special form is called "**Abhiplava**." "**Prishthya**" refers to the variant Soma-yaga where the first and fourth days are performed like Agnishtoma, and the remaining days like Ukthya.

**In the Agnishtoma-yaga, the day when the Soma juice is pressed and extracted is called "Sutya-dina."** Since Stotra and Shastra mantras are recited during the time of extracting the Soma juice, this day is also called "**Stutya-dina**." On this day, in the early morning — that is, after the previous night's midnight has passed, but before sunrise, from when the birds' calls first begin until the earliest light of dawn — **the mantras called the Pratar-anuvaka must be recited to completion.** This Pratar-anuvaka comprises three portions: the **Agneya-kratu** (Riks connected with Agni), the **Auṣasya-kratu**, and the **Aśvina-kratu**. Each portion must contain numerous mantras spanning the seven meters — Gayatri, Anushtubh, Trishtubh, Brihati, Ushnik, Jagati, and Pankti.

**After reciting the Pratar-anuvaka, the rite called "Prataḥ-savana" takes place.** "Savana" means: crushing the Soma creeper with stones and extracting its juice. This rite occurs at three separate times: extraction in the morning is called "**Prataḥ-savana**"; extraction at midday is called "**Madhyandina-savana**"; extraction in the evening is called "**Tritiya-savana**."

**Across these three Savanas together, twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras must be recited in total.** We have already explained their sequence on page 652.

**During the recitation of the Pratar-anuvaka mantras, the sukta "agnimīḷe" is recited — its application has already been explained.** Now, the second sukta, "vāyunā yāhi"...

### Page 671

**...the nine-versed sukta; and the third sukta, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ," comprising twelve Riks, are to be recited by the Hotṛ during the recitation of the mantras called the "Pralugat-shastra."** The sequence of these Pralugat-shastra mantras runs as follows — mantras praising the **seven deities**: **Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā, Aśvinau, Indraḥ, Viśve-devāḥ**, and **Sarasvatī**. Each deity is addressed by three Riks in turn. **In this nine-versed sukta "vāyunā yāhi": the first three Riks address Vāyu; Riks four through six address Indra-Vāyu; Riks seven through nine address Mitrā-Varuṇā. In the following sukta, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ": Riks one through three address the Aśvins; four through six, Indra; seven through nine, Viśve-devāḥ; and nine through twelve, Sarasvatī.** Together, these two suktas thus contain the Shastra-mantras for all seven deities, in seven groups of three Riks each. **The Hotṛ recites these — this second Pralugat-shastra — in the morning pressing, immediately after the Udgātṛ has sung the Ājya-stotra, following the earlier-recited [Sukta 1]. This is the application (viniyoga) of both this sukta and the following, third sukta.**

**This application is confirmed in the Aitareya Brahmana, in the section beginning "gṛhe'laṃ" (Aitareya Brahmana 3.1)**, and also by Ashvalayana himself in his own Shrauta-sutra, in the section beginning "stotram agre śakrāt" (Ashvalayana Sutra 5.10). **The Anukramaṇikā states this as follows:**

> वायो वायस्त्वं प्रे वायनस्त्वंत्रावरुणास्त्वाचि अग्निना द्वादशाश्च्वैन्द्रैश्वदेवसारस्वास्त्वैचास्त्वैचा प्रुलगदेवता ।
> *(this compressed Anukramaṇikā entry remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading; its overall sense, however, is confirmed by the clear surrounding prose)*

**That is: in the sukta "vāyav ā yāhi," each set of three Riks in turn is assigned one deity — Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā — and in the sukta "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ," the following four deities — Aśvinau, Indraḥ, Viśve-devāḥ, Sarasvatī — are similarly praised, three Riks each. All seven of these deities together bear the name "Pralugat-devatāḥ."**

**Regarding this sukta "vāyav ā yāhi" — as with the preceding "agnimīḷe" sukta, its meter throughout is Gāyatrī.** The sukta's first three Riks are Vāyu-related. Among them, the first Rik serves as the Puronuvākyā for the Vāyu-deity, and the second Rik serves as the Puronuvākyā for the Indra-Vāyu [offering] — this application is stated directly.

**Ashvalayana likewise states, in his own Shrauta-sutra:**

> वायुना याहि दर्शते न्द्रवायू इमे सुता इत्यनुवाक्ये ।
> *vāyunā yāhi darśate indravāyū ime sutā ity anuvākye |* (Ashvalayana Sutra 5.10[?])

**— that is: "vāyunā yāhi darśata" serves as one Puronuvākyā, and "indravāyū ime sutā" as another — this states the application of these Riks.**

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**दर्शत (darśata)** — one worthy of being looked upon, that is, one of beautiful form | **(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **आ याहि (ā yāhi)** — come (to this yajna we are performing) | **इमे सोमाः (ime somāḥ)** — these Soma-juices (the pressed Soma-juice that has been prepared) | **अरंकृताः (araṅkṛtāḥ)** — made ready, that is, embellished, by the pressing and other preparatory rites (made fit for drinking) | **तेषाम् (teṣām)** — of those Soma-juices, or from among those Soma-juices, your share | **पाहि (pāhi)** — drink | **हवम् (havam)** — the invocation we make (for the sake of the Soma-drinking) — the calling | **श्रुधि (śrudhi)** — hear.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Vāyu, your form is exceedingly beautiful. We have here, in this yajna, pressed out the Soma juice in the prescribed manner, and — through the recitation of Stotra-Shastra mantras and the like — refined it and made it ready for drinking. Hear the invocation we make with these mantras, come here, and drink this Soma-juice.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> Come hither, O handsome Vayu, these soma-draughts are prepared; drink of them, hear our invocation.

### Page 674

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Somāḥ"** — the Veda contains many mantras concerning Soma; the entire ninth Maṇḍala is devoted to praise of Soma. When many deities are being invoked, [Soma] is called to come to the yajna so that they may drink it. Many yajnas are connected with Soma, of which the **Agniṣṭoma** is chief. In this yajna, only a single animal (a goat) is offered to Agni. Through the recitation of Stotra-Shastra mantras and the like, the Soma is drawn out in the prescribed manner at all three pressings, consecrated, and drunk by the sacrificer and the ritvijs. In the other Soma-yajnas too, the same order is followed with certain variations.

**What, then, is "Soma"?** This needs some examination. Soma is a particular kind of creeper (a climbing plant). Its juice is extracted by placing it on a stone and crushing it with another stone. The lower stone is called "**adri**" (Rigveda Samhita, several citations); the pressing-stone is called "**grāvā**" and is referred to by that name in many contexts. Besides these, the stones are sometimes called "**ulūkhala**" (mortar) in some places.

**The juice that flows over the cloth from the crushed creeper is described in the Rigveda in many ways:** as tawny-brown (**babhru**), as reddish (**aruṇa**), as ruddy-hued (**aruṣa**), as golden-green (**hariḍvarṇa**), as red (**śoṇa**), and as white/bright (**śukra**).

**On its taste and smell, it is described as sweet (svādiṣṭa, svādu, madhu, madhumat)** and as fragrant. **The Shatapatha Brahmana states that when this juice is left for some days it becomes foul-smelling through fermentation, and that, taken in excess, it can cause vomiting** (Taittiriya Samhita and Shatapatha Brahmana, several citations).

**Professor Max Müller, drawing on the Ayurvedic work "Dhūrtasvāmi-bhāṣya-ṭīkā," gives this account:** the Soma creeper is somewhat blackish, leafless, its juice flows like milk, and the plant grows on a mountain, with many joints/nodes — which goats and other animals eat. Its juice, when freshly pressed, is sweet and fragrant, but after some days turns sour and foul-smelling.

### Page 675

**This Soma creeper is no longer found in the lands of India today.** The plant called **Homa (Haoma)**, described in the Zend Avesta (the Persian scripture), must be the very same as this Soma. **The German scientist Schindler**, while travelling in Persia, reported that this plant had come to his notice. According to him, it grows especially on mountains; he saw it growing at about 2,000 feet elevation, reaching about four feet in height. Its stem is bare and soft, reddish-brown with a mixture of pink; it has a rough, thorny body; its leaves are very few, small, and of a pinkish, thin sort; leaves generally fall off, and at the tips of the stems there are clusters resembling millet-like seed-heads. Its juice is mixed with a greenish tint; in taste it is somewhat sweet, though to some people it becomes sour if kept; the colour of the juice is a reddish-brown (*babhru*) mixed with a yellowish tint. Growing near large trees, it climbs around the trunk like a creeper. It grows here and there in scattered fashion, and those familiar with it can find it readily. **This German scholar's description closely agrees with the description Professor Max Müller drew from the Ayurvedic work.**

**This creeper grows in open ground, along riverbanks, and on mountains** — but the mountain-grown plant yields the most juice. The more elevated its place of growth, the more juice it yields. For this reason, the Rigveda in many places speaks of Soma as "brought from the mountains" (several citations). A mountain called **Mūjavat** is famed as a Soma-growing peak (Rigveda 10.34.1; Atharva Veda; Vajasaneyi Samhita; Nirukta; Shatapatha Brahmana, etc.), and the Avesta likewise says Soma is carried down from the mountains.

**The Rigveda says in several places that the Soma creeper is found in the lakes of a region called "Śaryaṇāvat"** (Rigveda 8.6.39[?] and others); in a place called **Ārjīka**; in a country called **Paśtyā**, where five tribes of people dwell; and in the regions around the river **Suṣomā** (whose name — "su" + "soma," "rich in Soma" — probably reflects that the area yielded good Soma). **From this we learn that in Vedic times, Soma grew freely on the open plains and along the riverbanks of what is now the Punjab.** Since the creeper growing in the open yields less juice than the mountain-grown plant, people carefully soaked it in water and used it...

### Page 676

*(The opening lines continue a string of Rigveda citations, whose exact chapter-verse numbers are not reproduced here.)*

**...[the creeper was] moistened in this manner with water; this soaking is called "ābhyāyana" (swelling/refreshing).** After the juice was pressed out of the creeper, it was purified by passing it through a filter called "**pavitra**" — a strainer of sheep's wool (Rigveda, several citations). **For these strainers they used the tuft of hair at the tail-end of the sheep** (called "*aṇva*"; the sheep's fleece is also called "avi"), which is why the word "**pavitra**" is said to arise from purifying with sheep's wool (Rigveda, several citations). **The juice thus purified was collected in vessels made of cow-hide** (called "kośa" or "pātra"; several Rigveda citations), and from there was poured into small vessels called "**kalaśa**" (pots). **The freshly pressed Soma-juice was then mixed with milk (Rigveda, many citations) or curds (dadhi), or with barley** (*yava*) — the mixed preparations bearing distinct names: **gavāśira** (mixed with milk), **dadhyāśira** (mixed with curds), **yavāśira** (mixed with barley); each mixture is called by its own name. **The milk and other substances mixed with Soma are called "āśir."** The vessel in which Soma-juice is offered to the deities is called "**camū**" (Rigveda, several citations); at times "camasa" is also used for such a vessel. **The Soma-juice and the milk called "āśir" were mixed in a vessel called "kalaśa."**

**The word "Soma," when speaking of the Soma-juice, is customarily used both in the singular ("somaḥ") and in the plural ("somāḥ" or "somāsaḥ").** This is because — since milk and other different substances were added to the Soma-juice — the prepared Soma came in many kinds, so the plural "somāḥ" can properly be used. More detail about the Soma creeper and its juice will be given when the ninth Maṇḍala is explained.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

*(This section takes up the derivation of "darśate" [darśata], using the Uṇādi rule for roots such as "bhṛ, mṛ, dṛś, yaj, pari-…" with the affix "ataC," and then other words of the verse, in the established dense sutra-citation register; not reproduced in detail.)*

### Page 677

*(This page continues the grammatical derivation of Rik 2.1 in the established dense sutra-citation register. The specific numbered citations are not reproduced verbatim; the readable substance is summarized below.)*

**"Darśata":** the root "dṛś" takes the affix "ataC" (per the Uṇādi rule covering roots like "bhṛ, mṛ, dṛś, yaj…"); with the guṇa substitution this yields "darśata." Since the affix carries the marker "C," the final syllable takes the udātta accent; as a vocative, the word is accordingly treated as "āmantrita," and its accent is adjusted by the rule for vocatives.

**"Somāḥ":** the word derives from the root "su" (in the senses of pressing/extracting, giving birth, going, and others) with the affix "manin" [glossed in the source via a long list of roots beginning "ṣu, ṣū, ṣuñ…" for pressing, and others meaning "to go," "to sustain," "to shine," "to worship"]; the resulting form takes the initial-udātta accent.

**"Araṅkṛtāḥ":** here "alam" changes its "l" to "r" (a Vedic feature), giving "aram." Since "alam" (as an indeclinable particle, meaning "enough/adequately") is treated as a "gati" (preverb-like element), the compound with "kṛta" follows the rule that a word compounded after such an element keeps the accent of its first member — so that the initial syllable is udātta, the following syllables lose their accent (anudātta), and the accent is finally resolved in the Saṃhitā as svarita and pracaya, giving "araṅkṛtāḥ."

**Progress: Through PDF page 705 (printed page 677) — 5-page batch covering the rest of Rik 2.1 (grammar, Pratipadartha, Bhavartha, English translation) and a long, genuinely interesting Viśeṣārtha excursus on Soma.** Highlights: the Rigveda's descriptions of the Soma creeper and its juice (colours, taste, smell, fermentation); Max Müller's and Schindler's botanical accounts, and the identification with the Avestan Haoma; the mountains and regions where Soma grew (Mūjavat, Śaryaṇāvat, Ārjīka, the Suṣomā river region); and the processing chain — soaking (ābhyāyana), pressing between stones, straining through a sheep's-wool pavitra, collecting in hide vessels and kalaśas, and mixing with milk, curds or barley (gavāśira, dadhyāśira, yavāśira).

### Page 678 — Sūkta 2, The Second Mantra

*(The grammatical derivation of Rik 2.1 concludes at the top of this page. Its readable substance: **"pāhi"** — the root "pā" (in the sense of drinking) in the second-person singular imperative takes the substitute "hi" for the personal ending; the Vedic accent-rules keep the verb unaccented after the vocative "vāyo," and, though the root would ordinarily take the substitute "piba" in later Sanskrit, the Vedic procedure means the substitution "piba" does not apply here. **"Śrudhi"** — from the root "śru" (to hear), imperative second person, with the affix "śnu"-class insertion and the substitution of "dhi" for "hi" in the Vedic language after such roots; the long "ī" seen in "śrudhī" of the Saṃhitā text arises by the rule of lengthening. **"Havam"** — from the root "hve" (to call), with contraction of the semi-vowel, giving "hava," accented on the final syllable as a root-derived noun. Specific sutra-numbers are not reproduced.)*

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायु॑ उ॒क्थेभि॑र्जरन्ते॒ त्वामच्छा॑ जरि॒तारः॑ ।
> सु॒तसो॑मा अह॒र्विदः॑ ॥२॥
>
> *vā́yav ukthébhir jarante tvā́m áchā jaritā́raḥ |*
> *sutásomā aharvídaḥ ||2||*

### Page 679

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । उक्थेभिः । जरन्ते । त्वाम् । अच्छ । जरितारः ।
> सुतऽसोमाः । अहःऽविदः ॥२॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे वायो जरितारः स्तोतार ऋत्विग्यजमानास्त्वामच्छ त्वामभिलक्ष्योक्थेभिराज्यप्रउगादिशस्त्ररूपैर्जरन्ते । स्तुवन्ति । कीदृशाः । सुतसोमा अभिषुतेन सोमेनोपेता अहर्विदः । अहःशब्द एकेनाह्ना निष्पाद्येऽग्निष्टोमादिक्रतौ वैदिकव्यवहारेण प्रसिद्धः । क्रत्वभिज्ञा इत्यर्थः ॥ अर्चति गायतीत्यादिषु चतुर्थत्वारिंशत्स्तुत्यर्चतिकर्मसु धातुषु जरते र्ह्वयतीति पठितम् । स्तुतेरप्यर्चनाविशेषत्वादौचित्येनात्र स्तुत्यर्थो जरतिधातुः ।
> *he vāyo jaritāraḥ stotāra ṛtvig-yajamānās tvām accha tvām abhilakṣyokthebhir ājya-praüga-ādi-śastra-rūpair jarante | stuvanti | kīdṛśāḥ | sutasomā abhiṣutena somenopetā aharvidaḥ | aḥ-śabda ekenāhnā niṣpādye'gniṣṭomādi-kratau vaidika-vyavahāreṇa prasiddhaḥ | kratv-abhijñā ity arthaḥ |*

**Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary:** "O Vāyu! The praisers — the ritvijs and sacrificers — directing themselves toward you, praise you with the 'ukthas,' that is, with Shastra-mantras such as the Ājya-shastra and Praüga-shastra. What kind of praisers? 'Sutasomāḥ' — those provided with pressed Soma; 'aharvidaḥ' — the word 'ahaḥ' (day) is known in Vedic usage to denote rites like the Agniṣṭoma that are completed within a single day; the sense is: those who know the rite (kratu). Among the roots listed in the sense of praising or worshipping, 'jarate' is read in the sense of 'praising'; the root 'jṛ' (jarati) is here used in the sense of praise."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **अहर्विदः (aharvidaḥ)** — those who properly know the time for performing yajnas and the like | **जरितारः (jaritāraḥ)** — the ritvijs, sacrificers and others who offer praise | **सुतसोमाः (sutasomāḥ)** — those who have prepared Soma through the pressing and other rites | **त्वामच्छ (tvām accha)** — directed toward you | **उक्थेभिः (ukthebhiḥ)** — with Shastra-mantras such as the Ājya and Praüga | **जरन्ते (jarante)** — offer praise.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Vāyu, the ritvijs, sacrificers and others know at what time and what work is to be done. Therefore they have now prepared the Soma-juice and are praising you with many hymns.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Vayu, the praisers who have pressed out the soma juice and know the proper season to offer it, are praising you with holy praises.

*(A brief grammatical note follows in the source on "jaritāraḥ" from the root "jṛ" [to praise], on the accent of "sutasomāḥ" as a bahuvrīhi compound, and on "aharvidaḥ" as a compound, in the established dense register.)*

### Page 680 — Sūkta 2, The Third Mantra

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics on Rik 2.2) ॥**

**"Ukthebhiḥ"** does not mean sung Stotras; it means the Shastra-mantras such as the Pṛhuga and others, which are recited rather than chanted. **"Jarate"** — of the four roots beginning "arcati" and "gāyati" [in the traditional list of praising-roots], the root "jṛ" is used in the sense of worshipping and singing, so "jarate" carries the sense of offering praise; likewise **"jaritāraḥ"** means "those who offer praise." **"Aharvidaḥ"** — in this word, "ahaḥ" means "day," referring to the Sutyā-day on which Soma-juice is pressed at the morning pressing and the others; this is a single day within the Agniṣṭoma. **"Sutasomāḥ"** — "those who have prepared the Soma-juice" — likewise makes clear that "ahaḥ" means the Sutyā-day specifically. Even so, one cannot say with certainty that the poet had precisely this sense in mind in using the word "aharvidaḥ."

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* The particle "accha" takes a lengthened vowel in the Saṃhitā by the rule that particles in mantras take lengthening. "**Sutasomāḥ**" is a bahuvrīhi compound ("those by whom Soma is pressed"), with the accent of the first member retained by the rule for bahuvrīhi. "**Aharvidaḥ**" is a compound whose final member, being a verbal derivative, keeps the stem accent.

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो॒ तव॑ प्रपृ॒ञ्चती॑ धे॒ना जि॑गाति दा॒शुषे॑ ।
> उ॒रू॒ची सोम॑पीतये ॥३॥
>
> *vā́yo táva prapṛñcatī́ dhenā́ jigāti dāśúṣe |*
> *urūcī́ sómapītaye ||3||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । तव । प्रऽपृञ्चती । धेना । जिगाति । दाशुषे ।
> उरूची । सोमऽपीतये ॥३॥

### Page 681

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे वायो तव धेना वाक् सोमपीतये सोमपानार्थं दाशुषे दाश्वांसं दत्तवन्तं यजमानं जिगाति गच्छति । हे यजमान त्वयो दत्तं सोमं पास्यामीत्येवं वायुर्ब्रूते इत्यर्थः । कीदृशी धेना । प्रपृञ्चती प्रकर्षेण सोमसंपर्कं कुर्वती । सोमगुणं वर्णयन्तीत्यर्थः । उरूची उरूनस्वभूजमानान् गच्छन्ती । ये ये सोमयोजिनस्तान् सर्वान् स्वर्णयन्तीत्यर्थः ।
> *he vāyo tava dhenā vāk somapītaye soma-pānārthaṃ dāśuṣe dāśvāṃsaṃ dattavantaṃ yajamānaṃ jigāti gacchati | he yajamāna tvayā dattaṃ somaṃ pāsyāmīty evaṃ vāyur brūte ity arthaḥ | kīdṛśī dhenā | prapṛñcatī prakarṣeṇa soma-saṃparkaṃ kurvatī | soma-guṇaṃ varṇayantīty arthaḥ | urūcī urūn [bahūn] yajamānān gacchantī |*

**Translation:** "O Vāyu! Your 'dhenā' — your speech — goes, for the drinking of Soma, to the sacrificer who has given the oblation (dāśuṣe). The sense is: 'O sacrificer, I shall drink the Soma you have offered' — thus says Vāyu. What kind of speech? 'Prapṛñcatī' — bringing about, in an excellent manner, association with the Soma, that is, describing the Soma's excellence. 'Urūcī' — going to the many sacrificers; that is, it reaches every one of those who have prepared Soma."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **प्रपृञ्चती (prapṛñcatī)** — describing the qualities of the Soma | **तव (tava)** — your | **धेना (dhenā)** — speech | **सोमपीतये (somapītaye)** — for the drinking of Soma | **दाशुषे (dāśuṣe)** — to the sacrificer who offers [Soma], and | **उरूची (urūcī)** — to the many other sacrificers who offer you Soma | **जिगाति (jigāti)** — goes.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Vāyu, the sacrificer who performs the yajna, and many others besides, call you for the drinking of Soma. Your speech, pleased by the hymns they offer and by their Soma-drinking, will gladden the sacrificer who calls you to drink the Soma, and many others as well.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Vayu, your approving speech goes to the giver (of the oblation) and to many (others) who invite you for drinking Soma.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥**

**"Dhenā"** — many scholars have held many opinions about this word's meaning. Yāska, in his Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta), placed this word "dhenā" among the fifty-seven words meaning "vāk" (speech). Some take "dhenā" to mean "tongue" (jihvā)...

### Page 682

**...[Some take "dhenā" to mean] "tongue" (jihvā)**, and on their view this Rik's sense would run: "O Vāyu, your long (Udvāta) tongue reaches the sacrificer who calls you for the drinking of Soma." **The German scholar Geldner**, after many investigations into the word "dhenā," concluded that it means "tongue" (in the sense of "speech," vāk); the sacrificer's Stotra (vāk), he says, generates in the deity a desire for the Soma-drinking. A Rik of the Rigveda supports this view: "**yaṃ te svadhāvan…**" (Rigveda 8.?). **But in a later study, this same scholar concluded that "dhenā" means "the milk-yielding cow's teat/milk-flow." According to Professor Max Müller, "dhenā" means "a stream of milk."** Both scholars hold that "dhenā" means "a cow that yields milk" and, by extension, "the drinking of milk." **In the Veda, the word "dhenā" is used in a variety of senses in different contexts:**

(1) A Rik in which "dhenā" refers to a beloved woman — used in the sense of "wife": "*striyo hi dāsa āyudhāni cakre kiṃ mā karann abalā asya senāḥ…*" (Rigveda 5.30.9[?]) — where "dhenā" is used for women who are objects of affection.

(2) "*ahan vyaṃsam uśadhag vaneṣv…*" and "*tvāvakro rathyo na dhenā rejante viśvā kṛtrimāṇi bhīṣā*" — in these Riks "dhenā" is used in the sense of "sister/mother-cow" [i.e., a milch-cow].

(3) "*viśvāḥ pinvathaḥ svasarasya dhenā anu vāmekaḥ pavir āvavarta*" (Rigveda 5.?) — here "dhenā" is used for a female animal, a cow.

(4) "*visṛṣṭadhenā bharate suvṛktir…*" and "*mādayasva haribhir ye ta indra viṣyasva śipre vi sṛjasva dhene*" (Rigveda 1.101.10[?]) — here, from the root "dhe" (to drink), the word "dhenā" arises with the meaning "milk-cow," and this sense is still found in the later-literature word "**stanandhaya**" (a suckling child — "one who drinks milk").

*(Several of the Rigveda verse-locators above are too small to read reliably at this resolution and are given only in approximate form; the Kannada text's citations in this passage should be checked against the source if precision matters.)*

### Page 683

**More Rigvedic uses of "dhenā"** (continuing the numbered list from the previous page):

(5) In several Riks — among them "*pitur…*" (Rigveda 3.1.6[?]), "*samyak sravanti saritro na dhenā…*" (Rigveda 4.?), "*yad īm upa hvarate sādhate matir ṛtasya dhenā anayanta sasrutaḥ*" (Rigveda 1.141.1[?]), "*dhiyo dhenā avasyavaḥ*", "*dhenā indrāvacākaśat*", "*viśaṃ-viśaṃ maghavā paryaśāyata janānāṃ dhenā avacākaśad vṛṣā*", "*indre dhenābhir iha mādayasva dhībhir viśvābhiḥ śacyā gṛṇānaḥ*", and "*vīreṇyaḥ kratur indraḥ suśastir utāpi dhenā puruhūtam ūtaye*" — the word is used in the senses of **speech, utterance, hymn of praise, and the act of praising.**

**M. Bloomfield**, in translating the Rik (10.104.10) cited above, remarks that the Vedic word "dhenā" is related to the Lithuanian word "*daina*" and the Avestan "*daena*." These words generally carry the senses of speech, song, hymn and lay. **Many scholars hold that in the Veda, "dhenā" chiefly and more often carries the sense of "speech, word."**

**"Prapṛñcatī"** — means "touching, making contact." **"Urūcī"** — "broad, extended, plentiful." The Bhashyakara has glossed this as "sacrificers performing Soma-yajnas"; but "urūcī" may instead be taken simply as a qualifier of the word "dhenā." **"Somapītaye"** — the meaning of this word is clear; its use is especially frequent across many Riks.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* **"Prapṛñcatī"** — here, by the rule concerning words ending in the "śatṛ" affix and lacking the augment "num," the feminine-forming "ṅīp" affix (a "nadī"-class affix) is added, and the accent is treated accordingly: the word is accented on its final syllable, and the case-endings following it (such as "śas") likewise take the udātta accent.

### Page 684 — Sūkta 2, The Fourth Mantra

*(The grammar of "prapṛñcatī" concludes: the "ṅīp"-type affix's long "ī" takes udātta even though its marker would otherwise leave it unaccented.)*

**"Dhenā"** — listed in the Nirukta (Nighaṇṭu 1.11) among the fifty-seven words for "vāk" ("speech": *ślokaḥ, dhārā, dhenā, gnāḥ*, …); this is why "dhenā" is glossed as "speech." **"Jigāti"** — listed among the words expressing movement (Nighaṇṭu 2.14), where "jigāti" is glossed "gacchati" (goes).

**Grammar (summarized):** since "jigāti" is a verb of motion, the recipient noun takes the accusative/dative ("dāśvān" → "dāśuṣe") by the rule that verbs of going govern a fourth-case (dative) object of destination — hence the dative "dāśuṣe." **"Urūcī"** — the "ṣit"-marked class of words (with "gaurādi" nouns) takes the feminine affix "ṅīṣ," which brings its own accent. **"Somapītaye"** — though not a bahuvrīhi, the initial member's accent is retained by a special rule.

> इ॒न्द्र॒वा॒यू इ॒मे सु॒ता उप॒ प्रयो॑भि॒रा ग॑तम् ।
> इन्द॑वो वामु॒शन्ति॒ हि ॥४॥

> *indravāyū imé sutā́ úpa práyobhir ā́ gatam |*
> *índavo vām uśánti hí ||4||*

### Page 685

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> एतस्या ऋचा ऐन्द्रवायवग्रहे द्वितीयपुरोनुवाक्यारूपेण विशेषविनियोगः पूर्वमेवोक्तः । हे इन्द्रवायू भवदर्थमिमे सोमाः सुताः अभिषुताः । तस्माद्युवां प्रयोभिरन्नैरस्मभ्यं दात्व्यैः सहोपसा गतं । अस्मत्समीपं प्रत्यागच्छतम् । हि यस्मादिन्दवः सोमा वां युवामुशन्ति कामयन्ते तस्मादागमनमुचितम् । इन्द्रवायूशब्दस्यामन्त्रितस्याद्युदात्तत्वम् । प्रीणयन्ति भोक्तॄनिति प्रयांस्यन्नानि ।
> *etasyā ṛcā aindravāyava-grahe dvitīya-puronuvākyā-rūpeṇa viśeṣa-viniyogaḥ pūrvam evoktaḥ | he indravāyū bhavad-artham ime somāḥ sutāḥ abhiṣutāḥ | tasmād yuvāṃ prayobhir annair asmabhyaṃ dātavyaiḥ sahopasā gataṃ | asmat-samīpaṃ pratyāgacchatam | hi yasmād indavaḥ somā vāṃ yuvām uśanti kāmayante tasmād āgamanam ucitam | indravāyū-śabdasyāmantritasyādyudāttatvam | prīṇayanti bhoktṝn iti prayāṃsy annāni |*

**Translation:** "The specific application of this Rik — as the second Puronuvākyā in the Indra-Vāyu-graha offering — was stated earlier. O Indra and Vāyu! For your sake these Soma-juices have been pressed. Therefore, come to our side together with the foods (*prayas*) that are to be given to us, coming close to us. For, since the Soma-drops desire you two, your coming is fitting. [Grammar:] the vocative 'indravāyū' takes initial-syllable udātta. 'Prayas' means foods, 'those which please the eaters.'"

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) इन्द्रवायू ((he) indravāyū)** — O Indra and Vāyu! (for your sake) | **इमे (ime)** — these Soma-juices | **सुताः (sutāḥ)** — pressed (prepared so as to be fit for drinking) | **प्रयोभिः (prayobhiḥ)** — together with foods and other things that please us | **उपागतम् (upāgatam)** — come to our side | **हि (hi)** — because | **इन्दवः (indavaḥ)** — these Soma-juices prepared for you | **वाम् (vām)** — you two | **उशन्ति (uśanti)** — desire.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! These Soma-juices have been thoroughly pressed and made ready to be drunk. Come to our side to accept them, bringing food and other things that will please us. For these Soma-juices that we have prepared are awaiting you — that is, we watch for your arrival so that you may drink.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and Vayu, here are Soma-libations (poured out for you). Come with food for us. For, the soma-drops are desiring You.

### Page 686

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**This Rik, as already stated, is applied as the second Puronuvākyā in the rite called the Aindravāyava-graha.** In this Rik, and in the two Riks that follow, Indra and Vāyu are invoked together. **The joint invocation or joint praise of two deities is often found in the Rigveda** — for example: *Indra-Vāyū, Indrāgnī, Agnīṣomau, Indrāsomau, Somārudrā, Indrāviṣṇū, Dyāvāpṛthivī, Uṣāsānaktā* (or *naktoṣāsā*), and so on.

**"Ime"** — these (Soma-juices): that is, freshly pressed, made fit for drinking through the preparatory rites. **"Sutāḥ"** — this word, formed from the root "su" (to press), shows that Soma-creeper, crushed between stones and pressed out in the filter, has become fit for drinking. **"Prayobhiḥ"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "with foods" or "with meals." Since the word derives from the root "prī" (to please, to gladden), the sense "things that please, that bring joy to the mind" is entirely fitting. Moreover the Bhashyakara himself, in the Rik "*pra yad vo yajñe…*" — where "prayāṃsi" occurs (Rigveda 3.?.?) — glosses it as "dear things." **In the Rigveda this word is used in many places in the sense of "food fit for sacrifice."** **"Indavaḥ"** — Soma-juices mixed with various admixtures; the word derives from the root "und" (to wet/moisten): since Soma-juice is a liquid, "kledana" (moistening) is the sense; and "indu" is accordingly used in place of "soma" in many passages.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* **"Indravāyū"** — the vocative takes initial-udātta accent. **"Prayāṃsi"** — "those which please the eaters" — by analysis, "prayas" derives from the root "prī" (to please) with the affix "asun" (added after all roots, per the Uṇādi rule), giving "prī + as," with guṇa and substitution "prayas"; being formed with an accent-bearing affix, it is accented on the first syllable.

### Page 687 — Sūkta 2, The Fifth Mantra

*(The grammar of "prayobhiḥ" concludes: the affix-final "s" becomes "ru" and then visarga, giving "prayobhiḥ.")* **"Gatam"** — the root "gam," in the second-person dual imperative, has its personal ending elided by the Vedic rule ("bahulaṃ chandasi"), and the nasal of the root is dropped when the following affix is marked as "kit" or "ṅit"; hence "gatam," not to be mistaken for a form ending in the "kta" affix. **"Indavaḥ"** — from the root "und" (to moisten), the affix "un" is added and the initial "u" becomes "i," giving "indu"; the affix marker makes the word accented on its first syllable. **"Vām"** — the dual pronoun "yuvām" is replaced by the enclitic "vām," which is therefore unaccented. **"Uśanti"** — a verb, hence normally unaccented; but here it is joined with "hi," which blocks the loss of accent, so the verb retains its own accent; "hi" itself, being a particle, takes initial accent.

> वायविन्द्र॑श्च चेतथः सु॒तानां॑ वाजिनीवसू ।
> तावा या॑त॒मुप॑ द्र॒वत् ॥५॥
>
> *vāyav índraś ca cetathaḥ sutā́nāṃ vājinīvasū |*
> *tā́v ā́ yātam úpa dravát ||5||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । इन्द्रः । च । चेतथः । सुतानाम् । वाजिनीवसू इति वाजिनीऽवसू ।
> तौ । आ । यातम् । उप । द्रवत् ॥५॥

### Page 688

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> अत्र चकारेणास्यः समुच्चीयते । संनिहितत्वाद्वायुरेव । हे वायो त्वमिन्द्रश्च युवामुभौ सुतानामभिषुतान्सोमान् चेतथः । जानीथः । यद्वा अभिषुतानां सोमानां विशेषणमित्यध्याहारः । कीदृशौ युवां । वाजिनीवसू । वाजिनीशब्दो यज्ञपुष्टोनामसु पठितस्तथास्य त्यासंभवात्रं गृह्यते । वाजोऽन्नं । तद्वत्यां हविःसंतत्तावस्ति सा वाजिनी । तस्यां वसतः इति तौ वाजिनीवसू । आमन्त्रितत्वादनुदात्तः । तौ तथाविधौ युवां द्रवत्क्षिप्रमुपसमीपे आ यातम् । आगच्छतम् ।
> *atra cakāreṇāsyaḥ samuccīyate | saṃnihitatvād vāyur eva | he vāyo tvam indraś ca yuvām ubhau sutānām abhiṣutān somān cetathaḥ | jānīthaḥ | … kīdṛśau yuvāṃ | vājinīvasū | vājinī-śabdo yajñapuṣṭo-nāmasu paṭhitaḥ … vājo'nnam | tadvatyāṃ haviḥ-saṃtatāv asti sā vājinī | tasyāṃ vasataḥ iti tau vājinīvasū | āmantritatvād anudāttaḥ | tau tathāvidhau yuvāṃ dravat kṣipram upa samīpe ā yātam | āgacchatam |*

**Translation:** "Here the word 'ca' combines [Indra] with the other deity — by proximity, Vāyu. O Vāyu, and Indra — you two — know the pressed Soma-juices. Or, as a qualifier of the pressed Somas, [it may be supplied]. What kind of pair are you? 'Vājinīvasū' — the word 'vājinī' is read among the words for 'sacrifice-nourishing'; 'vāja' means food. That in which there is a continuous stream of oblation-food is 'vājinī'; 'those two who dwell in it' are 'vājinīvasū' — unaccented as a vocative. You two, being such, come here quickly (*dravat*), near us."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **(त्वम्) इन्द्रश्च ((tvam) indraś ca)** — you, and Indra with you, both | **वाजिनीवसू (vājinīvasū)** — those who are foremost among the sacrificers, who are provided with oblation-food and the like | **(अतः तौ यूयम्)** — (you two, such as you) | **सुतानाम् (sutānām)** — of the pressed Soma-juices (that the Soma-juices are ready for drinking) | **चेतथः (cetathaḥ)** — know | **तौ (tau)** — you two, such | **द्रवत् (dravat)** — with alertness | **उप (upa)** — to our side | **आ यातम् (ā yātam)** — come.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! In yajnas equipped with oblation-shares and the like, you are honoured as chief. You know full well that the Soma-juice has been made ready for your drinking. Therefore, for the sake of drinking the Soma, come quickly and attentively to our side.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Vayu and Indra dwellers in the sacrifices, You are aware of these Soma-libations. You both come hither quickly.

### Page 689

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Vājinīvasū"** — many people have interpreted this word in many different ways. **The Bhashyakara** says that although "vājinī" is among the words that name Uṣas (the Dawn), that sense is impossible here and must be set aside; then "vāja" means food (the Vedic text says "*annaṃ vai vājaḥ*"), and "that in which there is oblation-food is 'vājinī'" — the sacrificial rite is thus called "vājinī" ("the yajna"). "*Tasyāṃ vasataḥ*" — "the two who dwell in it" are "vājinīvasū": the two who dwell in the yajna, hence so named.

**Authors of the Vedārtha-yatna [a modern commentary]** interpret the word thus: "vāji" means a horse, or a swift horse; "vasū" means those who possess them — that is, the two who possess swift horses. Or "vājinī" means "provided with horses" — a chariot; "vasū" means those who dwell or sit in it — those who sit in the chariot. Or "vājinī" may mean a mare, and "vasū" wealth — those who possess these. Or it may mean "givers." **The German scholar Grassmann** interprets "vājinīvasū" as "those who give abundant rewards."

**The Bhashyakara glosses the word "vājinī" in some places as "food"** (Rigveda 3.62.5[?] and many others); in some places as "sacrificial rite" (Rigveda 1.?; 3.?; and others); in some as "possessing food" (*annavatī*); in some as "strong" (*balavatī*); and **"vasu" as "one who dwells"** (Rigveda 1.?.?) and as "wealth, riches" (many citations).

**"Vasu"** is among the twenty-eight words for "wealth" in the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.10). Moreover, compounds ending in "vasu" are needed and found throughout the Rigveda, in which "vasu" generally means "wealth." A few examples follow:

**Śacīvasū** (Rigveda 1.139.[?]; 2.19.1[?]; 8.60.19); **Sūryavasū** (Rigveda 2.?.?); **Vibhāvasuḥ** (Rigveda 1.44.10; 3.2.?; 5.?; 8.?; and many others), and so on.

### Page 690

*(This page continues the list of compounds ending in "-vasu" begun on the previous page, each followed in the source by a string of Rigveda chapter-verse references. Those numeric references are very small and were not read reliably, so only the compound names are given here; they should be checked against the source if the exact locations matter.)*

**Further compounds ending in "vasu" in the Rigveda:** **Viśvāvasuḥ, Manāvasū, Viśvalāvasū, Snāvasuḥ, Tvāvasuḥ, Ṛtāvasū, Jenyāvasū, Divāvasū, Dhiyovasuḥ, Vṛṣaṇvasū, Puruvasū, Prabhūvasuḥ, Vibhūvasuḥ, Mahāvasū, Punarvasū, Aśvajivasū (?), Ābharadvasuḥ, Akṣitāvasuḥ, Kaitevasū (?), Gotrāvasuḥ, Pratevasū (?), Radāvasū, Vidadvasuḥ, Śatadvasuḥ**, and so on.

**In these words, "vasu" generally means "wealth."** In the Shatapatha Brahmana as well, the word occurs in "Amāvasu" and in "Citravasu"...

### Page 691

**"Vasu"** — the word derives from the root "vas" (to dwell), and signifies "one who dwells." The Bhashyakara has followed this sense and explained accordingly here.

**The word "vājinīvatī"** — which is a derivative of "vājinī" — is used in the Rigveda as a qualifier of Uṣas (the Dawn) in several Riks (several citations). **Yāska, in his Nirukta, when explaining one of these Riks, glosses "vājinīvatī" as "annavatī" (possessing food).** There "vājinī" means "food"; and when explaining another Rik, he gives the same sense again.

**Sāyaṇācārya has explained "vājinī" as "possessing oblation-food"; likewise Skandasvāmin, in his own Vedabhāṣya, glosses "vājinī" as "sacrifice."** Veṅkaṭamādhava, in explaining this word, interprets "*asmai vāsayitārau — vājinīvasū*" — hence for "vājinī," the principal senses that may be entertained are: (1) food or nourishment, (2) strength, and (3) speed. **"Vāji" is taken by some to mean "horse."** **Roth**, the scholar, translates "vājinīvasū" as "possessing quick horses." Since this word "vājinīvasū" is used by many rishis when praising deities such as Indra and the Aśvins, no single fixed sense has been established for it; it was evidently in common use, and especially frequent in yajnas involving Soma-drinking, so it is reasonable to suppose that Soma-juice and foods of every sort were freely offered in such rites.

**"Cetathaḥ"** — "you both know." **"Dravat"** — in the Nirukta (2.15.?), this word is listed among the sixteen or so words expressing "quickly, swiftly."

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* **"Vājinīvasū"** — although Yāska lists "vājinī" among the names of Uṣas, that sense does not fit here and is not adopted. "**Vājaḥ asyām asti**" — food is present in this: the affix "ini" is added after "vāja," and the "a" is dropped, then the feminine affix "ṅīp" is added, giving "vājinī." Then "vājinyāṃ vasataḥ" gives the compound "vājinīvasū," a vocative dual; and by the rule for vocatives, its accent becomes fully unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).

### Page 692 — Sūkta 2, The Sixth Mantra

**"Dravat"** — Yāska lists this among the sixteen words meaning "quickly" ("*su kṣipraṃ makṣu dravat*," Nirukta 2.15.?). Hence here, by the rule for such words, the final syllable takes the udātta accent.

**॥ Iti prathamāṣṭake prathamādhyāye tṛtīyo vargaḥ ॥**
*(Thus ends the third Varga of the first Adhyāya of the first Aṣṭaka.)*

> वा॒यवि॒न्द्र॑श्च सुन्व॒त आ या॑त॒मुप॑ निष्कृ॒तम् ।
> म॒क्ष्वि१त्था धि॒या न॒रा ॥६॥
>
> *vāyav índraś ca sunvatá ā́ yātam úpa niṣkṛtám |*
> *makṣv ítthā dhiyā́ narā ||6||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । इन्द्रः । च । सुन्वतः । आ । यातम् । उप । निःऽकृतम् ।
> मक्षु । इत्था । धिया । नरा ॥६॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे वायो त्वमिन्द्रश्च सुन्वतः सोमाभिषवं कुर्वतो यजमानस्य निष्कृतं संस्कृतं संस्कर्तारं वा सोममुपसा यातमागच्छतम् । नरा हे नरौ पुरुषौ पौरुषेण सामर्थ्येनोपेतौ युवयोरागतयोश्च सतोर्धियामुना कर्मणा मक्षु त्वरया संस्कारः संपत्स्यते । इत्था सत्यम् ॥
> *he vāyo tvam indraś ca sunvataḥ somābhiṣavaṃ kurvato yajamānasya niṣkṛtaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ saṃskartāraṃ vā somam upa yātam āgacchatam | narā he narau puruṣau pauruṣeṇa sāmarthyenopetau yuvayor āgatayoś ca satoḥ dhiyāmunā karmaṇā makṣu tvarayā saṃskāraḥ saṃpatsyate | itthā satyam ||*

**Translation:** "O Vāyu, and Indra with you! Come to the prepared (*niṣkṛta*, refined) Soma of the sacrificer who is pressing Soma — or to him who prepares it. 'Narā' — O two men, endowed with manly strength! When you two have come, by this rite the preparation will quickly be completed. 'Itthā' — truly."

*(The grammar that follows in the source — on the accent of "vāyo" as vocative, "indraḥ" as a word with the "ran" affix (final-syllable udātta), "ca" as a particle, "sunvataḥ" as a present participle in the class-5 conjugation, "niṣkṛtam" as a compound with the preverb "niḥ" taking the accent of its first member, "dhiyā" with an udātta case-ending, and "narā" as a dual vocative — is in the established dense register and is not reproduced in detail.)*
