### Page 693

**Application (viniyoga) of the next three Riks:** *"mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam"* and the following Riks — addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa — are applied in the Maitrāvaruṇa-graha of the morning pressing, and (as Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra states, "*mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam*") likewise in the Ābhiplava-ṣaḍaha and related rites. *(The Kannada gives the citations in a compressed run; only the sense is given here.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca)** — and Indra, both of you | **सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ)** — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | **निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam)** — Soma purified by the preparatory rites (for drinking) — or to the sacrificer who has readied the Soma-juice | **उप आ यातम् (upa ā yātam)** — come | **(हे) नरा ((he) narā)** — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength | **धिया (dhiyā)** — through this rite | **मक्षु (makṣu)** — quickly (the preparation will be accomplished) | **इत्था (itthā)** — this is true.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed out Soma-juice and made it pure through the preparatory rites, keeping it ready for you. O mighty ones, by your coming this rite — the yajna — is completed; that is, it is fully and correctly accomplished. Since you come and drink the Soma, the yajna will be carried through exactly as prescribed. This is true.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥**

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this as "**saṃskṛtam**," that is, "refined, purified"; the authors of the Vedārtha-yatna simply say "Soma." **Geldner** takes it as "arranged in order," and **Grassmann**...

### Page 694

**...[Grassmann] takes "niṣkṛta" as "a fixed [appointed] place" or "an enclosure/pen."** But the right sense is "niṣkṛta" = "completely accomplished" (*niḥśeṣeṇa saṃpāditam*), as in "*uta tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 1.20.6), where this same sense is found. And further:

(1) "*ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varsaḥ … niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭhaḥ*" (Rigveda 3.58.9[?])
(2) "*somo jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(3) "*baḷitthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat*" (Rigveda 5.?.?)
(4) "*indra dṛhyasva pūrasi bhadrā te eti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 8.?.?)
(5) "*vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(6) "*ukthā minoti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(7) "*kanikradad vṛṣā harir indrasyābhyeti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)

**In these Riks, "niṣkṛta" is used for a place where work (that is, sacrificial work) goes on — "the appointed place where the work of sacrifice is performed" — or, more simply, "a suitable place."** *(As on earlier pages, the exact Rigveda locators here were too small to read reliably and are not asserted.)*

**"Itthā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "truly." **Skandasvāmin** — "*itthā amutaḥ … asyā arthaḥ*": from there, from the intermediate region, from their own station; **Veṅkaṭamādhava** takes "itthā" as "in this manner."

**"Dhiyā"** — "by this rite": the Bhashyakara, following the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.?), explains "dhī" as "action, work" — "perform the sacrifice!" The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna take it as "by this our praise, made with heartfelt intent"; Geldner takes it as "as we desire." Skandasvāmin and Veṅkaṭamādhava take "dhiyā" as "by this work." In the Nighaṇṭu, "dhīḥ" is a synonym of "prajñā" (wisdom); but that sense does not suit here. Since Madhucchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma and offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" meaning "by this rite" fits best.

### Page 693

**Application (viniyoga) of this Rik:** the Rik "**mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam**" [the seventh Rik, next] and the two that follow are applied, in the Prātaḥ-savana, to the *Maitrāvaruṇa* Stotra — in the Ājya-śastra of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, and, as stated in the Aitareya Brahmana, in the Ṣaḍaha... The same is stated by Ashvalayana in the section beginning "*caturviṃśe hotājaniṣṭ…*": "*mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam*" (Ashvalayana 2.?), and in the section "*pariśiṣṭā nāvāpānu…*."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca)** — and Indra along with you (both of you) | **सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ)** — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | **निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam)** — Soma made pure through preparatory rites (for drinking), or [to the side of] the sacrificer who has readied the Soma-juice | **उप आ यातम् (upa ā yātam)** — come | **(हे) नरा ((he) narā)** — O two Indra-Vāyu, endowed with manly strength and the like | **धिया (dhiyā)** — through this rite | **मक्षु (makṣu)** — with alertness (the preparation will be completed) | **इत्था (itthā)** — this is true.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra-Vāyu, come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and made it pure through preparatory rites, for your sake. O manly ones! With your arrival, this yajna-rite becomes complete and properly furnished. By your coming and drinking the Soma, the yajna will proceed as prescribed and reach its completion. This is true.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥**

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam," i.e., "prepared, purified." **The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna** say it simply means "Soma." **Geldner** says it means "arranged, set in order"; **Grassmann**...

### Page 694

**...[Grassmann] takes "niṣkṛta" to mean "the appointed place" (the ritual ground).** Both "niṣkṛtam = niḥśeṣeṇa saṃpāditam" ("completely accomplished") — this is the sound sense. **The same sense appears in the Rik "*uta tyaṃ cemasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 1.20.6).** The word "niṣkṛta" is also used in the following Riks:

(1) "*ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kerikratu-tāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭhaḥ*" (Rigveda 3.58.?)
(2) "*somo jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?)
(3) "*baḷittthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat*" (Rigveda 8.?)
(4) "*indra dṛhyasva pūrasi bhadrā te eti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 8.?)
(5) "*vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?)
(6) "*ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?)
(7) "*kanikradad vṛṣā harir indrasyābhyeti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.100.?)

**In these Riks, "niṣkṛtam" indicates a place where a rite (a yajna-rite) is performed — "the appointed place where the work of sacrifice is performed" — or a place made ready.**

**"Itthā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "true" (*satya*). Skandasvāmin: "*amuta*" — "from there"; from this it is explained as "from that heaven, from their own abode of the sky"; Veṅkaṭamādhava glosses it as "in this manner."

**"Dhiyā"** — the Bhashyakara takes it as "amunā karmaṇā" — "by this rite" — as in the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 3.?): "*dhīḥ*" is glossed as "action; perform the yajna." **The authors of Vedārtha-yatna** take it as "by this our mindful praise"; **Geldner** as "as we desire." **Skandasvāmin and Nārāyaṇa** give "by this rite." In the Nighaṇṭu, "dhīḥ" is a synonym of "prajñā" (intelligence) — but that sense does not fit here. Since Madhuchandas and others were performing an Agniṣṭoma and offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" — "in this rite," "by this rite," "by performing this rite" — is the most fitting sense. The next Ṛca, beginning "**mitraṃ huve**"...

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (Rik 2.6) ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca)** — and Indra with you (both of you) | **सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ)** — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | **निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam)** — the Soma purified by consecrating rites (for drinking), or [the sacrificer's] presence, he who has got the Soma-juice ready | **आ यातम् (ā yātam)** — come | **(हे) नरा ((he) narā)** — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength | **धियः (dhiyaḥ)** — [through] this rite | **मक्षु (makṣu)** — with alertness (the preparation is completed) | **इत्था (itthā)** — this is true.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and, having purified it by consecrating rites, has kept it ready for you. O men of vigour! By your coming, this rite of yajna will be perfected — that is, made complete in all its parts. Since you come and drink the Soma, the yajna will proceed as prescribed and reach completion. This is true.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥**

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam" — that is, consecrated, purified. The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say it simply means "Soma." **The scholar Geldner** takes it to mean "arranged/put in order," and **Grassmann**...

### Page 694

**...[Geldner and Grassmann] take "niṣkṛta" to mean "the appointed place" or "the place of sacrifice."** That is: "niṣkṛta" = "that which has been completely prepared" — this is the right sense. The same sense holds in the Rik "*utā tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 1.20.6[?]). **Other Riks where "niṣkṛta" occurs:**

(1) *ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kerikṛtsnā tāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭaḥ* (Rigveda 3.58.9[?])
(2) *somo no jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(3) *baḷitthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat* (Rigveda 8.?.?)
(4) *indra dṛhyasva pūras ti bhadrā te iti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 5.?.?)
(5) *vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(6) *ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9.69.4[?])
(7) *kanikradad vṛṣā hariḥ indrasya abhy eti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9.100.?)

**In these Riks, "niṣkṛta" suggests a fixed place where the work of sacrifice is performed (the appointed place), or an established, prepared place.**

**"Itthā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "true" ("satya"). Skandasvāmin explains it: "*itthā amutaḥ*" — "from there" — that is, "from your own place, from the sky" [where you dwell]; Veṅkaṭamādhava glosses "itthā" as "in this manner."

**"Dhiyā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses "amunā karmaṇā" — "by this rite." The Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.?) lists "dhī" as meaning "action" (karma), which the commentators explain in the sense "perform, sacrifice." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say: "with our mindful (manaḥpūrvaka) stotra"; **Geldner**: "as we desire." Skandasvāmin and Veṅkaṭamādhava also give "by this rite." In the Nighaṇṭu "dhī" is listed as a synonym of "prajñā" (understanding), but that sense does not suit the present context. Since Madhuchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma at this moment, offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" — "by this rite, or through this act, or by performing this act" — is the natural sense.

### Page 693

**Application (viniyoga) note for the following Riks:** the three Riks beginning "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam" [Riks 2.7–9, addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa] are applied in the Maitrāvaruṇa-graha (the Mitra-Varuṇa offering) of the morning pressing — that is, they belong to the Maitrāvaruṇa Stotra-recitation; and this is also stated by Āśvalāyana in the section of his Shrauta-sutra beginning "*caturviṃśe hotā*" ("mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam…") — the sutra there giving these as the Puronuvākyā and Yājyā of the Mitra-Varuṇa offering, together with "mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca)** — and Indra with you (both of you) | **सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ)** — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | **निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam)** — the Soma made pure by the preparatory rites (for drinking), or [approach] the sacrificer who has readied the Soma-juice | **आ यातम् (ā yātam)** — come | **(हे) नरा ((he) narā)** — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength and the like! | **धिया (dhiyā)** — by this rite | **मक्षु (makṣu)** — quickly (the preparation will be completed) | **इत्था (itthā)** — this is true.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and, having purified it through the preparatory rites, has kept it ready for you. O manly ones! By your coming, this rite of sacrifice will be brought to completion — that is, will be made whole and complete. Since you will come and drink the Soma, the yajna will be concluded in accordance with the prescribed rules. This is true.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam," meaning "prepared, purified." **The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna** say that it here means simply "Soma." **Geldner** says it means "arranged/duly ordered," and **Grassmann** ...

### Page 694

**...Grassmann** takes "niṣkṛta" as "appointed, fixed," or a "prepared place" (a sacrificial ground). **But "niṣkṛtam" — meaning "completed without remainder (*niśśeṣeṇa*), brought to fulfilment" — is the truly fitting sense.** In the Rik "*ute tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 1.20.6) this very sense appears. Further examples (numbering as in the source, locators approximate):

(1) "*ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kariṣyat sutāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭhaḥ*" (Rigveda 3.?.?)
(2) "*somo jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(3) "*baliṭthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat*" (Rigveda 5.?.?)
(4) "*indra dṛhyasva pūr asi bhadrā te eti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 8.?.?)
(5) "*vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(6) "*ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.?.?)
(7) "*kanikradad dhvṛṣā hariṃ indrasyābhyeti niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 9.100.?)

**In these Riks, "niṣkṛtam" indicates a place where the work — the sacrificial rite — is carried on: a place appointed for the sacrifice (the assigned place where the work of sacrifice is performed), or a place that is set apart** — this is the sense suggested.

**"Itthā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "truth" (*satya*). Skandasvāmin gives "*amuta iti asyārthaḥ*" ("from that place" — the sense being "from there, from their own dwelling, from the sky"), while Veṅkaṭamādhava takes "itthā" to mean "in this manner."

**"Dhiyā ('amunā karmaṇā')"** — "by this rite," as the Bhashyakara explains, following the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2.?.?), where "dhīḥ" is listed as a word for "karma" (action, rite). The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say it means "by this our [prayer] made with mind and devotion"; **Geldner** says "as we desire"; Skandasvāmin and Mādhava give "by this rite." ("Dhīḥ" is in another sense a synonym of "prajñā," wisdom, but that sense does not fit here.) **Since the rishi Madhuchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma at the morning pressing and offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu, the sense "in this rite," "by this rite" or "by performing this rite" is the fitting one.** The next Ṛc-group then begins: "**mitraṃ huve…**"

### Page 695

**...that is, "mitraṃ huve," the sukta's [seventh] Rik, is said to be the first of three Riks concerning Mitra-Varuṇa.** On the day of the Sutyā (pressing), within the yajña beginning at the appointed hour, at the morning pressing, in the Maitrāvaruṇa-graha rite, this Rik's application follows. Further, the entire matter of the Abhiplava and Ṣaḍaha [six-day] rites has already been explained; the application of these Riks in the present sacrifice has also been explained. **Āśvalāyana, in the section of his Shrauta-sutra called "hotā-jani..." (Adhyāya 3, Section 8), states the application of the Riks concerning Mitra and Varuṇa individually,** and further, in the Adhyāya 8, Section 2, states the application of the Riks concerning Vāyu and the others. This has already been discussed above (see printed pages 671–672).

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Vāyo"** — since the vocative case is governed by the rule stated in the Adhyāya on vocatives, it is treated as unaccented.

**The words "udgātra, graha, viṣṭu, kubja, cambu, kṣurabhṛd, vedyoktra, bhairavabhelaka, śrūmāla,"** and others (Uṇādi 3.108[?]) are formed with the affix "ratna," pronounced with initial-udātta accent by the special rule for such formations. On this rule, the word "**indra**" is likewise established with the affix "ratna," pronounced with initial-udātta accent — this is well established in the grammar; the sense "one who is strong" is not further explained here, being clear enough.

**"Cāpadayo'nudāttāḥ"** (Phit-sutra 4.14) — words ending in "ca" and similar particles are unaccented; hence "ca" itself is unaccented.

**"Sunvataḥ"** — the word "śamerasumeṇaddhyādeḥ" (Panini 3.2.?) is used with the meaning of that word's own class.

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — here, in the sense of "carefully purified/consummated" (Nirukta 4.2), "niḥ" is used; the word "niḥ" being used with the sense of "carefully purified," in the sense "carried through by no remainder," and the meaning is thus established according to the various usages. **"Niṣkṛta"** is derived from "niḥ" + "kṛta" ("kṛ," to make); the resulting compound is formed by the rule concerning gati-compounds beginning at (Panini 1.4.60), where "kṛ" in the sense of "action" takes "kṛt" affix. Since "niḥ" is an indeclinable used with the root "kṛ" in the sense of "beginning," it is properly usable in the sense of the compound now beginning, "niṣkṛtam" indicating "the appointed place where the offering is begun." **"Makṣu"** — the word "kaḥ" and others, according to their own grammatical class, along with the appropriate preceding or following elements, take the udātta accent — hence "makṣu" carries this accent...

The surrounding Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, Bhāvārtha and Viśeṣārtha sections translated elsewhere in this project remain the more reliable material.)*

### Page 696 — Sūkta 2, The Seventh Mantra

*(The preceding grammar section concludes with brief remarks on "kṛta" and "dhiyā," in the same dense register; not reproduced in detail. The Kannada then confirms that "dhiyā" is treated as unaccented per the sutra "āmantritasya ca" — that is, as a case-form following a vocative — in agreement with the accent already seen in the printed Saṃhitā-text.)*

---

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> मि॒त्रं हु॑वे पू॒तद॑क्षं॒ वरु॑णं च रिशाद॒सम् ।
> धियं॑ घृ॒ताची॑ साध॒न्ता ॥७॥
>
> *mitráṃ huve pūtádakṣaṃ váruṇaṃ ca riśādasám |*
> *dhíyaṃ ghṛtā́cīṃ sādhantā ||7||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> मित्रम् । हुवे । पूतऽदक्षम् । वरुणम् । च । रिशादसम् ।
> धियम् । घृतऽअचीम् । साधन्ता ॥७॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> अहमस्मिन् कर्मणि हविष्प्रदानाय पूतदक्षं शवितबलं मित्रं हुवे । तथा रिशादसं रिशानां हिंसकानामत्तारं वरुणं च हुवे । आह्वयामि । कीदृशौ मित्रावरुणौ । घृतमुदकमञ्चतीति घृताचीं भूमिं प्रापयतीति यां धीर्वर्षणकर्म तां घृताचीं धियं साधन्तौ कुर्वन्तौ । मित्र-शब्दः पुंल्लिङ्गः प्रातिपदिकस्वरेणान्तोदात्तः । हुव इति ह्वयतेर्लुक् भवति शप्रीव लुक् सति शपः स्थाने संस्कारणम् । साः-अच्युवृत्तौ बहुलं भूतकाले चोदाहृतः ॥
> *aham asmin karmaṇi haviṣ-pradānāya pūtadakṣaṃ śavita-balaṃ mitraṃ huve | tathā riśādasaṃ riśānāṃ hiṃsakānām attāraṃ varuṇaṃ ca huve | āhvayāmi | kīdṛśau mitrāvaruṇau | ghṛtam udakam añcatīti ghṛtācīṃ bhūmiṃ prāpayatīti yāṃ dhīr varṣaṇa-karma tāṃ ghṛtācīṃ dhiyaṃ sādhantau kurvantau | mitra-śabdaḥ puṃllliṅgaḥ prātipadika-svareṇāntodāttaḥ | huva iti hvayater luk bhavati śapa iva luk sati śapaḥ sthāne saṃskāraṇam | sā-acyuvṛttau bahulaṃ bhūtakāle codāhṛtaḥ ||*

**Translation:** "In this rite, for the offering of the oblation, I call ('huve') upon Mitra, whose strength is pure ('pūtadakṣam'). Likewise I call upon Varuṇa, called 'riśādasam' — the devourer of the harmful ones (riśānām). What kind of pair are Mitra and Varuṇa? Those who accomplish the rain-bringing rite — 'dhiyam ghṛtācīm' — the rite that causes water (ghṛta) to reach the earth. The word 'mitra' is masculine and takes final-syllable accent by the ordinary noun-accent rule. 'Huve' — from the root 'hve' (to call), with elision of the class-marker affix 'śap' (as usual), and the resulting adjustment in its place."

*(The grammar continues in the dense register, working through "pūtadakṣam," "riśādasam," and "dhiyam ghṛtācīm.")*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(अश्विनोः कर्मणि हविष्प्रदानाय, इह यज्ञ-कर्मदल्लि हविस्सन्नु समर्पिसुवुदक्कागि)** — (for offering the oblation in this yajna-rite) | **मित्रं (mitraṃ)** — Mitra | **पूतदक्षं (pūtadakṣaṃ)** — whose strength is pure, that is, who is ever capable | **हुवे (huve)** — I call | **रिशादसं (riśādasaṃ)** — one who devours the harmful ones (rākṣasas), the destroyer of enemies | **वरुणं (varuṇaṃ)** — Varuṇa | **च (ca)** — and | **हुवे (huve)** — I call | **(मित्रावरुणौ) (mitrāvaruṇau)** — (Mitra and Varuṇa) | **घृताचीं (ghṛtācīṃ)** — the rite that causes rain to fall | **धियं (dhiyaṃ)** — the sacrificial rite | **साधन्ता (sādhantā)** — accomplishing.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

I invoke, into this rite of sacrifice, the deities Mitra and Varuṇa, that they may partake of the oblation. Among them, Mitra is of surpassing strength; his power knows no weakening. Varuṇa is mighty and destroys enemies. Moreover, in bringing about rain, Mitra and Varuṇa possess a particular capability. I invoke such Mitra and Varuṇa into this yajna, as the principal deities [of this Rik].

### Page 698

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> I invoke Mitra of pure strength, and Varuna the devourer of foes; the joint accomplishers of the act of bestowing water (on the earth).

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Pūtadakṣam"** — "pūta" means pure; "dakṣa" means strength; this is the Bhashyakara's sense, taking these as two separate words joined together within a compound ("pūta" occurring [inserted] between the syllables of a word meaning strength — Nighaṇṭu 3.9). **The Bhashyakara has explained the word following this Nighaṇṭu sense.** Several Riks illustrate this word's usage:

(1) "*jajñānā pūtadakṣasā*" (Rigveda 1.94.5[?])
(2) "*abudhne rājā varuṇo vanasyordhvaṃ stūpaṃ dadate pūtadakṣaḥ*" (Rigveda 1.24.7[?])
(3) "*mayo dadhe medhiraḥ pūtadakṣo divaḥ subandhur januṣā pṛthivyāḥ*" (Rigveda 3.1.?)
(4) "*arcanti tvā marutaḥ pūtadakṣāsteme sakhāyaḥ svidharā abhūvan*" (Rigveda 8.13.?)
(5) "*ni ketunā janānāṃ citekhe pūtadakṣā*" (Rigveda 8.44.?)
(6) "*utasya vo rathaḥ pūtadakṣāstvaṣṭasya pastyo adabdhā*" (Rigveda 1.?)
(7) "*prati vāṃ sūra udite sūkta ṛcā vartraṃ hunve varuṇa pūtadakṣam*" (Rigveda 2.?)
(8) "*ṛtāvānā samrāṭā pūtadakṣasā*" (Rigveda 8.25.10[?])
(9) "*ṛtāvānā yajase pūtadakṣāsā*" (Rigveda 7.?)
(10) "*arcanti pūtadakṣasaḥ*" (Rigveda 8.94.?)
(11) "*tyānnu kṣatriyāṃ diṣo yau martaḥ purukṛt tuve*" (Rigveda 8.?)
(12) "*indro mitro varuṇaḥ saṃ tvākratve pūtadakṣo bhagaḥ savitā pūtadakṣasaḥ*" (Rigveda 10.?)

— and so on. **The Bhashyakara, in explaining these Riks, glosses "pūtadakṣa" as: pure strength, power, or capability.** The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna, for this word, consider "*manaskeṃdu*"...

*(Note: given the density of citations on this page and the small print, several verse-locators above are given only approximately; several were left unread where illegible.)*

### Page 699

**...Geldner** takes "manaskeṃdu" [an intended-mind reading] in the sense of "purpose." **But the Bhashyakara's own sense — "capability" — as stated on the previous page, fits better.** In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda (6.2.1[?]), "dakṣa" is glossed as both "strength" and "wisdom." **Here, some of the Vedārtha-yatna authors explain "dakṣa" as meaning "sensory power" or "the power of the sense-organs," while others explain it as meaning "the capacity for action."** "Dakṣa" indicates a strength of mind and a strength of body alike.

**Some further Riks in which the word "dakṣa" appears:**

(1) "*dakṣaṃ dadhāte apasam*" (Rigveda 1.3.6[?])
— here "dakṣa" is used in the sense of a particular capability or the quality of skill in work.

(2) "*dakṣaṃ dadhāsi jīvase*" (Rigveda 1.60.?[?])

"*taṃ dakṣam abhi saṃvide kavim*" (Rigveda 1.?)

"*dyumattamaṃ dakṣaṃ dhehi sedhā janānāṃ pūrvyaḥ arātīḥ*" (Rigveda 8.44.9[?])

"*ya indro haryāśvo dakṣaṃ dadhāti taṃ riśo dakṣaṃ dhāti somini*" (Rigveda 2.?)

"*pra dakṣāya preṣṭheṣā*" (Rigveda 8.6.20[?])

**In all these Riks, the word "dakṣa" always carries the sense of "strength."** Elsewhere the word "dakṣa" is used in the sense of purpose, or determination, or an intended aim, and "kratu" (also meaning something like determination/resolve) too carries this same sense of "the power that gives shape to intent" — as in:

"*bhadraṃ no api vātaya manaḥ dakṣam uta kratum*" (Rigveda 10.25.1[?])
"*ā te niyantu manasaḥ purāṇi kratve dakṣāya jīvase*" (Rigveda 10.?)
"*uta svena kratunā saṃ vadeta śreyāṃsaṃ daksaṃ manasā jagṛbhyāt*" (Rigveda 10.?)
"*tvaṃ soma kratubhiḥ sukratur bhūḥ dakṣaḥ suṣaṃbhoḥ viśvavedāḥ*" (Rigveda 9.?)
"*ā no yajñāya takṣata śubhavantaḥ kratve dakṣāya suprajāvatīm iṣam*" (Rigveda 1.?)
"*adhā hy agne kratvor bhadrasya dakṣasya sādhoḥ*" (Rigveda 4.?)

### Page 700

**Further citations closing the "dakṣa" discussion:** "*pra vaḥ sutāso haraya iva pūrṇāḥ kṛtve dakṣāya harṣayanta kīlāḥ*" (Rigveda 5.?), and "*tvaṃ no agne āditye kṛtvā dakṣasya mekṣanā*" (Rigveda 8.?). **In all of these Riks, the word "dakṣa" bears various senses; in the present context, however, it should be understood to mean "resolve" (saṃkalpa) or "purpose" (uddeśa).**

---

**"Riśādasam"** — Yāska, in his Nirukta (2.16), states that "riśādas" means "**rekṣalayodāriṇī**" or, alternatively, "**rekṣalayodāsinaḥ**." He explains that those who protect against violence, being armed as it were with the weapons appropriate for use against those who inflict harm, are "**riśādasaḥ**." That is, they are "the destroyer of the harmful," "the protector against harm," the one who chastises those who do harm.

**Regarding the deities to whom this epithet applies: Nirukta scholars — Riśṭaṃ himsati** (i.e., "riśa" is destroyed [by the deity]); Riśaṃ hiṃsakaṃ dasyati (destroys the harmer); Riśam adyaṃ hiṃsanti dasyanti (destroy that which harms); **Riśam adyanti kṣipanti veti riśādasaḥ** — thus various authors explain it, some saying that they eat or consume the harmful, some that they hurl them away.** These are examined in Vaidika-nighaṇṭu, chapter 3.9. **Vāyu and other deities' epithets are likewise described using the word "riśādasaḥ" in many places.**

**Sāyaṇācārya explains this word, in his commentary, as meaning: "Riśānām" — "of the harmful ones" — "Attāram" — "devourer" or "eater," and in other places as: "one who protects" or "one who guards." At times he explains it as "one whose enemies dwindle away, or who destroys their strength."**

**Some who have written treatises on Vedic interpretation state:** "*riśat: hiṃsakah, ādaḥ-attā, riśādaḥ. riśāṃ hiṃsakāṇaṃ attā*" — "**Riśāt**" means "one who inflicts harm"; "**adaḥ**" means "eater"; "**riśādaḥ**" therefore means "eater of those who inflict harm." **This is stated to mean: "he who destroys the harmful," or "one who does away with the enemy."** Veṅkaṭamādhava explains it in the very same manner, connecting the sense with this compound word.

### Page 701

**Among Western scholars — Max Müller, Eggling, Grassmann, Hillebrandt** and others — most explain this word to mean "destroyer of enemies" (Destroyer of enemies). **The German scholar Ludwig** does not agree that the word means "destroyer of enemies." He is inclined to think the word "Riśat" refers to a particular tribe/people, and that the sense is "one who has vanquished them." **But this meaning has not gained acceptance here.** Many other scholars have proposed varied meanings for the word, but since these meanings are drawn merely from etymology, and none of them fits the actual context well, further discussion of them is not useful here.

---

**"Dhiyam"** — this word means an act of sacrifice, a rite. **Geldner** calls it "poem, composition" (Poem). Skandasvāmin, Veṅkaṭamādhava, and Sāyaṇa do not accept this. Skandasvāmin calls it "an act to be examined/investigated" (*vicāryaṃ karma*), and Sāyaṇa calls it "*varṣaṇa-karma*" (the rain-bringing rite). This is correct, because it is well established that Vṛṣṭi (rain) is brought about through the performance of yajnas in the Vedic period. **This sense is clearly evident in the Rik:**

> युद्धेनाशिं शतकतवे पुरोरुहेको होत्राय वृषकं कृतस्य दीधेत् । देवपत्रं वृष्णियं रराशेको बृहस्पतिर्नाचमश्यायच्छेत् ॥
> *yuddhenāśiṃ śatakatave puroruheko hotrāya vṛṣakaṃ kṛtasya dīdheta | devapatraṃ vṛṣṇiyaṃ rarāśeko bṛhaspatir nācamaśyāyacchet ||* (Rigveda 10.?.?)

*(this specific citation remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading given its compressed and archaic form)*

---

**"Ghṛtācīm"** — the Bhashyakara has interpreted this word: "*udakaṃ pṛthivīṃ prati yā gamayati sā ghṛtācī*" — that is, "the rite that causes water to reach the earth," on the analogy of "vṛṣṭi" (bringing water down). **The Māthava commentary [Veṅkaṭamādhava]** and others agree with this. The rite whereby, through yajnas performed, one brings water down onto the earth — this rite ("ghṛtācī") is thus glossed. **The Skandasvāmī commentary explains further: "phalasva bhūmiṃ prāsayati yā dhīrvarṣaṇakarma taṃ" — "the rite that carries water (in the form of ghee/rain) to the earth" — through this the two deities, Vāyu and [Mitra-Varuṇa], accomplish it, "vṛṣṇyaḥ" [rain-bringing].** Sāyaṇācārya says the same. **Sāyaṇācārya explains** "sphṛta udakaṃ āñcati bhūmiṃ prāsayati yā dhīrvarṣaṇakarma taṃ" — the rite by which water (in the form of the deity's own oblation) is caused to reach the earth — that rite, "ghṛtācī," and that which is accomplished — "vṛṣṭi" — as its result. **Māthava too accepts this sense.** Māthava, in one Brahmana-passage's citation, gives the example: "**mitraṃ vā ahaḥ vāruṇe rātrau. ca ahoratrābhyāṃ hi mitrāvaruṇāhorātrābhyāṃ tu varṣaṇyo**" — Mitra [rules] the day; Varuṇa, the night; and [through] Mitra-Varuṇa together, [ruling] both day and night, [rain is brought about]...

### Page 702

**...that is, Varuṇa causes lightning to occur through the day.** In the Rigveda too, elsewhere (several citations), it is said that Mitra-Varuṇa together summon the rain onto the earth. In the Nighaṇṭu, "udaka" (water) is included among the hundred-odd words listed as synonyms for water, in which "ghṛta" itself is one.

> त आ अनश्रे रत्नान्युपैषु घृतेन पृथिवी व्यूद्ये ।
> *ta ā anaśre ratnāny upaiṣu ghṛtena pṛthivī vyūdye |* (Rigveda 1.164.47[?])

**In this Rik, "ghṛtena pṛthivī vyūdye"** — "the earth is watered/moistened by ghṛta" — makes clear that "ghṛta" here means water (rain). **Yāska, in this context, discusses this word further.** Some Vedic-ritual scholars say that "ghṛta" means "flowing water" or "melted butter," and that whichever sense (water or ghee) is intended is decided by context — but that, in the present case, the sense of "water" clearly fits the surrounding sense.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)*

**"Mitraḥ"** derives with a kṛt-affix, giving final-syllable accent. **"Huve"** — from the root "hve" (to call), first person singular, the affix "iṭ" being added in a special sense for the "ātmanepada" middle form, giving "huve," accented on the final syllable (by the vocative-adjacent rule). **"Kartari śaḥ"** (Panini 3.1.68) — the class-affix "śa"; hence the "śap" affix is elided ("luk"), by the special rule applying widely to such roots. **"Riśādasam"** — the augment "sup" is inserted, and finally the compound resolves to a possessive/agentive derivative ending in "u+ṣu." **"Dhiyam"** — a derivative of the root "dhī" with the kṛt-affix "kvip," ending in consonantal stem, with accent falling on the base ("dhī"). **"Ghṛtācī"** — a compound of "ghṛta" and "añc" (going), with the "ac" ending replaced by "īṣ" in the feminine, giving "ghṛtācī," retaining the accent of its earlier member (by the rule for such gati-compounds).

**"Sādhantā"** — the roots "ṛdh, dāri, uśan" (Uṇādi 1.99[?]) — "ṛdh" means to prosper/flourish, "dāri" means to split/divide, "uś" means to desire — these three roots take the "unan" affix; hence "uśan" [likewise elsewhere in this Rik] takes the same affix. Consequently, this affix, being accentless, shifts the accent to the syllable preceding it, giving the udātta placement seen in the printed text.

*(Caveat: the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā section above, like page 695 earlier, is a lower-confidence best-effort reading of very dense grammatical shorthand; the specific sutra attributions and derivational chains should not be relied upon without independent verification. The Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, Bhāvārtha and Viśeṣārtha content translated on the surrounding pages remains the more solid material.)*

### Page 703

*(This page continues the grammatical derivation of "riśādasam" and "ghṛtācī" in the same extremely dense register as the previous page — working through the roots "riś" (to harm) and "ad" (to eat), the formation of the compound "riśādas," and detailed accent-rules for "ghṛtācī" as a feminine compound of "ghṛta" and "añc." Given the exceptional density of this stretch (continuing directly from the caveated section on the previous page), it is not reproduced line-by-line here; the overall senses already established in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and Viśeṣārtha above — "devourer of the harmful," and "the rain-bringing rite" — are the reliable takeaways.)*

---

**"Apna"** — among the words listed by the Nirukta as synonyms for "karma" (deed, act, rite), "apna" is one of the terms used to mean a sacrificial rite.

---

**"Ghṛtācīti"** — the word "ghṛta" is formed with the "in" affix, with the roots "ghṛt," "gṛdh," "gṛdhra," "sṛj," and others (per Uṇādi 3.94). **"Pūrvatrāsiddham"** (Panini 8.2.1) — this rule is applied here to govern the process. In the formation of certain roots, when "aj" (going) is a member of the compound, and the affix is "kvip," ending with the loss of the "j," the compound results as "ghṛta+añc," with a special "ni" affix (Uṇādi 6.144[?]) attached to some such formations. **In "adhyātmam"** — "cati," "jati," and other roots of this class form derivatives ending in the vowel; when preceded by a consonant, the affix following gives rise to a differing formation. **This is why word-forms such as "annavaṃśyoji"** arise in certain established usages.

**"Ajña keśvyo-siṃsyāṃ"** (Panini 7.4.?) — the Ātmanepada verb "yaśa+bham" arises here, and by a special rule regarding this class of feminine ("uṃs")-suffixed derivatives, "yaṣabham" arises, with the meaning "attaining a particular arrangement/adornment" (adopting a suitable form), the letter "bha" combining with the class-sign. **"Acaḥ"** (Panini 6.?.?) — the letter "ca" ends with elision, being combined with "bha," yielding "acaḥ."

**"Nabhiṣayasyāsiṃvedhya"** (Phit-sutra 3.8) — the exception-rule for words ending in "in-antodātta"-class declension: **"Ghṛtādīnāṃ ca"** (Phit-sutra 3.6) — words of the "ghṛtādi" group take accent on the final syllable — hence "ghṛtāci" is confirmed as final-syllable accented (**ghṛtācī**), matching the accent shown in the printed text.

### Page 705

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे मित्रावरुणौ युवां क्रतुं प्रवर्तमानमिमं सोमायागमाशाथे । व्याप्नुवन्तौ । केन निमित्तेन । ऋतेन । अवश्यंभावितया सत्येन फलेन । अस्पृष्टं फलं दातुमिच्छथ इत्यर्थः । कीदृशौ युवां । ऋतावृधौ । ऋतस्य सत्यस्य वर्धकौ ऋतस्पृशा ऋतस्य स्पृष्टारौ संस्पर्शकौ । केन विशेषेण । मित्रावरुणाविति महर्षिनामधेयेन । मित्रावरुणाविति देवतायोर्द्वे च । पूर्वपदस्यान्तोदात्तत्वं ऋतस्पृशेति वर्धयितारावाख्येयादृध्वर्थ फलम् आर्षेण द्वित्वं शेष्वाचाकिच्चेति निपातनात् । कीदृशं क्रतुम् । बृहन्तं महान्तं ।
> *he mitrāvaruṇau yuvāṃ kratuṃ pravartamānam imaṃ somāyāgam āśāthe | vyāpnuvantau | kena nimittena | ṛtena | avaśyaṃbhāvitayā satyena phalena | aspṛṣṭaṃ phalaṃ dātum icchatha ity arthaḥ | kīdṛśau yuvāṃ | ṛtāvṛdhau | ṛtasya satyasya vardhakau ṛtaspṛśā ṛtasya spṛṣṭārau saṃsparśakau | kena viśeṣeṇa | mitrāvaruṇāv iti maharṣi-nāmadheyena | … kīdṛśaṃ kratum | bṛhantaṃ mahāntaṃ |*

**Translation:** "O Mitra and Varuṇa! You both fully attend to and pervade this ongoing Soma-yajna. By what means? By 'ṛta' — through the true fruit that is bound to occur; the sense is 'you desire to bestow the fruit that is otherwise unattainable.' What kind of pair are you two? 'Ṛtāvṛdhau' — increasers of ṛta (truth); 'ṛtaspṛśā' — those who touch/directly bring about ṛta. [Grammar notes on accent and derivation follow.] What kind of rite (kratu)? 'Bṛhantam' — great, mighty."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) मित्रावरुणौ ((he) mitrāvaruṇau)** — O Mitra and Varuṇa! | **ऋतावृधौ (ṛtāvṛdhau)** — increasers of truth | **ऋतस्पृशा (ṛtaspṛśā)** — those who touch/uphold truth | **(यूयम्) ((yūyam))** — you two, being such | **ऋतेन (ṛtena)** — through the true and inevitable fruit | **बृहन्तं (bṛhantaṃ)** — great, mighty | **क्रतुम् (kratum)** — this rite (yajna) | **आशाथे (āśāthe)** — you fully pervade and attend to.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two are increasers of truth, and you uphold that truth; you accordingly bestow, without fail, the fruit that truly and certainly follows from this rite. You watch over this great sacrifice we now perform, so that it is duly and completely fulfilled.

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) मित्रावरुणौ ((he) mitrāvaruṇau)** — O Mitra and Varuṇa, (you two) | **ऋतावृधौ (ṛtāvṛdhau)** — increasers of water, or of truth, or of the yajna | **ऋतस्पृशा (ṛtaspṛśā)** — those who bring about water (in the form of rain) | **(such as you) ऋतेन (ṛtena)** — in order to give us, truly and certainly, the fruit obtained from the yajna | **बृहन्तं (bṛhantaṃ)** — exceedingly great, whole with all its parts | **क्रतुम् (kratum)** — toward this Soma-yajna we are now performing | **आशाथे (āśāthe)** — may you come, attending to it (come!).

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Mitra and Varuṇa! By your grace you cause rain to fall, so that water is abundantly available in the world; or, you cause dharma or the yajna to flourish, and through that bring about rain upon the earth. Therefore, come now to this great sacrifice we are performing — attended by many ritvijs, furnished with the materials needed for the rite, and thronged with many people amid great festivity — and graciously grant us its fruit.

### Page 707

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Mitra and Varuna, augmenters of water, presenters of water, you attend this big sacrificial rite and grant us its true reward.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Ṛtena"** — we have already fully discussed this word (see page 647). **"Ṛtāvṛdhau"** — the Bhashyakara states that "ṛta" here means "water," or, alternatively, "truth" or "the yajna." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna accept the sense "water"; Skandasvāmī has similarly explained it. **The Bhashyakara, accepting the sense "water," explains it accordingly.** Scholars of Vedic interpretation say that "ṛta" means "Dharma" (**Taking delight in the Sacred law**), and explain the word in this sense. In the present context, this meaning too is entirely fitting, since, in a Rik connected with Mitra-Varuṇa, some scholars accept the sense "rain" precisely because of the well-known connection between rain and Mitra-Varuṇa. **Others who hold that this is not the fitting sense here explain the word differently.** Various writers explain this word using three distinct meanings: **"satyam" (truth), "yajña" (the sacrifice), and "udaka" (water)**. The Bhashyakara has himself made use of all three senses across various contexts.

**In the present passage, the word "vṛdhau" is used in the sense of augmenting; the word "spṛśau" (in "ṛtaspṛśā") appears twice** — [used once each] with two distinct senses. **Since it would otherwise be redundant to repeat the same word "ṛtavṛdhau" and "ṛtaspṛśā" with an identical sense, several scholars hold that "ṛtāvṛdhau" means "increasers of truth or of the yajna," while "ṛtaspṛśā," within the same word, means "bringers of water"** — this being why the [same-looking] word carries different meanings in each place. **Some scholars, however, are of the view that "ṛta" applies with only the general sense of "truth" throughout, without needing this distinction.**

**Many hold that the sense "truth" fits best here.** In the context where Mitra-Varuṇa are being praised, since only the sense "truth" fits the reference clearly, it is regarded as the more suitable reading — while the fittingness of the sense "water" does not appear so clear in the other place. **"Yugas satyaṃ paraṃ brahma"** — the topic of universal righteousness and eternal order — is discussed further in the Taittiriya Upanishad (1.1.1[?]); this subject matter is treated more fully when that context is explained.

---

**"Ṛtaspṛśā"** — the Bhashyakara explains this word as meaning "those who cause rain (vṛṣṭi) and are graciously disposed [toward it]"; and Vedic interpreters explain it as "defenders of Dharma" (**defending the Sacred law**). The German scholar Geldner explains it as "fosterers of truth" (**fosterers of truth**).

### Page 708

**Māthava [Veṅkaṭamādhava] explains "ṛtaspṛśau" as meaning "creators who establish truth."** His sense and Geldner's sense mutually agree. **Therefore, the sense "those who establish truth" is preferred here as the more suitable reading for "ṛtaspṛśau."**

**"Āśāthe"** — "āśnute" means "pervades, reaches, attends to," and so on. Each author has interpreted this word according to what fits his own sense; whatever meaning one adopts, they all essentially arrive at the same overall sense.

**"Bṛhantam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this as "possessing every limb and part, complete." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain it as "great" ("*bṛhat*"); Skandasvāmī as "vast" (mahat); Māthava and others agree with this. **None of these authors differ in the essential sense.**

**"Kratum"** — the Bhashyakara explains this word as meaning "the Soma-yajna." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna take it as "desire" (**desire**); Geldner takes it as "insight, understanding" (**insight, understanding**). **However, since the rishi is engaged in performing this yajna, the sense "Soma-yajna" — as given by the Bhashyakara, Skandasvāmī, and Māthava — is the fitting one.** Geldner's and the Vedārtha-yatna's readings, when examined here, do not fit well.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Ṛtaḥ"** — being listed among the "ghṛtādi" group, by the rule "**ghṛtādīnāṃ ca**" (Phit-sutra 3.6), the word takes the udātta accent. **"Mitraś ca varuṇaś ca mitrāvaruṇau"** — a dvandva (copulative) compound, formed by the rule "**cārthe dvandvaḥ**" (Panini 2.2.29[?]). By the rule "**devatādvandve ca**" (Panini 6.3.26[?]) — in a dvandva compound of deity-names, the first member retains its accent — the udātta of "mitra" is retained. **"Na lokavikṣa-prātipadikāṃśasya**" (Panini 6.1.?) causes elision of accent here. **"Mitrāvaruṇau"** — thus formed. **"Ṛtasya vardhayitārau"** — a compound, where "ṛtasya," being the second member of a determinative compound with "vardhaka" ("increaser"), takes the "kṛtya" affix, giving "vṛdha," with the root "spṛś" (to touch) taking "kvip" ("**anyeṣām api dṛśyate**," Panini 6.3.137[?]) elided, retaining its original accent. **In the sandhi-analysis, this becomes "ṛtavṛdhau."** **"Ṛtaspṛśau"** — a similar compound with the affix "kvip" from the root "spṛś" giving "sukāḥ-" ("**susambodhane**," Panini 8.1.19[?]) yielding "ṛtaspṛśā" — both words functioning as the vocative dual. Since these are vocatives, both are treated, by the rule for such formations, as fully accentless in the Saṃhitā.

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**कवी (kavī)** — the two wise ones | **तुविजाता (tuvijātā)** — born so as to help many, that is, produced for the sake of many | **उरुक्षया (urukṣayā)** — dwelling in a vast, established abode, or possessed of a broad, stable dwelling | **मित्रावरुणा (mitrāvaruṇā)** — Mitra and Varuṇa, these deities | **नः (naḥ)** — for us | **दक्षं (dakṣaṃ)** — strength | **अपसं (apasaṃ)** — and work (the rite, i.e., the sacrifice) | **दधाते (dadhāte)** — uphold, bestow.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

We, who are engaged in performing this yajna, are aided by these deities Mitra and Varuṇa, who are exceedingly wise; upholding many, and refuge to those who come [to them], or protectors of many dwelling-places. May Mitra and Varuṇa in this way graciously bestow upon us strength, and the capability to perform yajnas and similar rites.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O, Wise Mitra and Varuna, you are born for the benefit of many, you are the refuge of multitudes; prosper our strength and work (sacrifice).

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Kavī"** — this word has already been discussed above. "Vipra," "dhīra," and "medhāvī" are all words that convey this same sense of wisdom; among the various senses of the word "kavi," "wise" is the one that fits here. Therefore here "kavi" is properly understood as meaning "wise."

**"Tuvijātā"** — "uru" and "tuvi" are words both meaning "many"; since the meaning "helper of many" fits well in this context, most scholars explain "tuvi" as meaning "helper," or, in this same sense, "many." "Tuvi" carries the sense "**strong or mighty**." Given this sense, the word "tuvijātā" is here explained as meaning "born in the lineage of the strong," or "born of mighty parents" (**Born of strong...**

### Page 714

**...race)" — this sense too fits well. Geldner** takes the same sense; the Bhashyakara and other authors adopt the meaning drawn from Yāska's own explanation, since the meaning proposed here does not appear inconsistent with that.

**"Urukṣayā"** — the Bhashyakara explains this as "possessed of a broad, established dwelling-place"; the authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain "urukṣaya" in the sense of "possessing a special, broad plain/settlement," reading it as a distinct compound (drawn from the widely established senses of the word). Given this, "urukṣaya" is taken to mean: those who possess a settled, established dwelling — a settlement across the extended earth.

**"Dakṣaṃ"** — this word, meaning "strength," is well known from the discussion given at the very outset of this sukta (see page 699 above). The Bhashyakara here explains "dakṣa" as meaning "the power/strength of the mind." Later, however, some interpret "dakṣa" as meaning "efficiency" ("**Intellectual faculty or power; efficiency in work both mental and physical**"). Others take "dakṣa" and "buddhi-śakti" (intellectual capacity) to carry the same sense; that, too, is fitting here.

**"Apasam"** — the Bhashyakara explains "apas" as meaning "karma" (action, rite). Further, some hold that "dakṣa" and "apas" together mean "one's own strength" and "the specific capability to accomplish the intended work." **But the fitting sense here is that "dakṣam" refers to strength itself, while "apasam" refers to that which is accomplished — the rite (the yajna).** This grants a sense to which the desire "may my rite prosper" is naturally connected.

---

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Mitrāvaruṇā"** — here, the word "Mitra" takes the accent of the accusative, connected with the Prātipadika accent-rule already discussed above. **"Varuṇaḥ"** — the derivation "**varṇāvarṇyor unan**" (Uṇādi 1.9[?]) is applied, giving "varuṇaḥ" from the root "vṛ" with the affix "unan," through the process of guṇa and other adjustments. **"Devatādvandve ca"** (Panini 6.3.26[?]) — in a dvandva-compound of deity-names, the first member retains its accent — hence the accent seen here.

**"Uru" + "tuvi"** — Yāska's Nirukta (2.?.?) states this word "tuvi" among words meaning "many"; many rishis in similar contexts have used "tuvijāta" as a compound meaning "born to help many." "**Tuvīnāṃ jātaḥ = tuvijātaḥ**" — a genitive compound, resolving by regular sandhi rules...

### Page 715

*(This page continues and closes the grammatical derivation of "tuvijātā," "urukṣayā," "dakṣaṃ," and "apasam" in the established dense register — not reproduced in full detail — before closing the sukta itself.)*

**"Asyeti"** — from the root meaning "to obtain a fruit through an action," a formation results; that is, "apas" (work) here means the action whose fruit is obtainable through the deed performed. **"Apasa kartryāyāṃ"** (Uṇādi 5.65[?]) — the affix "asun" gives "apas," meaning "work" in general. Since the root here means "to perform, to be diligent in an action," the affix produces the accent seen in the printed text — hence "**apasasyāre**" (Rigveda Samhita 1.?.?), reading "apas" in this same sense.

**Summary of Sūkta 2, all nine verses:**
1. "vāyav ā yāhi darśateme somā araṅkṛtāḥ..." — Come hither, O handsome Vayu, these soma-draughts are prepared; drink of them, hear our invocation.
2. "vāyav ukthebhir jarante..." — O Vayu, the praisers who have pressed out the soma juice and know the proper season to offer it, are praising you with holy praises.
3. "vāyo tava prapṛñcatī dhenā..." — O Vayu, your approving speech goes to the giver and to many others who invite you for drinking Soma.
4. "indravāyū ime sutā..." — O Indra and Vayu, here are Soma-libations poured out for you. Come with food for us.
5. "vāyav indraś ca cetathaḥ..." — O Vayu and Indra, dwellers in the sacrifices, you are aware of these Soma-libations. Come hither quickly.
6. "vāyav indraś ca sunvata ā yātam..." — O Indra and Vayu, come quickly to drink the Soma of the sacrificer; thus your coming will complete the rite.
7. "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣaṃ varuṇaṃ ca riśādasam..." — I invoke Mitra of pure strength, and Varuna the devourer of foes; the joint accomplishers of the act of bestowing water.
8. "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛśā..." — O Mitra and Varuna, augmenters of water, presenters of water, you attend this big sacrificial rite and grant us its true reward.
9. "kavī no mitrāvaruṇā tuvijātā urukṣayā..." — O Wise Mitra and Varuna, you are born for the benefit of many, you are the refuge of multitudes; prosper our strength and work.

**What made this sūkta distinctive:** unlike Sūkta 1, this one opened with an unusually long apparatus — the extended Jaimini-sutra debate on Stotra/Shastra (spanning roughly Jaimini 2.1.1–26), the full Agnishtoma ritual-structure summary, and the detailed seven-deity Pralugat-Shastra framework — before the verses themselves began. Once underway, the verse-by-verse commentary followed the now-familiar template throughout, with substantial Viśeṣārtha excursuses on Soma (its botany, geography, and processing), on "dhenā" (its many senses across Vedic usage), on "dakṣa"/"riśādasa," and on "ṛta" (water vs. truth vs. yajna) — each weighing Sāyaṇa's reading against Skandasvāmī, Veṅkaṭamādhava, the Vedārtha-yatna authors, and Western scholars (Geldner, Max Müller, Grassmann, Ludwig, Roth, Eggling, Hillebrandt, Bloomfield).

**Honesty note carried through this sūkta:** several stretches of Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (grammar) were exceptionally dense even by this project's standards — notably printed pages 695, 702–703, and 708–711 — and were flagged as lower-confidence rather than presented as reliable transcriptions, consistent with the project's standing caution around this register.

**Target for next session:** begin Sūkta 3 (Rigveda 1.3, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ") at PDF page 744 / printed page 716.

# ॥ ऋग्वेदमन्त्राणां वर्णानुक्रमसूचिः ॥
## Alphabetical Index of Rigveda Mantras (Varṇānukrama-sūcī)

*(⚠ Major structural shift: rather than continuing directly into Sukta 3 of the verse-by-verse commentary, the source here inserts a substantial appendix — a comprehensive alphabetical index (varṇānukramaṇikā) listing Rigveda mantras by their opening syllable, each followed by its Maṇḍala-Sūkta-Mantra locator, and, where applicable, cross-references to where the same mantra recurs in the Sāmaveda, Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, Atharvaveda, Taittirīya Saṃhitā/Brāhmaṇa/Āraṇyaka, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and Nirukta. This is evidently a standalone traditional reference tool — a complete concordance of the whole Rigveda's mantras — rather than part of the sukta-by-sukta commentary itself, and its presence here does not depend on how far the commentary proper has progressed.)*

**॥ Sūcane (Note) ॥**

**In this index, mantras are listed according to their division into Maṇḍala, Sūkta, and mantra-number.** For example — to locate the mantra "**aṃśaṃ duhanti svanayantam**" (9-42-6), the number given, "9-42-6," should be understood as: 9th Maṇḍala, 42nd Sūkta, 6th mantra. In this work, at the top right of every page, "Ma. A. Sū." (Maṇḍala, Anuvāka, Sūkta) is given; the reader should consult that accordingly. **Since some mantras also occur in the other Vedas, that information is given here too**, using these abbreviations: **Sāma** = Sāmaveda; **Vā. Ya** = Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā; **Atharva** = Atharvaveda; **Tai. Saṃ** = Taittirīya Saṃhitā; **Tai. Brā** = Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa; **Tai. Ā** = Taittirīya Āraṇyaka; **Śata. Brā** = Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; **Ni** = Nirukta; and so on.
